According to this provision, the Financial Services Commission may supervise the business of credit cooperatives and the central association and issue orders necessary for supervision (paragraph (1)); and the Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service may have his or her affiliated employees inspect the business and assets of a credit cooperative or the central association (paragraph (2)). Article 84(1) of the Credit Cooperatives Act provides that where executives or employees of a credit cooperative fail to perform the procedures and duties prescribed by law or by orders, articles of association, or regulations pursuant to law (hereinafter referred to as “unlawful acts”), the Financial Services Commission may require the credit cooperative to take measures such as improvement [improvement means dismissal of the executive who committed the unlawful act and election of a new executive], suspension of duties, or reprimand (subparagraph 1) with respect to the relevant executive, and disciplinary dismissal, suspension, reduction of salary, or reprimand (subparagraph 2) with respect to the relevant employee (hereinafter referred to as a “request for measures”).\\n\\nArticle 42 of the Credit Cooperatives Act and Article 16-4(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act provide that a credit cooperative may not extend a loan to the same person in excess of the greater of 20 percent of its equity capital at the end of the immediately preceding business year and 1 percent of its total assets, and that in this case, a loan made in another person’s name at one’s own calculation shall be deemed to be a loan by the person himself/herself. Article 99(2) subparagraph 2 of the Credit Cooperatives Act provides that where an executive or employee of a credit cooperative violates Article 42 and thereby extends a loan exceeding the loan limit for the same person, such person shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than 2 years or by a fine not exceeding 20 million won.\\n\\n(2) The Act on the Establishment of the Financial Services Commission, etc. (hereinafter the “Financial Services Commission Act”) provides that matters concerning “the supervision and inspection and sanctions (sanctions) of financial institutions” are among the affairs under the jurisdiction of the Financial Services Commission (Article 17 subparagraph 2), and that, where the Commission deems it necessary, it may require reports on matters concerning the business, etc. of the Financial Supervisory Service or inspect the business, etc. in accordance with what the Commission determines (Article 60). Pursuant thereto, the 「Regulations on Inspection and Sanctions of Financial Institutions」, which were publicly notified by the Financial Services Commission (hereinafter the “Notice at Issue”), provide for the methods of inspection conducted by the Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service, the disposition of inspection results and sanctions, and other necessary matters, and these apply not only to financial institutions inspected by the Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service (Article 2(1)) but also mutatis mutandis, within the necessary scope, to financial institutions inspected by the Financial Services Commission (Article 2(2)).\\n\\nArticle 18(1) of the Notice at Issue sets forth in stages, according to the degree of seriousness, the types and grounds of sanctions that may be imposed on executives of financial institutions under the financial-related statutes, including the Credit Cooperatives Act, in subparagraphs 1 through 5. Among them, item (a) of subparagraph 1 provides that where an executive of a financial institution has “greatly disturbed the financial order or seriously damaged the credibility of the financial institution by intentionally committing a serious unlawful or improper act,” the Financial Services Commission may issue a recommendation for dismissal [including a request for dismissal and a request for improvement (improvement). The same shall apply hereinafter]. Under paragraph (2) of the same Article, where an executive of a financial institution falls under the grounds of subparagraph 1 (recommendation for dismissal) or subparagraph 2 (suspension of all or part of the performance of duties), the Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service shall recommend to the Financial Services Commission that the corresponding measure be taken; and where the grounds fall under subparagraph 3 (warning of disciplinary accountability), subparagraph 4 (cautionary warning), or subparagraph 5 (caution), the Governor may directly take the corresponding measure.\\n\\n(3) Considering comprehensively the structure and contents of the relevant statutes, the legislative purpose, etc., Article 18(1) of the Notice at Issue specifically prescribes matters to become the content of statutes pursuant to the delegation under the Financial Services Commission Act and does not exceed the limits of the delegation by the Financial Services Commission Act; accordingly, it must be regarded as having the force of a legislative rule binding on the outside world when combined therewith (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2007DO4841, decided April 10, 2008).\\n\\nIf an executive or employee of a credit cooperative intentionally commits a serious unlawful act and thereby greatly disturbs the financial order or seriously damages the credibility of the financial institution, this may constitute grounds for a recommendation for dismissal under item (a) of subparagraph 1 of Article 18(1) of the Notice at Issue. Even where such person retired or resigned and then again became an executive of the same credit cooperative, such person must be deemed subject to a request for measures under subparagraph 1 of Article 84(1) of the Credit Cooperatives Act. This is because, if an executive or employee of a credit cooperative intentionally commits a serious unlawful act and thereafter again assumes office as an executive of the same credit cooperative, the credibility of the credit cooperative may be seriously damaged.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts may be known.\\n(1) The Plaintiff was newly appointed on August 1, 2012, as an employee (Executive Director) of ○○ Credit Cooperative (hereinafter the “○○ Credit Union”), and from May 27, 2013, served as the branch manager of the △△ Branch of the ○○ Credit Union, in overall charge of the branch’s affairs, until he retired upon reaching the mandatory retirement age on August 31, 2015.\\n(2) From around September 2013 to around May 2015, the Plaintiff extended loans exceeding the same-person loan limit of KRW 500 million of the ○○ Credit Union to Non-Party 1, the representative director of Ganghwa Land Industry Development Co., Ltd., in four installments totaling KRW 1.77 billion; to Non-Party 2, in five installments totaling KRW 877 million; and to Non-Party 3, the actual representative of Seongheung C&D Comprehensive Construction Co., Ltd., in two installments totaling KRW 900 million, for a total of 11 loans amounting to KRW 3.547 billion (hereinafter referred to as the “individual loans at issue”).\\n(3) In around November 2015, the Financial Supervisory Service conducted an inspection by sector of the ○○ Credit Union, confirmed the Plaintiff’s above-described same-person loan-limit-exceeding loans, and recommended to the Defendant sanctions against the Plaintiff; and in around December 2015, it requested the Incheon District Prosecutors’ Office to investigate the Plaintiff.\\n(4) The Plaintiff, citing business performance including the above same-person loan-limit-exceeding loans, was elected on February 26, 2016, as the chairman, an executive of the ○○ Credit Union, and the Defendant, on December 14, 2016, requested the ○○ Credit Union to take improvement measures against the Plaintiff pursuant to Article 84(1) subparagraph 1 of the Credit Cooperatives Act (hereinafter the “Disposition at Issue”).\\n(5) The Plaintiff was indicted for violating the Credit Cooperatives Act with respect to the individual loans at issue that exceeded the same-person loan limit, and on July 16, 2018, received a guilty judgment from the Incheon District Court.\\n\\nc. When the above factual relation is examined in light of the legal principles set forth above, the fact that the Plaintiff, while serving as branch manager of the △△ Branch of the ○○ Credit Union, carried out several same-person loan-limit-exceeding loans falls under the case where, by intentionally committing a serious unlawful act, he greatly disturbed the financial order or seriously damaged the credibility of the ○○ Credit Union, and thus becomes subject to a recommendation for dismissal under item (a) of subparagraph 1 of Article 18(1) of the Notice at Issue. Since the Plaintiff was not immediately detected and retired upon reaching the mandatory retirement age without being subjected to sanctions, and thereafter became chairman of the ○○ Credit Union, thereby continuing to seriously damage the credibility of the ○○ Credit Union, the Defendant must be deemed able, pursuant to Article 84(1) subparagraph 1 of the Credit Cooperatives Act, to request the ○○ Credit Union to take improvement measures against the Plaintiff.\\n\\nd. The appellate court’s determination to the same purport is proper, and there is no error in the appellate court’s determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in misconstruing the legal principles concerning the requirements for application of a request for measures under Article 84(1) of the Credit Cooperatives Act.\\n\\n2. Whether the regulation limiting the same-person loan limit was violated, etc. (Grounds for Appeal Nos. 2 and 3)\\na. The appellate court determined that the individual loans at issue constituted loans made in violation of the regulation limiting the same-person loan limit under Article 42 of the Credit Cooperatives Act, and that there was no justifiable reason for which the Plaintiff could not be blamed for violating the regulation limiting the same-person loan limit.\\nb. Examining in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in such determination by the appellate court, such as incomplete deliberation due to failure to exercise the right to clarify, or misconstruction of the legal principles concerning Article 42 of the Credit Cooperatives Act, which limits the same-person loan limit, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n3. Whether there was deviation from or abuse of disciplinary discretionary power (Ground of Appeal No. 4)\\na. The appellate court, based on the following circumstances, determined that it is difficult to regard the Disposition at Issue as excessively harsh toward the Plaintiff and therefore as a deviation from or abuse of discretionary power. ① A large portion of responsibility for the individual loans at issue lies with the Plaintiff. ② The loans extended in violation of the regulation limiting the same-person loan limit exceeded KRW 2 billion, and such unlawful loans resulted from the Plaintiff’s intent or gross negligence. ③ The Disposition at Issue does not deviate from the sanction standards concerning “extension of loans in excess of the same-person loan limit by executives or employees of credit cooperatives, etc.” among the sanction standards by industry and by type of violation in Article 46(2) [Attached Table 3] of the Detailed Rules for the Enforcement of the Regulations on Inspection and Sanctions of Financial Institutions, as determined by the Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service pursuant to the delegation under the Notice at Issue.\\n\\nb. Examining in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in such determination by the appellate court, such as misconstruction of the legal principles concerning deviation from or abuse of disciplinary discretionary power, as alleged in the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is without merit and is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged, in unanimous opinion of the Justices, as per the order."}

{"[2020DU39297]": "We examine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Relevant legal principles\\n\\na. To recognize a death as a “death caused by occupational reasons” under Article 5 item 1 of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, there must be a causal relationship between work and the disease that caused the death. Even if the principal cause of the disease’s onset is not directly related to the performance of work, if at least work-related overwork or stress overlapped with the principal cause of the disease and thereby caused or aggravated the disease, a causal relationship must be found to exist; and such causal relationship need not necessarily be clearly proved medically or scientifically, but should also be deemed proved where, in light of all the circumstances, it may be inferred that there is a substantial causal relationship between the work and the disease. In addition, this includes cases where a basic disease or pre-existing disease that ordinarily would allow normal work is rapidly aggravated beyond the natural progression rate due to excessive duties or the like. And at that time, whether there is a causal relationship between the work and the disease or between the death and the disease must be determined based on the health and physical condition of the worker concerned, not that of an ordinary average person (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2019DU62604 rendered on May 28, 2020).\\n\\nb. In an administrative appeal suit, whether an administrative disposition is unlawful must, absent special circumstances, be determined on the basis of the laws and regulations in force at the time of that disposition. The same applies to a disposition made upon application (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2019DA264700 rendered on January 16, 2020). However, because the “Matters Necessary for Determining Whether Cerebrovascular Diseases or Heart Diseases and Musculoskeletal Diseases Qualify as Occupational Diseases” (Ministry of Employment and Labor Notice No. 2013-32, dated June 28, 2013; hereinafter the “Pre-Amendment Notice”) do not have binding effect externally on the public or the courts, even where the Korea Workers’ Compensation & Welfare Service issued a disposition denying approval of industrial accident medical care by applying the “Pre-Amendment Notice” in force at the time of the disposition, the court in an administrative appeal suit against that denial disposition is not obligated to apply the “Pre-Amendment Notice” and may determine whether a substantial causal relationship exists by taking into account the content and purpose of the provisions of the “Matters Necessary for Determining Whether Cerebrovascular Diseases or Heart Diseases and Musculoskeletal Diseases Qualify as Occupational Diseases” amended after the denial disposition (Ministry of Employment and Labor Notice No. 2017-117, dated December 29, 2017; hereinafter the “Amended Notice”). The specific reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Taking the content, form, and legislative purpose of Article 37(1) item 2 and paragraph 5 of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act and Article 34(3) [Attached Table 3] of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act together, [Attached Table 3] of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, “Specific Criteria for Recognizing Occupational Diseases,” should be understood as setting forth exemplary cases that fall under “occupational diseases” prescribed in Article 37(1) item 2 of the same Act, and cannot be viewed as a provision that excludes all diseases arising in relation to work other than those set forth in those criteria from occupational diseases (see Supreme Court Decision 2012DU24214 rendered on June 12, 2014).\\n\\n2) [Attached Table 3] of the Enforcement Decree of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, “Specific Criteria for Recognizing Occupational Diseases,” delegates to the Minister of Employment and Labor the task of determining and publicly announcing the matters necessary for determining whether “cerebrovascular diseases or heart diseases” and “musculoskeletal diseases” are occupational diseases [item 1 (c) and item 2 (e)]. Since [Attached Table 3] of the Enforcement Decree of the Industrial Accident Compensation Insurance Act, the delegating basis, is merely an exemplary provision, the Ministry of Employment and Labor notice issued pursuant to that delegation cannot be regarded as a norm having binding effect externally on the public and the courts; rather, it should be regarded as an “administrative rule” by which the Minister of Employment and Labor, an upper administrative authority and supervisory authority, sets administrative internal work-handling guidelines or standards for interpretation and application of statutes for the Korea Workers’ Compensation & Welfare Service, which is under his or her guidance and supervision.\\n\\n3) Even under the Pre-Amendment Notice, whether a case corresponds to “chronic excessive work” must be determined by comprehensively considering the amount, time, intensity, and responsibility of the work; time off such as holidays and leave; work patterns such as shift work and night work; the degree of mental tension; sleeping hours; the work environment; and, in addition, the worker’s age, sex, and health condition, among others [I. 1. item (c), latter sentence]; working hours are merely one factor to be considered in determining whether there was occupational overwork and cannot be an absolute standard of judgment.\\n\\n4) The Amended Notice, in reflective consideration that the content of the Pre-Amendment Notice was excessively strict, deleted the previously prescribed “health condition” so that the victim’s underlying disease is not considered as a factor in determining work-relatedness [I. 1. item (c), latter sentence], and further provides that where the average weekly working hours during the 12 weeks before onset exceed 52 hours, the longer the working hours, the greater the relationship between work and the disease is evaluated to be, and in particular, where work schedules are difficult to predict, shift work is involved, or the work has a high physical intensity, the relationship between work and the disease is to be evaluated as strong [I. 1. item (c) 2)].\\n\\n2. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances may be ascertained.\\n\\na. The deceased, who was the Plaintiff’s spouse (hereinafter referred to as “the deceased”), was born in (date of birth omitted) and joined Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering Co., Ltd. on April 9, 2009, and while performing fitting assembly and automatic welding work such as member joining, tack welding, and plate-fitting automatic welding at the subassembly fitting site in the shipyard, worked in alternating day and night shifts.\\n\\nb. The deceased’s basic work pattern was to work day and night alternating shifts on a weekly basis, working an average of 4 days per week, with day shifts from 08:00 to 17:00 for 8 hours each day (excluding a 1-hour lunch break), and night shifts from 20:00 to 05:00 the next day for 7 hours each day (excluding a 1-hour late-night meal break and a 1-hour sleeping break), but examining the work record for the 12 weeks before death, the above work principle was in fact not well observed and the day and night work schedule was also irregular.\\n\\nc. Looking at the work record for the 12 weeks before the deceased’s death, the total work hours for the 1 week before death were 47 hours (of which 30 hours were night work), for 2 weeks before death 47 hours (10 hours of night work), for 3 weeks before death 30 hours (30 hours of night work), for 4 weeks before death 46 hours (10 hours of night work), for 5 weeks before death 49 hours (40 hours of night work), for 6 weeks before death 46 hours (10 hours of night work), for 7 weeks before death 40 hours (40 hours of night work), for 8 weeks before death 39 hours (20 hours of night work), for 9 weeks before death 56 hours (40 hours of night work), for 10 weeks before death 47 hours (10 hours of night work), for 11 weeks before death 56 hours (38 hours of night work), and for 12 weeks before death 44 hours (10 hours of night work).\\n\\nd. The deceased, after a day off on October 31, 2016, worked night shifts for 10 hours each on three consecutive days from November 1, 2016, to November 3, 2016, and during a night shift on November 4, 2016, suddenly felt pain and left work early, then went to the emergency room of Daewoo Hospital and was diagnosed with “acute myocarditis” (hereinafter the “disease in this case”), and died from the disease in this case on November 14, 2016.\\n\\ne. The deceased had symptoms such as diarrhea, body aches, and a slight fever from October 31, 2016, including upper respiratory infection and enteritis. According to the medical record appraisals at both the first instance and the appellate instance, it appears that the disease in this case occurred as the above initial infection worsened.\\n\\nf. Other than having suffered from “acute gastric ulcer with bleeding” around 2013, the deceased had no particular underlying disease, and there is no material to conclude that he had any abnormality in his usual health condition; his weight and blood pressure appear to have been normal, and he did not smoke.\\n\\ng. A co-worker of the deceased, the non-party witness, testified in the first-instance trial that the deceased worked as an employee of a subcontractor and was later hired as an experienced employee, and that, because he was an experienced employee, he was assigned many tasks that were more difficult and demanding than those assigned to new employees, and that Assembly Division 5, where the deceased worked, was a department newly established in 2009 and had many new hires, creating a competitive atmosphere. The witness also testified that, since August 2016, because of pressure to use up annual leave and strengthened control over overtime work, the actual number of workers and work hours had decreased while they still had to meet the same workload as before, so the work intensity per unit time was high.\\n\\nh. According to the reply to the factual inquiry made to Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering Co., Ltd., the usual period for promotion from Giseon (A) to Gijeong (B) is from 3 years to 5 years, but the deceased was promoted to Gijeong in his 3rd year.\\n\\n3. Examining these circumstances in light of the legal principles set forth above, there is a strong possibility of recognizing a substantial causal relationship between the deceased’s work and the disease in this case. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na. At the time the disease in this case occurred, the deceased was a healthy adult male of 37 years of age, had no particular underlying disease in ordinary times, and aside from work-related factors, no factor can be found that would have caused the initial infection to rapidly worsen into the disease in this case and lead to death. In particular, it is noteworthy that the disease in this case occurred while the deceased was working night shifts for four consecutive days without being able to rest properly after the initial infection developed.\\n\\nb. Since the deceased engaged in physical labor while working irregularly alternating day and night shifts over a long period of time, physical and mental fatigue appears to have accumulated. It is widely known that alternating day and night shifts cause fatigue and stress through irregular sleeping hours, sleep deprivation, and disruption of daily rhythms and biological rhythms, thereby themselves triggering disease or, through accumulated fatigue and stress, lowering the body’s immunity and negatively affecting the onset and aggravation of disease (see Supreme Court Decisions 2002DU8145 rendered on January 10, 2003, 2006DU4912 rendered on April 12, 2007, etc.). Moreover, if the schedule and cycle of alternating day and night shifts are irregular, it can readily be inferred that the adverse effects such as fatigue and stress suffered by the worker will be even greater.\\n\\nc. In light of the co-worker’s testimony and all other circumstances such as the timing of the deceased’s promotion, the deceased appears to have worked more diligently than average co-workers in ordinary times, and the intensity of his work appears to have been high. In addition, the workplace where the deceased worked appears to have been in a situation where the working personnel were somewhat insufficient, so that it seems difficult for workers to take leave using annual leave for personal reasons other than the days off scheduled by management.\\n\\nd. Under the Amended Notice, the deceased’s work falls within work in which multiple factors increasing work burden coexist, such as work with difficult-to-predict schedules, shift work, and work of high physical intensity; accordingly, even if the working hours during the 12 weeks before the onset of the disease in this case were less than the 52-hour weekly average, the relationship between work and disease should be deemed to have increased.\\n\\nf. Ultimately, there is a strong possibility of finding that the deceased developed the initial infection while in a state of lowered immunity due to accumulated physical and mental overwork from ordinary day and night shift work, and that despite this, while continuing night work without proper rest, the initial infection rapidly worsened, causing the disease in this case and leading to death.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, the court below determined that it was difficult to recognize a substantial causal relationship between the deceased’s work and the disease in this case solely on the grounds that the deceased’s working hours during the 12 weeks before the onset of the disease in this case fell short of the 60-hour weekly average standard set forth in the “Pre-Amendment Notice,” and the like. The judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning substantial causal relationship in occupational accidents and by failing to conduct the necessary deliberation.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and in order for the court below to retry and determine the case, the case is remanded to the court below. It is so adjudged unanimously by the participating Justices as per the Disposition."}

{"[2020DU43722]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds for final appeal filed after the period for submitting the statement of grounds for final appeal has elapsed shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for final appeal).\\n\\n1. Background of the case and the decision of the court below\\n\\nA. According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) On 2017. 3. 8., the Plaintiff filed with the Defendant an application for a building permit in the form of a composite civil complaint, including an application for a development activity permit, in order to construct one animal funeral facility (hereinafter referred to as “the animal funeral facility in this case”) on the land at Daegu Seo-gu (address omitted) and one other parcel (hereinafter referred to as “the application site in this case”) (hereinafter referred to as “the application in this case”).\\n\\n2) On 2019. 4. 10., the Defendant issued a disposition refusing the application in this case to the Plaintiff on the grounds of “traffic-related: insufficient materials concerning securing an access road based on 3-3-2-1 of the Development Activity Permit Operation Guidelines,” and “site appropriateness-related: does not satisfy the site appropriateness standard in relation to the distance restriction provision between schools and animal funeral facilities under the Animal Protection Act (enforced on 2019. 3. 25.)” (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition in this case”).\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, Articles 32(1) and 33(4)5.(b) of the Animal Protection Act, as partially amended by Act No. 16075 on 2018. 12. 24. and enforced from 2019. 3. 25. (hereinafter referred to as the “Amended Animal Protection Act”), provide that, in principle, registration as an animal funeral business may not be made where an animal funeral facility is to be installed within 300 m from a densely populated residential area of 20 or more units, a school, or other facility or place where the public frequently gathers. A ○○ High School is located within a straight-line distance of 200 m south of the application site in this case.\\n\\nB. The court below determined that: ➀ since the Development Activity Permit Operation Guidelines are a regulatory decree, and the application in this case fails to secure the width of the access road prescribed by the above guidelines, even if the Defendant, without going through deliberation by the Urban Planning Committee, immediately treated insufficient materials concerning securing the access road as a ground for refusal, it cannot be deemed that there was an error of deviation from or abuse of discretionary power; and ➁ in light of the purport of the provisions of the Amended Animal Protection Act, it cannot be deemed that the Defendant erred by deviating from or abusing discretionary power in finding that the application in this case does not satisfy the standard of “site appropriateness,” which is a requirement for a development activity.\\n\\n2. Portion of the grounds for final appeal alleging matters concerning the Development Activity Permit Operation Guidelines\\n\\nA. 1) Articles 58(1) and (3) of the Act on Planning and Use of National Territory (hereinafter referred to as the “National Land Planning and Utilization Act”) provide that a development activity permit or a permit for modification shall be granted only when the contents of the application for a development activity permit satisfy the standard that “the use of land in surrounding areas or the land-use plan, the height of structures, the gradient of the land, the condition of trees, drainage of water, drainage of rivers, lakes, wetlands, and the like shall be in harmony with the surrounding environment or landscape,” and that the standards for development activity permits shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree according to the classification in each of the following items, taking into account the characteristics of the area, the status of development in the area, the current status of infrastructure, and the like.\\n\\n2) Article 56(1) [Attached Table 1-2] of the Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, “Standards for Development Activity Permits,” constitutes externally binding delegated legislation enacted pursuant to the delegation under Article 58(3) of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act. However, since Article 56(4) of the Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act merely provides that the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport may establish “detailed review standards” for the standards for development activity permits under paragraph (1), the “Development Activity Permit Operation Guidelines” established by the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport as a Ministerial Instruction of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport pursuant thereto are merely administrative rules by which the superior administrative agency, namely the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport, has set detailed standards concerning the interpretation and application of the standards for development activity permits prescribed in the National Land Planning and Utilization Act and its subordinate statutes with respect to officials under his authority or subordinate administrative agencies in connection with development activity permit duties, and therefore have no external binding force. Accordingly, even if an administrative disposition was made in accordance with the above guidelines, whether the disposition is lawful must be determined according to whether it conforms to the standards for development activity permits prescribed in the National Land Planning and Utilization Act and its subordinate statutes and to general principles of law such as the principles of proportionality and equality (see Supreme Court Decisions 2017Du38874, decided 2019. 7. 11., and 2019Du60776, decided 2020. 8. 27., among others).\\n\\nB. 1) Therefore, it was not appropriate for the court below to premise the legal nature of the above guidelines as a regulatory decree and then to state their contents as the standard for determining whether the grounds for disposition are lawful.\\n\\n2) However, Article 56(1) [Attached Table 1-2] of the Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, “Standards for Development Activity Permits,” 1. Ma. sets forth, under “matters for review concerning infrastructure,” as item (1), the standard that “it shall not cause interference with traffic flow in the surrounding area,” and as item (2), the standard that “the relationship between the site and the road shall conform to the Building Act,” and the Development Activity Permit Operation Guidelines 3-3-2-1 provide, with respect to access to roads and criteria for securing roads, that “as a general rule, the site on which a building or structure is to be constructed shall connect to an urban or district planning road, etc., and accordingly the width of the access road to be opened (including road expansion) shall be at least 4 m where the development scale is less than 5,000㎡, and an appropriate width shall be secured considering traffic volume according to the scale of the development activity.” Therefore, the judgment of the court below on this point can ultimately be understood as a determination to the effect that the application in this case does not conform to the standards for development activity permits that “it shall not cause interference with traffic flow in the surrounding area” and “it shall conform to the standards under the Building Act concerning roads” as a result of failing to meet the requirement that “the width of the access road shall be at least 4 m.”\\n\\n3) Whether a matter falls within the requirements for a development activity permit under Article 56(1) of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act belongs to the realm of discretionary judgment by the administrative agency; thus, judicial review thereof, in light of the discretionary room afforded to the administrative agency’s public-interest judgment, is in principle limited to whether there has been deviation from or abuse of discretionary power, and whether there has been a factual mistake or a violation of the principles of proportionality and equality becomes the standard for such determination (see Supreme Court Decision 2016Du55490, decided 2017. 3. 15., among others). In addition, where an administrative rule concerns matters that fall within the discretion of the administrative agency that established it, the courts should respect it unless there are special circumstances such as a lack of objective rationality in the substance of the provision (see Supreme Court Decision 2017Du43319, decided 2019. 1. 10., and the aforementioned Supreme Court Decision 2019Du60776, decided 2020. 8. 27.).\\n\\nC. Taking the above legal principles together, the judgment of the court below is partly not appropriate, but as a result it can be upheld as meaning that there was no error of deviation from or abuse of discretionary power in the disposition in this case. The grounds for final appeal on this point are not accepted.\\n\\n3. Portion of the grounds for final appeal alleging matters concerning the Amended Animal Protection Act\\n\\nA. 1) Even when the statute serving as the basis for an administrative disposition has been amended, as a general rule the amended statute in force at the time of the disposition and the standards prescribed therein apply, unless otherwise provided by transitional provisions, and there may be room to restrict the application of the amended statute in order to protect citizens’ trust in the continued existence of the pre-amendment statute where such trust is recognized as more worthy of protection than the public interest demand concerning the application of the amended statute (see Supreme Court Decision 97Nu9918, decided 2000. 3. 10., among others). Where an administrative agency, after accepting an application, delays processing without justifiable reason and during that period the statute and compensation standards are changed, a disposition made in accordance with the changed statute and compensation standards is unlawful (see Supreme Court Decision 2004Du2974, decided 2006. 8. 25., among others). Whether there was a delay in processing without justifiable reason should be examined and determined mainly with reference to the specific circumstances or background that caused the disposition to be delayed, based on the statutory processing period or ordinary processing period, while also considering whether the administrative agency had a motive or intent to avoid applying the pre-amendment statute, whether there was a possibility of easily avoiding the delay in disposition, and the like (see Supreme Court Decision 2012Du23501, decided 2014. 7. 24.).\\n\\n2) As noted above, Article 56(1) [Attached Table 1-2] of the Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, “Standards for Development Activity Permits,” pursuant to the delegation under Article 58(1)4. and (2) of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, provides, in 3. B. 2), as matters for review by use zone, that “as an area to which development demand is flexibly applied according to the characteristics of the region, consider locational validity, the appropriateness of infrastructure, the impact of development on the environment, the protection and creation of the landscape, and the minimization of damage to aesthetics.”\\n\\nB. In light of these relevant provisions and legal principles and examining the reasons of the judgment of the court below against the record, although some parts of the judgment of the court below are not entirely appropriate, it cannot be said that the court below found that there was no error of deviation from or abuse of discretionary power in the disposition in this case in the sense that the requirements of the standards for development activity permits, which are regulatory decrees, were not satisfied in terms of “locational validity.” The grounds for final appeal on this point are likewise not accepted.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the final appeal are borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning the case are correct? (If there is any dispute, the answer is based on judicial precedents)

A owns X land, and on 2024. 2. 1. property tax on Y land, which is adjacent to X land and is clearly registered in the name of B in the registry, was imposed on A. A, who was not accurately remembering the location of his own land, did not pay it and was then given a demand notice under the Local Tax Collection Act on 2024. 4. 1., and after receiving further demand notices again on 2024. 5. 1. and 2024. 6. 3., paid the tax on 2024. 6. 17. A knows that he is not the person obligated to pay the property tax and seeks relief through litigation.
* The above case is hypothetical.
A: The Administrative Procedures Act does not apply to tax tribunal matters concerning a disposition imposing property tax under the Local Tax Act.
B: Under the Local Tax Collection Act, if a taxpayer is delinquent in property tax, the head of a local government may request the competent administrative authority for a business requiring permits, etc. not to grant such permits, etc. to that taxpayer.
C: If one contests the demand notice through litigation proceedings, the object of the dispute is the last demand notice dated 2024. 6. 3.
D: The property tax imposition disposition against A on 2024. 2. 1. is void ab initio because it imposed a duty to pay on a person who is not the obligor.
E: The property tax imposition disposition against A on 2024. 2. 1. is void ab initio because it imposed a duty to pay on a person who is not the obligor.
label: C

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the true statements (○) and false statements (X) concerning the legal interest under Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act? (Where there is a dispute, according to precedents)

(a) Where a third party other than the direct addressee of a disposition merely has an indirect, factual, or economic interest in the disposition, plaintiff standing to seek revocation of the disposition is not recognized.  
(b) Even if the disposition approving the establishment of a factory within a Development Restriction Zone was annulled in litigation on the ground that it was unlawful, if the factory construction permit disposition based on that approval disposition remains in existence, nearby residents still have a legal interest in seeking revocation of the factory construction permit disposition.  
(c) Where Incorporated Foundation A Research Foundation sent a notice to the President of B University terminating the BK21 agreement, which is a State research and development project, on the ground of improper expenditure of research and development funds, and ordering a three-year restriction on participation in the State research and development project for research team leader A, A has a legal interest in disputing the validity of the notice terminating the above agreement.  
(d) In a case where a decision and public notice of a change to the urban management plan were made to lift some settlements within a Development Restriction Zone from the Development Restriction Zone, the owner of land within the Development Restriction Zone omitted from the areas subject to lifting has a legal interest in seeking revocation of the above decision and public notice.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2007DU10242]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\nThe reasons in the original judgment regarding whether the instant action is lawful are as follows.\\nOn September 4, 2004, the Defendant made and publicly notified a decision on a change to the Namyangju Urban Management Plan, which lifted 24 settlements, including an area of 44,440 m² around 169-6, Jinjung-ri, Joan-myeon, among the Development Restriction Zones in Namyangju City (hereinafter referred to as “the Jungi settlement in this case”), from the Development Restriction Zone (hereinafter referred to as “the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case”). However, although 330 m² of housing site among the land in this case owned by the Plaintiff was required to be included in the subject area for lifting the Development Restriction Zone under Namyangju City’s guidelines for lifting the Development Restriction Zone, it was omitted from the subject area for lifting the Development Restriction Zone due to a clerical error by the responsible public official. Nevertheless, since, like the owners of other land lifted from the Development Restriction Zone by the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case, the Plaintiff was in a status in which the above housing site portion among the land in this case could have been lifted from the Development Restriction Zone, when the constitutional principles of equality and guarantee of property rights are taken together, the Plaintiff has a legal interest in seeking revocation of the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case.\\nHowever, the above determination by the original court cannot be upheld for the following reasons.\\nIn order to file an action for revocation concerning an administrative disposition, there must be a legal interest in seeking revocation of the administrative disposition; such legal interest refers to a case where there exists a direct and concrete interest protected by the statute that is the basis of the disposition in question, and cases in which a person merely has indirect or factual or economic interests do not fall within this category (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2000DU2136, decided July 10, 2001).\\nHere, the land in this case remained designated as a Development Restriction Zone both before and after the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case; therefore, the Plaintiff, as its owner, does not, by reason of the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case, come to bear any new public-law restriction on the use, profit from, or disposition of the above land, nor does the Plaintiff become subject to a more disadvantageous status than before. In addition, even if the portion relating to the Jungi settlement among the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case were revoked as requested in the Plaintiff’s claim, the result would merely be that the lands owned by third parties that were lifted from the Development Restriction Zone by the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case would remain in the Development Restriction Zone as before; it would not result in the land in this case owned by the Plaintiff being lifted from the Development Restriction Zone. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff has a direct and concrete interest in seeking revocation of the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case concerning land owned by third parties.\\nNevertheless, the original court held that the Plaintiff has standing to seek revocation of the decision on change to the urban management plan in this case; thus, there is an error of law in the original court’s determination concerning the Plaintiff’s standing in an administrative litigation. The argument in the grounds of appeal pointing out this issue is well-founded.\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the original court is reversed and the case is remanded to the original court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2012DU28704]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (supplemental briefs on the grounds of appeal, etc., filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal, shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Concerning the argument on the standing of the Plaintiff to challenge the notice of termination of the agreement\\n\\na. Even if a third party is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition, if that third party’s legally protected interest has been infringed by the administrative disposition in question, such third party is entitled to file an action for revocation and obtain a judicial determination of its merits. The legally protected interest referred to here means an individual, direct, and concrete interest protected by the enabling provisions for the disposition in question and related provisions, and does not include a merely factual or economic interest, such as a general, indirect, and abstract interest commonly shared by the public at large as a result of the protection of the public interest. Further, the legally protected interest protected by the enabling provisions for the disposition in question and related provisions includes not only a legally protected interest expressly protected by the enabling provisions for the disposition in question, but also a legally protected interest expressly protected by the enabling provisions for a series of related staged dispositions intended to achieve the administrative purpose of the disposition in question, even if such interest is not protected by the enabling provisions for the disposition in question, and even where there is no express provision in the enabling provisions or related provisions of the disposition in question expressly protecting such interest, if it is construed, by a reasonable interpretation of the enabling provisions and related provisions, that the reasons for restricting the administrative agency in those provisions include a purport to protect individual, direct, and concrete interests, and not merely the protection of the public interest (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DU33044 rendered on 2013. 9. 12.).\\n\\nb. (1) Article 12-2(1) of the Act on the Promotion of Academic Research and the Credit Guarantee for Student Loans provides that the Minister of Education, Science and Technology may, for the promotion of academic research, contribute, within the limits of the budget, all or part of the expenses necessary for academic research, etc. to institutions such as schools under Article 2 of the Higher Education Act. Article 11(1) of the former Special Act on Support for Science and Engineering Personnel for Strengthening National Science and Technology Competitiveness (prior to its amendment by Act No. 10769 on 2011. 6. 7.) provides that the Government may provide necessary support to universities that place emphasis on research activities in order to efficiently promote creative research and development and the fostering of science and engineering personnel. The foregoing statutes (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “Academic Promotion Act, etc.”) form the direct legal basis for the implementation of the project and the execution of the budget for the “Phase 2 Brain Korea (BK)21 Project for the Training Program for Development of Basic Materials for High-Value-Added Foods, Cosmetics, and Traditional Medicines Derived from Marine Organisms” (hereinafter referred to as the “Project at issue”).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Framework Act on Science and Technology (as amended by Act No. 12673 on 2014. 5. 28.; hereinafter the same) uniformly governs matters concerning the operation and management of various national R&D projects such as the Project at issue, and Article 11(2) thereof provides that “when the Government promotes national R&D projects, it shall do so in accordance with each of the following subparagraphs,” and among those subparagraphs provides that the Government shall strengthen support to enhance research and development capabilities, including by creating the best possible research environment for research institutions and researchers (item 2), and that when the Government establishes systems or regulations related to national R&D projects, it shall give the highest priority to the autonomy of research institutions and researchers (item 3).\\n\\nIn addition, pursuant to the delegation of the Framework Act on Science and Technology, the former Regulations on the Management, etc. of National R&D Projects (prior to amendment by Presidential Decree No. 22721 on 2011. 3. 28.; hereinafter referred to as the “Regulations at issue”) provide in Article 7 that project beneficiaries for R&D tasks applied for by researchers belonging to a lead research institution such as a university shall be selected through review, in Article 9 that, for the tasks so selected, project agreements shall be concluded between the head of the central administrative agency or the head of a specialized agency entrusted with the relevant work by such head and the head of the lead research institution, so that R&D funds may be provided, in Article 12 that the head of the central administrative agency shall pay the contributed R&D funds to the head of the lead research institution for management and execution, and in Article 11 that where grounds arise such as “when it becomes difficult to perform R&D due to a serious breach of the agreement by the lead research institution (item 2)” by the head of the central administrative agency, the agreement may be terminated in accordance with the agreement (paragraph 1); and, in particular, in cases of termination of the agreement attributable to the lead research institution, etc., the whole or part of the contribution may be recovered and measures restricting the relevant persons’ participation in national R&D projects may be taken (paragraph 3).\\n\\n(2) In light of the legislative purpose and contents of the Academic Promotion Act, etc. and the Framework Act on Science and Technology, and also considering, inter alia, the following: 1) under a reasonable interpretation of the Academic Promotion Act, etc. and the Framework Act on Science and Technology, the State’s contribution of R&D funds to a university, which is the lead research institution in the Brain Korea (BK)21 Project, appears to aim not only at fostering a “research-oriented university” but also, separately, at strengthening the capabilities of the research personnel belonging to the university; 2) as a matter of principle, the provision of R&D funds for national R&D projects is for R&D tasks applied for by each certain research unit (hereinafter referred to as the “research team”) belonging to a university, and not on the basis of the university to which it belongs; 3) a university is merely a party to the agreement as the formal recipient of the R&D funds under the Academic Promotion Act, etc. and as the external entity in charge of their management and execution, and the substantive interests arising from the agreement should be regarded as belonging to the research team that is the entity performing the relevant R&D task; and 4) furthermore, under the Framework Act on Science and Technology regulations, the notice of termination of a project agreement is not merely a declaration of intent terminating a public law contract formed in the position of equal parties from the position of a contracting party, but constitutes an administrative disposition by which the administrative agency, from a superior position, produces legal effects such as recovery of R&D funds and restriction of participation in national R&D projects by the persons concerned (see Supreme Court Decision 2010DU23859 rendered on 2011. 6. 30.); accordingly, researchers whose legal status is affected thereby are deemed to have an individual, direct, and concrete interest in challenging the effectiveness of the notice of termination of the agreement at least through the team leader representing their interests — when these circumstances are examined in light of the legal principles stated above, the Plaintiff, who was the team leader of the research team for the Project at issue, has a legally protected interest in challenging the effectiveness of the notice of termination of the agreement concerning the Project at issue.\\n\\nc. (1) Nevertheless, the court below erred by holding otherwise, namely, by determining that the Plaintiff lacked standing to challenge the notice of termination of the agreement concerning the Project at issue, and thereby dismissing this part of the action, thereby misapprehending the legal principles concerning “standing of the Plaintiff in an action for revocation.”\\n\\n(2) However, according to the reasons stated in the judgment of the first instance court cited by the court below and the evidence adopted therein, when the Defendant, the President of ○○ University, and the Plaintiff concluded the agreement concerning the Project at issue on 2009. 4. 14., the contents thereof provided that the President of ○○ University and the Plaintiff were to faithfully manage the project funds in accordance with the “Directive on the Management and Operation of the Phase 2 Brain Korea (BK)21 Project” and the “Guidelines on the Management and Operation of the Phase 2 Brain Korea (BK)21 Project” (Article 8), and that the Defendant may terminate the agreement, pursuant to the said Directive, where the President of ○○ University or the research team leader fails to perform major contractual matters, etc. (Article 10); that, according to the said Directive and Guidelines, “participating graduate students” who may be affiliated with the research team and receive research scholarships, etc. are limited to full-time graduate students among the students under the guidance of professors participating in the Project at issue, and those who are registered as research students among degree candidates who have completed the coursework; and that, notwithstanding the foregoing, the Plaintiff registered Nonparty 1, 2, 3, and 4, etc., who did not qualify as such “participating graduate students,” as research students in his research team and received a total of KRW 18,207,300 in research scholarships, international cooperation expenses, conference participation expenses, etc.; and that the Defendant, on 2011. 1. 11., issued the notice at issue to the President of ○○ University, on the ground that the Plaintiff’s conduct constituted “improper execution of R&D funds,” thereby terminating the agreement at issue and further ordering, inter alia, a three-year restriction on the Plaintiff’s participation in national R&D projects.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing relevant statutes and regulations, the facts as determined above amount to “a case where it becomes difficult to perform R&D due to a serious breach of the agreement by the lead research institution” under Article 11(1) item 2 of the Regulations at issue, and thus constitute grounds for termination of the agreement as provided in Article 10 of the agreement at issue; accordingly, the Defendant’s termination of the agreement at issue on the basis of such grounds was proper, and this part of the claim seeking revocation thereof lacks merit.\\n\\n(3) Therefore, since this part of the Plaintiff’s claim is bound to be dismissed on the merits, even if the Plaintiff’s ground of appeal on this point were well-founded and the judgment of the court below were reversed, the court below would still have no choice but to dismiss the Plaintiff’s appeal on this point under the principle prohibiting reformatio in peius; consequently, the error in the court below’s determination concerning standing of the Plaintiff has no effect whatsoever on the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\n2. Concerning the argument on whether the portion of the notice at issue that requested university-imposed disciplinary action against the Plaintiff constitutes an administrative disposition\\n\\nAn administrative disposition subject to an administrative appeal litigation refers to an act by an administrative agency under public law that directly causes a change in the specific rights and duties of citizens by ordering the establishment of rights or the assumption of obligations with respect to a particular matter according to law, or otherwise producing legal effects; acts such as internal acts within the administrative power, solicitations, recommendations, or factual notices, which do not directly produce legal changes in the legal status of the addressee or other interested persons, cannot be the subject of an administrative appeal litigation (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2008DU3500 rendered on 2008. 4. 24.).\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the first instance court cited by the court below, the court below dismissed this part of the action on the ground that the Defendant’s request to the President of ○○ University for university-imposed disciplinary action against the Plaintiff constitutes a recommendation or factual notice without legally binding force and therefore falls under an act that does not directly produce legal changes in the Plaintiff’s legal status, such as rights and duties, and thus does not constitute an administrative disposition subject to an administrative appeal litigation.\\n\\nExamining the record in light of the legal principles stated above, the court below’s determination in this regard is proper, and there is no illegality in misapprehending the legal principles concerning administrative dispositions subject to an administrative appeal litigation.\\n\\n3. Concerning the argument on the illegality of the portion of the notice at issue imposing a restriction on the Plaintiff’s participation in national R&D projects\\n\\nArticle 11-2(1) of the Framework Act on Science and Technology provides that the head of the central administrative agency may, within a period not exceeding 5 years, restrict the participation in the relevant national R&D projects of the principal investigators, etc. who have participated in the national R&D projects under his or her jurisdiction, if any of the following items applies, and among such items includes “where R&D funds have been used for a purpose other than the intended purpose (item 5).”\\n\\nFurther, Article 27(1) of the Regulations at issue, which pursuant to the delegation under Article 11-2(5) of the Framework Act on Science and Technology sets forth specific standards for the period of participation restriction according to each ground for restriction, classifies “where R&D funds have been used for a purpose other than the intended purpose (item 5)” into: “where R&D funds have been embezzled, fraudulently obtained, or misappropriated, from 3 years to 5 years (subitem a)”; “where R&D funds have been intentionally improperly executed, from 2 years to 3 years (subitem b)”; and “where R&D funds have been temporarily diverted and used for another purpose, within 2 years (subitem c).”\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment of the first instance court cited by the court below, the court below, after recognizing the facts as stated in its opinion, determined that the Plaintiff’s act of causing unqualified persons who could not participate as graduate students under the agreement at issue to participate so that they received research scholarships, etc. constitutes “a case where R&D funds were intentionally improperly executed” under Article 27(1) item 5(b) of the Regulations at issue, and on the premise that the ground for disposition was established, held that the Defendant’s disposition imposing a three-year participation restriction within the scope of the disposition standards under the relevant laws and regulations was not illegal.\\n\\nExamining the foregoing relevant statutes and the record, the court below’s determination in this regard is proper, and there is no illegality in finding facts contrary to the rules of logic and experience, thereby exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the interpretation of the requirements of the participation restriction provision above under the Framework Act on Science and Technology regulations or the legal principles concerning deviation from or abuse of discretion.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party; accordingly, it is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2015DU3485]": "The grounds of appeal of the Defendant and the Defendant-intervenor are examined together.\\n\\n1. On the legal interest to seek revocation of the factory building permit disposition\\n\\na. A third party who is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition and who files a revocation action on the ground that the disposition has infringed, or is likely to infringe, his or her environmental interest must prove that such environmental interest is an interest individually, directly, and concretely protected by the statute forming the basis of the disposition or by related statutes, that is, a legally protected interest, in order for standing to sue to be recognized (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DU14001 rendered on Dec. 22, 2006). In addition, the latter sentence of Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that “in cases where there exists a legal interest to be restored by the revocation of the disposition, etc., even after the effect of the disposition, etc. has been extinguished due to the lapse of time, the execution of the disposition, etc., or any other reason,” a revocation action may be filed, thereby allowing the filing of a revocation action even with respect to an administrative disposition whose effect has already ceased to exist, where the necessity of legal protection is recognized. In determining, in a specific case, whether there is a necessity of legal protection, in light of the purport of Article 27(1) of the Constitution, which guarantees the people’s right to a trial, and the purpose of the Administrative Litigation Act, which seeks to effectively remedy infringements of rights and interests caused by administrative dispositions, consideration must be given to the request that litigation to redress such infringements be allowed not only where the people’s rights and interests are in fact being infringed due to the existence of the administrative disposition, but also where there is a concrete and realistic risk of infringement of rights and interests (see, e.g., Supreme Court en banc Decision 2003DU1684 rendered on Jun. 22, 2006). Therefore, where a disposition remains validly in force, unless there are special circumstances, it must be deemed that there is a necessity of legal protection to file a revocation action in order to remove the actual infringement or realistic risk of infringement caused by the existence of that disposition.\\n\\nb. Under the former Act on the Activation of Industrial Cluster and Factory Establishment (before amendment by Act No. 9426 on Feb. 6, 2009; hereinafter referred to as the “former Industrial Cluster Act”), to newly establish, expand, or change the business type of a factory with a factory building area of at least 500 square meters (hereinafter referred to as “factory establishment, etc.”), approval from the competent authority must be obtained pursuant to the Presidential Decree (Article 13(1)), and a person who has obtained approval for factory establishment, etc. may construct a factory building only after separately obtaining a building permit or filing a building report under the Building Act and its subordinate statutes, or after the building permit or building report is deemed to have been made (Article 13-2(1)16 and Article 14). Furthermore, the competent authority shall not grant, under the relevant statutes, a permit for the construction of a factory, operation, or the like to a person who has not obtained approval for factory establishment, etc. (Article 50), and where it is deemed difficult to carry out the project because a person who has obtained approval for factory establishment, etc. uses the site or building for a purpose different from that approved without justifiable grounds, the approval for factory establishment, etc. may be revoked and restoration of the land to its original condition may be ordered (Article 13-5(4)).\\n\\nTaken together, the above provisions mean that, since it is permissible to issue a factory building permit disposition after, or concurrently with, a factory establishment approval disposition, if the factory establishment approval disposition is revoked, the factory building permit disposition based on that approval disposition must also be revoked, and where a change in the form and quality of land has been made based on the factory establishment approval disposition, restoration to the original condition shall, as a matter of principle, be made. Therefore, even if the disposition approving factory establishment in a development restriction zone was litigated and revoked on the ground that it was unlawful, so long as the factory building permit disposition based on that approval disposition remains in existence, it cannot be concluded merely from the circumstance that the factory establishment approval disposition was revoked that the state in which the environmental interests of nearby residents are infringed, or are at risk of being infringed, has ended or that the stage at which it can be corrected has passed; nearby residents must still be deemed to have a legal interest in seeking revocation of the factory building permit disposition (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DU24474 rendered on Mar. 14, 2013).\\n\\nc. On the same purport, the court below determined that, even if a judgment revoking the factory establishment approval disposition against the Defendant-intervenor had become final in the revocation action concerning the factory establishment approval disposition filed by nearby residents, so long as the factory building permit disposition at issue, which was made on the basis of the above factory establishment approval disposition, remains validly in force, the Plaintiffs are recognized as having a legal interest in seeking revocation of the factory building permit disposition at issue. The court below’s determination in this regard contains no error of law concerning legal interest in a revocation action.\\n\\n2. On the unlawfulness of the factory building permit disposition\\n\\na. According to the record, it can be seen that the Defendant issued to the Defendant-intervenor on Jul. 13, 2009 a factory establishment approval disposition for newly establishing a ready-mixed concrete factory, but a judgment revoking it became final on the grounds that it did not fall under “an act of changing the use for the purpose of changing a factory into an urban-type factory” or “the reconstruction of an existing building,” which are exceptionally permitted within a development restriction zone, etc. (Supreme Court Decision 2012DU24474 rendered on Mar. 14, 2013).\\n\\nb. According to the legal principles discussed above, since the judgment revoking the factory establishment approval disposition against the Defendant-intervenor became final, the factory building permit disposition that the Defendant made against the Defendant-intervenor in this case lost its basis and is unlawful.\\n\\nOn the same purport, the court below determined that the factory building permit disposition at issue is unlawful and must therefore be revoked. The court below’s determination in this regard contains no error of law concerning restrictions on acts in development restriction zones, requirements for a factory building permit, factory establishment area, succession of defects, restrictions on revocation of beneficial administrative acts, binding force of a decision on review by the Board of Audit and Inspection, or exercise of the court’s duty to clarify. The arguments in this part of the grounds of appeal are, in the end, merely intended to criticize the already final judgment revoking the factory establishment approval disposition, and thus cannot be accepted.\\n\\n3. Whether the court below violated the obligation of mandatory remand\\n\\nAccording to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act and Article 418 of the Civil Procedure Act, even when the first-instance judgment dismissing the action as unlawful is reversed, if the case has been sufficiently tried for the first-instance court to render a judgment on the merits, the appellate court may render a judgment on the merits by itself.\\n\\nExamining the record in light of these statutes and legal principles, it was proper for the court below to proceed to and determine the merits without remanding the case to the first-instance court while reversing the first-instance judgment dismissing the action, and there is no error of law concerning mandatory remand. \\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal arising from the intervention shall be borne by the Defendant-intervenor, while the remainder shall be borne by the losing Defendant. It is so adjudged as per the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated in the decision."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning the following case is incorrect? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)

On 2009. 6. 1., A Church applied to the head of B District Office of A City for a road occupancy permit with respect to the underground portion of a road owned by B District, for the purpose of using it as part of the site for church facilities to be constructed in the underground space during the process of newly constructing the church building at that time. Accordingly, on 2010. 4. 6., the head of B District Office issued a road occupancy permit disposition (hereinafter, “the disposition at issue”) allowing A Church to occupy the underground portion of part of the above road (hereinafter, “the road at issue”) from 2010. 4. 9. to 2019. 12. 31., and A Church, after the disposition at issue, obtained a building permit for the newly built church building including the underground portion of the road at issue and installed facilities such as a chapel from the first basement level to the fifth basement level. Accordingly, a resident of B District seeks to challenge the disposition at issue through a residents’ lawsuit under the Local Autonomy Act.
A: Any resident of B District who has made a residents’ audit request may bring a residents’ lawsuit, and a filing by one person is also possible.
B: In the case of a residents’ lawsuit, which has the character of objective litigation, the illegality of the disputed disposition should be construed in the same way as the general “illegality of a disposition” in appeal litigation.
C: As, with respect to residents’ lawsuits, the Administrative Litigation Act applies except as otherwise provided in the Local Autonomy Act, a judgment on the basis of circumstances is also permitted in residents’ lawsuits.
D: In a case where confirmation of nullity of the disposition at issue is sought through a residents’ lawsuit, unlike in an action for confirmation of nullity, which is an appeal litigation, it is subject to the filing period under the Local Autonomy Act.
E: If it is confirmed in the case that there are circumstances showing that the effect of the building permit issued on the basis of the disposition at issue cannot be directly challenged by a resident, then the benefit of suit to challenge the disposition at issue through a residents’ lawsuit is denied.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2018DU104]": "The grounds for appeal are examined (the statements in the supplemental brief of the grounds for appeal submitted after the filing period for the brief of the grounds for appeal has expired are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Whether the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case is subject to a resident suit\\n\\nA. According to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act and the latter sentence of Article 436(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, a court to which a case has been remanded or transferred is bound by the factual and legal determinations that the Supreme Court used as grounds for reversal. Therefore, in accordance with the binding force of the Supreme Court’s decision of reversal and remand dated May 27, 2016 in 2014DU8490, there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, in the lower court’s misapprehension of the legal nature of the permission for occupation of the road in this case and the legal principles concerning the subject of a resident suit, in its judgment proceeding to the merits on the premise that the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case falls under “matters concerning the management and disposal of property” under Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nB. Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act merely provides that a resident who has requested an audit concerning “matters relating to the acquisition, management, or disposal of property” may, with respect to unlawful acts or negligent performance of duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested, bring an action against the head of the relevant local government as the opposing party, and does not limit the subject of a resident suit to matters concerning the “acquisition, management, or disposal of property that caused damage to local finances.” Therefore, the argument in the grounds for appeal that the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case does not constitute a subject of a resident suit because it did not cause damage to local finances is contrary to the clear language of the above provision of the Local Autonomy Act prescribing the subject of a resident suit, and is thus rejected.\\n\\n2. Whether the filing period has expired\\n\\nThe lower court determined that the Plaintiffs filed a resident audit request on December 7, 2011, which was within 2 years from April 9, 2010, when the Defendant rendered the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case, and therefore complied with the resident audit request period under Article 16(2) of the Local Autonomy Act; that they filed this resident suit on August 29, 2012, which was within 90 days from June 1, 2012, when the Mayor of Seoul notified the audit results, and therefore complied with the filing period for a resident suit under Article 17(4) of the Local Autonomy Act; and that, with respect to a resident audit request and a resident suit premised thereon, the filing period for an ordinary action for revocation prescribed in Article 20(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act does not apply.\\n\\nSuch determination of the lower court is proper as it follows the relevant statutory provisions, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the filing period for a resident audit request and a resident suit.\\n\\n3. Whether the right to sue was extinguished because incontestability arose with respect to the disposition granting building permission\\n\\nA. Once a judgment revoking an administrative disposition on the ground that it is unlawful becomes final and binding, the administrative agency has the duty, in accordance with the binding force of the revocation judgment, to render a new disposition excluding the unlawfulness confirmed in that judgment or to take measures to eliminate the unlawful consequences (see Article 30 of the Administrative Litigation Act, and Supreme Court Decision dated October 29, 2015 in 2013DU27517, etc.). And when an administrative disposition becomes final and binding due to the lapse of the period for objection, such finality merely means that the person whose legal interests have been infringed by the disposition can no longer contest the effect of the relevant disposition or adjudication; it does not further mean that res judicata, as in the case of a judgment, is recognized, so that the factual relations or legal determinations underlying the disposition become final and the parties or the court become bound thereby and unable to make contradictory allegations or determinations (see Supreme Court Decision dated July 8, 2004 in 2002DU11288, etc.).\\n\\nB.
