If, in this resident suit, a judgment revoking the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case becomes final and binding, the Defendant may, in accordance with the binding force of the revocation judgment and as part of measures to eliminate unlawful consequences, order the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side to suspend the occupation of the road in this case and restore the original condition pursuant to Articles 73, 96, and 100 of the Road Act, and, if this is not complied with, take measures such as administrative compulsory execution or imposition of an enforcement fine, thereby making it possible to eliminate the unlawful state caused by the disposition granting permission for occupation of the road in this case.\\n\\nIn addition, although the building permit in this case is not revoked or extinguished directly as a result of the revocation judgment, the building permit in this case, which was granted on the premise that the permission for occupation of the road in this case validly existed, loses part of its legal and factual basis. Accordingly, within the scope of complying with the legal principles concerning the limitation on ex officio revocation of beneficial administrative acts, the Defendant has the duty, under certain requirements, to take measures such as ex officio revocation or alteration of part thereof. Therefore, even if the Plaintiffs cannot directly contest the validity of the building permit in this case in this resident suit, that cannot serve as grounds for denying the Plaintiffs’ legal interest in seeking revocation of the permission for occupation of the road in this case.\\n\\nC. On the same reasoning, the lower court held that even if, in this resident suit, a judgment dismissing the claim for revocation of the building permit in this case becomes final and binding, and the Plaintiffs are thereby unable to directly contest the validity of the building permit in this case, the legal interest in seeking revocation of the permission for occupation of the road in this case is not extinguished. Such determination of the lower court is based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning legal interest in a lawsuit or the incontestability of administrative dispositions.\\n\\n4. Standard for examining unlawfulness of a disposition in a resident suit\\n\\nA. Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act provides that if the administration of affairs within the authority of a local government and its head is “in violation of statutes or recognized as significantly detrimental to the public interest,” residents of that local government in a prescribed number or more may request an audit. Article 17(1) provides that a resident who has requested an audit concerning matters relating to public expenditure, matters relating to the acquisition, management, or disposal of property, matters relating to the conclusion or performance of sales, lease, or construction contracts or other contracts to which the relevant local government is a party, or matters concerning the neglect of assessment and collection of public charges such as local taxes, usage fees, charges, or administrative fines, may bring an action against the head of the relevant local government “with respect to unlawful acts or negligent performance of duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested.”\\n\\nFurthermore, Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act provides, as types of actions that residents may bring pursuant to paragraph (1), “an action seeking revocation or alteration of the relevant act, which is an administrative disposition, or seeking confirmation of the validity or nonexistence of that act,” and Article 17(17) provides that, with respect to actions under paragraph (1), the Administrative Litigation Act shall apply except as otherwise provided in the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nB. Considering the content and structure of these relevant provisions, together with the legislative purpose and legal nature of the resident suit system as discussed below, the unlawfulness of the disposition challenged in a resident suit should be determined, as in an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act, on the basis of whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, such as the Constitution, statutes, subordinate regulations, and general principles of law; it is not to be determined solely on the basis of whether the disposition caused a loss to the finances of the local government.\\n\\n(1) The Local Autonomy Act merely enumerates the subjects of resident suits in Article 17(1) and does not separately prescribe a standard for reviewing the unlawfulness of a disposition in a resident suit; nor does Article 17(2) item 2 require, as a condition for seeking revocation or alteration of an administrative disposition, that it have caused a loss to the finances of the local government.\\n\\n(2) The resident suit system was introduced in the Local Autonomy Act as amended by Act No. 7362 on January 27, 2005, for the purpose of enhancing the accountability of local administration by expanding resident participation, through allowing residents of a local government to petition a court to rectify the local government’s unlawful “acquisition, management, or disposal of property,” etc. It constitutes a popular action under the Administrative Litigation Act. A popular action means “an action brought directly to seek correction of an act of a state or public entity that violated statutes, irrespective of one’s own legal interests,” and may be brought “only by persons prescribed by law in cases prescribed by law” (Article 3(3) and Article 45 of the Administrative Litigation Act), thereby being distinguished from an appeal litigation that may be brought by a person having a legal interest in seeking revocation of a disposition (Article 3(1) and Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act).\\n\\nThus, the resident suit system was introduced for the purpose of specially recognizing a legal standing permitting the filing of an action seeking revocation, etc. of a disposition, on the premise that a prescribed number or more residents undergo the procedure of requesting an audit pursuant to Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act, in order to remedy the problem that ordinary residents belonging to a local government lack a legal interest in seeking such revocation and therefore cannot bring an appeal litigation seeking revocation of the local government’s unlawful “acquisition, management, or disposal of property,” etc. There is little basis to find that the legislative intent was to restrict the merits review standard in a resident suit to whether damage was caused to the finances of the local government.\\n\\n(3) As noted above, Article 17(17) of the Local Autonomy Act provides that resident suits shall be governed by the Administrative Litigation Act except as specially provided in the Local Autonomy Act, and Article 46(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that, for a popular action seeking revocation of a disposition, the provisions concerning an action for revocation shall apply mutatis mutandis insofar as they are not contrary to its nature. Therefore, unless the Local Autonomy Act provides otherwise concerning the subject of a resident suit, the filing period, standing of the plaintiff, etc., a resident suit and an action for revocation should not be treated differently; accordingly, in a resident suit seeking revocation of an administrative disposition, the review of unlawfulness should, absent special circumstances, be conducted in the same manner as the review of unlawfulness in an action for revocation.\\n\\n(4) It is the Supreme Court’s established view that the object of litigation in an action for revocation is “the general unlawfulness of the disposition” (see Supreme Court Decisions dated March 23, 1990 in 89NU5386, and March 8, 1994 in 92NU1728, etc.). In an action for revocation, the court must determine the unlawfulness of the disposition on the basis of whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, such as the Constitution, statutes, subordinate regulations, and general principles of law, and the same applies in a resident suit.\\n\\nC. On the same reasoning, the lower court held that the unlawfulness of a disposition in a resident suit must be interpreted in the same way as “the general unlawfulness of a disposition” in appeal litigation, and that the disposition should be revoked not only when it violates explicit laws concerning finance and accounting, but also when it is unlawful because it has deviated from or abused discretion by violating general principles of law such as the principles of proportionality, equality, and protection of trust. There is no error in such determination of the lower court, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the standard for reviewing unlawfulness of a disposition in a resident suit.\\n\\n5. Whether Article 13 of the former Public Property and Commodity Management Act (as in force prior to amendment by Act No. 10006 of February 4, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Public Property Act”) was violated\\n\\nA. (1) The former Public Property Act is a statute enacted for the purpose of protecting public property and commodities and promoting the propriety of their acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposal (Article 1), and it provides that, with respect to the acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposal of public property and commodities, the former Public Property Act shall apply except where other statutes contain special provisions (Article 2).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Road Act is a statute enacted for the purpose of contributing to the development of transportation and the enhancement of public welfare by providing for the establishment of plans concerning roads, designation or recognition of routes, management, facility standards, preservation, and expenses, in order to improve the road network and ensure proper road management (Article 1). It comprehensively regulates roads, including not only roads falling under administrative property and general property under the State Property Act and the Local Finance Act, but also cases in which the land for roads belongs to private ownership.\\n\\n(2) Considering the content and structure of the above relevant provisions together with the legislative purposes of the two statutes, the Public Property and Commodity Management Act has the nature of a general law governing matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposal of public property and commodities, whereas the Road Act, taking into account the functional characteristics of roads as facilities provided for public traffic, should be regarded as a special law that applies preferentially over the Public Property and Commodity Management Act when roads constitute public property, because it imposes special public-law regulation regardless of ownership (see Supreme Court Decisions dated November 10, 1981 in 80NU618, and May 26, 2011 in 2010DU28106, etc.).\\n\\nB. (1) Article 13 of the former Public Property Act provides that no person other than the head of the relevant local government may construct buildings, ditches, bridges, other structures, or other permanent facilities on public property, while its proviso allows such construction by persons other than the head of the relevant local government in cases where there is no impediment to the use and enjoyment of the public property and in cases prescribed by Presidential Decree. Pursuant to that delegation, Article 9 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Public Property and Commodity Management Act (as in force prior to amendment by Presidential Decree No. 25441 of July 7, 2014) provides that permanent facilities may be constructed on public property in cases such as “where a structure is installed above ground, on the surface, or underground of the relevant public property to the extent that it does not impede the present use and enjoyment of the public property by the local government” (item 9).\\n\\nBy contrast, Article 38 of the former Road Act (as in force prior to amendment by Act No. 10156 of March 22, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Road Act”) provides that a person who intends to construct, rebuild, alter, or remove structures, objects, or other facilities, or to occupy a road for other purposes within a road area, shall obtain permission from the managing authority (paragraph (1)), and delegates to Presidential Decree the necessary matters concerning the types of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupancy permission may be granted (paragraph (2)). Pursuant to that delegation, Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act (as in force prior to amendment by Presidential Decree No. 24205 of November 27, 2012; hereinafter referred to as the “former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act”) prescribes the types of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupancy permission may be granted.\\n\\n(2) Considering the content and structure of Article 38 of the former Road Act, each item of Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, and [Table 1-2] of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, which sets forth the structural standards for structures or facilities subject to road occupancy permission, together with the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, the Road Act and its subordinate regulations are special provisions concerning Article 13 of the former Public Property Act. Therefore, with respect to occupation of roads, the provisions of the Road Act and its subordinate regulations apply preferentially, and Article 13 of the former Public Property Act does not apply.\\n\\nC. The lower court held that, although road occupancy permission may be granted for the installation of underground structures, the former Public Property Act Article 13 applies to the permission for occupation of the road in this case; and because the permanent facilities underground the road that the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side intended to install through the permission for occupation of the road in this case do not fall under permanent facilities whose construction on public property is permitted under the proviso to Article 13 of the former Public Property Act, the permission for occupation of the road in this case is unlawful as it violates Article 13 of the former Public Property Act.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles discussed above, this aspect of the lower court’s determination contains an error of law concerning the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, but, as explained below, insofar as the lower court’s conclusion that the permission for occupation of the road in this case is unlawful as it constitutes a deviation from or abuse of discretion is proper, there is no error that affected the judgment.\\n\\n6. Whether there was unlawfulness arising from deviation from or abuse of discretion\\n\\nA. According to the record and the reasons for the lower court’s judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) On June 1, 2009, after purchasing 6,861.2 square meters of land in the Special Planning District II of the ○○ Zone (△△△ Area) among lands in the area of Seoul Seocho-gu (address omitted) that had then been designated as a district-unit planning zone, the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side applied to the Defendant for road occupancy permission for the underground portion of Cheonnari-gil, a local road owned by Seocho-gu, Seoul, for the purpose of constructing an access passage to an underground parking lot and using it as part of the site for a chapel facility to be built in the underground space in the course of constructing a new church building.\\n\\n(2) Accordingly, on April 6, 2010, the Defendant imposed a condition that 325 square meters of the southern underground first floor of the new church building be donated and entrusted as a child-care center, and granted the disposition permitting occupation of the road in this case so that the underground portion of “a road with a width of 7 meters × a length of 154 meters” out of the total width of 12 meters, consisting of the above Cheonnari-gil plus the 4-meter-wide portion that the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side was scheduled to widen and donate to the Defendant under the district-unit plan, could be occupied by the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side from April 9, 2010 to December 31, 2019.\\n\\n(3) After the permission for occupation of the road in this case, the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side installed facilities such as the main sanctuary, video worship room, Bible study room, choir room, and broadcasting room from underground first floor to underground fifth floor beneath the new church building, including the underground portion of the road in this case, and installed facilities such as parking lots, machine rooms, and storage rooms from underground sixth floor to underground eighth floor.\\n\\nB. The lower court held that occupation of the underground space through the installation of underground structures such as a chapel, choir room, and broadcasting room is not only difficult to restore to the original condition, but also entails considerable risks and responsibilities for maintenance, management, and safety; that if such occupation is permitted, it will be difficult in the future to refuse similar applications for road occupancy permission, thereby creating a risk that the underground portion of roads will be used indiscriminately and public safety will be endangered; and that the underground portion of the road in this case would be used practically permanently and exclusively as part of the church building, making it impossible to respond flexibly and actively to changes in the circumstances around the road. On such grounds, the lower court determined that the permission for occupation of the road in this case violated the principles of proportionality and equity, and rejected the Defendant’s argument that, with respect to road occupancy permission within a district-unit planning zone, broad planning discretion is recognized, as in the formulation and decision of an administrative plan.\\n\\nC. In light of the reasons of the lower court’s judgment, the provisions and relevant legal principles discussed above, and the record, there is no error in the lower court’s above determination, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning deviation from or abuse of discretion or planning discretion.\\n\\n7. Remaining grounds for appeal\\n\\nA. Whether the legal principles concerning revocation of beneficial administrative dispositions apply in an action for revocation\\n\\nThe legal principle that the exercise of the right to revoke a beneficial administrative disposition, etc. may be allowed only when there is a substantial public interest necessity justifying the infringement of vested rights or a necessity to protect the interests of a third party (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 14, 1991 in 90NU9780, etc.) applies only when the administrative agency revokes or withdraws a beneficial administrative disposition ex officio, and does not apply in the case of litigation revocation. There is no error in the lower court’s determination to the same effect, insofar as it misapprehended the legal principles limiting the revocation and withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\n\\nB. Whether it is subject to a judgment based on circumstances\\n\\nThe lower court held that a judgment based on circumstances, as provided in Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act, should be recognized only in very exceptional cases where revoking or altering an unlawful administrative disposition would instead be significantly contrary to the public welfare; that there does not appear to be a public interest necessity to preserve the effect of the permission for occupation of the road in this case; and that it would be difficult to eliminate the unlawful state through supplementary measures by the Defendant, who is the road managing authority, and on such grounds determined that there is no justification for a judgment based on circumstances regarding the permission for occupation of the road in this case.\\n\\nUpon examining the reasons for the lower court’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in such determination of the lower court, as alleged in the grounds for appeal, such as misapprehension of the legal requirements for a judgment based on circumstances or failure to conduct the necessary deliberation on balancing public and private interests.\\n\\nC. Whether the portion of Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act concerning “matters relating to the acquisition, management, or disposal of property” (hereinafter referred to as the “provision at issue”) is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) The principle of clarity, which is an expression of the rule of law, is required for all legislation restricting fundamental rights. However, requiring the principle of clarity to be rigorously realized in a mathematical sense is impossible or markedly difficult as a matter of legislative technique, so the use of abstract general clauses and indeterminate concepts is inevitable in legislative drafting. Therefore, even if a certain degree of ambiguity is inherent in the wording of a statute, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity if the meaning and content of the wording can be ascertained through the supplementary value judgment of a judge and such supplementary interpretation is not likely to vary according to the interpreter’s personal preference (see Constitutional Court en banc decision dated December 26, 2013 in 2012HEONBA375, etc.).\\n\\nEven though the provision at issue uses the general and abstract term “matters relating to the acquisition, management, or disposal of property,” the concepts of “property,” “acquisition,” “management,” and “disposal” are terms widely used in numerous statutes, and their meaning can in particular be understood through provisions of related statutes such as the Local Autonomy Act and the former Public Property Act, which regulate matters concerning the property of local governments. Whether an act concerning “the acquisition, management, or disposal of property” becomes the subject of a resident suit is ultimately an area in which the court must, considering the legislative purpose of the resident suit system, conduct a specific review and make a determination.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Supreme Court has held: “Where a permit for occupation of a road, etc. or other public property allowing a specific private person to use it exclusively is evaluated as being for realizing and utilizing its value of use regardless of the road’s original function and purpose, it shall be deemed to fall under the management or disposal of property subject to a resident suit” (see Supreme Court Decision dated May 27, 2016 in 2014DU8490). Thus, the Court has presented specific standards for determining the subject of a resident suit.\\n\\nTherefore, the provision at issue does not contravene the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, the disadvantage suffered by the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side as a result of the revocation of the permission for occupation of the road in this case is merely an effect arising from the combination of the fact that Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act establishes a resident suit system that seeks revocation or alteration of unlawful administrative dispositions or confirmation of the validity or nonexistence of an administrative disposition, and the fact that the permission for occupation of the road in this case was originally unlawful and should not have been granted from the outset. It cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional result caused by the provision at issue itself.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the argument in the grounds for appeal that the provision at issue contravenes the principle of clarity and is unconstitutional because it is contrary to the trust of the addressee of the disposition and causes a serious restriction on the relevant fundamental rights is rejected.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal arising from the participation by intervention shall be borne by the Intervenor on the Defendant’s side, and the remainder shall be borne by the Defendant, and the judgment is rendered as follows by the unanimous opinion of the Justices who reviewed the case."}

rendered on 2010DU28106 on 2011. 5. 26., among others).\\nb. (1) Article 13 of the former Public Property Act provides that no person other than the head of the relevant local government may construct buildings, structures such as ditches and bridges, or other permanent structures on public property, while its proviso permits a person other than the head of the relevant local government to construct buildings, structures such as ditches and bridges, or other permanent structures on public property “in cases prescribed by Presidential Decree where there is no hindrance to the use and enjoyment of the public property.” Pursuant thereto, Article 9 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Public Property and Goods Management Act (the version before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 25441 on 2014. 7. 7.) provides that permanent structures may be constructed on public property in cases such as “where structures are installed in the air, on the ground, or underground of the relevant public property within a scope that does not interfere with the current use and enjoyment of the public property by the local government” (subparagraph 9).\\nBy contrast, Article 38 of the former Road Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 10156 on 2010. 3. 22.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Road Act”) requires a person who seeks to newly construct, rebuild, alter, or remove structures, objects, or other facilities, or to occupy a road for other purposes, within a road zone, to obtain permission from the managing authority (paragraph 1), and delegates to Presidential Decree the necessary matters concerning the types of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupation permission may be granted (paragraph 2). Pursuant thereto, Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act (the version before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 24205 on 2012. 11. 27.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act”) provides for the types of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupation permission may be granted.\\n(2) Taking into comprehensive consideration the content and structure of Article 38 of the former Road Act, the subparagraphs of Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, and Attached Table 1-2 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, which sets forth structural standards for structures or facilities subject to road occupation permission, as well as the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, the provisions of the Road Act and its subordinate regulations are special provisions with respect to Article 13 of the former Public Property Act; therefore, with respect to occupation of roads, the above provisions of the Road Act and its subordinate regulations apply preferentially, and Article 13 of the former Public Property Act does not apply.\\nc. The lower court held that although road occupation permission may be granted for the installation of underground structures, Article 13 of the former Public Property Act applies to the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue, and the permanent structure to be installed underground of the road by the Defendant-Intervenor through the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue does not fall under the category of permanent structures whose construction on public property is permitted pursuant to the proviso of Article 13 of the former Public Property Act; therefore, the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue is unlawful in violation of Article 13 of the former Public Property Act.\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, such determination by the lower court contains an error of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, but as discussed below, insofar as the lower court’s conclusion that the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue is unlawful because it deviates from and abuses discretion is proper, there is no error that affected the judgment.\\n\\n6. Whether there is unlawfulness due to deviation from or abuse of discretion\\na. According to the record and the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n(1) On 2009. 6. 1., after purchasing 6,861.2 square meters of land in Special Planning Zone II of the ○○ Zone (△△△ Area) among the land in the area of Seocho-gu, Seoul (address omitted), which had then been designated as a district unit planning area, the Defendant-Intervenor applied to the Defendant for road occupation permission for the underground portion of Chamnari-gil, a local road owned by Seocho-gu, Seoul Metropolitan City, for the purpose of constructing an access passage to an underground parking lot beneath the road and using it as part of the site for a sanctuary to be built in the underground space during the construction of a new church building.\\n(2) In response, on 2010. 4. 6., the Defendant issued the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue, attaching a condition that 325 square meters of the southern basement level 1 of the new church building be donated to and accepted as a child-care center, and permitting the Defendant-Intervenor to occupy the underground portion of the road measuring “7 m in width × 154 m in length” out of the total width of 12 m, which includes the 4 m-wide portion of Chamnari-gil that, under the district unit plan, the Defendant-Intervenor was scheduled to widen and donate to the Defendant, from 2010. 4. 9. until 2019. 12. 31.\\n(3) After the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue, the Defendant-Intervenor installed in the basement of the new church building, including the underground portion of the road at issue, facilities such as the main sanctuary, video worship room, catechism study room, choir room, and broadcasting room from basement level 1 through basement level 5, and facilities such as parking lots, machine rooms, and storage rooms from basement level 6 through basement level 8.\\nb. The lower court found that occupation of the underground portion by the installation of underground structures such as a sanctuary, choir room, and broadcasting room is not only difficult to restore to its original condition, but also entails considerable risks and responsibilities in maintenance, management, and safety; that if such form of occupation is permitted, it becomes difficult in the future to refuse applications for road occupation permission with similar content, thereby raising the concern that the underground portion of the road will be used indiscriminately and create a danger to public safety; and that the underground portion of the road at issue will, as a practical matter, be used permanently and exclusively as part of the church building, making it impossible to respond flexibly and actively to changes in circumstances around the road; on such grounds, it determined that the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue violated the principles of proportionality and fairness, and rejected the Defendant’s argument that a broad planning discretion is recognized in granting road occupation permission within a special planning zone, just as in the formulation and decision of administrative plans.\\nc. In light of the provisions and relevant legal principles discussed above, and the record, the reasons stated in the lower court judgment do not contain an error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning deviation from or abuse of discretion or planning discretion.\\n\\n7. Remaining grounds of appeal\\na. Whether the legal principles concerning cancellation of beneficial administrative dispositions apply to revocation litigation\\nThe legal principle that the exercise of the right to revoke, etc. a beneficial administrative disposition is permitted only when there is a serious public interest need sufficient to justify the infringement of vested rights or a need to protect the interests of a third party (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 90NU9780 on 1991. 5. 14., among others) applies only when the administrative agency revokes or withdraws a beneficial administrative disposition ex officio, and does not apply in the case of litigious revocation. The lower court’s determination to the same effect contains no error of misunderstanding the legal principles limiting the revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\nb. Whether the case is subject to a judgment based on circumstances\\nThe lower court determined that a judgment based on circumstances prescribed in Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act should be recognized only in extremely exceptional cases where cancelling or modifying an unlawful administrative disposition would, contrary to expectations, be manifestly unsuitable for the public welfare; that the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue does not appear to involve a public-interest need to maintain its effect; and that it would be difficult to eliminate the unlawful state through the Defendant’s supplemental measures as the road management authority; on such grounds, the lower court determined that there is no justification for a judgment based on circumstances with respect to the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue.\\nReviewing the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in such determination, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as a misunderstanding of the legal requirements for a judgment based on circumstances or a failure to conduct the necessary deliberation on balancing public and private interests.\\nc. Whether the part of Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act concerning “matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposal of property” (hereinafter referred to as the “statutory provision at issue”) is unconstitutional\\n(1) The principle of clarity, which is an expression of the principle of a state governed by the rule of law, is required for all legislation restricting fundamental rights; however, it is practically impossible or markedly difficult to rigidly and arithmetically enforce the principle of clarity, and therefore the use of abstract general clauses and indefinite concepts is unavoidable in legislative technique. Accordingly, even if a certain degree of ambiguity is inherent in the wording of a statute, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity so long as the meaning and content of the wording can be ascertained through the supplementary value judgment of a judge and such supplementary interpretation is not likely to depend on the interpreter’s personal preference (see Constitutional Court en banc decision rendered on 2012HEONBA375 on 2013. 12. 26., among others).\\nEven though the statutory provision at issue uses the general and abstract terms “acquisition, management, and disposal of property,” the concepts of “property,” “acquisition,” “management,” and “disposal” are terms widely used in numerous statutes, and in particular, their meaning can be ascertained through the provisions of related statutes such as the Local Autonomy Act and the former Public Property Act, which regulate matters concerning the property of local governments; whether an act concerning the “acquisition, management, and disposal of property” becomes subject to a resident suit is ultimately an area in which the court must make a concrete determination after considering the legislative purpose of the resident suit system.\\nFurthermore, the Supreme Court has held that “where a permit for occupation allowing a specific private party to use public property, such as roads, or public-use property, exclusively, is evaluated as being intended to realize and utilize its use value irrespective of the road’s original function and purpose, it should be deemed to constitute management and disposal of property subject to a resident suit” (see Supreme Court judgment rendered on 2014DU8490 on 2016. 5. 27.), thereby presenting a concrete standard for determining the subject of a resident suit.\\nAccordingly, the statutory provision at issue does not violate the principle of clarity.\\n(2) Furthermore, the disadvantage suffered by the Defendant-Intervenor as a result of the cancellation of the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue is merely the effect arising from the combination of the fact that Article 17(2) subparagraph 2 of the Local Autonomy Act establishes a resident suit system that requests cancellation or modification of an unlawful administrative disposition or confirmation of the validity or existence of an administrative disposition, and the fact that the disposition granting permission for the occupation of the road at issue was originally unlawful and should not have been permitted in the first place; it cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional result caused by the statutory provision at issue itself.\\n(3) Therefore, the grounds of appeal asserting that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of clarity and, contrary to the trust of the addressee of the disposition, causes a serious restriction on the relevant fundamental rights and is therefore unconstitutional are rejected.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the portion of the appellate costs arising from the intervention in support of the Defendant shall be borne by the Defendant-Intervenor, and the remainder by the Defendant; and it is so adjudged, with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[2018DU104]": "The Grounds of Appeal are examined (statements in a supplementary brief on the grounds of appeal filed after the expiry of the filing period for the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only within the scope of supplementing the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Whether the disposition granting permission to occupy the road at issue is subject to a residents' suit\\n\\nA. Pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act and the latter sentence of Article 436(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, the court to which the case has been remanded or transferred is bound by the factual and legal determinations that the court of final appeal used as grounds for reversal. Accordingly, in line with the binding force of the Supreme Court Decision 2014DU8490, rendered on 2016. 5. 27., reversing and remanding, there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in the lower court's misunderstanding of the legal nature of the road occupation permit in this case and the legal principles concerning the subject of a residents' suit, in its determination proceeding to the merits on the premise that the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case falls under a matter concerning 'the management and disposition of property' under Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nB. Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act provides only that a resident who has requested an audit concerning 'the acquisition, management, and disposition of property' may bring an action against the head of the relevant local government with respect to an unlawful act or omission to perform duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested; it does not limit the subject matter of a residents' suit to matters concerning the 'acquisition, management, and disposition of property that caused damage to local finances.' Accordingly, the grounds of appeal asserting that the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case is not subject to a residents' suit because it did not cause damage to local finances are contrary to the clear wording of the above provision of the Local Autonomy Act governing the subject of a residents' suit, and are therefore not accepted.\\n\\n2. Whether the filing period has expired\\n\\nThe lower court determined that the Plaintiffs filed a resident audit request on 2011. 12. 7., within 2 years from 2010. 4. 9., when the Defendant rendered the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case, and therefore complied with the period for a resident audit request under Article 16(2) of the Local Autonomy Act; that they filed the residents' suit in this case on 2012. 8. 29., within 90 days from 2012. 6. 1., when the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City notified the audit results, and therefore complied with the filing period for a residents' suit under Article 17(4) of the Local Autonomy Act; and that, with respect to a resident audit request and a residents' suit premised thereon, the filing period for an ordinary action for revocation prescribed in Article 20(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act does not apply.\\n\\nSuch determination of the lower court is proper as it follows the provisions of the relevant statutes, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the filing periods for resident audit requests and residents' suits.\\n\\n3. Whether the action has lost its benefit because non-contestability has arisen with respect to the disposition granting building permission\\n\\nA. Once a judgment canceling an administrative disposition as unlawful becomes final and conclusive, the administrative agency has the duty, in accordance with the binding force of the judgment of cancellation, either to make the disposition again in a state excluding the grounds of illegality confirmed in that judgment or to take measures to remove the unlawful result (see Article 30 of the Administrative Litigation Act, Supreme Court Decision 2013DU27517, rendered on 2015. 10. 29., etc.). Moreover, if an administrative disposition becomes final and conclusive due to the lapse of the period for objection, such finality merely means that the person whose legal interest has been infringed by the disposition may no longer contest the validity of the disposition or adjudication; it does not further mean that res judicata, as in a judgment, is recognized, so that the factual relations or legal determinations underlying the disposition are not fixed and the parties or the court become bound thereby, making contradictory assertions or determinations impossible (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DU11288, rendered on 2004. 7. 8., etc.).\\n\\nB. If a judgment canceling the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case becomes final and conclusive in this residents' suit, the Defendant, pursuant to the binding force of the judgment of cancellation, can, as part of measures to remove the unlawful result, order the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side to discontinue occupation of the road in this case and restore it to its original state pursuant to Articles 73, 96, and 100, etc. of the Road Act, and, if such order is not complied with, take measures such as administrative compulsory execution or imposition of an enforcement fine, thereby making it possible to remove the unlawful condition resulting from the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case.\\n\\nIn addition, although the building permission in this case will not be canceled by the direct effect of the judgment of cancellation or lose its validity, the building permission in this case, which was granted on the premise that the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case validly existed, will lose part of its legal and factual basis; accordingly, the Defendant has the duty, within the scope of compliance with the legal principles concerning the restriction on ex officio revocation of beneficial administrative acts, to take measures such as ex officio cancellation or modification of part thereof under certain requirements. Therefore, even if the Plaintiffs cannot directly contest the validity of the building permission in this case in the residents' suit in this case, that cannot serve as a basis for denying the benefit of action seeking cancellation of the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case.\\n\\nC. In the same vein, the lower court determined that even if, in the residents' suit in this case, a judgment dismissing the claim for cancellation of the building permission in this case becomes final and conclusive, and thus the Plaintiffs can no longer directly contest the validity of the building permission in this case, the benefit of action seeking cancellation of the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case does not thereby disappear. Such determination of the lower court is based on the legal principles discussed above, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the benefit of action and the non-contestability of administrative dispositions.\\n\\n4. Standard for reviewing the unlawfulness of a disposition in a residents' suit\\n\\nA. Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act provides that if the handling of affairs within the authority of a local government and its head is deemed to violate statutes or seriously harm the public interest, residents above a certain number of the relevant local government may request an audit; and Article 17(1) provides that a resident who has requested an audit concerning matters of expenditure of public funds, matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposition of property, matters concerning the conclusion or performance of sales, lease, or outsourcing contracts or other contracts to which the relevant local government is a party, or matters concerning the neglect of levying and collecting public funds such as local taxes, usage fees, charges, and fines for negligence, may bring an action against the head of the relevant local government 'with respect to an unlawful act or omission to perform duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested.'\\n\\nFurther, Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act provides, as types of actions that residents may bring pursuant to paragraph (1), 'an action seeking cancellation or modification of the relevant act, which is an administrative disposition, or seeking a declaration as to whether the act is effective or whether it exists,' and Article 17(17) provides that, with respect to actions under paragraph (1), the Administrative Litigation Act shall apply except as otherwise provided in the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nB. Considering the content and structure of these relevant provisions, together with the legislative purpose and legal nature of the residents' suit system as discussed below, the unlawfulness of the disposition challenged in a residents' suit must be determined, as in an appeal-type suit under the Administrative Litigation Act, by whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, including the Constitution, statutes, subordinate statutory regulations, and general principles of law; it is not to be determined solely on the basis of whether the disposition caused loss to the local government's finances.\\n\\n(1) The Local Autonomy Act merely enumerates the subject matters of residents' suits in Article 17(1) and does not separately prescribe the standard for reviewing the unlawfulness of a disposition in a residents' suit; nor does Article 17(2) item 2 require, as a condition for seeking cancellation or modification of an administrative disposition, that the disposition caused loss to the local government's finances.\\n\\n(2) The residents' suit was introduced by the Local Autonomy Act as amended by Act No. 7362 on 2005. 1. 27., as a system intended to increase accountability in local administration by expanding residents' participation, through which residents of a local government request the court to correct that local government's unlawful 'acquisition, management, and disposition of property,' etc. It corresponds to a popular action under the Administrative Litigation Act. A popular action means \"an action brought by a national or public entity's organ, when it has committed an act contrary to statutes, in order to seek correction thereof, without direct relation to one's own legal interest,\" and may be brought \"only by a person prescribed by statute in cases prescribed by statute\" (Article 3(3) and Article 45 of the Administrative Litigation Act), and is therefore distinguished from an appeal-type suit that may be brought by a person who has a legal interest in seeking cancellation of the disposition (Article 3(1) and Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act).\\n\\nThus, the residents' suit was introduced for the purpose of specially recognizing the legal standing to bring an action seeking cancellation, etc. of unlawful 'acquisition, management, and disposition of property' by a local government, by residents above a certain number, on the premise that they undergo the procedure of requesting an audit under Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act, in order to remedy the problem that ordinary residents of a local government cannot bring an appeal-type suit seeking cancellation of the local government's unlawful 'acquisition, management, and disposition of property,' etc. because they are not recognized as having a legal interest in seeking such cancellation. There is no basis to find that the legislative intent was to restrict the standard for merits review in a residents' suit to whether it caused loss to the local government's finances.\\n\\n(3) As noted above, Article 17(17) of the Local Autonomy Act provides that, with respect to residents' suits, the Administrative Litigation Act shall apply except as specially provided in the Local Autonomy Act, and Article 46(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that, in an action seeking cancellation of a disposition as a popular action, the provisions concerning actions for revocation shall apply mutatis mutandis insofar as they are not contrary to its nature. Therefore, unless otherwise provided in the Local Autonomy Act regarding the subject of the residents' suit, the filing period, standing of the plaintiff, etc., residents' suits and actions for revocation are not to be treated differently; accordingly, in a residents' suit seeking cancellation of an administrative disposition, the review of unlawfulness should, absent special circumstances, be conducted in the same manner as the review of unlawfulness in an action for revocation.\\n\\n(4) It is the Supreme Court's established view that the subject matter of an action for revocation is the 'unlawfulness of the disposition in general' (see Supreme Court Decision 89NU5386, rendered on 1990. 3. 23.; Supreme Court Decision 92NU1728, rendered on 1994. 3. 8.; etc.). In an action for revocation, the court must determine the unlawfulness of the disposition by whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, including the Constitution, statutes, subordinate statutory regulations, and general principles of law, and the same applies in a residents' suit.\\n\\nC. In the same vein, the lower court determined that the unlawfulness of a disposition in a residents' suit should be construed in the same manner as the 'unlawfulness of the disposition in general' in an appeal-type suit, and that the relevant disposition must be canceled not only when it violates explicit fiscal and accounting-related statutes, but also when it is unlawful because it exceeds or abuses discretionary power by violating general principles of law such as the principles of proportionality, equality, and protection of trust. There is no error in such determination of the lower court, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the standard for reviewing the unlawfulness of a disposition in a residents' suit.\\n\\n5. Whether Article 13 of the former Act on the Management of Public Property and Goods (as amended by Act No. 10006 on 2010. 2. 4., hereinafter the 'former Public Property Act') was violated\\n\\nA. (1) The former Public Property Act was enacted for the purpose of protecting public property and goods and promoting the appropriateness of their acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposition (Article 1), and provides that, with respect to the acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposition of public property and goods, the provisions of the former Public Property Act shall apply except where special provisions exist in other statutes (Article 2).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Road Act was enacted for the purpose of contributing to the development of transportation and the enhancement of public welfare by establishing plans concerning roads, designating or recognizing routes, management, facility standards, preservation, and costs, in order to improve the road network and manage roads properly (Article 1), and it comprehensively and integrally regulates roads, including not only roads falling under administrative property and general property under the State Property Act and the Local Finance Act, but also cases in which the road site is privately owned.\\n\\n(2) Considering the content and structure of the above relevant provisions, together with the legislative purposes of the two statutes, the Act on the Management of Public Property and Goods has the nature of a general law governing matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposition of public property and goods in general, whereas the Road Act, in light of the functional characteristics of roads as facilities provided for public traffic, is a statute that imposes special public-law regulation regardless of ownership, and must therefore be regarded as a special law that applies in preference to the Act on the Management of Public Property and Goods when a road constitutes public property (see Supreme Court Decision 80NU618, rendered on 1981. 11. 10.; Supreme Court Decision 2010DU28106, rendered on 2011. 5. 26.; etc.).\\n\\nB. (1) Article 13 of the former Public Property Act provides that no person other than the head of the relevant local government may construct buildings, structures such as ditches and bridges, or other permanent installations on public property, while its proviso permits persons other than the head of the relevant local government to construct buildings, structures such as ditches and bridges, or other permanent installations on public property in cases prescribed by Presidential Decree as cases where there is no impediment to the use and enjoyment of public property. Pursuant to that delegation, Article 9 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Management of Public Property and Goods (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 25441 on 2014. 7. 7.) provides that permanent installations may be constructed on public property in cases such as 'where structures are installed above ground, on the surface, or underground of the relevant public property within a scope that does not interfere with the current use and enjoyment of the public property by the local government' (item 9).\\n\\nBy contrast, Article 38 of the former Road Act (as amended by Act No. 10156 on 2010. 3. 22.; hereinafter the 'former Road Act') provides that a person who intends to newly construct, rebuild, alter, or remove structures, objects, or other facilities, or occupy a road for any other purpose within a road zone, must obtain permission from the managing authority (paragraph (1)), and delegates to Presidential Decree the matters necessary concerning the types, etc. of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupation permission may be granted (paragraph (2)). Pursuant to that delegation, Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 24205 on 2012. 11. 27.; hereinafter the 'former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act') provides for the types of structures, objects, and other facilities for which road occupation permission may be granted.\\n\\n(2) Considering the content and structure of Article 38 of the former Road Act, each item of Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, and [Attached Table 1-2] of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act setting forth the structural standards for structures or facilities subject to road occupation permission, together with the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, the Road Act provisions are special provisions concerning Article 13 of the former Public Property Act; therefore, with respect to occupation of roads, the above provisions of the Road Act shall apply preferentially and Article 13 of the former Public Property Act shall not apply.\\n\\nC. The lower court held that, although a road occupation permit may be granted for the installation of an underground structure, Article 13 of the former Public Property Act applies to the road occupation permit in this case, and the permanent structure underground the road that the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side intends to install through the road occupation permit in this case does not fall under a permanent installation permitted to be constructed on public property under the proviso to Article 13 of the former Public Property Act; accordingly, the road occupation permit in this case is unlawful because it violates Article 13 of the former Public Property Act.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles discussed above, although there is an error in such determination of the lower court in that it misunderstood the legal principles concerning the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, as discussed below, there is no error affecting the judgment insofar as the lower court's conclusion, as discussed below, that the road occupation permit in this case is unlawful because it exceeds or abuses discretionary power is upheld as proper.\\n\\n6. Whether there is unlawfulness in that discretion was exceeded or abused\\n\\nA. According to the record and the reasons of the lower court judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\n(1) On 2009. 6. 1., after purchasing 6,861.2 square meters of land in Special Planning Zone II of the OO Zone (TTT Area) in Seocho-gu, Seoul, which had previously been designated as a district unit planning zone, the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side applied to the Defendant for road occupation permission for the underground portion of Chamnari-gil, a neighborhood road owned by Seocho-gu, Seoul, for the purpose of constructing an access passage for an underground parking lot and using it as part of the site for worship facilities to be constructed underground in the course of rebuilding a church building.\\n\\n(2) In response, on 2010. 4. 6., the Defendant rendered the disposition granting permission to occupy the road in this case, attaching a condition that 325 square meters on the first basement level on the south side of the newly built church building be donated and transferred as a daycare center, permitting the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side to occupy the underground portion of a road measuring '7 m in width × 154 m in length' out of the total width of 12 m, which includes the 4 m-wide portion that, under the district unit plan, the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side was scheduled to widen and donate and transfer to the Defendant, from 2010. 4. 9. to 2019. 12. 31.\\n\\n(3) After the road occupation permit in this case, the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side installed facilities such as the main sanctuary (worship hall), video worship room, catechism study room, choir room, and broadcasting room from the first basement level to the eighth basement level in the underground of the newly built church building, including the underground portion of the road in this case, and facilities such as parking lots, machine rooms, and storage rooms from the sixth basement level to the eighth basement level.\\n\\nB. The lower court determined that occupying the underground through the installation of underground structures such as a worship hall, choir room, and broadcasting room is not easy to restore to the original state, and entails considerable risks and responsibilities in maintenance, management, and safety; that if such type of occupation is permitted, it will be difficult to refuse future applications for road occupation permission of a similar nature, leading to indiscriminate use of the underground portion of roads and the risk of harm to public safety; and that, as the underground portion of the road in this case is actually used permanently and exclusively as part of the church building, flexible and active responses to changes in conditions around the road become impossible, and for such reasons, the road occupation permit in this case violated the principle of proportionality and fairness. The lower court rejected the Defendant's argument that broad planning discretion is recognized for road occupation permits within a special planning zone, just as in the drafting and determination of administrative plans.\\n\\nC. In light of the provisions and relevant legal principles discussed above, as well as the record, the reasons of the lower court judgment contain no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning excess or abuse of discretion or planning discretion.\\n\\n7. Other grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Whether the legal principles concerning cancellation of beneficial administrative dispositions apply to an action for revocation\\n\\nThe legal principle that the exercise of cancellation rights, etc. with respect to a beneficial administrative disposition may be permitted only when there is a substantial public interest necessity sufficient to justify infringement of vested rights, or a necessity to protect the interests of a third party (see Supreme Court Decision 90NU9780, rendered on 1991. 5. 14., etc.), applies only when the disposition authority ex officio cancels or withdraws a beneficial administrative disposition; it does not apply in the case of contested revocation. The lower court's determination to the same effect contains no error in misunderstanding the legal principles restricting cancellation and withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\n\\nB. Whether it is subject to a judgment of circumstances\\n\\nThe lower court determined that a judgment of circumstances prescribed in Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act should be recognized only extremely exceptionally, where canceling or modifying an unlawful administrative disposition would instead be manifestly inconsistent with the public welfare; that the road occupation permit in this case does not appear to have a public interest necessity to sustain its effectiveness, and that it would also be difficult to eliminate its unlawful condition through supplementary measures by the Defendant, who is the road managing authority; and on these grounds, the lower court held that no justification exists for rendering a judgment of circumstances regarding the road occupation permit in this case.\\n\\nReviewing the reasons of the lower court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in such determination of the lower court, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for a judgment of circumstances or failing to conduct the necessary review regarding the balancing of public and private interests.\\n\\nC. Whether the provision of Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act concerning 'matters relating to the acquisition, management, and disposition of property' (hereinafter the 'statutory provision at issue') is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) The principle of clarity, as an expression of the rule-of-law principle, is required for all legislation restricting fundamental rights; however, requiring the principle of clarity to be realized with arithmetical rigor is impossible or extremely difficult as a matter of legislative technique, and the use of abstract general clauses and indeterminate concepts is inevitable as a matter of legislative technique. Accordingly, even if a certain degree of ambiguity is inherent in the wording of a statute, if the meaning of the wording can be ascertained through supplementary value judgments by judges, and such supplementary interpretation is not likely to depend on the individual preferences of the interpreter, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity (see Constitutional Court en banc Decision 2012HEONBA375, rendered on 2013. 12. 26., etc.).\\n\\nEven though the statutory provision at issue uses the general and abstract terms 'the acquisition, management, and disposition of property,' the concepts of 'property,' 'acquisition,' 'management,' and 'disposition' are terms widely used in numerous statutes; in particular, their meaning can be ascertained through the provisions of the Local Autonomy Act and related statutes such as the former Public Property Act, which regulate matters concerning the property of local governments, and whether an act concerning the 'acquisition, management, and disposition of property' is subject to a residents' suit is ultimately an area that the court must examine and determine in detail, considering the legislative purpose of the residents' suit system.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Supreme Court has held that \"where a road occupation permit, etc. that allows a specific private person to use a public thing or public facility exclusively is assessed as being for realizing and utilizing its use value unrelated to the road's original function and purpose, it shall be regarded as constituting the management and disposition of property subject to a residents' suit\" (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DU8490, rendered on 2016. 5. 27.). Thus, the Supreme Court has presented specific criteria for determining the subject matter of a residents' suit.\\n\\nTherefore, the statutory provision at issue does not contravene the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, the disadvantage suffered by the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side as a result of the cancellation of the road occupation permit in this case is merely an effect arising from the combined operation of the fact that Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act establishes a residents' suit system that seeks cancellation or modification of an unlawful administrative disposition or a declaration as to whether an administrative disposition is effective or exists, and the fact that the road occupation permit in this case was originally unlawful and should not have been granted in the first place; it cannot be deemed a constitutionally impermissible result caused by the statutory provision at issue itself.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the grounds of appeal asserting that the statutory provision at issue violates the principle of clarity and is unconstitutional because it contravenes the trust of the addressee of the disposition and causes a serious restriction on the relevant fundamental rights are not accepted.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the portion of the appeal costs arising from the intervention by the co-litigant intervenor on the Defendant's side shall be borne by that co-litigant intervenor, and the remainder by the Defendant, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2018DU104]": "The grounds of appeal are to be determined (the statements in the supplemental statement of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal are to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Whether the road occupancy permit disposition in this case is subject to a resident suit\\n\\nA. According to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act and the latter sentence of Article 436(2) of the Civil Procedure Act, the court to which a case has been remanded or transferred is bound by the factual and legal determinations that the Supreme Court took as grounds for reversal. Therefore, in accordance with the binding force of the reversed and remanded judgment rendered by the Supreme Court on 2014DU8490 decided on May 27, 2016, there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in the judgment of the court below, which proceeded to the merits on the premise that the road occupancy permit disposition in this case falls under ‘matters concerning the management or disposition of property’ under Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act, inasmuch as it misapprehended the legal nature of the road occupancy permit in this case and the legal principles concerning the subject of a resident suit.\\n\\nB. Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act provides only that a resident who has requested an audit concerning ‘matters concerning the acquisition, management, or disposition of property’ may file a lawsuit against the head of the relevant local government with respect to unlawful acts or failure to perform duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested; it does not limit the subject matter of a resident suit to matters concerning the ‘acquisition, management, or disposition of property that caused damage to local finances.’ Accordingly, the ground of appeal asserting that the road occupancy permit disposition in this case is not subject to a resident suit because it did not cause any damage to local finances is contrary to the clear wording of the above provision of the Local Autonomy Act prescribing the subject of a resident suit, and is therefore not accepted.\\n\\n2. Whether the period for filing suit has expired\\n\\nThe court below determined that the Plaintiffs filed a resident audit request on December 7, 2011, within 2 years from April 9, 2010, when the Defendant issued the road occupancy permit disposition in this case, and thus complied with the period for a resident audit request under Article 16(2) of the Local Autonomy Act; that the Plaintiffs filed the resident suit in this case on August 29, 2012, within 90 days from June 1, 2012, when the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government notified the audit results, and thus complied with the period for filing a resident suit under Article 17(4) of the Local Autonomy Act; and that, with respect to a resident audit request and a resident suit based thereon, the period for filing an ordinary cancellation suit prescribed in Article 20(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act does not apply.\\n\\nSuch determination by the court below is proper as it accords with the provisions of the relevant statutes, and there is no error therein, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the period for filing a resident audit request and a resident suit, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Whether the benefit of suit has ceased because unchallengeability arose with respect to the building permit disposition\\n\\nA. Once a judgment annulling an administrative disposition as unlawful becomes final and conclusive, the administrative agency has the duty, in accordance with the binding force of the cancellation judgment, to make a new disposition excluding the unlawful cause identified in that judgment, or to take measures removing the unlawful consequences (see Article 30 of the Administrative Litigation Act and Supreme Court Decision 2013DU27517 decided on October 29, 2015, among others). And when an administrative disposition becomes final and conclusive upon the lapse of the period for objection, such finality merely means that a person whose legal interest has been infringed by the disposition can no longer contest the validity of that disposition or adjudication; it does not further mean that res judicata, as in the case of a judgment, is recognized, so that the factual relations or legal determinations forming the basis of the disposition become final and conclusive, and the parties or the court are bound thereby and cannot make inconsistent assertions or determinations (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DU11288 decided on July 8, 2004, among others).\\n\\nB. If a judgment annulling the road occupancy permit in this case becomes final and conclusive in this resident suit, the Defendant may, in accordance with the binding force of the cancellation judgment, order the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant to suspend the occupancy of the road in this case and restore the original condition pursuant to Articles 73, 96, and 100 of the Road Act, as part of measures to remove the unlawful consequences, and if that order is not complied with, may take measures such as administrative execution or imposition of an enforcement fine, thereby making it possible to remove the unlawful state arising from the road occupancy permit in this case.\\n\\nIn addition, although the building permit in this case is not annulled or rendered void by the direct effect of the cancellation judgment, the building permit in this case, which was granted on the premise that the road occupancy permit in this case validly exists, loses part of its legal and factual basis; accordingly, within the scope of complying with the legal principles concerning the limitations on ex officio cancellation of beneficial administrative acts, the Defendant has the duty, under certain requirements, to take measures such as canceling or modifying part of it ex officio. Therefore, even if the Plaintiffs cannot directly contest the validity of the building permit in this resident suit, that cannot serve as grounds for denying the benefit of suit seeking cancellation of the road occupancy permit in this case.\\n\\nC. On the same purport, the court below determined that even if, in this resident suit, the portion of the claim seeking cancellation of the building permit in this case was dismissed and became final and conclusive, so that the Plaintiffs could no longer directly contest the validity of the building permit in this case, the benefit of suit seeking cancellation of the road occupancy permit in this case would not thereby also be extinguished. Such determination by the court below is based on the legal principles stated above, and there is no error therein, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the benefit of suit or the unchallengeability of administrative dispositions, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Standard for reviewing illegality of a disposition in a resident suit\\n\\nA. Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act provides that if the handling of affairs falling within the authority of a local government and its head is “deemed to violate statutes or to seriously harm the public interest,” residents in a prescribed number or more of that local government may request an audit; Article 17(1) provides that a resident who has requested an audit concerning matters relating to the expenditure of public funds, matters concerning the acquisition, management, or disposition of property, matters concerning the conclusion or performance of contracts of sale, lease, or construction work, or other contracts to which the relevant local government is a party, or matters concerning the failure to levy or collect public charges such as local taxes, user fees, charges, or penalties, may file a lawsuit against the head of the relevant local government “with respect to unlawful acts or failure to perform duties related to the matters for which the audit was requested.”\\n\\nFurthermore, Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act provides, as a type of lawsuit that a resident may file under paragraph 1, “a lawsuit seeking the revocation or modification of the relevant act, which is an administrative disposition, or seeking a determination as to whether such act is valid or exists,” and Article 17(17) provides that, with respect to lawsuits under paragraph 1, the Administrative Litigation Act shall apply except as otherwise provided in the Local Autonomy Act.\\n\\nB. When the content and structure of these relevant provisions are combined with the legislative purpose and legal nature of the resident suit system, as seen below, the illegality of a disposition challenged in a resident suit must, like in an appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act, be determined on the basis of whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, such as the Constitution, statutes, subordinate statutes, and the general principles of law, and not solely on the basis of whether the disposition caused a loss to the local government’s finances.\\n\\n(1) The Local Autonomy Act merely enumerates, in Article 17(1), the subjects of a resident suit, and does not separately prescribe a standard for reviewing the illegality of a disposition in a resident suit; nor does Article 17(2) item 2 require, as a prerequisite for seeking the revocation or modification of an administrative disposition, that the disposition caused a loss to local government finances.\\n\\n(2) A resident suit was introduced in the Local Autonomy Act as amended by Act No. 7362 on January 27, 2005, as a system intended to enhance accountability in local administration by expanding resident participation, through residents of a local government petitioning a court to rectify the local government’s unlawful “acquisition, management, or disposition of property,” etc. It corresponds to a public-interest action under the Administrative Litigation Act.
