Since a public-interest action is “a lawsuit brought by a state or public organization’s organ to seek rectification when it has committed an act in violation of statutes, irrespective of its own legal interest,” and may be brought “only by a person prescribed by statute in cases prescribed by statute” (Article 3 item 3 and Article 45 of the Administrative Litigation Act), it is distinguished from an appeal litigation, which may be brought by a person having a legal interest in seeking revocation of a disposition (Article 3 item 1 and Article 12 of the Administrative Litigation Act).\\n\\nIn this way, the resident suit was introduced for the purpose of specially recognizing the legal status of allowing residents, subject to the premise that a prescribed number or more of residents undergo the procedure of requesting an audit under Article 16 of the Local Autonomy Act, to file a lawsuit seeking revocation, etc. of a disposition, in order to supplement the problem that ordinary residents of a local government cannot file an appeal litigation seeking revocation of the local government’s unlawful “acquisition, management, or disposition of property,” etc., because legal interest in seeking such revocation is not recognized. There is no basis to find that a legislative intent to limit the standard for merits review in a resident suit to whether it caused a loss to local government finances is reflected therein.\\n\\n(3) As noted above, Article 17(17) of the Local Autonomy Act provides that, with respect to resident suits, the Administrative Litigation Act shall apply except as otherwise specially provided in the Local Autonomy Act, and Article 46(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that, for lawsuits seeking revocation of a disposition as a public-interest action, the provisions concerning cancellation suits shall apply mutatis mutandis insofar as they do not run contrary to its nature. Therefore, unless the Local Autonomy Act provides otherwise regarding the subject of a resident suit, the period for filing suit, standing to sue, etc., a resident suit should not be treated differently from a cancellation suit; accordingly, in a resident suit seeking revocation of an administrative disposition, the review of illegality should, absent special circumstances, be conducted in the same manner as the review of illegality in a cancellation suit.\\n\\n(4) It is the Supreme Court’s established view that the subject matter of a cancellation suit is “the general illegality of the disposition” (see Supreme Court Decision 89NU5386 decided on March 23, 1990, Supreme Court Decision 92NU1728 decided on March 8, 1994, among others). In a cancellation suit, the court must determine the illegality of the disposition on the basis of whether it violates all legal norms constituting the objective legal order, such as the Constitution, statutes, subordinate statutes, and the general principles of law; the same applies to a resident suit.\\n\\nC. On the same purport, the court below determined that, in a resident suit, the illegality of a disposition must be interpreted in the same way as the “general illegality of the disposition” in an appeal litigation, and that the disposition must be revoked not only when it violates explicit fiscal and accounting statutes, but also when it is unlawful because it deviated from or abused discretionary power by violating general principles of law such as the principles of proportionality, equality, and protection of trust. There is no error in such determination by the court below, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the standard for reviewing the illegality of a disposition in a resident suit, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n5. Whether Article 13 of the former Public Property and Goods Management Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 10006 on February 4, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Public Property Act”) was violated\\n\\nA. (1) The former Public Property Act was enacted for the purpose of protecting public property and goods and promoting the appropriateness of their acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposition (Article 1), and provides that, with respect to the acquisition, maintenance, preservation, operation, and disposition of public property and goods, the provisions of the former Public Property Act shall apply except where other statutes contain special provisions (Article 2).\\n\\nMeanwhile, the Road Act was enacted for the purpose of contributing to the development of transportation and the enhancement of public welfare by establishing plans concerning roads, designating or recognizing routes, management, facility standards, preservation, and costs for the maintenance of a road network and proper road management (Article 1), and it comprehensively regulates roads, including not only roads falling under state property and administrative or general property under the Local Finance Act, but also cases where the road site belongs to private ownership.\\n\\n(2) When the content and structure of the above relevant provisions and the legislative purpose of both Acts are comprehensively considered, the Public Property and Goods Management Act has the character of a general law governing matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposition of public property and goods in general, whereas the Road Act, taking into account the functional characteristics of roads as facilities provided for the traffic of the general public, is a statute that imposes special public-law regulation regardless of ownership, and when a road constitutes public property, it should be regarded as a special law that applies in preference to the Public Property and Goods Management Act (see Supreme Court Decision 80NU618 decided on November 10, 1981, Supreme Court Decision 2010DU28106 decided on May 26, 2011, among others).\\n\\nB. (1) Article 13 of the former Public Property Act provides that no person other than the head of the relevant local government may erect buildings, structures such as ditches or bridges, or other permanent facilities on public property; however, its proviso permits a person other than the head of the relevant local government to erect buildings, structures such as ditches or bridges, or other permanent facilities on public property in cases prescribed by Presidential Decree where there is no hindrance to the use and enjoyment of the public property. Article 9 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Public Property and Goods Management Act (the version before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 25441 on July 7, 2014), enacted pursuant thereto, provides that permanent facilities may be erected on public property in cases such as “where a structure is installed above, on, or below the ground of the relevant public property within the extent that it does not interfere with the present use and enjoyment of the public property by the local government” (item 9).\\n\\nOn the other hand, Article 38 of the former Road Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 10156 on March 22, 2010; hereinafter referred to as the “former Road Act”) provides that a person who intends to newly install, reconstruct, alter, or remove a structure, object, or other facility in a road area, or to occupy a road for any other purpose, must obtain permission from the managing authority (paragraph 1), and delegates to Presidential Decree matters necessary concerning the kinds of structures, objects, and other facilities for which a road occupancy permit may be granted (paragraph 2). Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act (the version before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 24205 on November 27, 2012; hereinafter referred to as the “former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act”) provides for the kinds of structures, objects, and other facilities for which a road occupancy permit may be granted.\\n\\n(2) When the content and structure of Article 38 of the former Road Act, the items of Article 28(5) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, and [Attached Table 1-2] of the former Enforcement Decree of the Road Act, which prescribes the structural standards for structures or facilities subject to a road occupancy permit, together with the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, are comprehensively considered, the Road Act regulations are special provisions with respect to Article 13 of the former Public Property Act. Therefore, with respect to the occupancy of roads, the above Road Act regulations apply preferentially, and Article 13 of the former Public Property Act does not apply.\\n\\nC. The court below determined that, although a road occupancy permit may be granted for the installation of underground structures, Article 13 of the former Public Property Act applies to the road occupancy permit in this case, and the permanent facilities to be installed underground on the road by the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant pursuant to that permit do not fall within the category of permanent facilities whose erection on public property is permitted under the proviso to Article 13 of the former Public Property Act; accordingly, it held that the road occupancy permit in this case is unlawful because it violates Article 13 of the former Public Property Act.\\n\\nIn light of the legal principles stated above, although there is an error in such determination by the court below in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning the relationship between the Public Property Act and the Road Act, as seen below, insofar as the court below’s conclusion that the road occupancy permit in this case is unlawful because it abused or deviated from discretionary power is proper, there is no error that affected the judgment.\\n\\n6. Whether there is unlawfulness due to deviation from or abuse of discretionary power\\n\\nA. According to the record and the reasons of the court below’s judgment, the following facts may be found.\\n\\n(1) On June 1, 2009, the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant purchased 6,861.2 square meters of land in Special Planning Zone II of the ○○ District (△△△ Area) among the land in the Seocho-gu, Seoul (address omitted) area, which had been designated as a district unit planning zone at the time, and, in the course of constructing a new church building, applied to the Defendant for a road occupancy permit for the underground portion of Chamnari-gil, a local road owned by Seocho-gu, Seoul Metropolitan Government, for the purpose of constructing an access passage to the underground parking lot beneath the road and using it as part of the site for a chapel to be constructed in the underground space.\\n\\n(2) Accordingly, on April 6, 2010, the Defendant issued the road occupancy permit disposition in this case, with a condition that the 325 square meters of the south side, basement level 1 of the new church building be donated and vested in the local government for use as a daycare center, permitting the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant to occupy, from April 9, 2010 to December 31, 2019, the underground portion of the road having a total width of 12 meters, which includes the 4-meter-wide portion of Chamnari-gil that the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant was scheduled under the district unit plan to widen and donate and vest in the Defendant, namely, the road portion of “7 meters in width × 154 meters in length” (hereinafter referred to as the “road in this case”).\\n\\n(3) After the road occupancy permit in this case, the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant installed facilities such as the main sanctuary (worship hall), video worship room, doctrinal study room, choir room, and broadcasting room on basement levels 1 through 5 of the newly built church building, including the underground portion of the road in this case, and installed facilities such as parking lots, machine rooms, and storage rooms on basement levels 6 through 8.\\n\\nB. The court below, taking into account circumstances such as that occupancy of the underground space through the installation of underground structures such as a chapel, choir room, and broadcasting room is not easily restored to the original condition and entails considerable risks and responsibilities in maintenance, management, and safety, and that if such an occupancy were permitted it would be difficult in the future to refuse similar applications for road occupancy permits, thereby creating a concern that the underground portion of the road would be used indiscriminately and harm public safety would arise; and that the underground portion of the road in this case would be used de facto permanently and exclusively as part of the church building, making it impossible to respond flexibly and proactively to changes in the circumstances around the road, determined that the road occupancy permit in this case violated the principle of proportionality and fairness, and rejected the Defendant’s argument that, for a road occupancy permit within a special planning zone, broad planning discretion is recognized just as in the formulation and determination of an administrative plan.\\n\\nC. In light of the provisions and relevant legal principles discussed above and the record, there is no error in the court below’s above determination, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning deviation from or abuse of discretionary power or planning discretion, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n7. Remaining grounds of appeal\\n\\nA. Whether the legal principles concerning revocation of a beneficial administrative disposition apply to a cancellation suit\\n\\nThe legal principle that the exercise of the power to revoke, etc. a beneficial administrative disposition may be permitted only when there exists a serious public interest necessity sufficient to justify infringement of vested rights or a necessity to protect the interests of a third party (see Supreme Court Decision 90NU9780 decided on May 14, 1991, among others) applies only when the administrative agency revokes or withdraws a beneficial administrative disposition ex officio, and does not apply to revocation in litigation. There is no error in the court below’s determination to the same effect, such as misapprehension of the legal principles limiting revocation or withdrawal of beneficial administrative dispositions.\\n\\nB. Whether it is subject to an adjudication of circumstances\\n\\nThe court below determined that the adjudication of circumstances prescribed in Article 28(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act should be recognized only exceptionally, where revoking or modifying an unlawful administrative disposition would, conversely, be markedly contrary to the public welfare; and that, since the road occupancy permit in this case does not appear to have a public interest necessity for maintaining its effect, and it would also be difficult to remedy the unlawful state through supplementary measures by the Defendant, who is the road managing authority, there is no justification for rendering an adjudication of circumstances with respect to the road occupancy permit in this case.\\n\\nReviewing the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles, there is no error in such determination by the court below, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the requirements for an adjudication of circumstances or failure to conduct the necessary examination regarding the balancing of public and private interests, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nC. Whether the portion of Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act stating “matters concerning the acquisition, management, or disposition of property” (hereinafter referred to as the “provision at issue”) is unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) The principle of clarity, as an expression of the rule-of-law principle, is required for all legislation restricting fundamental rights. However, because it is technically impossible or markedly difficult to strictly and mathematically enforce the principle of clarity, the use of abstract general clauses and indeterminate concepts in legislative technique is inevitable. Accordingly, even if a certain degree of ambiguity is inherent in the statutory language, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity if the meaning and content of the statutory language can be ascertained through supplementary value judgments by judges, and if such supplementary interpretation is not likely to depend on the interpreter’s personal preference (see Constitutional Court Decision 2012HEONBA375 decided on December 26, 2013, en banc, among others).\\n\\nEven though the provision at issue uses the general and abstract term “acquisition, management, or disposition of property,” the concepts of “property,” “acquisition,” “management,” and “disposition” are terms widely used in numerous statutes, and in particular, their meaning can be ascertained through the provisions of related statutes such as the Local Autonomy Act and the former Public Property Act, which regulate matters concerning the property of local governments; whether an act concerning the “acquisition, management, or disposition of property” falls within the subject matter of a resident suit is ultimately a matter for the court to examine and determine specifically, taking into account the legislative purpose of the resident suit system.\\n\\nFurthermore, the Supreme Court has stated that “where a permit to occupy public objects or public property such as roads, allowing a particular private person exclusive use, is evaluated as being for the realization and utilization of the use value unrelated to the original function and purpose of roads, etc., it should be regarded as constituting management or disposition of property subject to a resident suit” (see Supreme Court Decision 2014DU8490 decided on May 27, 2016). Thus, specific standards for determining the subject matter of a resident suit have been presented.\\n\\nTherefore, the provision at issue does not contravene the principle of clarity.\\n\\n(2) Furthermore, the disadvantage suffered by the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant due to the revocation of the road occupancy permit in this case is merely the effect arising from the combination of the fact that Article 17(2) item 2 of the Local Autonomy Act provides a resident suit system seeking the revocation or modification of an unlawful administrative disposition, or a determination as to whether the validity or existence of an administrative disposition exists, and the fact that the road occupancy permit in this case was originally unlawful and should not have been granted in the first place; it cannot be regarded as an unconstitutional consequence caused by the provision at issue itself.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, the ground of appeal asserting that the provision at issue violates the principle of clarity and is therefore unconstitutional because it is contrary to the trust of the addressee of the disposition and causes a grave restriction on the relevant fundamental rights is not accepted.\\n\\n8. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal, insofar as they arise from the intervention in support, shall be borne by the Intervenor Supporting the Defendant, and the remainder shall be borne by the Defendant, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}

{"[89NU5386]": "With respect to the grounds of appeal by the Defendant’s litigation representative, we hold as follows.\\n\\n1. The lower court, for the following reasons in substance, held that the correction disposition in this case, by which the Defendant corrected the tax base and tax amount on September 16, 1988, so as to impose corporate tax of 17,884,950 won and defense tax of 3,940,160 won against the Plaintiff, was unlawful, and therefore upheld the Plaintiff’s claim seeking revocation of the correction disposition in this case.\\n\\nThat is, the Plaintiff is a company whose business purpose is the manufacture and sale of corrugated base paper. On the ground that, in producing corrugated cardboard, it had discharged pollutants exceeding the emission standards under Article 14 of the Environmental Conservation Act, it received from Gyeonggi-do, the competent authority, notices of payment of emission charges under Article 19-2 of the same Act in the amounts of 14,457,360 won on July 1, 1985 and 43,281,140 won on December 16, 1985, respectively, and paid them. Thereafter, the Plaintiff included the total amount of the above emission charges, 57,738,500 won, in deductible expenses, reported the tax base for corporate tax for the fiscal year 1985 as 125,194,501 won, and reported and paid corporate tax of 22,790,845 won and defense tax of 7,488,420 won calculated on the basis of that tax base; but the Defendant, on the ground that the above emission charges fall under the non-deductible expense provision of Article 16, item 4 of the Corporate Tax Act, denied inclusion in deductible expenses and corrected the tax base, and then, after deducting the already reported and paid corporate tax and defense tax from the corporate tax of 40,675,802 won and defense tax of 11,428,584 won calculated on the basis of this corrected tax base, rendered the correction disposition in this case. Having found these facts, the lower court further held that, considering the structure of the Environmental Conservation Act, which separately provides penal provisions under Articles 66 et seq. for cases punishable by imprisonment or fine, and specifically enumerates cases where a fine for negligence may be imposed under Article 69-2, and also considering the content of Article 19-2 of the same Act, the above emission charges may be regarded as a type of burden borne by the beneficiary or the person causing the event, but cannot be regarded as falling under “fines, petty fines (including amounts equivalent to fines or petty fines under a notice disposition), fines for negligence (including petty fines and negligence penalties), surcharges and expenses for disposition for delinquent payment,” which are expenses not included in deductible expenses under Article 16, item 4 of the Corporate Tax Act; and since the provision of Article 16, item 4 of the Corporate Tax Act must, in light of the principle of tax legality, be construed as a provision of exhaustive enumeration, even if there are expenses that appear similar to the expenses prescribed in that Article, they cannot be recognized as non-deductible expenses. Accordingly, the lower court held that the Defendant’s correction disposition in this case, which denied the Plaintiff’s inclusion of the above emission charges in deductible expenses, was unlawful.\\n\\n2. When the relevant provisions of the Environmental Conservation Act are considered in their entirety, the lower court’s determination that the emission charges prescribed in Article 19-2 of the same Act do not fall under the “fines, petty fines, fines for negligence, surcharges and expenses for disposition for delinquent payment,” which are expenses not included in deductible expenses under Article 16, item 4 of the Corporate Tax Act, is proper and acceptable.\\n\\nHowever, Article 16, item 5 of the Corporate Tax Act provides that “public charges and dues other than those prescribed by Presidential Decree” (excluding, however, the “taxes and public charges” included in deductible expenses pursuant to Article 9, paragraph (3) of the same Act and Article 12, paragraph (2), item 10 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act) are expenses not included in deductible expenses, and Article 25 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act provides that the “public charges and dues” under Article 16, item 5 of the Act (those included in deductible expenses) shall be those listed in each item below, without providing that the emission charges prescribed in Article 19-2 of the Environmental Conservation Act are public charges and dues included in deductible expenses. Since “public charges and dues” mean all public burdens compulsorily imposed by the State or a public body on the people or members of a public body, the above emission charges must also be regarded as a kind of “public charges and dues” that are expenses not included in deductible expenses.\\n\\n3. Originally, a taxation disposition is a procedure that specifically confirms and establishes the content of a tax claim objectively and abstractly formed by the satisfaction of the tax requirements prescribed by law. Since the subject matter of a lawsuit seeking revocation of a taxation disposition is general illegality, which constitutes the cause for revocation, and the object of adjudication is the objective existence or nonexistence of the tax base and tax amount, which are the tax liabilities confirmed by the taxation disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 78NU435 dated 1980.10.14.; Supreme Court Decision 85NU418 dated 1985.12.10.; Supreme Court Decision 86NU491 dated 1987.11.10.; Supreme Court Decision 87NU647 dated 1989.4.11.; etc.), even if, in determining or correcting the tax base and tax amount of corporate tax, the tax authority denied inclusion in deductible expenses on the mistaken legal interpretation that expenses recorded by the taxpayer corporation as deductible expenses fall under Article 16, item 4 of the Corporate Tax Act, if those expenses are in any event determined to be expenses not included in deductible expenses under item 5 of the same Article, the tax authority’s decision or correction disposition cannot be regarded as unlawful.\\n\\n4. Therefore, although the Defendant’s correction disposition in this case, which denied inclusion in deductible expenses by determining the above emission charges to be expenses not included in deductible expenses, cannot be regarded as unlawful, the lower court focused only on the point that the above emission charges do not fall under “fines, petty fines, fines for negligence, surcharges and expenses for disposition for delinquent payment,” which are expenses not included in deductible expenses, and without properly examining whether they fall under “public charges and dues,” which are expenses not included in deductible expenses, held that the Defendant’s correction disposition in this case was unlawful. Thus, the lower court judgment cannot but be said to contain an error in the interpretation and application of the law, and such error is manifestly one that affected the judgment. Accordingly, the argument pointing this out is well founded, and the lower court judgment cannot escape reversal.\\n\\n5. Therefore, the lower court judgment is reversed, and in order to have the case further heard and determined, the case is remanded to the lower court, and the judgment is rendered as follows, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[92NU1728]": "We shall determine the 3rd and 4th grounds of appeal advanced by counsel for the Plaintiffs (the supplemental grounds of appeal stated in the supplementary brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the petition of appeal only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. Summary of the reasons of the judgment of the court below.\\n\\na. Findings of fact concerning the circumstances in which the Defendant came to issue the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue.\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs received, from the Defendant, each a permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages (a business that purifies mineral water or groundwater so as to make it suitable for drinking) between 1976.1.23. and 1987.6.23. under the condition that the products be wholly exported or sold only to foreigners in Korea (provided, however, that Plaintiff Seorim Co., Ltd. was subject to the condition that its products be wholly exported), but the Plaintiffs were caught around 1990.7. selling the preserved beverages they had manufactured to Korean nationals in violation of the above permit conditions; and as a result of a water quality test conducted around June of the same year, general bacteria in the preserved beverages manufactured and sold by Plaintiff Sansu Beverage Co., Ltd. and Plaintiff Goryeo General Co., Ltd. were detected in excess of the allowable standard of not more than 100 per 1 ml, and accordingly the Defendant, on 1990.8.30., issued to the Plaintiffs the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue, imposing, in each case, a surcharge in lieu of a 4-month suspension of business.\\n\\nb. Determination as to whether the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue is lawful.\\n\\nThe court below rejected the Plaintiffs’ claim seeking revocation of the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue, by determining as follows.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiffs argue that the above permit conditions attached to the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages granted to the Plaintiffs are unlawful because they are not related in any way to the purpose of the Food Sanitation Act and, moreover, they violate the principle of proportionality and the principle of equality and thus deviate from the limits on the imposition of ancillary conditions granted by the Food Sanitation Act to the licensing authority; however, Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act (before its full amendment by Act No. 3823 dated 1986.5.10.) (the current Food Sanitation Act after amendment, Article 24(1), Item 4, is to the same effect) provides that where an occupation or item designated by the Minister of Health and Social Affairs is found to require restriction of the permit in the public interest, no permit for the business or for the manufacture of the item may be granted; and Article 2, Item 11 and Article 4, Item 1 of the former Standards for Permitting Food Manufacturing Businesses (as amended by Notice of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs No. 34 dated 1975.9.1.) provide that no new permit shall be granted for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, except that a new permit may be granted in the case of a joint venture or technical tie-up pursuant to the Foreign Capital Inducement Act where the entire output is exported; and Article 1, Item 6 and Article 2, Item 4 of the former Standards for Permitting Food Manufacturing Businesses (as amended by Notice of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs No. 84-38 dated 1984.5.28.) provide that the business of manufacturing preserved beverages shall be a business subject to permit restrictions under Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act, but that a permit may be granted where the business is intended wholly for export or for sale to foreigners in Korea. Therefore, the above permit condition attached by the Defendant to the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, namely, that the products be wholly exported or sold only to foreigners in Korea, is of a different nature from the ancillary conditions attached at the discretion of the licensing authority, because it is a so-called statutory condition imposed directly by law to restrict the effect or validity of a specific administrative act, and thus the issues of deviation from the limits of purpose or the limits of proportionality and equality concerning the imposition of ancillary conditions do not arise.\\n\\n(2) The Plaintiffs also argue that the above permit conditions violated the constitutional rights of consumers’ choice, which are fundamental rights of the people, by depriving the people of the right to drink preserved beverages according to their own choice; that they violated the right to equality by unreasonably and unjustly discriminating against Korean nationals as compared with foreigners residing in Korea, etc., without rational basis and by discriminating against manufacturers of preserved beverages as compared with manufacturers of water purifiers; and that they violated the freedom of occupation, which forms part of the content of the freedom to choose one’s occupation, a fundamental right of the people, by restricting the business target of manufacturers of preserved beverages to foreign countries or foreigners residing in Korea, and therefore are contrary to the Constitution and void ab initio; accordingly, they contend that the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue, made on the ground of violation of the above permit conditions, is unlawful. However, even the freedom to choose one’s occupation, the right to drink clear and clean water according to one’s own choice, and the right of Korean nationals not to be treated unequally as compared with foreigners, may be restricted by law to the extent necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare pursuant to Article 37(2) of the Constitution, provided that the essential content of such freedoms and rights is not infringed. If the sale of preserved beverages to Korean nationals were permitted without restriction, it would cause the majority of the people who use tap water as drinking water to feel uneasy that tap water is not suitable for drinking, and further induce them to avoid using tap water as drinking water, thereby ultimately causing considerable confusion in the administration of drinking water supply; moreover, it would create a sense of alienation between the class that drinks preserved beverages and the class that drinks tap water, with a high probability of deepening conflicts among income classes; and there is also a public necessity to supply preserved beverages as drinking water to foreigners residing in Korea or Korean workers abroad who cannot adapt to tap water in Korea. Accordingly, Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act, Article 24(1), Item 4 of the current Food Sanitation Act, and the above Standards for Permitting Food Manufacturing Businesses based thereon, in principle, do not permit the granting of a business permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, but exceptionally permit such a business permit only in the case where the business is intended wholly for export or for sale to foreigners residing in Korea; and the Plaintiffs accepted the permit conditions as above and obtained the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, or succeeded to the status of the person who had obtained such permit as it stood. In addition, the people’s right to drink clear and clean water according to their own choice can also be pursued by means such as improving the quality of tap water, using groundwater or medicinal spring water beverages, using soft drinks, or using water purifiers; therefore, even if the sale of preserved beverages to Korean nationals is not permitted, the essential content of the above right is not infringed. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the above permit conditions attached by the Defendant to the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages against the Plaintiffs infringe the essential content of the Plaintiffs’ freedom of occupation; and even if the Plaintiffs are placed in a relatively unfavorable position compared with manufacturers of water purifiers, it is difficult to say that such treatment lacks rational basis; nor can it be said that the essential content of the people’s rights to pursue happiness, consumers’ choice, and equality is infringed by the above legal restriction for public welfare, and therefore the above permit conditions do not violate the Constitution.\\n\\n(3) Plaintiff Sansu Beverage Co., Ltd. and Plaintiff Goryeo General Co., Ltd. argue that general bacteria do no harm to the human body, and that among foreign water quality standards, the majority do not establish an allowable standard for general bacteria; yet the water quality standard for general bacteria in preserved beverages was set at not more than 100 per 1 ml, and the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue, which was made on the ground that general bacteria in the preserved beverages manufactured and sold by the above Plaintiffs were detected in excess of the above allowable standard, deviated from or abused discretion and is therefore unlawful. However, water quality standards for drinking water may be set differently depending on the natural conditions of the relevant country, etc.; Article 7(1) of the Food Sanitation Act provides that the Minister of Health and Social Affairs may, where it is recognized as necessary for public health, establish and publicly announce standards concerning methods of manufacturing food, etc. for sale and the standards concerning their ingredients; paragraph (4) of the same Article restricts the sale of food, etc. that do not conform to the above standards and specifications; and Article 58 of the same Act provides that permits may be revoked, etc. for violations thereof. Where general bacteria exceeding the allowable standard of not more than 100 per 1 ml, as prescribed by the Rules on Drinking Water Quality Standards, etc. (Ministerial Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs No. 744 dated 1984.3.31.), established on the basis of Article 30(2) of the Public Sanitation Act, Article 4 of the Waterworks Act, etc., were detected in the preserved beverages manufactured and sold by the above Plaintiffs, such products become subject to administrative dispositions such as suspension of business, and it cannot be said that the Defendant’s imposition of a surcharge in lieu of a 4-month suspension of business for the above violation by the above Plaintiffs deviated from or abused discretion.\\n\\n2. Concerning the permit conditions at the time the Plaintiffs obtained the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages and the nature of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs notice that formed the basis therefor.\\n\\nUnder Article 23(1) and Article 22(1) of the former Food Sanitation Act, a person who intends to engage in a business, such as the manufacture of food or additives, prescribed by Presidential Decree must obtain a permit from the Minister of Health and Social Affairs, etc. in accordance with the Presidential Decree; Item 28 of Article 9(1) of the former Enforcement Decree of the Food Sanitation Act (before its full amendment by Presidential Decree No. 12,000 dated 1986.11.11.) prescribed the business of manufacturing preserved beverages as a business for which the above permit must be obtained; and Article 22(1) and Article 21 of the current Food Sanitation Act, as well as Item (n) of Item 1 of Article 7 of the same Act’s Enforcement Decree, are to the same effect (however, pursuant to the amendment to the Enforcement Decree of the Food Sanitation Act on 1991.3.11., the name and content of the business of manufacturing preserved beverages were changed to the business of manufacturing mineral beverages. Thereafter, this shall be referred to as “the business of manufacturing preserved beverages” based on the time when the Plaintiffs obtained the permit). Meanwhile, Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act and Article 24(1), Item 4 of the current Food Sanitation Act provide that where an occupation or item designated by the Minister of Health and Social Affairs is found to require restriction of the permit in the public interest, no permit for the business or for the manufacture of the item may be granted; and the Standards for Permitting Food Manufacturing Businesses (as amended by Notice of the Ministry of Health and Social Affairs No. 85-17 dated 1985.3.11.), which were issued by the Minister of Health and Social Affairs as a notice designating businesses subject to permit restrictions pursuant to this provision and which apply to the permit at issue obtained by the Plaintiffs (Item 2 of the Supplementary Provisions of the above notice provides that persons who obtained a permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, etc. before the enforcement of this notice shall be deemed to have obtained a permit pursuant to the provisions of Article 2, Item 4 of this notice. Therefore, in the present case where the Plaintiffs obtained permits between 1976.1.23. and 1987.6.23., the above notice as amended on 1985.3.11. applies. Thereafter, this notice shall be referred to as “the Notice”) provide in Article 2, Item 4 and Article 1, Item 6 that the business of manufacturing preserved beverages may not be permitted, but that such permit may be granted only where requirements such as wholesale export of the products or sale only to foreigners residing in Korea are satisfied.\\n\\nIn light of the above provisions of the relevant laws and regulations, the above Notice was issued by the Minister of Health and Social Affairs pursuant to Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act, which granted the authority to designate types of businesses for which permits may not be granted for public interest reasons, and it appears to have the nature of a rule-making administrative regulation that has the external binding force by combining with and supplementing the content of the statutory provisions in substance (see this Court Decisions 86NU484, decided 1987.9.29.; 87NU1028, decided 1988.5.10., etc.). Since the business of manufacturing preserved beverages is prescribed in the above Notice as being permittable only where requirements such as wholesale export of the products or sale only to foreigners residing in Korea are satisfied, and the Plaintiffs obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages pursuant to the above Notice, it should be said that the Plaintiffs directly assumed the obligation, by virtue of the regulatory effect of the above Notice, to export the products wholly or sell them only to foreigners residing in Korea. Therefore, even if the permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages obtained by the Plaintiffs were attached with permit conditions to the above effect, this merely confirms the content of the obligations directly assumed pursuant to the above Notice, and such conditions are the so-called statutory conditions and are not ancillary conditions of an administrative act in the original sense attached by the will of the administrative agency. Accordingly, the general principle concerning the limits on attaching ancillary conditions to administrative acts does not apply to such statutory conditions.\\n\\nHowever, if the above Notice violates the Constitution as infringing fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, then it must be regarded as having no effect; therefore, it would be unlawful to impose a surcharge on the Plaintiffs on the ground that they failed to perform the obligations assumed pursuant to the above Notice.\\n\\nOriginally, all freedoms and rights of the people may be restricted by law only when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, and even when restricted, the essential content of freedoms and rights may not be infringed, as provided in Article 37(2) of the Constitution (the same as former Article 35(2) of the Constitution, which was in force when the above Notice was enforced). Since the above Notice was issued pursuant to the relevant provisions of the former Food Sanitation Act, which allow restrictions on permits for businesses, etc. where necessary for public interest, there is a legal basis for restricting the permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages; however, if the above Notice restricts the people’s fundamental rights and is not necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, or even if necessary, if the objective can be achieved by other means that less restrict the freedoms and rights of the people, or if the disadvantages suffered by the people as a result of such restriction are greater than the public interest achievable by such restriction, then such restriction cannot escape being in violation of the Constitution, even if it does not infringe the essential content of freedoms and rights. Accordingly, we shall examine whether the above Notice, by imposing the above obligations on persons who have obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, violates the Constitution.\\n\\n3. Whether the above Notice infringes the freedom of occupation.\\n\\na. Freedom of occupation and its restriction.\\n\\nArticle 15 of the Constitution (the same as former Article 14 of the Constitution) guarantees freedom to choose one’s occupation as one of the fundamental human rights of the people, and among the freedoms guaranteed by this provision are not only freedom of occupational choice in the original sense, but also freedom of occupational activity, which permits, in principle, free determination of the content, manner, etc. of one’s activities while engaging in the chosen occupation. It may be said that not only natural persons but also juristic persons can be the subjects of freedom of occupation.\\n\\nHowever, the above Notice restricts the freedom of business by allowing persons who have obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages to export the manufactured beverages in their entirety or sell them only to foreigners residing in Korea, thereby prohibiting sales to Korean nationals within the country. Thus, it is clear that it restricts freedom of occupation, and the issue is whether such restriction on freedom of occupation is indeed consistent with the Constitution.\\n\\nOriginally, occupations differ widely in kind, nature, content, social significance, and influence, and the social reasons or purposes requiring regulation of such occupations are also manifold, with differing degrees of importance; accordingly, restrictions on freedom of occupation take various forms depending on the concrete case, and thus whether they are unconstitutional cannot be discussed uniformly, but must be carefully determined by examining and comparing the purpose, necessity, content of the restriction, the nature and content of the freedom of occupation being restricted, and the degree and method of restriction in the specific restrictive measure.\\n\\nIn general, where a restriction on freedom of occupation does not restrict the choice of occupation itself but only restricts the content or manner of occupational activity, such restriction is regarded as lighter in degree than a restriction on the freedom of occupational choice; therefore, the scope within which freedom may be restricted is broader, and the necessity and rationality of the restriction may be affirmed relatively easily. However, this distinction is not necessarily absolute; if the restriction on freedom of occupational activity is so substantial that, although formally it appears to restrict only freedom of occupational activity, it is in substance no different from restricting freedom of occupational choice, then the rationality of such restriction should not be easily affirmed, and only where such restriction is recognized as necessary to protect a very important public interest superior to individual freedom should it be regarded as constitutional.\\n\\nAlso, where the restriction consists of prohibiting a certain act, the degree of restriction may vary depending on whether the prohibition is relative, recognizing exceptions in certain cases, or absolute, recognizing no exceptions at all; accordingly, the determination of whether it is constitutional may also vary.\\n\\nb. Degree to which freedom of occupation is restricted.\\n\\nThe above Notice, while granting a permit to a person who seeks a permit for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, prohibits only the sale of the manufactured beverages to Korean nationals within the country (hereinafter abbreviated as “domestic sales”), and therefore, formally, there is room to view it as restricting the freedom of business only lightly, by restricting only freedom of occupational activity. However, although that may appear so on the surface, in substance the restriction imposed on the Plaintiffs by the above Notice cannot be said to be anything other than very serious.\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs argue that, as of 1987, the export volume of preserved beverages accounted for only 1.3% of total production (record page 34), and there is no material in the record to support a finding that such assertion is contrary to fact, nor does it appear that such ratio has materially changed up to the present. In addition, even if the quantity sold to foreigners within the country is considered, almost all of the preserved beverages manufactured by the Plaintiffs must be sold within the country to Korean nationals; closing almost the entire potential market for such preserved beverages is, in substance, a restriction as significant as permitting the business of manufacturing preserved beverages in full while limiting only the conditions for the permit (which would fall under a restriction on freedom of occupational choice), and therefore a substantial restriction on freedom of business, which is no different from restricting freedom of occupational choice.\\n\\nMoreover, even in the content of the restriction on freedom of business, domestic sales are completely prohibited and no exception is recognized in any case; accordingly, the degree of restriction is absolute, and it cannot be said that freedom of occupation is being severely restricted.\\n\\nTherefore, in order to restrict freedom of occupation to such an extent, it must be recognized that such restriction is necessary to protect a very important public interest.\\n\\nc. Purpose of the restriction and its necessity.\\n\\nWe shall now examine whether the purpose of the above Notice restricting the Plaintiffs’ freedom of business is legitimate.\\n\\n(1) One of the purposes recognized by the court below, based on the Defendant’s argument, as the purpose of the above Notice in restricting the freedom of business of persons obtaining permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages is that, if domestic sales of preserved beverages to Korean nationals are permitted without restriction, the majority of the people who use tap water as drinking water would become uneasy that tap water is not suitable for drinking, and would further avoid using tap water as drinking water, thereby ultimately causing considerable confusion in the drinking water supply administration; another purpose is that it is highly likely to create a sense of alienation between the class that drinks preserved beverages and the class that drinks tap water, thereby deepening conflicts among income classes (the court below additionally stated that there is a public necessity to supply preserved beverages as drinking water to foreigners residing in Korea or Korean workers abroad who cannot adapt to tap water; however, since it is clear that such reason cannot serve as a basis for prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages, we shall not further examine this point).\\n\\n(2) However, the second purpose recognized by the court below, namely the prevention of a sense of alienation, cannot be said to be a legitimate purpose that would justify restricting domestic sales of preserved beverages. The sense of alienation asserted by the Defendant is a kind of relative deprivation; that is, it is understood to mean that if domestic sales of preserved beverages are permitted, it would not directly disadvantage those who previously drank tap water and, due to their circumstances, will have no choice but to continue drinking tap water because they cannot afford to drink preserved beverages in the future, but that when those persons see others drinking preserved beverages, they will feel that they are relatively disadvantaged compared with them. Such a phenomenon, absent special circumstances such as the occurrence of a serious social disturbance as a result, is not itself something to be regulated by law. Even if permitting domestic sales of preserved beverages would mean that only part of the people could drink preserved beverages, that in itself would mean that the scope of beverage choices available to the people has thereby expanded, and as seen below, it would constitute a state in which the people’s right to pursue happiness is realized; from the perspective of the nation or society as a whole, it would amount to an increase in public welfare. Such an increase in public welfare cannot be blocked merely on the ground that another part of the people might feel relative deprivation as a result. Nor can the prevention of such relative deprivation be justified under the principle of equality.\\n\\nIndeed, allowing only domestic sales of preserved beverages to foreigners residing in Korea might even be viewed as creating the above-mentioned sense of alienation to a greater degree.\\n\\n(3) By contrast, the first purpose recognized by the court below, namely that if domestic sales of preserved beverages are permitted, the majority of the people would become uneasy about tap water and further avoid using tap water as drinking water, ultimately causing considerable confusion in the drinking water supply administration, and that such confusion should therefore be prevented, may in itself be regarded as a legitimate purpose for maintaining order or public welfare. However, the issue is whether, for that reason alone, prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages can truly be recognized as necessary and rational to achieve that purpose. This is because even if the purpose of restricting the people’s fundamental rights is legitimate, rationality is not recognized unless there is a balance between the purpose and the means.\\n\\nIf the people’s uneasiness about tap water arises from domestic sales of preserved beverages itself, the matter would be different; however, the people’s uneasiness about tap water should fundamentally be viewed as arising from the people’s inability to trust the quality of tap water (the question of how the quality of tap water is to be objectively assessed is a separate matter), and thus a connection between domestic sales of preserved beverages and the people’s uneasiness about tap water cannot be recognized. Of course, if the Minister of Health and Social Affairs were to permit domestic sales of preserved beverages, one might think that the government itself would thereby be acknowledging that the quality of tap water is poor, and that the people’s uneasiness about tap water would increase; however, whether that would in fact be so, and if so, to what extent the people’s uneasiness about tap water would increase, cannot be said to be clear.\\n\\nFurthermore, even if a connection between domestic sales of preserved beverages and the people’s uneasiness about tap water were recognized, it is questionable whether, for that reason alone, it could be justified to permit sales only to foreigners residing in Korea and to impose such a strong restriction on the freedom of occupation of persons who have obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages as to absolutely prohibit domestic sales. The fundamental solution to alleviating the people’s uneasiness about tap water would be to improve the quality of tap water or to clearly inform the people, on the basis of objective data, that such uneasiness is unfounded. Since prohibiting only domestic sales of preserved beverages, without taking such measures, does not fundamentally resolve the people’s uneasiness about tap water, prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages cannot be said to be a necessary and appropriate means to alleviate the people’s uneasiness about tap water.\\n\\n(4) If so, prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages solely for the purposes recognized by the court below cannot but be said to infringe the freedom of occupation, which is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution to persons who have obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, and therefore to violate the Constitution; and, in light of the purpose of the Food Sanitation Act, which seeks to contribute to the promotion of public health by preventing sanitary hazards arising from food and by promoting the qualitative improvement of food nutrition (Article 1), it cannot be regarded that the Minister of Health and Social Affairs, pursuant to Article 23-3, Item 4 of the former Food Sanitation Act or Article 24(1), Item 4 of the current Food Sanitation Act, issued the above Notice restricting the freedom of occupation of persons obtaining permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages in a manner as above that was absolutely necessary and rational for maintaining order or public welfare. Thus, the above Notice can only be regarded as having no effect.\\n\\n4. Whether the above Notice infringes the right to pursue happiness.\\n\\nArticle 10 of the Constitution (the same as former Article 9 of the Constitution) provides that all people have dignity and value as human beings and have the right to pursue happiness, thereby making clear that the right to pursue happiness is a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. The ability of a human being to freely choose the food he or she wishes to eat or the beverage he or she wishes to drink constitutes one of the most basic means of pursuing happiness as a human being and forms an important part of the right to pursue happiness. Therefore, there must be sufficient reason to restrict the people’s freedom to choose the beverage they wish to drink.\\n\\nHowever, the above Notice, even with respect to persons who have obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, prohibits them from selling preserved beverages to Korean nationals within the country, thereby indirectly causing a restriction on the people’s right to pursue happiness to choose and drink such beverages.\\n\\nIt has already been made clear, without need for further explanation, as seen in section 3 above, that the people’s above-mentioned right to pursue happiness cannot be restricted on the ground alone that it will alleviate the people’s uneasiness about tap water and prevent confusion in the drinking water supply administration.\\n\\nMoreover, even assuming that the public purpose of preventing the people’s uneasiness about tap water from increasing is legitimate, and that prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages is recognized as a necessary and appropriate means for that purpose, if one compares such public purpose with the result that the people’s right to pursue happiness is restricted by prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages, the loss suffered by the people as a result of the restriction or infringement of the right to pursue happiness is greater; therefore, on this point as well, prohibiting domestic sales of preserved beverages must be deemed impermissible. If the people harbor doubts as to the quality of tap water as a beverage, it is natural that they will seek other beverages; to prohibit the people from choosing other beverages and compel them to drink only tap water, under the pretext of preventing the people’s uneasiness about tap water, cannot but be regarded as unfair.\\n\\nIn particular, Article 35(1) of the Constitution provides that all people have the right to live in a healthy and pleasant environment (former Article 33 of the Constitution also provides to substantially the same effect); therefore, if the people doubt the quality of tap water and are reluctant to drink it, the State should endeavor to remove such doubt by taking necessary measures such as improving the quality of tap water, and if the people’s uneasiness or doubt regarding tap water is difficult to resolve in a short period of time, it would be the State’s natural duty to allow the people to choose and drink other beverages. Nevertheless, instead of taking such measures, the State’s action in prohibiting only domestic sales of preserved beverages merely shifts to preserved beverages the responsibility for doubts arising regarding the quality of tap water, and is unfair because it indirectly compels the people to continue drinking only tap water, thereby restricting the people’s environmental rights.\\n\\nThe court below stated that the people’s right to drink clear and clean water can also be pursued by means such as improving the quality of tap water, using groundwater or medicinal spring water beverages, using soft drinks, or using water purifiers, and thus the essential content of the right to pursue happiness is not infringed. However, such means cannot be definitively said to be easier than purchasing and drinking preserved beverages (improving the quality of tap water is not something that can be achieved by the efforts of individual citizens alone); and in restricting the freedoms and rights of the people, the side seeking regulation must search for other means that less restrict the people’s fundamental rights, whereas from the perspective of the people whose rights are restricted, the mere existence of other means to realize such rights does not, by itself, justify the restriction of fundamental rights. Accordingly, the above reasoning stated by the court below cannot but be regarded as reversing the order of reasoning.\\n\\n5. Conclusion.\\n\\nIf so, the above Notice, by prohibiting the Plaintiffs, who obtained permits for the business of manufacturing preserved beverages, from making domestic sales of preserved beverages, infringes the constitutionally guaranteed freedom of occupation and the people’s right to pursue happiness, and therefore violates the Constitution and has no effect. Accordingly, the administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue, by which the Defendant imposed a surcharge on the Plaintiffs on the premise that the above Notice, though void, was effective, is unlawful. Therefore, the judgment of the court below, which took a different view and held that the Defendant’s administrative disposition imposing the surcharge at issue was lawful, is unlawful in that it erred in its understanding of the legal principles concerning freedom of occupation and the right to pursue happiness, and since such error is manifestly one that affected the judgment, the argument pointing out this point has merit. Without determining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and the opinions of the participating Justices are unanimous, and the judgment is rendered as follows."}

question:
Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (✕) concerning the principle of protection of trust under administrative law? (Where disputed, according to case law)

(a) In order for the principle of protection of trust to apply, there must be no attributable fault on the part of the individual with respect to the reliance placed on the administrative agency’s expression of view as being justified; here, the presence or absence of attributable fault must be determined with respect to all persons concerned, including the addressee of the expression of view and any mandatary entrusted by that person with certain acts therefrom.
(b) Even though the administrative agency had an opportunity to exercise its authority, if it has not exercised that authority for a long period and there are justifiable grounds for the public to believe that the authority will not be exercised, it shall not exercise that authority, and the same applies even where there is a risk of substantially harming the interests of a third party.
(c) Even where broad legislative discretion is recognized in amending statutes, if the party’s trust in the continued existence of the statute is reasonable and justifiable and the loss caused to the party by the amendment is so severe that the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new statute cannot justify the destruction of such trust, the legislator must take appropriate measures to protect the party’s trust, such as providing transitional provisions.
(d) Even if a resident registration number and the corresponding resident registration card were assigned by an administrative agency, pursuant to a birth registration, to A, who was born to a Korean-national father and a People’s Republic of China-national mother who were not legally married, once the family relation register was cancelled by the administrative agency as a “birth registration of a child born out of wedlock to a foreign mother,” the Minister of Justice’s determination that A does not possess Korean nationality on the ground that A is not a holder of Korean nationality can be justified.
(e) If, after an administrative agency has expressed an official view, the circumstances change, it is difficult to regard that official view as still being a subject of trust for the individual; therefore, absent special circumstances, the administrative agency may issue a disposition contrary to that expression of view.
