{"[2003DU12899]": "We consider the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. With respect to the grounds of appeal concerning whether the principle of protection of trust was violated\\n\\na. The rule of law, which our Constitution adopts as a basic principle, does not stop at formal rule of law, under which matters concerning the rights and duties of the people are to be prescribed by law, but aims at substantive rule of law, under which the purpose and content of such law must conform to the constitutional ideal of guaranteeing fundamental rights, and, for the realization of such substantive rule of law, legal stability in the process, no less than the requirement that state action be carried out on the basis of law, must also be given important consideration.\\n\\nThe principle of such substantive rule of law is typically embodied in Article 13 of the Constitution, which provides for the prohibition of retroactive effect of criminal statutes, the prohibition of double jeopardy or double punishment, and the prohibition of deprivation of property rights by retroactive legislation. Accordingly, not only in cases where there are such express provisions, but also where reasonable and legitimate trust of the people has been formed with respect to the existing legal order, the so-called principle of protection of trust, under which such trust must be protected within an appropriate scope, is likewise, for the same reason, to be regarded as falling within the principle of the rule of law, which is a basic principle of our Constitution. In other words, if the State gives no protection whatsoever to a situation where the people, on the basis of reasonable and legitimate trust that a certain statute or regulation will continue unchanged in the future, have taken concrete actions corresponding to that statute or regulation and thereby formed a certain legal status or living relationship, then the people’s trust in the legal order will collapse, and the future legal effects of present acts will become unforeseeable, thereby greatly undermining legal stability; accordingly, it may be said that the legislature, in amending statutes or regulations, must promote legal stability by taking appropriate measures to protect such trust. Of course, such protection of trust is not absolute nor uniform in every sphere of life, and the degree and method of protection may differ depending on the freedoms, rights, interests, etc. involved in each individual case; where the public interest purpose sought to be realized through a new statute or regulation is superior, it may be restricted in light thereof.\\n\\nTherefore, in amending statutes or regulations, if a party’s trust in the continued existence of the former statute or regulation is reasonable and legitimate, and if the damage suffered by the party due to the amendment is so severe that the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new statute or regulation cannot justify the destruction of such trust, the legislature must take appropriate measures to protect the party’s trust, such as establishing transitional provisions, and it cannot be permitted to implement or apply the new statute or regulation as is without such appropriate measures, because, as stated above, doing so would violate the principle of protection of trust derived from the principle of the rule of law, which is a basic principle of the Constitution. In order to determine whether there has been a violation of such principle of protection of trust, on the one hand, one must comprehensively compare and balance the value of the interest infringed, the degree of seriousness of the infringement, the degree to which trust has been damaged, the manner of infringement of trust, etc., and on the other hand, the public interest purpose sought to be realized through the new statute or regulation (see, e.g., Constitutional Court Decision 2002HEONBA45 (en banc), decided November 28, 2002).\\n\\nb. According to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, ① the Enforcement Decree of the Patent Attorney Act, amended by Presidential Decree No. 16867 on June 27, 2000, changed the Patent Attorney Examination, first and second stages, conducted by the Defendant, from the former “relative grading system” to an “absolute grading system” under which all examinees obtaining 40 points or more in each subject and an average of 60 points or more across all subjects are to pass (Article 4), in accordance with the Regulatory Reform Committee, a body directly under the President, having sought to expand the number of professional license holders such as patent attorneys by converting the selection examination into a qualification verification examination system, and, for the preparation of its implementation, provided a grace period of about one and a half years and thus was to be implemented from January 1, 2002 (proviso to Supplementary Provision, paragraph 1); ② on January 10, 2002, the Defendant announced in the “Notices” section of the Korean Intellectual Property Office Internet homepage that the first examination of the 39th Patent Attorney Examination, which was to be the first examination to be administered under the absolute grading system pursuant to the above Enforcement Decree provision (hereinafter referred to as “the examination at issue”), would be held on March 31 of the same year; ③ however, two days later, on January 12 of the same year, the Defendant deleted the above announcement, and, on January 17 of the same year, on the ground of “efficient examination administration,” a legislative notice of an amendment to the Enforcement Decree of the Patent Attorney Act, changing the first examination back from the “absolute grading system” to the “relative grading system,” was published in the Official Gazette; on March 25 of the same year, Article 4, etc. of the Enforcement Decree of the Patent Attorney Act were amended and promulgated in the same content as the above legislative notice (Presidential Decree No. 17551; hereinafter the amended decree is referred to as the “Amended Enforcement Decree,” and the decree before amendment as the “Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree”), and the supplementary provisions of the Amended Enforcement Decree provided that “this Decree shall enter into force on the date of its promulgation”; ④ on March 26 of the same year, the day after the promulgation of the Amended Enforcement Decree, the Defendant announced the implementation plan for the 39th Patent Attorney Examination, and then conducted the examination at issue on May 26 of the same year; ⑤ on July 25 of the same year, the Defendant announced 1,047 successful candidates for the examination at issue, and treated the Plaintiffs as unsuccessful candidates for the examination at issue on the ground that the Plaintiffs’ scores fell short of the average passing score of 66.88 points under the relative grading system; ⑥ there were in total 689 examinees, including the Plaintiffs, who obtained 40 points or more in each subject and an average of 60 points or more across all subjects, which are the passing standards under the absolute grading system, but were treated as failed in the examination at issue; ⑦ meanwhile, during the several years before the examination at issue, the passing score of the first examination conducted under the relative grading system was determined between 70 points and 82 points; and ⑧ the time required to pass the Patent Attorney Examination would vary depending on the individual circumstances of the examinee, but generally it would take about 3 to 4 years, and even according to the Defendant’s contention, at least one year or more would be required merely for basic preparation.\\n\\nc. In light of the purpose and background of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, which introduced the absolute grading system, the passing scores of the first examination conducted under the relative grading system during the several years before the examination at issue, the grace period after promulgation of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, and the series of facts concerning the legislative notice and promulgation of the Amended Enforcement Decree and the subsequent announcement of the examination, etc., it was a universal expectation, to the extent that even the Defendant, who is the legislator, foresaw it, that if the first examination were conducted under the absolute grading system pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, the number of successful candidates would be much greater than under the former relative grading system; and since the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, while converting the first examination to the absolute grading system, had set a considerable grace period of about one and a half years and was to be implemented from 2002, it is sufficient to conclude that the examinees for the Patent Attorney Examination, in reliance on the expectation that the examination at issue in 2002 would be conducted pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, prepared for the examination in a manner suitable to the passing standard on the premise of the level of difficulty of the examinations up to that time, and such conduct constituted the exercise of a reasonable and legitimate trust. Moreover, although it may not have been entirely unforeseeable for such examinees that Article 4 of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree itself, which provided for the absolute grading system for the first examination, could be amended, it is reasonable to deem that they could not possibly have anticipated that, at a time when the examination at issue was imminent, the Enforcement Decree would be amended so as to revert the absolute grading system under the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree to the relative grading system, without ever having implemented the absolute grading system under the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree even once, and that it would be put into immediate effect.\\n\\nIf so, the examinees who prepared for the examination in accordance with the passing standard required by the absolute grading system on the basis of such reasonable and legitimate trust were, at a point when only two months remained until the first examination was to be held, caused to suffer a great disruption in their preparation for the examination as a result of the change in the passing standard due to the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree, and thus such trust was greatly damaged; in particular, the reliance interest of the Plaintiffs, who were treated as unsuccessful despite obtaining 40 points or more in each subject and an average of 60 points or more across all subjects, which are the passing standards under the absolute grading system, was severely infringed. On the other hand, the public interest purpose achievable by introducing the relative grading system through the Amended Enforcement Decree is limited to avoiding the difficulty of administering the second examination due to an excessively large number of successful candidates in the first examination, and securing the selection of first-examination passers above a certain level by raising the passing score of the first examination. However, these problems that may arise when the first examination is conducted under the absolute grading system were fully foreseeable at the time of promulgation of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, and, since a preparation period for implementation of about one and a half years was already allowed by transitional provisions and there is no indication that resolution by another method was impossible, it is difficult to find any reasonable basis for the realization of such public interest purpose by immediately implementing the Amended Enforcement Decree and applying it to the examination at issue, which was just imminent. Accordingly, even taking into account the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree, the infringement upon the Plaintiffs’ reliance interest caused by such immediate implementation is so excessive that it cannot be justified. Furthermore, the fact that the adjustment of the method and period for preparing for the examination under the Amended Enforcement Decree was applied uniformly to the examinees who took the examination at issue cannot justify the infringement of the above reliance interest, and even if the Plaintiffs took the examination at issue as announced in accordance with the content of the Amended Enforcement Decree, in social common sense this alone cannot be deemed to constitute a waiver of any and all reliance interest in the continued existence of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree.\\n\\nTherefore, applying Article 4, paragraph (1) of the Amended Enforcement Decree, which provides for the relative grading system in the first examination, to the examination at issue in 2002 cannot be permitted in light of the constitutional principle of protection of trust; accordingly, the portion of the supplementary provisions of the Amended Enforcement Decree that set the time of its entry into force so that Article 4, paragraph (1) would be immediately applied to the examination at issue is in violation of the Constitution and therefore null and void.\\n\\nAlthough the reasoning differs, the conclusion of the court below that the portion of the supplementary provisions which provided that Article 4, paragraph (1) of the Amended Enforcement Decree be immediately applied to the examination at issue is in violation of the Constitution and void is proper, and there is no legal error regarding the principle of protection of trust, violation of logic and experience rules, lack of adequate examination, or contradiction of reasons or absence of reasons, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe ground of appeal on this point is without merit.\\n\\n2. With respect to the grounds of appeal concerning the scope of application of the principle of protection of trust\\n\\nThe infringement of a reliance interest by a new statute or regulation is not an issue only when the new statute or regulation is applied retroactively to past facts or legal relations; the principle of protection of trust may also apply where a new statute or regulation governs facts or legal relations that arose in the past but have not yet been completed and are ongoing, thereby infringing the reliance interest in the continued existence of the previously applicable statute or regulation.\\n\\nEven if the examination at issue was conducted after the day set as the effective date of the Amended Enforcement Decree, the Plaintiffs’ acts of preparing for the examination in reliance on the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree had continued from before that time, and therefore the court below was correct in applying the principle of protection of trust to the infringement of the Plaintiffs’ reliance interest caused by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree; there is no legal error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, concerning the scope of application of the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nThe ground of appeal on this point is also without merit.\\n\\n3. With respect to the grounds of appeal concerning whether the Act on the Promulgation of Statutes, etc. applies\\n\\nArticle 13 of the Act on the Promulgation of Statutes, etc. provides that Presidential Decrees, etc. shall take effect upon the lapse of 20 days from the date of promulgation unless otherwise specially provided; however, the Amended Enforcement Decree contains a supplementary provision that specially provides that the date of promulgation shall be the effective date. As stated above, even if the portion of the supplementary provision, which provided that Article 4, paragraph (1) be immediately applied to the examination at issue, is unconstitutional and void and its application is excluded, as long as that supplementary provision exists, there is no room for Article 13 of the Act on the Promulgation of Statutes, etc. to apply to the Amended Enforcement Decree.\\n\\nAccordingly, the ground of appeal, which is premised on the contrary and alleges legal error, contradiction of reasons, or absence of reasons in the judgment of the court below on the assumption that the above statutory provision applies to the Amended Enforcement Decree, is without merit.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as per the operative part.\\n\\nWith respect to this judgment, the opinions of the participating justices were unanimous except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Yong-dam, Kim Hwang-sik, and Ahn Dae-hee, and there is a supplementary opinion to Justice Kim Yong-dam’s dissenting opinion.\\n\\n5. The dissenting opinions of Justices Kim Yong-dam, Kim Hwang-sik, and Ahn Dae-hee are as follows.\\n\\na. The majority opinion held that it is reasonable and legitimate for the examinees of the Patent Attorney Examination, in reliance on the fact that the examination at issue would be conducted under the absolute grading system pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, to prepare for the examination in a manner suitable to the passing standard on the premise of the level of difficulty of the examinations up to that time; furthermore, the infringement of the examinees’ reliance interest caused by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree is so excessive that it cannot be justified even taking into account the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree, and therefore applying Article 4, paragraph (1) of the Amended Enforcement Decree, which provides for the relative grading system for the first examination for patent attorneys, to the examination at issue cannot be permitted in light of the constitutional principle of protection of trust, so that the portion of the supplementary provisions of the Amended Enforcement Decree that provided that Article 4, paragraph (1) be immediately applied to the examination at issue is in violation of the Constitution and void; however, for the following reasons, I cannot agree with the majority opinion.\\n\\nb. First, I examine whether the trust mentioned by the majority opinion, and the exercise of such trust, is reasonable and legitimate and thus deserving of legal protection.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that, if the first examination were conducted under the absolute grading system, the number of successful candidates would be much greater than under the relative grading system; since this was the legislative intent of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree and at the same time a universal expectation to the extent that even the legislator, the Defendant, foresaw it, it is sufficient to conclude that the examinees, in reliance on the fact that the examination would be conducted under the absolute grading system, prepared for the examination in a manner suitable to the passing standard on the premise of the level of difficulty of the examinations up to that time, and that this constituted the exercise of reasonable and legitimate trust.\\n\\nHowever, as stated above, even if the relative grading system for the first examination was changed to the absolute grading system in accordance with the policy of the Regulatory Reform Committee, at least from a legal and institutional perspective, such change does not necessarily mean that the number of successful candidates will increase, nor does such change legally guarantee an increase in the number of successful candidates. Moreover, since there is no basis whatsoever for the level of difficulty of the examination necessarily to remain as before, the number of successful candidates may vary depending on the adjustment of the level of difficulty. In other words, the absolute grading system is not a legal mechanism that guarantees more successful candidates than the relative grading system.\\n\\nThe legislative intent of the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree, namely expanding the number of professional license holders such as patent attorneys, can ultimately be achieved by increasing the number of successful candidates in the second Patent Attorney Examination, and since the first examination is merely a preliminary examination that grants eligibility to take the second examination, as long as the framework for producing a reasonable number of first-examination passers who can sit for the second examination is maintained and operated reasonably, the method of determining successful candidates in the first examination should be regarded as a matter within the authority of the Defendant.\\n\\nIf so, even if there existed on the part of the Plaintiffs an expectation or trust that the examination at issue would be conducted under the absolute grading system pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree and that the level of difficulty of the examination would remain at the previous level, such expectation was merely factual and based on the Plaintiffs’ subjective interests, and was not of the nature that the Defendant must protect as a matter of law, since it lacks legal legitimacy and reasonableness.\\n\\nMoreover, preparing for the examination in a manner suitable to the passing standard on the premise of the level of difficulty of the examinations up to that time—that is, adopting an examination strategy or tactic of not devoting one’s utmost effort to the first examination, but merely preparing just enough to pass—cannot be regarded as legitimate and therefore cannot be characterized as the exercise of reasonable and legitimate trust deserving of protection.\\n\\nIn addition, since the Defendant can sufficiently adjust the number of persons to be passed in the first examination by controlling the difficulty of the examination even under the absolute grading system, regardless of whether the Defendant chooses an absolute or relative grading method, the final pass or fail of the examination will ultimately be determined by the individual examinees’ mastery of the examination subjects, and, for examinees who have prepared for the already scheduled subjects, unless there is a sudden change in such subjects, the mere change in the grading method cannot be said to have operated as a decisive factor affecting pass or fail in the examination, making it difficult to view the examination’s being conducted under the relative grading system itself as infringing the examinees’ expected interests. Even if examinees who took the examination under the belief that it would be graded relatively obtained scores that could have resulted in passing under the absolute grading system, that would merely be a factual result of the examination, and it would not be logically proper to say that their expected interests were thereby infringed.\\n\\nc. Furthermore, even if the trust mentioned by the majority opinion, and the exercise of such trust, were reasonable and legitimate and deserving of legal protection, I next examine whether the infringement of the examinees’ reliance interest caused by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree is so excessive that it cannot justify the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by such immediate implementation.\\n\\nThe passing standards and the method of determining successful candidates for examinations designed to select professional license holders such as patent attorneys are matters that may be changed at any time according to changes in legislative policy, and in fact the Patent Attorney Examination has undergone several changes, including conversion from the absolute grading system to the relative grading system and then back to the absolute grading system pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree. In light of this, the examinees’ expectation and trust that the examination at issue would be conducted under the absolute grading system pursuant to the Pre-Amendment Enforcement Decree are merely relative and variable. Moreover, the subjects of the examination at issue are four in number and there is no major change from before; more than four months of preparation time was allowed from the time of legislative notice to the time of the examination; and although the examination is conducted under a relative grading system, the ratio of the number of first-examination passers to the final successful candidates is 2.4 times in the case of the Judicial Examination, 2 times in the case of the Certified Public Accountant Examination, and 4 to 5 times in the case of the Higher Civil Service Examination. Compared with these, the Defendant caused 1,047 candidates, more than five times the number of final successful candidates, to pass the examination at issue, thereby limiting the degree of infringement on the examinees’ reliance interest to the minimum necessary. In light of these circumstances, it cannot be said that the infringement of the examinees’ reliance interest caused by the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree is so excessive that it cannot justify the public interest purpose of proper administration and management of the examination and selection of first-examination passers above a certain level, which are the purposes of the immediate implementation of the Amended Enforcement Decree.\\n\\nd. Nevertheless, the court below held that the portion of the supplementary provisions providing for the immediate application of Article 4, paragraph (1) of the Amended Enforcement Decree to the examination at issue was null and void in light of the constitutional principle of protection of trust, and therefore concluded that the Defendant’s disposition at issue was unlawful. Since this judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the outcome by misapprehending the law concerning the principle of protection of trust, it is appropriate to reverse the judgment of the court below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination. However, the majority opinion takes a different view, and I therefore dissent from it.\\n\\n6. The supplementary opinion to the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Yong-dam is as follows.\\n\\na. On the point that the majority opinion regards this case as a matter of constitutional adjudication\\n\\n(1) Our Constitution, in Article 101, paragraph (1), provides that “judicial power shall vest in courts composed of judges,” and, in Article 111, paragraph (1), provides that “the Constitutional Court shall adjudicate the following matters,” and then enumerates the matters within its jurisdiction, thereby adopting a dual structure that separates the matters within the jurisdiction of the Constitutional Court from judicial power.\\n\\nThe five matters within the jurisdiction of the Constitutional Court enumerated in Article 111, paragraph (1), each have different inherent functions, and the adjudicatory procedures accordingly also differ, so questions may arise as to whether they can be encompassed within a single unified concept of constitutional adjudication. However, as judicial power under the Constitution and the adjudicatory power of the Constitutional Court are separated and independent from each other, the question of how the scope and limits of the latter should be understood and established marks the boundary between the two, and because if that boundary collapses it would raise a very important constitutional issue in which the independence of the courts and the Constitutional Court may mutually encroach upon each other, it must be explored with careful attention.\\n\\nConstitutional adjudication is ordinarily referred to as “independent adjudication on constitutional issues” or “judicial action concerning constitutional matters,” and the constitutional issues or constitutional matters referred to here must be understood as issues directly related to the provisions of the Constitution, including the fundamental rights clauses, or the major principles of the Constitution. With respect to the constitutional adjudicatory power regarding review of unconstitutional statutes or regulations, the Constitution further subdivides this by assigning review of unconstitutional statutes to the Constitutional Court (Article 107, paragraph (1), and Article 111, paragraph (1), item 1), while vesting the power to review unconstitutional orders and rules in the Supreme Court (Article 107, paragraph (2)). However, in exercising constitutional adjudication, the Constitutional Court must of course not endlessly expand its constitutional adjudicatory power by reducing every legal issue to a constitutional issue, and likewise the Supreme Court, in reviewing the constitutionality or legality of orders and rules, must clearly distinguish whether the matter is constitutional adjudication concerning the unconstitutionality of the order or rule, or an exercise of judicial power raising the issue of legality. If one mindlessly adheres to the doctrine of hierarchical legal norms and thinks that every legal issue can ultimately be transformed into a constitutional issue, that is incompatible, at the very least, with our Constitution, and must in the end be regarded as a dangerous way of thinking that denies the independence of judicial power.\\n\\n(2) In order for an expectation or trust regarding the creation, maintenance, amendment, or abolition of a certain system itself to be protected as a constitutional expectation or trust, the creation, maintenance, amendment, or abolition of that system must be directly expected and trusted from the Constitution; if the system was first established by statutes or regulations other than the Constitution, then the question of expectation and trust regarding the creation, maintenance, amendment, or abolition of that system is, in principle, a matter under those statutes or regulations. Therefore, with respect to a system established by statute, as in this case, a change in the method of implementation by an order, rule, or ordinance delegated by statute to implement it should primarily be treated as a matter of statute, not as a matter of the Constitution.\\n\\nThe majority opinion states that “in amending statutes or regulations, if a party’s trust in the continued existence of the former statute or regulation is reasonable and legitimate, and if the damage suffered by the party due to the amendment is so severe that the public interest purpose sought to be achieved by the new statute or regulation cannot justify the destruction of such trust, it cannot be permitted to implement or apply the new statute or regulation as is without appropriate measures such as transitional provisions protecting the party’s trust, because doing so would violate the principle of protection of trust derived from the principle of the rule of law, which is a basic principle of the Constitution.” In so doing, it appears to take the position that, regardless of whether the source of the party’s trust derives from the Constitution, if it derives from statutes, orders, rules, or even ordinances, all such matters are converted into issues of constitutional violation. However, such an attitude, as pointed out above, cannot be tolerated because it destroys the boundary between judicial power and the adjudicatory power of the Constitutional Court.\\n\\nIn the past as well, issues of protection of trust under orders and rules have been dealt with merely as matters of statute, and I wish to point out that attempts to treat them as constitutional issues may also be connected with the problem of encroachment upon judicial power.\\n\\n(3) In particular, the majority opinion here raises only the effective date of the supplementary provisions of the Amended Enforcement Decree as an issue. According to Article 13-2 of the Act on the Promulgation of Statutes, etc., it is provided that “laws, Presidential Decrees, Prime Minister’s Decrees, and Ministerial Decrees directly related to restriction of rights or imposition of duties on the people shall, unless there is a special reason that they must be urgently implemented, be implemented from a date at least 30 days after the date of promulgation.” Therefore, the validity of the supplementary provisions of the Amended Enforcement Decree is a matter to be dealt with within the scope of this Act, and is not a constitutional issue but a statutory issue.\\n\\nb. On the point that the judiciary intervenes in the effective date of the Amended Enforcement Decree in this case\\n\\n(1) The majority opinion, by stating that “preparing for the examination in a manner suitable to the passing standard was sufficiently the exercise of reasonable and legitimate trust,” regards the object of protection of trust as “preparation for the examination suitable to the passing standard.” Although it is not clear what “preparation for the examination suitable to the passing standard” means, summarizing the majority opinion as a whole, it amounts to saying that “it is not permissible under the principle of protection of trust to have made the (first) examination easier to pass and then suddenly change it to a system under which passing is difficult.”\\nHowever, if the legislative notice procedure was complied with and the statutory notice period for the examination was observed, it is questionable whether this can be described as “sudden,” or, in the words of the majority opinion, whether “it could not possibly have been anticipated that it would be put into immediate effect.” Moreover, it is even more difficult to understand that failing to prepare for the examination or preparing less for it could be regarded as the object of trust protection that should be protected in law, or even in the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) The power to determine the effective date of an amended statute or regulation belongs to the person authorized to amend that statute or regulation. The authority of the legislator to determine the effective date of an amended statute or regulation is the correlative of the authority to determine the scope and content of the amended statute or regulation, and is a natural component of legislative power (Article 40 of the Constitution) and the power to enact orders and rules (Articles 75 and 95 of the Constitution).\\n\\nIn particular, as to the effective date, not the content, of a statute or regulation, it is ordinarily provided in the supplementary provisions of each statute or regulation that it shall enter into force on the date of promulgation; and laws, Presidential Decrees, Prime Minister’s Decrees, and Ministerial Decrees directly related to restriction of rights or imposition of duties on the people shall, as stated above, be implemented from a date at least 30 days after the date of promulgation. If there is no special provision determining the effective date, it is expressly provided in the Constitution and statutes that laws, Presidential Decrees, Prime Minister’s Decrees, and Ministerial Decrees take effect upon the lapse of 20 days from the date of promulgation (Article 53, paragraph (7) of the Constitution, Articles 13 and 13-2 of the Act on the Promulgation of Statutes, etc.). In addition, the National Assembly and the Executive have established systems such as legislative notice (Article 82-2 of the National Assembly Act) and administrative notice (Article 46 of the Administrative Procedures Act) to prevent unforeseen harm when statutes and regulations are enacted or amended, and legislative notice is to be carried out in accordance with the methods and procedures prescribed by the rules of the National Assembly, while the period for administrative notice is to be determined in consideration of the nature of the notice content, etc., and, unless there are special circumstances, set at 20 days or more, thereby providing their own institutional devices to prevent the implementation of statutes and regulations from being accelerated or delayed. Therefore, determining the effective date of a statute or regulation that has gone through such procedures is a matter left to the discretion of the National Assembly or the Executive. Judicial review of the effective date of a statute or regulation is not excluded, but the room for judicial intervention concerning the effective date of a statute or regulation is that much reduced, and judicial review can be justified only where there is a manifest departure from the limits of the authority to amend statutes or regulations.\\n\\n(3) Recently, judicial activism is sometimes spoken of as though it were an ideology to be pursued by the courts; however, in a state with separation of powers and a relatively clear meaning of the language of statutes and regulations in a written-law system, judicial activism may rather obscure the plain language of clear statutes and regulations, thereby undermining the rule of law and encroaching upon other powers. Therefore, I believe that the exercise of judicial power must be carried out cautiously with this aspect also taken into account."}

{"[2018DU34732]": "The grounds of appeal are to be determined (the statement in the petition of appeal submitted after the period for filing the petition of appeal has elapsed, insofar as it supplements the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. With respect to Grounds of Appeal Nos. 5 and 6 (the portion concerning the validity of the resolution of the extraordinary general meeting of members held on 2015. 12. 27. for amending the articles of association and the resolution of the general meeting of members held on 2016. 1. 14. for approval of change in the incorporation of the association in the present case)\\n\\na. The general meeting of an association is the supreme decision-making body of a redevelopment maintenance project association, and since amendments to the articles of association and the formulation or amendment of the management and disposition plan are matters to be resolved by the general meeting, the general meeting of an association has autonomy and discretion to withdraw or change the contents of a prior resolution of the general meeting by a new resolution of the general meeting in accordance with the higher statutes and the articles of association (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DU35281 rendered on 2018. 3. 13.). The former Act on the Maintenance and Improvement of Urban Areas and Dwelling Conditions for Residents (before amendment by Act No. 13912 on 2016. 1. 27.; hereinafter referred to as the “former Urban Improvement Act”) provides that “where a redevelopment maintenance project association intends to amend the articles of association concerning the association’s burden of expenses, it shall obtain approval from the Mayor/County Governor with the consent of at least two-thirds of the members, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 16(2)” (Article 20(3), Article 20(1) item 8), and provides that “the procedures, timing, and voting method for convening the general meeting shall be prescribed by the articles of association” (Article 24(6)); therefore, unless the articles of association of the association contain provisions stricter than those prescribed by the former Urban Improvement Act, which is the higher statute, with respect to the procedures for convening the general meeting or the voting method concerning the association’s burden of expenses, the quorum applicable to a resolution of the general meeting to amend the articles of association concerning the association’s burden of expenses is the approval of at least two-thirds of the members, and even if the contents of the amended articles of association directly affect the interests of a specific group such as commercial unit owners, etc., it cannot be said that Article 16(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act applies or applies by analogy.\\n\\nMeanwhile, even if there is a procedural defect such as a notice of convocation in the general meeting of an organization, if there was no hindrance whatsoever to the members’ participation in the general meeting, such procedural defect is minor and the resolution of the general meeting is valid (see Supreme Court Decision 91DA29071 rendered on 1992. 3. 27.).\\n\\nb. The court below, on the grounds stated in its reasoning, held that the fact alone that the agenda items were publicly notified and posted 14 days before the date of the general meeting, in violation of the procedure for public notice and posting of agenda items 20 days before the date of the general meeting prescribed by the articles of association in this case, cannot lead to the conclusion that the resolution of the general meeting held on 2015. 12. 27. in this case is void, and further held that, with respect to the resolution of the general meeting of members for amending the articles of association concerning the method of calculating the rights value of commercial unit members, only the provisions of Article 20(3), Article 20(1) item 8 of the former Urban Improvement Act apply, and Article 16(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act does not apply by analogy, and therefore determined that the extraordinary general meeting resolution of members held on 2015. 12. 27. and the general meeting resolution of members held on 2016. 1. 14. in this case for application for approval of change in the incorporation of the association are valid.\\n\\nc. Examining the record in accordance with the legal principles stated above, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no error in misapprehending the legal principles concerning defects in the convocation procedure of a redevelopment association or the scope of application of the quorum under Article 16(2) of the former Urban Improvement Act.\\n\\n2. With respect to Grounds of Appeal Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4 (the portion concerning whether the principle of protection of trust applies to the management and disposition plan dated 2016. 1. 20. in this case)\\n\\na. In principle, the principle of protection of trust is applied on the premise that the circumstances existing at the time when the administrative agency expressed its official view remain unchanged; therefore, where such circumstances have changed thereafter, it is difficult to regard the official view as still being a subject of reliance for the individual, and, absent special circumstances, it cannot be said that the administrative agency violates the principle of protection of trust even if it takes a disposition contrary to the expression of view (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2014DU3839 rendered on 2015. 1. 29.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, once an internal norm has been established in a redevelopment association, the members come to have trust that it will continue to exist, absent special circumstances, and thus the interest to be achieved through changing the internal norm must outweigh the interests of the members who relied on the continuation of the prior internal norm. In order to determine whether a resolution of the general meeting that changes the internal norm of the association violates the principle of protection of trust, one must comprehensively compare and balance various circumstances, such as whether there exist objective circumstances and necessity to alter the contents of the prior internal norm, what interest the association seeks to achieve thereby, to what extent the interests infringed upon the members by the change of the internal norm are worthy of protection and what the degree of infringement is, and what efforts the association made to minimize the infringement of the members’ trust in the continuation of the prior internal norm (see the above Supreme Court Decision 2016DU35281).\\n\\nb. The court below, on the grounds stated in its reasoning, held that, under the premise that in order to find that the Defendant association’s resolution of the general meeting or amendment to the articles of association contrary to its previously expressed intent, and the management and disposition plan established on that basis, violate the principle of protection of trust and are defective, the circumstances existing at the time of the prior expression of intent must not have changed by the time of the disposition and, despite that, the administrative agency must have, without reasonable grounds, taken a disposition different from the previously expressed intent and thereby seriously infringed the other party’s legal interest, the Defendant association’s adoption of a resolution of the general meeting contrary to what had been promised by the Promotion Committee and its amendment of the prior articles of association, followed by the management and disposition plan in this case, is reasonable because, after the expression of intent, the business promotion method was changed from the fixed share system to the contracting system in the course of the project, and thereby the circumstances changed so that establishing the management and disposition plan in accordance with the prior expression of intent would have a substantial impact on the interests of ordinary members as well; and further held that the interest of the commercial unit members infringed by the resolution of the general meeting or the amendment to the articles of association contrary to the prior expression of intent cannot be said to be a significant interest that can be legally enforced, and therefore determined that the management and disposition plan dated 2016. 1. 20. in this case, based on the resolutions of the general meetings of members dated 2015. 12. 27. and 2016. 1. 14. in this case, does not violate the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nc. Examining the record in accordance with the legal principles stated above, the following is determined.\\n\\n(1) In light of the wording and the circumstances of the conclusion, etc. of the agreement dated 2007. 11. 28. entered into between the Promotion Committee, the predecessor of the Defendant association, and the commercial unit members (hereinafter referred to as the “Agreement in this case”), the Agreement in this case recognizes for the commercial unit owners the right, where they directly negotiate with the contractor concerning the rights value of the commercial units and an agreement is reached, to have the agreed matters reflected in the management and disposition plan, and the Defendant association reflected the Agreement in this case in the initial articles of association at the time of approval for establishment of the association. However, since the Agreement in this case does not provide anything as to how the rights value is to be determined where the commercial unit owners and the contractor fail to reach an agreement concerning the rights value of the commercial units, it cannot be viewed as granting the commercial unit owners the right to have a rights value at the level they demand reflected in the management and disposition plan even in cases where agreement on the rights value is not smoothly reached. There are also no circumstances suggesting that the Promotion Committee, prior to concluding the Agreement in this case, gave the commercial unit owners including the Plaintiffs trust in the granting of such right.\\n\\n(2) The Agreement in this case was concluded on the premise that the redevelopment project in this case would be implemented under the fixed share system, but thereafter, as the project implementation method was changed to the contracting system, circumstances changed, such as the fact that if only the rights value of ancillary and welfare facilities, such as commercial units, is calculated higher than that of apartment housing, the apartment housing owners may suffer corresponding disadvantages. Given the characteristics of a redevelopment project that is scheduled to be implemented over a long period by numerous interested parties, if project conditions, etc. change in the course of the project, such circumstances may make it inevitable to revise the project contents, etc. accordingly.\\n\\n(3) Before formulating the draft management and disposition plan in this case, the Defendant association held several rounds of consultation with the commercial unit owners including the Plaintiffs concerning the rights value of the commercial units, but failed to reach an agreement; and there are no circumstances showing that the Defendant association engaged in the consultations in bad faith or that the Defendant association bears full responsibility for the failure to reach a final agreement.\\n\\n(4) The method of calculating the rights value for ancillary and welfare facilities, etc. in the management and disposition plan in this case, namely by arithmetic averaging the amounts appraised by two appraisal corporations, cannot be said to essentially infringe the Plaintiffs’ prior right as commercial unit owners concerning property valuation.\\n\\n(5) Taking the above circumstances together, even if the Defendant association changed the Agreement in this case and the prior articles of association accordingly, and established a management and disposition plan contrary to the Agreement in this case, it cannot be said that this violates the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\nd. Accordingly, the court below’s determination is proper, and there is no error in exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the validity of the Agreement in this case dated 2007. 11. 28., rescission of contract due to change of circumstances, the scope of application of Article 48(5) item 1(a) of the former Urban Improvement Act, or the requirements for application of the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n3. With respect to the remaining challenged portion\\n\\nThe Plaintiffs also appealed the portion of the judgment below that upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing the claim for confirmation of invalidity of the resolution for change in establishment of the association; however, they did not set forth any specific grounds of appeal therefor in the petition of appeal or the statement of grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing parties. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2022DU60011]": "We decide on the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the lower court and the record, the following facts are established.\\n\\na. Plaintiff 1 and Plaintiff 2 were born between their father, Non-Party 1, a national of the Republic of Korea, and their mother, Non-Party 2, who at the time was a national of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as \"China\"); at the time of the Plaintiffs' birth, Non-Party 1 and Non-Party 2 were not legally married.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiffs' father filed birth registrations for the Plaintiffs on June 14, 2001, and around that time Resident Registration Numbers were assigned to the Plaintiffs on the premise that they had acquired Korean nationality, and, as the Family Relations Registration Act was implemented on January 1, 2008, family relation registers for the Plaintiffs were also prepared on the premise that the Plaintiffs were nationals of the Republic of Korea.\\n\\nc. The Plaintiffs' parents filed a marriage registration on December 23, 2008; however, the competent administrative agency, on the ground that the Plaintiffs' birth registrations fell under \"birth registrations of a child born out of wedlock to a foreign mother\" and were therefore subject to correction, cancelled the Plaintiffs' family relation registers on February 13, 2009. Accordingly, the Plaintiffs' father, Non-Party 1, filed acknowledgments concerning the Plaintiffs on May 8, 2009. The Plaintiffs were entered in Non-Party 1's family relation register as Non-Party 1's children, but their nationality was indicated as China, and no separate family relation register for the Plaintiffs was prepared.\\n\\nd. In 2015 and 2017, the years in which the Plaintiffs each turned 17, Resident Registration Cards were issued to the Plaintiffs. The Plaintiffs' mother, Non-Party 2, was naturalized as a national of the Republic of Korea on February 13, 2017, but the Plaintiffs, who were minors at that time, did not undergo the nationality acquisition procedure incident to nationality acquisition prescribed in Article 8 of the Nationality Act.\\n\\ne. Meanwhile, the Immigration and Foreigners Policy Headquarters informed the Plaintiffs' parents on two occasions, on May 28, 2013 and February 8, 2017, that, on the premise that the Plaintiffs had not acquired Korean nationality, they should proceed with the nationality acquisition procedure by acknowledgment prescribed in Article 3 of the Nationality Act.\\n\\nf. After they had become adults, the Plaintiffs applied to the Defendant for a determination of nationality retention pursuant to Article 20 of the Nationality Act on January 8, 2019, but the Defendant, on the ground that the Plaintiffs were not holders of Korean nationality, rendered a determination of non-possession of nationality to the Plaintiffs on October 1, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as \"the determination in this case\").\\n\\n2. The Judgment of the Lower Court\\nThe lower court held that the determination in this case did not violate the principle of protection of trust for the following reasons. Even though Resident Registration Numbers were assigned to the Plaintiffs and family relation registers were prepared for them pursuant to the Plaintiffs' birth registrations, the family relation registers for the Plaintiffs were thereafter cancelled, the Plaintiffs' nationality was entered as China in the family relation register of the Plaintiffs' father, and the immigration administrative agency informed the Plaintiffs' parents of the need for nationality acquisition procedures for the Plaintiffs, and thus, even if there had been an official representation by the administrative agency that the Plaintiffs had acquired Korean nationality, that representation had been withdrawn, or there was attributable fault on the part of the Plaintiffs' parents who trusted that the representation was proper.\\n\\n3. The Judgment of the Supreme Court\\nHowever, the lower court's judgment is not readily acceptable for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Legal Doctrine on the Application of the Principle of Protection of Trust\\nGenerally, in legal relations under administrative law, for the principle of protection of trust to apply to an act of an administrative agency, first, the administrative agency must have made an official representation that becomes the object of trust to an individual; second, there must be no attributable fault on the part of that individual in trusting that the administrative agency's representation was proper; third, the individual must have trusted the representation and acted on the basis thereof; and fourth, as a result of the administrative agency making a disposition contrary to the aforementioned representation, the individual who trusted that representation must suffer infringement of his or her interests. When an administrative disposition satisfies these requirements, it is unlawful as an act contrary to the principle of protection of trust, unless there is a risk of seriously harming the public interest or the legitimate interests of a third party (see Supreme Court Decisions 98DU19070 dated March 9, 1999, 2004DU46 dated June 9, 2006, etc.).\\n\\nMeanwhile, in determining whether there was an official representation by an administrative agency, it is not necessarily bound by the formal allocation of authority within the administrative organization; rather, the matter must be determined substantively in light of the organizational status and duties of the person in charge, the specific circumstances leading to the relevant conduct, and the reliability thereof from the standpoint of the other party.\\n\\nb. Whether the Determination in this Case Violated the Principle of Protection of Trust\\n1) Existence of an Official Representation\\nIn light of the fact that Resident Registration Numbers and Resident Registration Cards are made public externally and constitute important grounds for inferring the lawful existence of administrative acts both internally and externally, the act by which the administrative agency assigned to the Plaintiffs Resident Registration Numbers endowed with public credibility and Resident Registration Cards accordingly should be deemed an official representation to the Plaintiffs that they had acquired Korean nationality (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DU10931 dated January 17, 2008). Therefore, even if the family relation registers for the Plaintiffs were cancelled or the Plaintiffs' parents were informed that the Plaintiffs needed to acquire nationality, as long as the Plaintiffs' resident registration remained maintained, the official representation that the Plaintiffs had acquired Korean nationality must also be deemed to have remained maintained.\\n\\n2) The Plaintiffs' Acts in Reliance on the Official Representation\\nArticle 3 of the Nationality Act provides the procedure by which a minor foreigner can acquire Korean nationality by filing a notification with the Minister of Justice when the child is acknowledged by a father who was a national of the Republic of Korea at the time of birth, and Article 8 of the Nationality Act separately provides the procedure by which a minor person who is the child of a foreigner can acquire Korean nationality incident to the naturalization permission of the father or mother.\\n\\nIf the Plaintiffs had known while they were minors that they did not hold Korean nationality, they could have held Korean nationality by following the simplified nationality acquisition procedure prescribed in Article 3 or Article 8 of the Nationality Act. However, as a result of administrative acts being repeatedly taken on the premise that the Plaintiffs held Korean nationality, the Plaintiffs, while still minors, relied thereon and became adults without proceeding with the nationality acquisition procedures under Article 3 and Article 8 of the Nationality Act.\\n\\n3) Interests of the Plaintiffs Infringed by the Determination in this Case Contrary to the Official Representation\\nThe determination in this case, contrary to the official representation made while the Plaintiffs were minors, held that the Plaintiffs, after becoming adults, did not hold Korean nationality. As described above, as a result of giving the Plaintiffs the trust that they held Korean nationality while they were minors and then, once they became adults, making a disposition contrary thereto, the Plaintiffs, now just adults, lost the opportunity to acquire nationality easily under Article 3 and Article 8 of the Nationality Act.\\n\\nEven if the adult Plaintiffs could acquire Korean nationality through the special naturalization procedure prescribed in Article 7 of the Nationality Act, during the period required to obtain special naturalization they would inevitably have to live in the Republic of Korea with unstable status, and moreover, because special naturalization is an act in which the administrative agency has broad discretion (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2018DO6913 dated November 29, 2018), the possibility that naturalization may not be permitted for the Plaintiffs depending on the administrative agency's discretion cannot be ruled out. Nationality is the most fundamental prerequisite for a national of the Republic of Korea to enjoy rights guaranteed by the Constitution and laws. Through the determination in this case, the Plaintiffs were denied the Korean nationality they believed they had held throughout their lives and were placed in a situation where whether they had acquired that nationality became unstable, and as a result they suffered a serious disadvantage in that even the qualification to stay in the Republic of Korea, where they were born and raised, was altered, thereby shaking the foundation of the lives they had maintained throughout their lives.\\n\\n4) Existence of Attributable Fault\\nThe Plaintiffs' parents were negligent in not proceeding with the nationality acquisition procedures for the Plaintiffs until the Plaintiffs became adults, even though the family relation register for the Plaintiffs had been closed and they had been informed by the Immigration and Foreigners Policy Headquarters that the Plaintiffs needed to acquire nationality. However, insofar as there is no material to find that the same notification was also made to the Plaintiffs themselves, rather than only to their parents, it is difficult to deem that the Plaintiffs knew that they had not acquired Korean nationality or that they did not know of this through gross negligence. Rather, as Resident Registration Cards were issued to the Plaintiffs in the year each of them turned 17, it appears that the Plaintiffs reasonably trusted, until becoming adults, that they had held Korean nationality.\\n\\nParents of minors must exercise parental authority with the child's welfare as the foremost consideration (see Article 912 of the Civil Act). If, as a result of the Plaintiffs' parents not properly exercising parental authority, the Plaintiffs, who bear no attributable fault, are pushed into a situation where the question whether they hold nationality becomes unstable immediately after becoming adults, this does not accord with the purpose of the legal representative system, which seeks to protect the interests of minors first. Since it is difficult to find attributable fault in the Plaintiffs' trust that they had acquired Korean nationality, the determination in this case made contrary to the Plaintiffs' trust should be deemed to violate the principle of protection of trust.\\n\\n5) Conclusion on the Above\\nNevertheless, the lower court held that the determination in this case did not contravene the principle of protection of trust merely because the official representation that the Plaintiffs had acquired nationality had been entirely withdrawn, or because the Plaintiffs' parents, who trusted such official representation, bore attributable fault. The lower court's judgment contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal doctrine concerning the criteria for determining the existence of an official representation and attributable fault.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nTherefore, the judgment of the lower court is reversed, and the case is remanded to the lower court for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the case."}

question:
Which combination correctly matches the following explanations concerning State compensation liability as correct (○) and incorrect (X)? (If there is a dispute, according to precedents)

(a) Where, in the course of executing public administrative affairs entrusted by the State, an officer or employee of a public juridical person or its servant violates laws and regulations intentionally or through negligence and thereby causes damage to another person, such officer or employee of the public juridical person or its servant qualifies as a public official prescribed in Article 2 of the State Compensation Act, and therefore bears liability for compensation only where there is intent or gross negligence.

(b) The proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act concerning soldiers, civilian military employees, and others applies, regardless of whether the person has actually exercised the right or is exercising the right, so long as a compensation system is provided for in another statute and, the conditions prescribed in that statute having been met, the right to receive compensation has arisen for the persons listed in the said proviso.

(c) Where the State or a local government, in the course of carrying out administrative procedures, committed an illegality by failing to guarantee procedural rights such as residents’ submission of opinions, and thereafter corrected this and carried out the procedure again, if there are special circumstances from which it may be deemed that even such measures still leave mental suffering resulting from the infringement of the residents’ procedural rights, the State or the local government is liable to compensate for the damage caused by such mental suffering, and, at this time, the burden of allegation and proof as to the existence of special circumstances lies with the residents claiming such compensation.

(d) A public structure cannot be said to be defective merely because it does not possess a high degree of safety sufficient to maintain a state of complete perfection in its installation and management; it is sufficient if it possesses relative safety expected from the common-sense and orderly use of the public structure by users.

supporting_precedents: {"[2015DA221668]": "We examine the grounds of appeal (written briefs, etc. submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal, to the extent that they supplement it).\\n\\n1. Whether liability for damages arising from infringement of residents’ right to participate in administrative procedures is recognized (Grounds of appeal by the Defendant)\\n\\na. Case outline\\n\\nAccording to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\n(1) The Defendant, upon the approaching expiration of the period of use of a waste landfill located in Boseong-gun, Jeollanam-do (address 1 omitted), promoted and carried out, from around August 2006, a project to install a waste disposal facility (hereinafter referred to as “the waste landfill at issue”) in Boseong-gun, Jeollanam-do (address 2 omitted), and, around 2009. 11. 24., filed a notice of commencement of use with the Governor of Jeollanam-do and thereafter operated the waste landfill at issue. The Plaintiff (selected party, hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiff”) and selected person Nonparty 1 (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the Plaintiff, etc.”) are persons residing in a village approximately 1.9 km in a straight line from the waste landfill at issue.\\n\\n(2) Around 2007. 12. 4., the Defendant applied to the Governor of Jeollanam-do for approval of the installation of the waste landfill at issue. The working-level official of Jeollanam-do requested that the Defendant supplement the related documents, such as the notice of decision and public notice of the site selection plan and the documents concerning the formation of the Site Selection Committee and the decision and public notice of the site selection, on the ground that the waste landfill at issue constituted a facility included among those subject to the site selection plan under the relevant statutes and regulations.\\n\\n(3) In connection with the project to install the waste landfill at issue, the Defendant requested the Boseong-gun Council to recommend two county council members for the formation of the Site Selection Committee and the resident support consultative body, and received the recommendation notice. Nevertheless, without going through any procedure regarding the formation of the Site Selection Committee and site selection, on 2008. 1. 2., the Defendant determined the site of the waste landfill at issue and issued a “Decision and Public Notice of the Site of the Boseong-gun Rural Waste Integrated Disposal Facility,” setting the inspection period for the related drawings and the period for submitting residents’ opinions from 2008. 1. 2. to 2008. 2. 1.\\n\\n(4) Thereafter, Nonparty 2, a public official in charge of the Defendant, forged related documents in early February 2008, including the “Notice of Decision and Public Notice of the Site Selection Plan for the Boseong-gun Rural Waste Integrated Disposal Facility,” the “recommendation letter from resident representatives” recommending experts to form the Site Selection Committee, the official document “Notice of a Meeting of the Rural Waste Integrated Disposal Facility Site Selection Committee,” and the minutes of the Site Selection Committee meeting. Around 2008. 2. 14., the Defendant submitted the forged documents as above to the Governor of Jeollanam-do and re-applied for approval of the installation of the waste landfill at issue. Around 2008. 2. 20., the Governor of Jeollanam-do approved the installation of the waste landfill at issue, together with notice to the Defendant that the installation plan for the waste landfill at issue was approved.\\n\\n(5) Nonparty 2 was indicted on charges including forgery of official documents, was convicted, and the judgment became final and conclusive.\\n\\n(6) The Plaintiff, etc. claimed damages for consolation money against the Defendant on the ground that, by failing to follow the administrative procedures that should be observed in the process of installing the waste landfill at issue, such as the formation of the Site Selection Committee and the resident support consultative body required by the relevant statutes and regulations and the decision and public notice of the surrounding impact area of the waste disposal facility, the Defendant infringed the Plaintiff, etc.’s right to participate in administrative procedures as residents of the surrounding impact area, and further caused the Plaintiff, etc. mental damage through tortious conduct that infringed their right to live in a pleasant environment and the like by operating the waste landfill at issue in an unsound manner.\\n\\nb. The judgment below and the issue\\n\\nThe court below accepted the Plaintiff, etc.’s argument for the following reasons and held that the Defendant is under an obligation to pay consolation money to the Plaintiff, etc. The relevant statutes and regulations applicable to this case are intended to directly protect the interests of each resident, but the Defendant violated those provisions and completely excluded the Plaintiff, etc., who are residents of the area where the waste landfill at issue was to be installed, from having the opportunity to participate in the site selection decision-making process. The Defendant’s public official in charge caused mental suffering to the Plaintiff, etc. by forging the related official documents, etc. as if the Defendant had gone through all the procedures prescribed by statute.\\n\\nThe issue is whether the Defendant, a local government, bears liability for compensation for mental damage under Article 2 of the State Compensation Act on the ground, inter alia, that the Defendant’s public official committed unlawful acts, such as failing to go through the procedure for collecting residents’ opinions prescribed by the relevant statutes and regulations in connection with the installation of the waste landfill at issue.\\n\\nc. Whether liability for damages arising from infringement of residents’ right to participate in administrative procedures is recognized and the scope of such recognition\\n\\n(1) The “Act on the Promotion of the Installation of Waste Disposal Facilities and Support for Surrounding Areas” (hereinafter referred to as the “Waste Disposal Facilities Promotion Act”) aims to promote environmental preservation and improve the quality of national life by facilitating the installation of waste disposal facilities and promoting the welfare of residents through the promotion of securing sites for waste disposal facilities and support for residents in the surrounding areas (Article 1). Article 9(3) of the Waste Disposal Facilities Promotion Act provides that, “Where the installing agency of a waste disposal facility publicly notifies the site selection plan for the waste disposal facility, it shall, without delay, establish a Site Selection Committee with the participation of resident representatives and have the committee select the site of the waste disposal facility.” According to Article 7 [Attached Table 1] of the former Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Promotion of the Installation of Waste Disposal Facilities and Support for Surrounding Areas (as amended by Presidential Decree No. 21543 on 2009. 6. 16., hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree”), resident representatives shall be selected by the relevant city, county, or district council from among the residents residing in the city, county, or district where the relevant waste disposal facility is to be located, but at least one resident representative residing in the candidate site shall be included, and resident representatives have the authority to recommend expert members. The Site Selection Committee so constituted deliberates and resolves on “the selection and change of the site of the waste disposal facility, whether a feasibility study of the candidate site is necessary, whether a public hearing or briefing session is to be held,” etc. (Article 11(1) of the Enforcement Decree), and local residents may inspect the process and results of the feasibility study conducted by the Site Selection Committee and then submit their opinions thereon to the Site Selection Committee (Article 10 of the Enforcement Decree).\\n\\nThe Site Selection Committee is the decision-making body for selecting the site of a waste disposal facility. The purpose of requiring that the Site Selection Committee include a certain number or more of resident representatives and experts recommended by resident representatives, and of allowing residents to submit opinions to the Site Selection Committee, is to ensure that the interests and views of residents are substantially represented in the site selection procedure for waste disposal facilities, thereby preventing the rights of residents from being unfairly infringed by the local government’s arbitrary exercise of power or by the imprudent decisions of a small number of resident representatives, and to secure democratization and trust in administration (see Supreme Court decision 2003DO7118 rendered on 2003. 11. 14., Supreme Court decision 2006DO20150 rendered on 2007. 4. 12., etc.).\\n\\nAs such, from the stage of site selection onward, substantive resident participation is guaranteed, and after the site of the waste disposal facility is selected and the installation plan for the waste disposal facility is publicly notified, the surrounding impact area that will be affected environmentally by the installation and operation of the waste disposal facility is determined, and in that process as well, opportunities for resident participation are guaranteed through the formation and activities of the resident support consultative body (Articles 17 and 17-2 of the Waste Disposal Facilities Promotion Act).\\n\\n(2) In the course of the State or a local government implementing a public project, residents in the vicinity of the project site may have an opportunity to exercise procedural rights prescribed by statute, such as participation in administrative procedures through the submission of opinions, and thereby protect private interests such as environmental rights or property rights. However, what the statutes and regulations prescribe regarding residents’ participation in administrative procedures is, in substance, only to guarantee residents an opportunity to reflect their own will and interests, secure fairness, transparency, and reliability in administration, and protect the rights and interests of the people; the right to participate in administrative procedures itself does not possess the nature of a private right. Since administrative procedures, as such, are not independently meaningful in and of themselves but are highly significant as a public-law means of ensuring fairness and propriety in administration, it cannot be immediately concluded that the State or a local government bears an obligation to compensate residents for mental damage merely because residents were temporarily deprived of the right to participate in administrative procedures, without examining whether the relevant administrative disposition was established or whether it was null and void or revoked.\\n\\nIn light of the nature and content, etc. of such procedural rights, even if the State or a local government committed an illegality in the course of conducting administrative procedures by failing to guarantee residents’ procedural rights such as submission of opinions, if it later corrects the defect and conducts the procedure anew, or if the process does not ultimately reach the stage of an administrative disposition, or if the disposition is revoked ex officio or withdrawn, or if a judgment revoking the disposition or confirming its nullity becomes final and conclusive through administrative litigation, the purpose of residents’ exercise of procedural rights to protect private interests such as environmental rights or property rights is substantially achieved; accordingly, unless there are special circumstances, compensation for mental suffering arising from infringement of procedural rights is not recognized. However, if there are special circumstances under which it can still be deemed that mental suffering caused by the infringement of residents’ procedural rights remains even after such measures, the State or local government is liable to compensate for the damage caused by such mental suffering. At this time, the burden of alleging and proving the existence of special circumstances rests with the residents claiming such compensation, and whether special circumstances exist must be determined by comprehensively considering the purpose of guaranteeing residents the right to participate in administrative procedures, the circumstances and degree of infringement of the right to participate in administrative procedures, and the progress of implementation of the project subject to the relevant administrative procedure.\\n\\n(3) Examining the following circumstances ascertainable from the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record in light of the foregoing legal principles, there is room to recognize special circumstances under which residents near the waste landfill at issue suffered mental distress due to the Defendant’s unlawful conduct, and such mental distress of the residents can still be deemed to remain even if the nullity of the relevant administrative disposition has been confirmed.\\n\\n(a) On 2018. 5. 31., after the waste landfill at issue had been installed, a judgment was rendered confirming the nullity of the disposition deciding and publicly notifying the site of the waste landfill at issue and the disposition approving the installation plan of the waste landfill at issue on the ground that the defect of not constituting the Site Selection Committee pursuant to the relevant statutes and regulations, including the Waste Disposal Facilities Promotion Act, was serious and objectively obvious (Gwangju District Court decision 2015GUHAP912 rendered on 2018. 5. 31.).
