This judgment became final and conclusive as rendered, because the parties did not appeal.\\n\\n(b) In light of the circumstances that the Defendant, upon receiving a request from the working-level official of Jeollanam-do to supplement the procedures such as the formation of the Site Selection Committee, requested recommendation of county council members from the Boseong-gun Council in order to form the Site Selection Committee, it may be deemed that the Defendant’s public official in charge clearly recognized that the site of the waste landfill at issue had to be decided through the formation and operation of the Site Selection Committee with the participation of resident representatives, etc. Nevertheless, the Defendant’s public official in charge forged related documents as if such procedures had been completed and submitted those documents to the Governor of Jeollanam-do to apply for approval of the installation of the waste landfill at issue, while excluding the formation of the Site Selection Committee and the site-selection process through that committee. Such conduct by the Defendant’s public official clearly has fault and is conduct that is unacceptable under social norms, as it completely excluded the opportunity of local residents to reflect their own will and interests regarding the installation of the waste landfill at issue and thereby nullified the legislative intent of the relevant provisions.\\n\\n(c) The waste landfill at issue was installed and used from around November 2009. However, the Defendant operated the waste landfill at issue in an unsound manner, including by leaving for a long time in the landfill the vinyl and tires, combustible materials used to cover the landfill area under the roof of the waste landfill at issue that had been lost by a typhoon, even after the roof restoration work had been completed.\\n\\n(4) However, the judgment below, which held that the Defendant is liable for damages to the Plaintiff, etc., cannot be accepted as is for the following reasons.\\n\\n(a) The court below stated that the Defendant’s series of acts of installing the waste landfill at issue by completely excluding residents of the surrounding impact area from the opportunity to participate in the site selection decision-making process and by forging related documents constituted a tort, and that the time of the tort was, at the latest, around 2008. 2. 14., when the Defendant forged the related documents and applied for approval of the installation of the waste landfill at issue. If so, the persons who suffered mental distress due to the Defendant’s tort are, at minimum, limited to those who were able to participate in the site selection decision-making process but were deprived of that opportunity, namely, those who resided in the surrounding impact area of the waste landfill at issue at the time of the tort.\\n\\n(b) In general, in an action for damages arising from a tort, the burden of proving the occurrence of damage and the causal relationship between the injurious act and the occurrence of damage lies with the claimant, i.e., the victim (see Supreme Court decision 2012DA68613 rendered on 2014. 7. 24.). In this case, in which the Plaintiff, etc. seek damages from the Defendant on the ground that their right to participate in administrative procedures, etc. was infringed, the fact that the Plaintiff, etc. were residents of the relevant area at the time the site of the waste landfill at issue was determined should have been alleged and proved by the Plaintiff, etc.\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Plaintiff, etc. did not expressly allege or submit evidence that they were residents of the relevant area at the time the site of the waste landfill at issue was determined and approval for its installation was applied for.\\n\\n(5) Nevertheless, without exercising the right to clarify by confirming whether the Plaintiff, etc. were residents of the relevant area even at the time the site selection decision-making process for the waste landfill at issue was underway and urging proof thereof, the court below recognized liability for damages for the Plaintiff, etc.’s mental suffering on the ground that the Defendant completely excluded the Plaintiff, etc. from the opportunity to participate in the site selection decision-making process. The judgment below contains an error affecting the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the State Compensation Act liability arising from infringement of residents’ right to participate in administrative procedures and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well taken.\\n\\n2. Whether tort liability arising from infringement of environmental rights and infringement of the right to safe passage concerning the access road is recognized (Grounds of appeal by the Plaintiff)\\n\\nThe court below did not accept the Plaintiff, etc.’s argument for damages liability on this point on the ground that, even if the Defendant had operated the waste landfill at issue in an unsound manner or the width of the access road leading to the waste landfill at issue was narrow and cracks and settlement occurred, there was no evidence to recognize that concrete and direct damage thereby arose to the Plaintiff, etc.\\n\\nExamining the reasons stated in the judgment below in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the judgment below does not contain an error affecting the conclusion of the judgment by, as asserted in the grounds of appeal, failing to conduct the necessary examination, thereby exceeding the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in violation of the rules of logic and experience, or by misapprehending the legal principles regarding the establishment of a tort, or by omitting a determination.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nWithout addressing the grounds of appeal concerning the Plaintiff’s amount of damages, we reverse the portion of the judgment below concerning the claim for damages arising from infringement of the right to participate in administrative procedures and remand this part of the case to the court below for further trial and determination; and as for the Plaintiff’s appeal concerning the portion of the claim for damages arising from infringement of environmental rights and infringement of the right to safe passage concerning the access road, since it is without merit, we dismiss it. Accordingly, by unanimous opinion of the Justices, the judgment is rendered as stated in the order.\\n\\n[Appendix] List of selected persons: omitted"}

{"[2015DA226137]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. a. Article 29(2) of the Constitution provides, “A soldier, military civilian employee, police public official, or other person prescribed by Act may not claim compensation from the State or a public entity, in addition to compensation prescribed by Act, for damage suffered in connection with the performance of duties such as combat or training,” and the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act based thereon provides, “Where a soldier, military civilian employee, police public official, or member of the Local Reserve Forces dies in action, dies on duty, or suffers injury or disease in connection with the performance of duties such as combat or training, and the person himself/herself or his/her bereaved family members are able to receive compensation such as disaster compensation, survivor pension, or disability pension under other statutes, no claim for damages under this Act or the Civil Act may be made.”\\n\\nThe legislative intent of Article 29(2) of the Constitution and the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act is that the State or a public entity (hereinafter referred to as “the State, etc.”) operates a damage-compensation system for soldiers, military civilian employees, police public officials, or members of the Local Reserve Forces (hereinafter referred to as “soldiers, etc.”) who perform dangerous duties, thereby ensuring that soldiers, etc. who suffer damage in connection with the performance of duties may, through a simple compensation procedure, receive certain and uniform damage compensation without the risk of insolvency, irrespective of whether they were at fault or the degree thereof; and, in return, by preventing injured soldiers, etc. from claiming damages from the State, etc. for torts committed in the performance of official duties by public officials, it aims to prevent excessive fiscal expenditure and imbalance that may arise from both compensation and indemnification being made by the State, etc. for the same damage to soldiers, etc., and also to prevent the harms arising from litigation concerning the official misconduct of soldiers, etc., who are the wrongdoers, and soldiers, etc., who are the victims (see Supreme Court en banc Decision dated 2001. 2. 15., 96DA42420).\\n\\nAs such, the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act is a provision that absolutely excludes the very right of soldiers, etc., who are the persons enumerated in the above statutory provision, to claim damages under the State Compensation Act or the Civil Act against the State where they have died in action, died on duty, or suffered injury or disease in connection with the performance of duties such as combat or training, in order to prohibit double compensation, if a separate compensation system such as disaster compensation, survivor pension, disability pension, etc. has been established; accordingly, they may not exercise a claim for damages against the State (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1992. 2. 11., 91DA12738, etc.). Therefore, once a compensation system is prescribed in another statute, and the conditions prescribed in that statute are satisfied so that a right to receive compensation arises for soldiers, etc., the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act must be deemed applicable, regardless of whether the soldiers, etc. have actually exercised that right or are exercising that right (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2002. 5. 10., 2000DA39735, etc.).\\n\\nAnd compensation for fallen soldiers and police officers, etc. under the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, and compensation for soldiers and police officers who died from a disaster, etc. under the Act on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans’ Compensation, constitute “compensation under other statutes” as provided in the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act (see Supreme Court Decision dated 1993. 5. 14., 92DA33145, etc.).\\n\\nb. Meanwhile, Article 12 of the Supplementary Provisions of the Act on the Honorable Treatment and Support of Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, as amended by Act No. 11041 on 2011. 9. 15. and enforced on 2012. 7. 1. (hereinafter referred to as the “Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State,” and the version before amendment by that Act as the “Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State”), provides, as a transitional measure concerning registration, “A person who, as of the enforcement of this Act, is registered as a person of distinguished services to the State and his/her bereaved family or family member pursuant to the former provisions (including a person registered pursuant to paragraph (2)) shall be deemed to have been registered as a person of distinguished services to the State and his/her bereaved family or family member under this Act.” (paragraph (1)), while it provides, “With respect to registration of a person who, as of the enforcement of this Act, has applied for registration to become a person of distinguished services to the State and his/her bereaved family or family member pursuant to the former provisions, and a person who falls under former Article 73-2, the former provisions shall apply.” (paragraph (2)); and Article 19 of the above Supplementary Provisions, as a transitional measure concerning compensation for soldiers and police officers equivalent to persons of distinguished services to the State, provides, “With respect to compensation for a person who, as of the enforcement of this Act, is registered as a person falling under former Article 73-2 (including a person registered pursuant to Article 12(2) of the Supplementary Provisions), the former provisions shall apply notwithstanding the amended provisions of Article 73-2.”\\n\\nAnd Article 4 of the Act on Support for Persons Eligible for Veterans’ Compensation, enacted by Act No. 11042 on 2011. 9. 15. and enforced on 2012. 7. 1. (hereinafter referred to as the “Veterans’ Compensation Act”), provides that a person who wishes to become a person eligible for veterans’ compensation, his/her bereaved family, or family member shall apply for registration to the head of the Office of Patriots and Veterans Affairs, as prescribed by Presidential Decree (paragraph (1)); and it provides that, with respect to a person who applies for registration under that Act in order to become a person of distinguished services to the State as prescribed in the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, the application for registration shall be deemed to have been filed under Article 4(1) of the Veterans’ Compensation Act on the date on which the application was made (paragraph (2)).\\n\\n2. The court below, after comprehensively considering the facts as found in the judgment, including the fact that the deceased person concerned enlisted as a candidate for a naval noncommissioned officer and was commissioned as a sergeant, and, after being commissioned, was diagnosed with severe depression and, while serving as the chief engineer of the vessel at issue, took his own life between 2011. 3. 27. and the following day while under intensified stress from excessive workload, and the fact that the Plaintiffs, who were the parents of the deceased person concerned, inherited the deceased person concerned, determined that although urgent measures were necessary for the deceased person’s depression, the superior officer of the deceased person or the commander of the unit to which the deceased person belonged was negligent in failing to fulfill the duty to protect the deceased person, and that a proximate causal relationship could be recognized between such negligence and the deceased person’s suicide; then, (2) since the deceased person concerned died before the enforcement of the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, it determined that whether the deceased person concerned fell under a person of distinguished services to the State or a person eligible for compensation equivalent to a person of distinguished services to the State as prescribed in former Article 73-2 of the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State (hereinafter referred to as a “person eligible for support”) must be determined under the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State; and, (3) on the basis of the circumstances as found in the judgment, it recognized that the Plaintiffs fell under persons eligible for support as prescribed in the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, but that there was no evidence to recognize that the Plaintiffs had been registered as persons eligible for support or had applied for such registration as of the enforcement of the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, and therefore recognized that they could not receive compensation as persons eligible for support; and, (4) rejected the Defendant’s argument that the Plaintiffs could not claim damages against the State pursuant to the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act.\\n\\n3. However, in light of the legal principles and relevant provisions set forth above, (1) if, as determined by the court below, it is not recognized that the Plaintiffs applied for registration under the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State as of the enforcement of the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State, or that the deceased person concerned and the Plaintiffs were registered as persons of distinguished services to the State or persons eligible for support and their bereaved family members, then whether the Plaintiffs fall under the case of “being able to receive compensation under other statutes” as provided in the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act should be determined not under the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State but under the provisions of the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State and the Veterans’ Compensation Act; and (2) if the Plaintiffs satisfy the requirements prescribed in the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State or the Veterans’ Compensation Act and a right to receive compensation arises, then, unless special circumstances exist, even if they did not actually exercise that right by, for example, applying for registration under each Act, the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act must be deemed applicable, and the Plaintiffs may not exercise a claim for damages against the State.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below should have determined whether the deceased person concerned fell under a fallen soldier or police officer, etc. prescribed in the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State or under a soldier or police officer, etc. who died from a disaster, etc. prescribed in the Veterans’ Compensation Act, and thereby whether the Plaintiffs acquired a right to claim compensation thereunder, and through such examination, should have determined whether the Plaintiffs could not exercise a claim for damages against the Defendant pursuant to the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act.\\n\\n4. Nevertheless, the court below, without sufficiently examining whether the Plaintiffs could receive compensation under other statutes, held outright that, solely because the Plaintiffs were not registered as persons eligible for support under the Former Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State or did not apply for such registration, the proviso to Article 2(1) of the State Compensation Act did not apply and they could exercise a claim for state compensation; in so doing, the court below erred in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the prohibition of double compensation under the State Compensation Act and the Amended Act on Persons of Distinguished Services to the State and the Veterans’ Compensation Act, and failed to conduct the necessary examination, thereby affecting the judgment. The ground of appeal raising this point is well-founded.\\n\\n5. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision."}

{"[2019DA260197]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the Case and Issues\\n\\na. According to the reasoning of the judgment below, the following circumstances may be found.\\n\\n(1) The Plaintiff completed the Judicial Research and Training Institute as the 35th class on January 31, 2006, and applied to the Defendant Korean Bar Association (hereinafter referred to as the “Defendant Association”) for initial lawyer registration as a member of the Seoul Bar Association. On March 9, 2006, the Plaintiff completed lawyer registration and had been engaging in the practice of law, when the Plaintiff was found guilty of the crime of forgery of an official document for altering a court’s certificate of monetary deposit, was sentenced to a judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence (suspended sentence: imprisonment for 6 months), and on September 15, 2015, the above judgment became final and conclusive. Accordingly, the Defendant Association, on September 22, 2015, issued a disposition canceling the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration pursuant to Article 18(1)2 of the Attorney-at-Law Act.\\n\\n(2) After the lapse of the “2-year period of disqualification from lawyer registration following a judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence” prescribed in Article 5(3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, the Plaintiff submitted an application for lawyer registration to the Seoul Bar Association on September 19, 2017, attaching only a certificate of finality of the above judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence and not attaching a criminal record inquiry certificate at that time.\\n\\n(3) On October 13, 2017, the Seoul Bar Association sent the Defendant Association the Plaintiff’s registration application, attaching an opinion stating that “since 2 years had elapsed after the judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence against the Plaintiff became final and conclusive on September 15, 2015, there is no ground for refusal of registration against the Plaintiff, and therefore it is appropriate to register the Plaintiff as a lawyer.”\\n\\n(4) Defendant 2, the head of the Defendant Association, on October 18, 2017, on the premise that there existed grounds for refusal of registration as prescribed in Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, referred the question of whether to register the Plaintiff as a lawyer to the agenda of the Defendant Association’s Registration Review Committee.\\n\\n(5) At the review dates held on November 21, 2017 and December 11, 2017, the Registration Review Committee required the Plaintiff to submit copies of the investigative records relating to the above crime of forgery of an official document and examined the circumstances of the crime and the existence or nonexistence of additional offenses; and, even reviewed whether the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration could be refused by applying Article 8(1)4 of the Attorney-at-Law Act on the ground that the Plaintiff was “unethical” (as will be seen below, this provision is inapplicable to the Plaintiff because it constitutes a ground for refusal of lawyer registration for a person who served as a public official and thereafter retired). Ultimately, however, the Committee resolved to the effect that the Plaintiff had no grounds for refusal of registration under Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act and that the application for lawyer registration should be accepted. Accordingly, the Defendant Association completed the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration on December 12, 2017. During this registration review process, neither Defendant 2, who decided to refer the matter to the agenda, nor the Registration Review Committee, which reviewed the agenda, requested the Plaintiff to submit a criminal record inquiry certificate in order to verify whether the Plaintiff had received a final and conclusive judgment of conviction for any crime other than the above crime of forgery of an official document.\\n\\n(6) The Plaintiff filed this action asserting that, although the Defendant Association had a duty to immediately accept the Plaintiff’s application for lawyer registration and complete registration because there were no grounds for refusal of registration prescribed in Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, Defendant 2’s act of referring the question of whether to register the Plaintiff as a lawyer to the Registration Review Committee was unlawful; that as a result, the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration was delayed for approximately 2 months, causing the Plaintiff pecuniary damage in that the Plaintiff was unable to engage in the practice of law during that period; and that because the Plaintiff suffered mental distress due to the improper review procedure of the Registration Review Committee, Defendant 2, as a tortfeasor, and the Defendant Association, pursuant to Article 35 of the Civil Act, which provides for a juristic person’s liability for tortious acts of its organ, were jointly and severally liable to compensate the Plaintiff for lost earnings in the amount of 12,829,520 won and solatium in the amount of 3,000,000 won.\\n\\nb. The issues in this case are: (1) whether the response or conduct of Defendant 2, etc. in the process of reviewing the Plaintiff’s application for lawyer registration constitutes unlawful execution of duties that has lost objective justification, thereby establishing the Defendant Association’s liability to compensate for damages arising from the delay in the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration, and, in connection therewith, whether intent or gross negligence may be recognized on the part of Defendant 2; and (2) if the Defendant Association’s liability for damages is recognized, whether the scope of such damages includes damages equivalent to the Plaintiff’s lost earnings.\\n\\n2. The Holding of the Lower Court\\n\\na. Claim against the Defendant Association\\n\\n(1) Whether liability for damages is recognized\\n\\nThe court below, for the following reasons, recognized the Defendant Association’s liability for damages to the Plaintiff, holding that Defendant 2 was negligent in referring to the Registration Review Committee the agenda of refusal of registration against the Plaintiff merely on the basis of simple suspicion even though the Plaintiff did not fall under any of the grounds for refusal of lawyer registration prescribed by law.\\n\\n① If the head of the Defendant Association were permitted to refer all applications for registration to the Registration Review Committee merely on the basis of a vague suspicion that an applicant for lawyer registration might have some other disqualification, this would run contrary to the purport of the Attorney-at-Law Act, which in principle requires registration procedures to be carried out without delay for applications for lawyer registration made through a local bar association, while requiring review by the Registration Review Committee only when the application falls under a ground for refusal specifically prescribed by law.\\n\\n② Whether a certain period after the pronouncement and execution of a sentence has elapsed is a matter of simple fact, and Defendant 2 could easily have verified it by directly obtaining from the Plaintiff a criminal record inquiry certificate or by having the competent standing director, etc. investigate it, but no such measure was taken at all.\\n\\n③ Furthermore, in this case, apart from the fact that the Plaintiff had received a judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence for the crime of forgery of an official document, there appears to have been no other related additional offenses concerning the Plaintiff, nor any reasonable basis or special circumstance to suspect that, despite such offenses, the Plaintiff concealed them and proceeded to file the present lawyer registration application.\\n\\n(2) Scope of damages\\n\\nDue to Defendant 2’s negligence, the Plaintiff had to respond to the registration review procedure, which entailed attendance before the Committee, statements of opinion, and submission of materials; and it is apparent by the rule of experience that the Plaintiff would have suffered mental distress in the process, so the Defendant Association is obligated to pay 3,000,000 won in solatium.\\n\\nHowever, since the Defendant Association completed the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration within the “3 months from the date of application for registration” prescribed in Article 8(3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, it cannot be said that the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration was unjustifiably delayed, and therefore the Plaintiff’s claim for compensation for lost earnings lacks merit.\\n\\nb. Claim against Defendant 2\\n\\nThe court below denied Defendant 2’s liability for damages to the Plaintiff for the following reasons.\\n\\nDefendant 2’s act of referring the agenda of refusal of the Plaintiff’s registration to the Registration Review Committee was an internal, intra-organizational act performed by the head of the Defendant Association, which was entrusted under the Attorney-at-Law Act with authority to process affairs concerning guidance and supervision of lawyers. Since there were no special circumstances indicating that such act exceeded the scope of ordinary acts within the scope of duties, the injured party, the Plaintiff, may only claim damages against the Defendant Association, which is the external legal subject, and may not directly claim damages against Defendant 2 individually, who is the person in charge of the organ.\\n\\n3. The Supreme Court’s Holding\\n\\nAlthough the part of the court below’s judgment recognizing the Defendant Association’s liability to pay solatium is acceptable, the part denying the Defendant Association’s liability to pay lost earnings and the reasons given in denying Defendant 2’s liability for damages are difficult to accept as they stand for the following reasons.\\n\\na. Legal status of the Defendants and legal principles concerning state compensation liability\\n\\n(1) Where, in the course of executing public administrative affairs entrusted by the State to a public juristic person, an executive officer or employee of the public juristic person intentionally or negligently violates the law and thereby causes damage to another, the public juristic person bears liability to compensate in its capacity as the administrative subject of the entrusted public administrative affairs; however, the executive officer or employee of the public juristic person is a person who performed public duties in a substantive sense and thus falls under the public official prescribed in Article 2 of the State Compensation Act, and accordingly bears liability to compensate only where there is intent or gross negligence, and is exempt from liability where there is slight negligence (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DA82950, 82967 dated January 28, 2010, etc.). Meanwhile, gross negligence of a public official means a state of marked lack of care that is close to intent, such as where, even without the degree of reasonable care ordinarily required of a public official, the official nevertheless carelessly overlooks a situation in which an unlawful or harmful result could easily have been foreseen with even slight attention (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DA34521 dated September 8, 2011, etc.).\\n\\n(2) The Defendant Association is a public juristic person established under the Attorney-at-Law Act for the purpose of handling affairs concerning guidance and supervision of lawyers and local bar associations, and lawyer registration constitutes a public administrative affair entrusted to and performed by the Defendant Association from the State pursuant to the Attorney-at-Law Act (see Constitutional Court Full Bench Decision 2017HEONMA759 dated November 28, 2019). Accordingly, Defendant 2, as the head of the Defendant Association, falls under the public official prescribed in Article 2 of the State Compensation Act within the scope of performing the “affairs concerning lawyer registration,” which are public administrative affairs entrusted by the State.\\n\\nb. Legal principles concerning lawyer registration\\n\\n(1) Lawyer registration is part of a “qualification system” that, after the legislature has comprehensively restricted the constitutionally guaranteed freedom to choose an occupation by statute enacted for the public interest, restores the freedom to choose an occupation only to those possessing certain qualifications, and is a system that enables a person to lawfully engage in the occupation of lawyer by examining whether the person possesses the qualifications prescribed by statute and registering in the roster those found to possess such qualifications (see Constitutional Court Full Bench Decision 2017HEONMA759 dated November 28, 2019).\\n\\n(2) The Attorney-at-Law Act prescribes the qualifications of lawyers in Article 4 and the grounds for disqualification of lawyers in Article 5, while in Article 7 it provides that a person who wishes to commence practice as a lawyer must apply for registration through a local bar association to the Defendant Association (paragraphs (1) and (2)); the local bar association may, upon receiving the application for registration, attach an opinion on whether the lawyer is qualified (paragraph (3)); and the Defendant Association, upon receiving the application for registration, must register the applicant in the roster of lawyers without delay (paragraph (4)). In Article 8, it provides that where a person who has applied for registration falls under any ground for refusal of registration prescribed in each item, the Defendant Association may, through resolution of the Registration Review Committee, refuse registration (main clause of paragraph (1)); and where the Defendant Association neither registers nor refuses registration by the time 3 months have elapsed from the date on which it received the application for registration, the registration is deemed to have been made (paragraph (3)).\\n\\nArticle 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act enumerates the following grounds for refusal of lawyer registration: “a person who lacks the qualifications of a lawyer under Article 4” (item 1); “a person who falls under the grounds for disqualification under Article 5” (item 2); “a person who is significantly difficult to perform the duties of a lawyer due to mental or physical incapacity” (item 3); “a person who, during service as a public official, was subject to criminal prosecution (excluding cases in which indictment was brought for a negligent offense) or disciplinary action [excluding dismissal, removal from office, expulsion, and suspension (limited to cases before the period of suspension under the relevant disciplinary action has ended)], or who retired in connection with such unlawful act and is deemed significantly unsuitable to perform the duties of a lawyer” (item 4); and “a person whose registration was refused because the person fell under item 4 or whose registration was canceled pursuant to Article 18(2) because the person fell under item 4, and the prohibition period on registration has not yet elapsed” (item 5).\\n\\n(3) In light of the content and structure of these provisions of the Attorney-at-Law Act concerning lawyer registration, together with the nature of lawyer registration as a “qualification system” and the legislative history in which the legislature newly added grounds for refusal of registration in each item of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act in response to social necessity or public interest demands, it is appropriate to view the grounds for refusal of registration prescribed in each item of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act as an exhaustive enumeration. Accordingly, the Defendant Association may refuse lawyer registration only where the applicant for registration falls under a ground for refusal prescribed in each item of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, and the Defendant Association’s refusal or delay of lawyer registration on grounds other than those prescribed by law, such as the Attorney-at-Law Act, is in direct contravention of the legislative purpose of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act and of the “principle of legal reservation,” under which restrictions on fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution must be based on law, and therefore cannot be permitted.\\n\\n(4) However, it is clear that a suspicion that an applicant for lawyer registration may have committed some crime does not fall under any of the grounds for refusal of registration prescribed in each item of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act. Even if the applicant for registration actually committed a crime, such suspicion constitutes a ground for refusal of registration only where there exists a final and conclusive guilty judgment imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment (including cases in which a suspended pronouncement of sentence or suspended execution is imposed) (Article 8(1)2, Article 5(1), (2), and (3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act), or where the crime was committed while serving as a public official and the person was subject to criminal prosecution or disciplinary action or retired in connection with the crime (Article 8(1)4 of the Attorney-at-Law Act).\\n\\nMeanwhile, Article 5 of the Attorney-at-Law Act prescribes the grounds for disqualification of lawyers as follows: “a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment and for whom 5 years have not elapsed since the execution of the sentence ended or since it became finally determined that the sentence would not be executed” (item 1); “a person who has been sentenced to a suspended execution of imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment and for whom 2 years have not elapsed since the end of the suspension period” (item 2); “a person who has received a suspended pronouncement of sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment and who is within the suspension period” (item 3); “a person who has been dismissed by impeachment or disciplinary action or expelled pursuant to this Act, and for whom 5 years have not elapsed” (item 4); “a person who has been removed by disciplinary action and for whom 3 years have not elapsed” (item 5); “a person who has been relieved from office by disciplinary action and for whom 2 years have not elapsed” (item 6); and “a person who, during service as a public official, has been suspended by disciplinary action and is within the period of suspension (in such case, even if the person retires during the period of suspension, the person shall be deemed to be within the period of suspension until the period of suspension under the relevant disciplinary action has ended)” (item 7), etc. These provisions may be regarded as embodying the constitutional principle of proportionality by the legislature’s differentiated setting of periods of disqualification from lawyer registration according to the degree of the violation of duty, etc., in relation to the crimes committed by the applicant for lawyer registration or acts of breach of official duty. Accordingly, it is clear that even if the periods of disqualification prescribed in each item of Article 5 of the Attorney-at-Law Act have already elapsed, it cannot be permitted for the Defendant Association to further refuse or delay lawyer registration by again invoking the applicant’s prior criminal record.\\n\\nc. As to whether the Defendant Association’s liability for damages is recognized (the Defendants’ incidental grounds of appeal)\\n\\nThe above factual circumstances are examined in light of the relevant provisions and legal principles.\\n\\n(1) In the Plaintiff’s case, the Plaintiff received a judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence for the crime of forgery of an official document committed during the Plaintiff’s practice as a lawyer, and, pursuant to the provisions of the Attorney-at-Law Act, the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration was canceled and the Plaintiff has already been subjected to the sanction of being unable to obtain lawyer registration for 2 years; and, as stated in the opinion of the Seoul Bar Association concerning the Plaintiff’s application for lawyer registration, there were no grounds for refusal of registration prescribed in each item of Article 8(1) of the Attorney-at-Law Act as of the time of the application for registration.\\n\\nHowever, focusing on the circumstance that the Plaintiff did not attach a criminal record inquiry certificate when submitting the lawyer registration application, it cannot be said that Defendant 2 had no room to suspect that, in addition to the above judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence, for which the disqualification period had already elapsed, the Plaintiff had a “final and conclusive judgment of conviction imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment,” which would constitute a ground for refusal of registration under Article 8(1)2, Article 5(1), (2), and (3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act.\\n\\nNevertheless, even in such case, it appears that Defendant 2 could have, within a short time, clearly verified by means of the submitted materials whether there existed, in addition to the ground for disqualification arising from the above judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence, any other grounds for refusal of registration prescribed by the Attorney-at-Law Act, after requiring the Plaintiff to submit explanatory materials such as a criminal record inquiry certificate. Therefore, with respect to referring the Plaintiff’s agenda of refusal of registration to the Registration Review Committee on the basis of only a vague level of suspicion without going through such verification procedure, it is difficult to accord objective justification in light of the above legal principles concerning lawyer registration and the legal status and social standing of the Defendant Association. Likewise, it is difficult to avoid the same evaluation with respect to the fact that the members of the Registration Review Committee had the Plaintiff submit copies of the investigative records relating to the above crime of forgery of an official document and further delayed the registration review period by stating that they were inquiring into the existence or nonexistence of additional offenses based merely on suspicion founded on the blameworthiness of the above crime of forgery of an official document.\\n\\n(2) As above, since negligence is recognized on the part of Defendant 2 and the members of the Defendant Association’s Registration Review Committee in referring the Plaintiff’s agenda of refusal of registration and proceeding with the review procedure, if damage thereby occurred to the Plaintiff, the Defendant Association must bear liability to compensate in its capacity as the administrative subject to which Defendant 2 and the members of the Registration Review Committee belong. The court below’s determination to the same effect is proper, and the Defendants’ incidental grounds of appeal asserting no liability to compensate the Plaintiff are without merit and are not accepted.\\n\\nd. As to whether Defendant 2’s intent or gross negligence is recognized (Ground 2 of the Plaintiff’s appeal)\\n\\n(1) Taking together the circumstances stated by the court below, such as the fact that, because the Plaintiff did not submit a criminal record inquiry certificate, there was room to suspect that, in addition to the judgment of suspended pronouncement of sentence for forgery of an official document, for which the disqualification period had already elapsed, there existed another final and conclusive judgment of conviction imposing a sentence of imprisonment without prison labor or more severe punishment that would constitute a ground for refusal of registration; and the fact that Article 14(4) of the Defendant Association’s Rules Concerning Lawyer Registration, etc. provides that the chairperson of the Association must, without delay, refer to the Registration Review Committee an agenda concerning refusal of registration not only when the result of the review recognizes that there are grounds for refusal of registration, but also when it is “suspected,” it is difficult to evaluate Defendant 2’s referral of the Plaintiff’s agenda of refusal of registration to the Registration Review Committee as having involved intent or marked carelessness close to intent.\\n\\n(2) If, with respect to Defendant 2’s referral of the Plaintiff’s agenda of refusal of registration, only slight negligence is recognized rather than intent or gross negligence, Defendant 2 bears no liability to compensate the Plaintiff under the legal principle of exemption for public officials with slight negligence. Therefore, although the reasons given by the court below in denying Defendant 2’s liability for damages are not appropriate, the conclusion dismissing the Plaintiff’s claim for damages against Defendant 2 is nevertheless proper. There is no error in the court below’s judgment that affected the outcome by misapprehending the legal principles concerning recognition of gross negligence on the part of a public official, etc.\\n\\ne. As to whether the Defendant Association’s liability for damages equivalent to lost earnings is recognized (Ground 1 of the Plaintiff’s appeal)\\n\\n(1) Article 7(4) of the Attorney-at-Law Act provides that when the Defendant Association receives an application for lawyer registration, it must register the applicant in the roster of lawyers without delay and notify the applicant of that fact, and Article 8(3) provides that if the Defendant Association neither registers nor refuses registration by the time 3 months have elapsed from the date on which it received the application for registration, the registration is deemed to have been made.\\n\\nThese provisions concerning the registration review period include not only the purpose of guaranteeing the time necessary for the Defendant Association to properly perform its duties, but also the purpose of setting the limits of the Defendant Association’s discretion regarding the registration review period so that the processing period for registration applications is not unjustifiably delayed, thereby protecting subjective interests such as the freedom of occupation and income-generating activities of lawyers through prompt lawyer registration and deemed registration. Accordingly, where the lawyer’s property damage occurs because registration is unlawfully delayed by the intent or negligence of an executive officer or employee of the Defendant Association, the Defendant Association should be regarded as bearing liability for the delayed period, and it cannot be said merely because Article 8(3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act allows a maximum review period of 3 months that the Defendant Association’s liability is always exempted during that period.\\n\\n(2) In light of the above facts and the circumstances appearing in the record, it may sufficiently be inferred that, due to the Defendant Association’s unlawful delay in lawyer registration, the Plaintiff was unable to engage in the practice of law and thereby suffered pecuniary damage in the form of reduced income; accordingly, unless there are other special circumstances, the Defendant Association must be deemed obligated to compensate the Plaintiff for the amount of income the Plaintiff failed to obtain due to the unlawful delay in lawyer registration.\\n\\nHowever, the lost earnings subject to compensation here are limited to the “earned income” that the Plaintiff could have obtained by providing labor while engaging in occupational activities as a lawyer after completing lawyer registration. Since income that a lawyer could obtain by engaging in occupational activities as a sole proprietor or as a member of a law firm, rather than by being employed by another person after completing lawyer registration, constitutes “business income,” the portion thereof remaining after deducting personal and material expenses and capital income is the lost earnings subject to compensation. Where it is difficult, due to the absence of objective materials, to calculate actual lost earnings by such a method, lost earnings may also be calculated based on the remuneration equivalent for employing a person with the same level of education, legal career, management ability, and specialized field expertise as the Plaintiff, that is, replacement hiring cost (see Supreme Court Decision 95DA1439 dated February 23, 1996, etc.). In addition, if, during the period in which lawyer registration was unlawfully delayed, the Plaintiff obtained wage income by being employed by another person as an ordinary worker without lawyer qualifications, such wage income must be deducted from the amount of lost earnings subject to compensation (offset by gain and loss).\\n\\n(3) Nevertheless, the court below determined that, merely because the Defendant Association completed the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration within the “3 months from the date of application for registration” prescribed in Article 8(3) of the Attorney-at-Law Act, it could not be said that the Plaintiff’s lawyer registration was unjustifiably delayed. There is an error in the court below’s judgment that affected the outcome by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the registration review period, etc. under the Attorney-at-Law Act. The Plaintiff’s ground of appeal pointing out this point is well taken.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the part of the judgment below against the Plaintiff shall be reversed insofar as it concerns the Plaintiff’s claim against the Defendant Association for lost earnings, and this part of the case shall be remanded to the court below for further trial and determination; the remainder of the Plaintiff’s appeal and the Defendant Association’s incidental appeal shall all be dismissed. The costs arising from the Plaintiff’s appeal against Defendant 2 shall be borne by the Plaintiff, and the judgment is rendered by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as set forth in the order."}

{"[2022DA225910]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. Facts\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be found.\\n\\nA. Status of the accident site\\n\\n1) Around March 2017, in front of (address omitted) in Seogwipo-si, there was a “┫”-shaped intersection (hereinafter referred to as “the intersection at issue”) where Iljudong-ro, a one-way three-lane road connecting the east and west, and Sehojungang-ro, connected to the north, met.\\n\\n2) At that time, from the Sumoru direction (east) of Iljudong-ro at the intersection at issue toward E-Mart (west), a three-color (red, yellow, green) traffic signal (hereinafter referred to as “the signal light at issue”) and a U-turn instruction sign and, as an auxiliary sign thereto, a sign reading “When turning left, when the pedestrian signal is on / only for small passenger cars and two-wheeled vehicles” (hereinafter referred to as “the sign at issue”) were installed; however, because the signal light at issue had no left-turn signal, the portion of the sign at issue stating that a U-turn was to be made when turning left did not conform to the signal system, and moreover, because there was no road on the left for making a left turn when driving while facing the signal light at issue, the sign at issue did not conform to the road structure either. Meanwhile, from the E-Mart direction (west) of Iljudong-ro toward the Sumoru direction (east), a four-color (red, yellow, left-turn arrow, green) traffic signal (hereinafter referred to as “the opposite-side signal light”) was installed, and on both sides of Iljudong-ro at that intersection, two crosswalks and pedestrian signal lights (hereinafter referred to as “the pedestrian signal lights”) were installed.\\n\\n3) At that time, the signal-change pattern of the traffic signals installed at the intersection at issue as stated above was as shown in the table below (excluding cases where yellow is illuminated between signal changes).\\n\\n<IMAGE1-0>\\n\\nB. Circumstances of the occurrence of the accident\\n\\n1) Plaintiff 1 and his friends, Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2, came to Jeju-do together on March 29, 2017, rented motorized bicycles (hereinafter referred to as “motorcycles”), and were driving them separately at around 17:52 on Iljudong-ro from the Sumoru direction toward E-Mart. At the intersection at issue, they stopped in the first lane, which was a U-turn-only lane, in the order of Plaintiff 1, Nonparty 1, and Nonparty 2, and waited for the signal.\\n\\n2) When the signal light at issue changed from green to red, a short time later Plaintiff 1, after saying words to the effect that they should go to Nonparty 1 and Nonparty 2 and signaling with his hand, made a U-turn and entered the third lane of the opposite roadway, and Nonparty 1 also made a U-turn following Plaintiff 1. Nonparty 2, however, did not begin the U-turn and remained stopped in the first lane.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, a Trax vehicle driven by Nonparty 3 at the time entered the intersection at issue from the opposite side, namely from the E-Mart direction of Iljudong-ro toward the Sumoru direction, at a speed of approximately 71 km/h, and, while continuing straight in accordance with the straight-through and left-turn signals of the opposite-side signal light, it collided with the rear end of Plaintiff 1’s motorcycle, which had just made a U-turn and entered the third lane (hereinafter referred to as “the accident at issue”).\\n\\n4) As a result of the accident at issue, Plaintiff 1 suffered injuries including traumatic subdural hemorrhage and fell into a coma, and had not regained consciousness by the time the oral argument in the court below was concluded.\\n\\n2. Regarding the existence of a defect in the installation or management of the public structure\\n\\nA. The “defect in the installation or management of a public structure” prescribed in Article 5(1) of the State Compensation Act means a state in which a public structure devoted to public purposes does not possess the safety that it should normally have according to its intended use. Whether such safety is present shall be determined on the basis of whether the installer or manager of the public structure fulfilled the duty to take protective measures generally required in society in proportion to the danger of the public structure, and financial, human, and material constraints of the installer or manager shall also be taken into consideration. Therefore, it cannot be concluded that a public structure is defective merely because it does not possess a high degree of safety sufficient to maintain a flawless condition in its installation and management; it is sufficient if it possesses relative safety that would permit the common-sense and orderly use expected of users of the public structure (see Supreme Court Decision 2002DA9158 dated August 23, 2002, Supreme Court Decision 2013DA208074 dated October 24, 2013, etc.).\\n\\nB. The court below, on the grounds stated in its opinion, determined that the sign at issue had a functional defect inconsistent with the road structure of the intersection at issue, and that such functional defect constituted a “defect in the installation or management of a public structure” prescribed in Article 5(1) of the State Compensation Act.\\n\\nC. However, in light of the legal principles set forth above, the court below’s such determination is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Since the sign at issue is a traffic safety facility installed for the purpose of preventing dangers on the road and securing traffic safety and smooth flow, its content must, in principle, conform to the structure or conditions of the place of installation and to the signal system.\\n\\n2) In particular, the sign at issue is a U-turn auxiliary sign that tells a person driving a motor vehicle or the like on the road (hereinafter referred to as “the driver”) under what signal a U-turn may be made; thus, if the content of the sign causes error or confusion to the driver, the risk of traffic accidents may increase significantly, and this makes the foregoing all the more so.\\n\\n3) Whether the content of the sign at issue is likely to cause error or confusion to the driver must be determined on the basis of the perception of an ordinary and average driver. Even if the content of the sign at issue contains some defect, if a common-sense and orderly method of use can be expected from the standpoint of an ordinary and average driver, it cannot be concluded on that basis that there is a defect in the installation or management of the sign at issue.\\n\\n4) Because the sign at issue states “When turning left, when the pedestrian signal is on,” it is understood to mean that a U-turn is possible when the signal light at issue is a left-turn signal or when the pedestrian signal light is green. However, at the time the accident at issue occurred, there was no road installed at the intersection at issue for making a left turn from the Sumoru direction to the E-Mart direction, and the signal light at issue also had no left-turn signal. Therefore, among the two cases in which a U-turn is permitted according to the sign at issue, the case where the signal light at issue becomes a left-turn signal cannot occur. In this case, an ordinary and average driver would appear to make a U-turn under the remaining case in which a U-turn is permitted according to the sign at issue, namely, when the pedestrian signal light is green.\\n\\n5) The circumstance that, before the accident at issue, no civil complaint was raised that the sign at issue had been installed incorrectly, and that no accident had ever occurred due to the sign at issue, also supports that point.\\n\\n6) In light of the foregoing, even if there is a part of the sign at issue that does not conform to the signal system of the signal light at issue and the road structure of the intersection at issue, it is difficult to regard such part as constituting a defect in installation or management in which the safety that it should normally possess is lacking.\\n\\nD. Nevertheless, the court below found that the sign at issue had a defect in installation or management solely for the reasons stated in its opinion; thus, the court below’s determination contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning defects in the installation or management of a public structure.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for appeal, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning administrative plans is incorrect? (In cases of dispute, in accordance with precedents)
A: Even in the case of land that continued to be used as agricultural land according to its land category after being designated as an urban planning facility (park), if a person who acquired ownership of the land after the designation is also in a situation where the land can continue to be used as agricultural land, and even if its use and profit are de facto impossible, if the right to demand purchase can be exercised under the law, it cannot be concluded that the designation of the park area excessively infringed the private interests of the landowner.
B: Where a reconstruction association privately concludes with an individual association member, who is part of the entire membership, an agreement concerning occupancy of the newly built commercial building related to reconstruction, in light of the nature of the management and disposition plan as a binding administrative plan and the public-law discretion that the reconstruction association possesses as an administrative subject, the reconstruction association is not directly bound by that private-law agreement.
C: In a revocation action brought against a newly established city management plan formulated by an administrative agency after a judgment annulling a disposition that rejected a proposal by residents, etc. to formulate a city management plan has become final and conclusive, even if the content of the city management plan does not violate the binding force of the revocation judgment, the court must separately examine and determine whether it deviates from the limits of planning discretion.
D: Where the person authorized to change an industrial complex development plan changes the industrial complex development plan so that a specific waste treatment company can expand its waste incineration facility, under the principle of equity, the person authorized to change must also change the industrial complex development plan so that nearby companies of the same kind can enjoy the same benefit.
E: Where a local government, without undergoing an objective review concerning landscape damage, issues a non-approval disposition against A's high-rise apartment construction project plan on the grounds of the surrounding landscape, there is room to recognize the local government's State compensation liability.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2017DA249219]": "We examine the grounds for appeal on points of law (the supplemental briefs for the grounds of appeal filed after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal shall be considered to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n1. Facts\\nAccording to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, the following facts can be found.\\n\\na. In order to carry out a high-rise apartment construction project, the Plaintiff purchased, around October 2003 and May 2005, 4 parcels of land totaling 69,041.4 square meters in Yeosu City (address omitted), etc., located within a Type 2 General Residential Area (hereinafter referred to as “the Project Site at issue”). In a Type 2 General Residential Area, multi-family housing exceeding 15 stories cannot be constructed. However, as a result of the Plaintiff’s inquiries to the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division and the Ministry of Construction and Transportation, the Plaintiff was informed that, pursuant to the National Land Planning and Utilization Act, if the Project Site at issue were designated as a Type 1 district unit zone and its plan were formulated, high-rise apartments exceeding 15 stories might be constructed even without changing the use district.\\n\\nFrom around July 2006, the Plaintiff consulted with the Defendant’s relevant departments for about 5 months regarding the high-rise apartment construction project plan, and on December 22, 2006, the Plaintiff submitted to the Defendant, together with an application for approval of a housing construction project plan (hereinafter referred to as “the Project at issue”), a proposal for the formulation of designation of a Type 1 district unit zone for a housing construction project plan to construct apartments consisting of 10 buildings in 3 complexes, with 23 to 39 stories above ground, 2 basement floors, and a total of 1,023 units on the Project Site at issue.\\n\\nFrom December 26, 2006 to June 25, 2007, the Defendant repeatedly requested the Plaintiff to supplement matters such as the traffic impact assessment report, financing plan, and results of environmental review, and received supplementary materials. After receiving conditional approval from the Jeollanam-do Local Traffic Impact Deliberation Committee in relation to the traffic impact assessment on June 26, 2007, the Plaintiff finally submitted supplementary materials, including the traffic impact assessment report and the draft Type 1 district unit plan, to the Defendant on July 7, 2007.\\n\\nb. On July 4, 2007, Non-party 1, who was the Defendant Mayor at the time, while receiving a report on urban planning affairs from the public officials in charge at the Urban Planning Division, expressed a negative opinion to the effect that “high-rise buildings adjacent to the coastline are unsightly” in relation to the Project Plan at issue. Thereafter, the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division prepared a review report stating that “formulating a Type 1 district unit plan for the Project Site at issue does not conform to the purpose of designation of a Type 2 General Residential Area, and considering the surrounding circumstances and the formation of the skyline of the entire area, it is reasonable to allow apartments not exceeding 15 stories to be built in accordance with the current use district,” and on August 9, 2007, it replied to the Defendant’s Architecture Division, the competent department in charge of approval of the Project Plan at issue, with an opinion of inappropriateness to the same effect.\\n\\nOn October 26, 2007, the Defendant notified the Plaintiff that approval of the Project Plan at issue would be denied on the ground that “as a result of a comprehensive review of the surrounding landscape, traffic, and linkage with neighboring areas, the Project Plan at issue does not conform to the purpose of designation of the current use district (15 stories or less)” (hereinafter referred to as “the Refusal Disposition at issue”).\\n\\nc. The Plaintiff filed an administrative appeal against the Defendant Mayor with the Jeollanam-do Administrative Appeals Commission seeking revocation of the Refusal Disposition at issue, but when the claim was dismissed, the Plaintiff filed a lawsuit under Gwangju District Court Case No. 2008GUHAP2354. During the administrative appeal proceedings, in order to prove the validity of the grounds for the Refusal Disposition at issue, the Defendant submitted the “Landscape Analysis of Buildings Before Project Implementation” and the “Landscape Analysis by the Photo Montage Technique” prepared by Non-party 2, a public official in charge at the Urban Planning Division (hereinafter collectively referred to as “the Analysis Materials at issue”), and thereafter also submitted them to the court seized of the administrative lawsuit. In response, the Plaintiff contested that the Analysis Materials at issue were falsely prepared.\\n\\nThe Gwangju District Court, by judgment dated April 30, 2009, found the Refusal Disposition at issue unlawful on the following grounds, on the basis that it had been made by deviating from and abusing discretion, and rendered a judgment revoking it; that judgment became final and conclusive as of May 23, 2009. 1) With respect to traffic and linkage with neighboring areas, the Plaintiff had already completed the review by supplementing and submitting the draft Type 1 district unit plan in accordance with the conditional approval of the Jeollanam-do Local Traffic Impact Deliberation Committee, and therefore it is difficult to say that serious problems in traffic or linkage with neighboring areas would arise from the Project at issue. 2) The Analysis Materials at issue do not appear to have been prepared by scientific and professional methods, and it cannot be said that the exercise of the Defendant’s discretion based on them was carried out according to objective, reasonable, and proper standards. There are also no materials showing that the Project at issue would cause a problem in the landscape due to serious disharmony with the surrounding landscape.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Jeollanam-do conducted a special audit of the public officials involved in the Refusal Disposition at issue in response to complaints filed by the Plaintiff. The Jeollanam-do Audit Office determined that “the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division positively reviewed approval of the Project Plan at issue and requested supplementation, but after the personnel appointment of the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division in June 2007, the policy changed, thereby causing the Plaintiff significant damage,” and requested the Defendant to take disciplinary action against Non-party 2 and other public officials in charge.\\n\\nd. As the judgment in favor of the Plaintiff in the administrative litigation became final and conclusive as stated above, the Defendant approved the Project Plan at issue on August 12, 2009. However, with respect to the Project Site at issue, a public auction procedure had been underway since August 22, 2008, and Booyoung Housing Co., Ltd. acquired ownership thereof around March 2011; thereafter, the Defendant revoked the approval disposition dated August 12, 2009.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\nUnlike the first-instance court, the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim for damages liability for the following reasons.\\n\\na. There is an aspect in which the Defendant’s public officials in charge handled part of their duties improperly before reaching the Refusal Disposition at issue.\\nThe Defendant had never requested the Plaintiff to supplement the issue of landscape damage until the Refusal Disposition at issue. It was after the Defendant Mayor made the negative remark regarding the Project Plan at issue that the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division established a policy of refusal, and it does not appear that the Defendant Mayor made the above remark based on any specific review results. The Jeollanam-do Audit Office also determined that the Defendant had been positively reviewing approval of the Project Plan at issue and requesting supplementation, but that the policy changed due to the personnel appointment of the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division. The Analysis Materials at issue, which formed the basis for the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division’s adverse opinion regarding the issue of landscape damage, being the reason for the Refusal Disposition at issue, cannot be regarded as having been prepared by scientific and professional methods, in that some of the locations described as places from which the subject site was observed are different from the actual ones, the location of the apartments to be constructed according to the Project Plan at issue differs from the location set forth in the Project Plan at issue, and the impact of those apartments on the surrounding landscape is distorted. Even if, as the Defendant asserts, the Analysis Materials at issue were prepared in anticipation of the administrative appeal or administrative lawsuit after the adverse opinion was returned, the Defendant has not submitted objective materials serving as the basis for the adverse opinion.\\n\\nb. However, even considering the foregoing circumstances, it is difficult to find that, on the standard of an ordinary public official, the Defendant’s public officials in charge committed acts amounting to a loss of objective legitimacy in the course of handling the approval work for the Project Plan at issue.\\n\\nApproval of the Project Plan at issue, as well as designation of the Type 1 district unit zone and formulation of the plan for that purpose, are all a kind of administrative planning, and the Defendant Mayor, as the approval authority, has broad discretion. According to the relevant laws and regulations, in order for the Defendant to designate a Type 1 district unit zone, it must closely examine the validity of whether the purpose intended by the district unit plan can be achieved, taking into consideration the land use, traffic conditions, and related plans of the surrounding area together; and in planning the height of buildings, it must consider locational characteristics, a stepwise skyline, and harmony with the surrounding environment. The Defendant had long pursued the construction of a marine tourism city and had no choice but to give priority to the impact that super-high-rise apartments to be built adjacent to the coastline would have on the surrounding landscape; and, while recognizing that a dispute with the Plaintiff was foreseeable and that the Plaintiff would suffer enormous damage, the Defendant decided to refuse approval of the Project Plan at issue, giving priority to the need of the public interest. Non-party 2 prepared the Analysis Materials at issue using materials obtained through direct on-site inspection, and even if there are some errors or mistakes therein, it is difficult to regard them as having been prepared after the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division internally and unfairly adopted a policy of refusal and then with the intent to justify it. Although the refusal disposition was not based on objective and scientific materials, it is appropriate to view the Defendant as having made the Refusal Disposition at issue for its own reasonable reasons. It cannot be said that there was no balancing of interests at all before reaching the Refusal Disposition at issue, or that balancing of interests was carried out without legitimacy or objectivity.\\n\\n3. Supreme Court’s determination\\na. Even if an administrative disposition is later found unlawful and revoked in an appeal litigation, that alone does not necessarily mean that the administrative disposition constitutes a tort caused by intent or negligence of a public official. When viewed by the standard of an ordinary public official, if the public official in charge of an unlawful administrative disposition failed to exercise objective due care and, as a result, the administrative disposition lost objective legitimacy, the State compensation liability prescribed in Article 2 of the State Compensation Act may be established. Whether objective legitimacy has been lost is to be determined by comprehensively considering various circumstances such as the manner and purpose of the act, whether and to what extent the victim was involved, the type of interest infringed, and the extent of the damage, and it must also be examined whether there is a substantial reason for the State or a local government to bear liability for compensation of the damage (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision dated May 12, 2000, 99DA70600).\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing legal principles, examining the facts set forth above, there is a strong possibility that the Defendant is liable for damages under Article 2 of the State Compensation Act. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\nThe Plaintiff completed the purchase of the Project Site at issue and then prepared the project for more than 2 years, consulted with the Defendant’s relevant departments for several months, filed an application for approval of the Project Plan at issue, and thereafter, over several months, complied with the Defendant’s requests for supplementation and satisfied the requirements necessary for approval of the Project Plan. Even considering that approval of the Project Plan at issue, etc. is an act for which the Defendant is recognized to have broad discretion, in such circumstances the Defendant needed to carefully balance the Plaintiff’s interests that would be infringed and the public interests to be protected if it intended to issue a refusal disposition concerning the Project Plan at issue. In particular, with respect to issues such as landscape damage and traffic impact, the Defendant had not previously raised the issue or had requested supplementation from the Plaintiff and received related materials, and therefore if it intended to refuse approval on such grounds, it needed to present more objective and reasonable grounds.\\n\\nAfter the Defendant Mayor made a negative remark regarding the Project Plan at issue, the Defendant’s Urban Planning Division prepared a review report and returned an adverse opinion to the Defendant’s Architecture Division, and as a result the Defendant issued the Refusal Disposition at issue. Before issuing the Refusal Disposition at issue, all the work performed by the Defendant’s public officials in charge to examine whether there would be landscape damage consisted of going to the site, taking photographs, and preparing the Analysis Materials at issue; there are no other objective materials concerning the matter. Examining the contents of the Analysis Materials at issue, the main descriptions differ from the actual facts, and the contents cannot be said to have been prepared in an objective and fact-conforming manner, in that they distort the impact of the apartments to be constructed under the Project at issue on the surrounding landscape. Such materials cannot serve as evidence supporting landscape damage, regardless of the time of their preparation. Therefore, the Refusal Disposition at issue can be viewed as having been made without an objective review of landscape damage. In light of the progress of the approval work for the Project Plan as noted above, the scale of the Project at issue, and the need for a reasonable and careful review to determine whether there would be landscape damage, the performance of duties by the Defendant’s public officials in charge can be regarded, on the standard of an ordinary public official, as having failed to exercise objective due care.\\n\\nFurthermore, in light of the foregoing circumstances, there is substantial reason to hold the Defendant liable for compensating the Plaintiff’s damages arising from the Refusal Disposition at issue.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim on the ground that it was difficult to find that the Defendant’s public officials in charge committed acts amounting to a loss of objective legitimacy while handling the approval work for the Project Plan at issue. The judgment of the court below contains errors that affected the judgment, in that, contrary to the rules of logic and experience, it went beyond the limits of the principle of free evaluation of evidence or misapprehended the legal principles concerning the establishment of State compensation liability under Article 2 of the State Compensation Act.\\n\\nd. Meanwhile, according to the reasoning of the judgment of the court below, in the first instance the Plaintiff limited its claim for damages to only the amount corresponding to financing costs among the damages alleged to have arisen from the Defendant’s tort, but at the stage of the court below expanded the claimed amount to include construction design service fees, personnel expenses, and damages related to development profits.\\n\\nUpon remand, the court below must determine the scope and amount of damages caused by the Defendant’s tort. In cases where the fact that damage has occurred is recognized but proving the specific amount of damages is extremely difficult, the court must not easily dismiss the claim for damages, and must actively exercise its power to elucidate the issues and prompt proof, etc., and examine the specific amount of damages (see Supreme Court Decision dated March 26, 2020, 2018DA301336). If the specific amount of damages is still unknown thereafter, pursuant to Article 202-2 of the Civil Procedure Act, the court may determine as the amount of damages a sum it deems reasonable by comprehensively considering all circumstances recognized from the purport of the entire arguments and the results of the examination of evidence. The circumstances to be considered at that time include the relationship between the parties, the circumstances in which the damage arose from the tort, the nature of the damage, and the circumstances after the damage occurred (see Supreme Court Decision dated August 20, 2009, 2008DA19355, Supreme Court Decision dated May 27, 2021, 2017DA230963, etc.).\\n\\nIn particular, in this case, if the Plaintiff was negligent, the degree of such negligence must of course be taken into account; moreover, the amount of damages may be determined by comprehensively considering the legal nature of the approval of the Project Plan at issue, the characteristics of the Project Site at issue and the surrounding environment, the type of damages incurred, whether the Plaintiff assumed to some extent the risk that the Project Plan at issue could be disapproved for reasons such as the purpose of designation of the Project Site at issue, and the circumstances at the time of the Refusal Disposition at issue and the policy direction of the Defendant.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\nThe Plaintiff’s appeal is well founded; the judgment of the court below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination. Accordingly, the Court renders judgment as stated in the disposition by unanimous opinion of the Justices."}

{"[2019DU57404]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n1. Overview of the case and issue  \\na.
