According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) As the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City effected a replotting disposition in the Yongdong (1st and 2nd Districts) land readjustment project on December 26, 1991, the Korea Land Development Corporation was allotted, by way of replotting, the 10,562.3 square meters of school site in Seocho-gu, Seoul, (address 1 omitted) that had been included in the project area, and acquired ownership thereof. Meanwhile, with respect to the total of 13,176.9 square meters comprising the school site at issue and the adjacent 2,614.6 square meters of school site at (address 2 omitted), a decision to designate urban planning facilities (school) had been made by Seoul Metropolitan City Notice No. 308 on May 17, 1986.\\n\\n2) On April 12, 2001, the Defendant purchased the land at issue from the Korea Land Development Corporation, and thereafter, around that time, received a building permit for a temporary structure from the head of Seocho-gu Office of Seoul Metropolitan City (hereinafter, the “head of Seocho-gu Office”) and constructed a neighborhood living facility (Building A) and an athletic facility (Building B) (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “temporary structures at issue”) on the land at issue. The Defendant then continues to operate an outdoor golf practice range, etc., while repeatedly extending the period of existence thereof.\\n\\n3) On October 24, 2014, the Defendant proposed to the head of Seocho-gu Office the formulation of a district unit plan containing provisions to abolish the decision to designate urban planning facilities (school) for the land at issue and to maintain the building use of the temporary structures at issue, and the head of Seocho-gu Office formulated a district unit plan proposal (hereinafter, the “plan at issue”) by substantially accepting that proposal as is. The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, through the head of Seocho-gu Office, gave notice to the Defendant on January 28, 2016 that he refused to establish a district unit plan in accordance with the plan at issue on the grounds that the plan at issue did not reflect 25% public contribution and did not include the outdoor golf practice range among the prohibited uses (hereinafter, the “prior refusal disposition”).\\n\\n4) Accordingly, the Defendant filed a lawsuit against the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City seeking cancellation of the prior refusal disposition, and a judgment cancelling the prior refusal disposition was rendered and became final on the ground that the prior refusal disposition was unlawful because it was defective in balancing of interests in the following two respects (Seoul Administrative Court Judgment dated September 23, 2016, 2016GUHAP54916; Seoul High Court Judgment dismissing the appeal dated February 23, 2017, 2016NU70255, hereinafter, the “prior judgment”).\\n\\n① The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City knew, at the time the Defendant purchased the land at issue, that urban planning restrictions had been imposed on the land at issue, and required that 25% public contribution be reflected in the plan at issue on grounds such as the need for donation and acceptance for the expansion of infrastructure in light of local conditions. This prioritized the aspect of establishing a development plan and ignored the aspect of relieving the disadvantages of the landowner, and thus cannot be regarded as being based on a balancing of interests with legitimacy and objectivity.\\n\\n② The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City required that the outdoor golf practice range be included among the prohibited uses in the plan at issue on grounds including that, in apartment districts, the outdoor golf practice range is not permitted pursuant to the “Seoul Metropolitan City Ordinance on Formulation of the Basic Plan for Apartment District Development” (hereinafter, the “Apartment District Ordinance”). However, in light of the fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City had established a policy of gradually lifting existing apartment districts, and that the plan at issue also presupposed the exclusion of the land at issue from the apartment district, it cannot be regarded as being based on a balancing of interests with legitimacy and objectivity.\\n\\n5) On April 14, 2017, the Defendant applied against the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City for indirect enforcement on the ground that no re-disposition had been made in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment, and the Seoul High Court issued an indirect enforcement order stating, “If the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City fails to make an urban management plan decision for the Defendant in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment within 120 days from the date on which a certified copy of this decision is served, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City shall pay to the Defendant the amount calculated at the rate of KRW 6.5 million per day from the day following the expiration of that period until the date of the urban management plan decision” (Seoul High Court Decision dated July 19, 2017, 2017RU1273), and a certified copy of this decision was served on the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City on July 24, 2017. The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City filed a final appeal therefrom, but as the Supreme Court issued a decision dismissing the final appeal, the indirect enforcement order became final as rendered (Supreme Court Decision dated November 21, 2017, 2017MU750).\\n\\n6) On November 16, 2017, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City gave public notice of: ① an urban management plan decision abolishing the existing decision to designate urban planning facilities (school) and designating the school site at issue as a special planning district (Seoul Metropolitan City Notice No. 2017-411); and ② a decision to partially amend the Basic Plan for the Development of the Banpo Apartment District and the Improvement Plan for the 3rd Section of the Banpo Apartment District, which changes the land use plan for the school site at issue in the Banpo Apartment District from urban planning facility land (school site) to other land, while having the building regulation matters follow Seoul Metropolitan City Notice No. 2017-411 (Seoul Metropolitan City Notice No. 2017-418) (hereinafter collectively referred to as the “decision at issue”).\\n\\n7) In the decision at issue, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City specified as the reason for designating the special planning district that there was a need for systematic urban management planning linked with the efficient land use of a large parcel following the abolition of the decision to designate urban planning facilities (school) and with the development status (plan) of the surrounding area, and for a plan to minimize adverse effects on the surroundings through a concrete development plan taking into consideration the Banpo Apartment District district unit plan currently being formulated and the characteristics of the surrounding area. In the special planning district guidelines, the floor area ratio was decided as follows: “standard floor area ratio of 120% or less, permitted floor area ratio of 150% or less, maximum floor area ratio of 200% or less, maximum floor area ratio = standard (permitted) floor area ratio × (1 + 1.3 × a) or less.”\\n\\n8) The Plaintiff, the local government to which the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City belongs, filed the present action of objection to execution on January 10, 2018, arguing that, if the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, within 120 days from July 24, 2017, the date on which the certified copy of the indirect enforcement order was served, performed the disposition again in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment by making the decision at issue on November 16, 2017, then this would constitute performance of the duty to re-dispose in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment.\\n\\nb. The issue in this case is whether the content of the decision at issue violates the binding force of the prior judgment, so that it cannot be deemed that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City performed the duty to re-dispose in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment.\\n\\n2. The judgment of the court below  \\na. The court below held that the decision at issue violated the binding force of the prior judgment for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) In the decision at issue, the standard floor area ratio and permitted floor area ratio for the land at issue were substantially reduced compared with the content determined in the plan at issue, while the maximum floor area ratio was set at 200% or less; thus, in order for the Defendant to be subject to a floor area ratio of 200% or less, the same as the standard floor area ratio and permitted floor area ratio under the plan at issue, the Defendant must necessarily make public contribution such as donation and acceptance of at least 20% or more. Considering that the provision concerning floor area ratio in “Seoul Metropolitan City Guidelines for Formulating District Unit Plans” (hereinafter, the “formulation standards at issue”), which are discretionary guidelines of the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, provides that, in a Class-2 General Residential Area where there is no change in the use district, both the standard floor area ratio and the permitted floor area ratio shall be set at 200% or less, and that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City appears to have applied the amended standards as they are with respect to floor area ratio unless special circumstances existed, the floor area ratio-related part of the decision at issue is, in substance, tantamount to requiring public contribution, which the prior judgment found to be unlawful.\\n\\n2) In the decision at issue, the abstract prohibited uses for the land at issue are set as “other uses that harm the surrounding residential environment, educational environment, landscape, etc.,” and there is sufficient room to interpret this by its wording as including an outdoor golf practice range. In light of the fact that, according to the Apartment District Ordinance, the outdoor golf practice range is not permitted in apartment districts within Seoul Metropolitan City, and that the Apartment District Ordinance would ultimately have to apply to the land at issue because the land at issue was not excluded from the apartment district, the decision at issue is, in substance, tantamount to deciding the land at issue as a use in which an outdoor golf practice range is not permitted.\\n\\n3) The fact that the land at issue was designated as a special planning district cannot be evaluated as either a new circumstance arising after the prior refusal disposition or a circumstance different in basic factual relations from the grounds for disposition that the prior judgment found unlawful due to defective balancing of interests, namely, the request for public contribution and the request for changing the use plan. As the “Implementation Plan for the Improvement of the Apartment District Urban Management System” (hereinafter, the “Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan”) is merely an internal administrative guideline of the Second Deputy Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, and since the legal basis for designating a special planning district had already existed even before the implementation of the above guidelines, the implementation of the Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan cannot be regarded as corresponding to a change in the law or facts concerning the designation of a special planning district.\\n\\nb. However, the foregoing judgment of the court below is difficult to accept as is for the following reasons.\\n\\n3. The judgment of the Supreme Court  \\na. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) According to Article 30 of the Administrative Litigation Act, a final judgment canceling a disposition, etc. binds the administrative agency that is a party to the case and other related administrative agencies with respect to that case (paragraph 1). Where the disposition canceled by the judgment consists of refusing an application by a party, the administrative agency that made the disposition shall again make a disposition on the prior application in accordance with the purport of the judgment (paragraph 2). Accordingly, once a judgment holding an administrative disposition unlawful and cancelling it becomes final, the administrative agency has, in accordance with the binding force of the cancellation judgment, the duty to make a new disposition in a state in which the grounds for illegality confirmed in that judgment are excluded, or to take measures to remove the unlawful result (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment dated October 29, 2015, 2013DU27517).\\n\\n2) An administrative plan means an activity standard or the act of establishing such standard, which is set to realize a certain order at a future point in time by comprehensively coordinating related administrative means on the basis of specialized and technical judgment regarding administration in order to achieve a specific administrative objective such as the construction, rearrangement, or improvement of a city. An administrative agency has a relatively broad discretion in formation when formulating and deciding a concrete administrative plan. However, such discretion of formation by the administrative agency cannot be unlimited, and administrative plans are subject to the limitation that the interests of the persons concerned therewith must be fairly compared and weighed not only between the public interest and private interest but also between public interests and between private interests. Therefore, if, when formulating and deciding an administrative plan, the administrative agency does not perform any balancing of interests at all, omits matters that ought to be included among the considerations in balancing of interests, or performs balancing of interests but lacks legitimacy and objectivity, the decision on the administrative plan may become unlawful due to a defect in balancing of interests. This legal principle applies equally where the administrative agency, pursuant to the National Land Planning and Utilization Act (hereinafter, the “National Land Planning Act”), decides whether to accept the proposal of residents, etc. for formulating an urban management plan and make an urban management plan decision (see, e.g., Supreme Court Judgment dated October 12, 2018, 2015DU50382).\\n\\n3) In light of the legal principles concerning the scope of the binding force of a final cancellation judgment and the discretion granted to the administrative agency in the formulation and decision of an urban management plan, even if a judgment that cancels a disposition refusing the proposal of residents, etc. for an urban management plan on the ground of defective balancing of interests has become final, it cannot be said that the administrative agency has the duty to establish an urban management plan that fully accepts the proposal. Rather, if the administrative agency again conducts new balancing of interests and actively formulates an urban management plan, it should be deemed to have fulfilled the duty to re-dispose pursuant to the binding force of the cancellation judgment. However, since whether there is a violation of the binding force of the cancellation judgment and whether the limits of planning discretion have been exceeded are separate issues, even if the content of the urban management plan actively established by the administrative agency does not violate the binding force of the cancellation judgment, whether the limits of planning discretion have been exceeded must be separately examined and determined.\\n\\nb. When the following circumstances ascertainable from the record are comprehensively considered, it is difficult to regard the part of the “request to reflect 25% public contribution,” which the prior judgment pointed out as a defect in the balancing of interests of the prior refusal disposition, as having been directly or in substance included in the decision at issue.\\n\\n1) The decision at issue contains no wording expressly requiring the Defendant to make public contribution for the development, etc. of the land at issue. The prior refusal disposition consisted of the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City refusing, on the ground that 25% public contribution was not reflected in the plan at issue, the abolition itself of the existing urban planning facility decision that had remained unexecuted for a long period with respect to the school site at issue, whereas the decision at issue abolishes the existing urban planning facility decision with respect to the school site at issue and, by stipulating that the floor area ratio be applied differentially according to the ratio of the area provided as public facility site in future construction projects, gives the builder a choice. In this respect, there is a substantial difference.\\n\\n2) The purport of the prior judgment is not that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City must necessarily accept the “standard (permitted) floor area ratio of 200% or less” part of the plan at issue. Therefore, even if under the floor area ratio provision of the decision at issue, when a construction project is carried out in the future on the land at issue, 20% of the land at issue must be provided as public facility site in order for the same result of a floor area ratio of 200% as presented in the plan at issue to be achieved, it cannot be said that the floor area ratio provision of the decision at issue was devised for the purpose of circumventing the binding force of the prior judgment.\\n\\n3) Under Article 78(1)1(a), paragraph 2 of the National Land Planning Act, Article 85(1)4 of the former Enforcement Decree of the National Land Planning and Utilization Act (before amendment by Presidential Decree No. 30031 on August 6, 2019), and Article 55(1)4 of the “Seoul Metropolitan City Urban Planning Ordinance,” the administrative agency is granted discretion to determine the floor area ratio of a Class-2 General Residential Area within the range of “200% or less.” The fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City set “120%,” which falls within the range of “200% or less,” as the upper limit of the standard floor area ratio, and “150%” as the upper limit of the permitted floor area ratio, respectively, conforms to the relevant statutes and ordinances concerning floor area ratio. Meanwhile, in light of the structure of the provisions concerning floor area ratio, the fact that the formulation standards at issue, which are merely administrative rules, prescribe the standard floor area ratio and permitted floor area ratio for a Class-2 General Residential Area as “200% or less” must also be understood in the same manner as the content of the provisions of the relevant statutes and ordinances.\\n\\n4) It is also difficult to conclude that there exists an established administrative practice within Seoul Metropolitan City of determining the upper limit of the standard floor area ratio for a Class-2 General Residential Area as 200%. Even if there are many cases in which the upper limit of the standard floor area ratio for a Class-2 General Residential Area was determined as 200%, it would be inappropriate to conclude on that basis alone that such an administrative practice has been established, because doing so would, in substance, negate the particularity of each planning zone and the administrative agency’s broad planning discretion.\\n\\nc. Next, when the following circumstances ascertainable from the record are comprehensively considered, it is also difficult to say that the part of the “request to include the outdoor golf practice range among the prohibited uses,” which the prior judgment pointed out as a defect in the balancing of interests of the prior refusal disposition, has been directly or in substance included in the decision at issue.\\n\\n1) The decision at issue merely enumerates massage parlors, funeral parlors, etc. as building uses prohibited in the special planning district and provides “other uses that harm the surrounding residential environment, educational environment, landscape, etc.,” and does not provide that outdoor golf practice ranges are prohibited. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the construction of an outdoor golf practice range on the land at issue was prohibited by the decision at issue.\\n\\n2) Initially, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City required that the outdoor golf practice range be included among the prohibited uses in the plan at issue on grounds including that, in apartment districts, the outdoor golf practice range is not permitted pursuant to the Apartment District Ordinance. Article 9(1) of the Apartment District Ordinance provides that buildings constructed in apartment districts shall be planned within the scope of [Attached Table 2], while [Attached Table 2] does not permit the construction of outdoor golf practice ranges in the district center, block center, subdivision center, residential land, school site, park land, or road land among apartment districts. However, because the land at issue was classified as “other land” among apartment districts by the decision at issue, it cannot be said that the construction of an outdoor golf practice range on the land at issue was prohibited by [Attached Table 2] of Article 9(1) of the Apartment District Ordinance. Rather, the fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City classified the land at issue as “other land” among apartment districts in the decision at issue may be seen as the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City’s own decision not to regulate the scope of buildings permitted on the land at issue according to [Attached Table 2] of Article 9(1) of the Apartment District Ordinance.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, the formulation standards at issue provide, as a “regulation on the location of aesthetically harmful facilities” along arterial roads, that “a golf practice range with an outdoor tower” may be designated as a building use that may be prohibited, but this is merely an internal standard to be referenced by the administrative agency when formulating a district unit plan. In addition, although the “Draft Decision on the District Unit Planning Zone and Plan of the Banpo Apartment District” publicly inspected and announced by the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City on April 12, 2018, explicitly listed “a golf practice range with an outdoor iron tower installed among athletic facilities” as a building use prohibited in the Banpo Apartment District, even if the district unit plan for the Banpo Apartment District were formulated and decided as such, the prohibition of constructing an outdoor golf practice range on the land at issue would merely be the effect of a separate urban management plan decision and would be unrelated to the decision at issue.\\n\\nd. Finally, when the following circumstances ascertainable from the record are comprehensively considered, it is appropriate to view the decision at issue as having been made by the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City by additionally considering new circumstances that were not considered at the time of the prior refusal disposition.\\n\\n1) First, the “Guidelines for Formulating District Unit Plans,” a directive issued by the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport pursuant to delegation under Article 49(2) of the National Land Planning Act, define a special planning district as a district within a district unit planning zone in which it is necessary to accept a creative development proposal through a design competition, etc., or in which, because a considerable period is expected to be required for the formulation and realization of the plan, it is necessary to have sufficient time to create a separate development proposal and decide to accept it as a district unit plan (3-15-1), and provide that, as targets for designation as special planning districts, where implementation of public projects, construction of large-scale buildings, or joint development by landowners of two or more parcels, or other cases in which designation and development as a special planning district is necessary to achieve the purposes of designation of the district unit planning zone, etc. (3-15-2). The formulation standards at issue designate as target areas for designation as special planning districts areas where planned development is necessary due to large-scale relocated sites such as schools and areas where a change in the use district or zone is necessary, and prescribe the scale for the designation standard for special planning districts as “5,000 square meters or more in the case of vacant lots and relocated sites (including small lots to be induced and regularized)” (1-8-3). The fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City designated the school site at issue, including the land at issue, as a special planning district conforms to the relevant provisions.\\n\\n2) Before the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City issued the prior refusal disposition, in the process of going through a prior feasibility consultation procedure for the plan at issue, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City presented, on April 7, 2015, a consultative opinion to the head of Seocho-gu Office requesting a review as to whether it conformed to the formulation and designation standards for special planning districts. In response, the Defendant submitted a corrective action plan on April 30, 2015 stating that the land at issue did not conform to the standards for formulation and designation as a special planning district. Although the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City did not expressly state in the prior refusal disposition that there was a need to designate the land at issue as a special planning district, this circumstance alone cannot be regarded as showing that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, through the prior refusal disposition, expressed an official view that the school site at issue would not be designated as a special planning district in the future.\\n\\nRather, when the process by which the prior refusal disposition and the decision at issue were made, as well as the wording of each disposition document, are comprehensively considered, it appears that, in the prior refusal disposition, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City did not actively consider the “need to designate the school site at issue as a special planning district” because the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City refused, on the ground that the plan at issue proposed by the Defendant was inappropriate, the very act of abolishing the existing urban planning facility decision and newly establishing an urban management plan with respect to the school site at issue. Thereafter, in the process of newly establishing an urban management plan in accordance with the purport of the prior judgment and making the decision at issue, it appears that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City designated the school site at issue as a special planning district in consideration of the need, following the abolition of the existing urban planning facility decision, to establish a development plan consistent with the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan),” the separate urban plan “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront,” and the “Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan” then in progress. Accordingly, it cannot be said that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City’s designation of the school site at issue as a special planning district in the decision at issue, after considering other administrative plans, violates the binding force of the prior judgment.\\n\\n3) Even if the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan)” or the “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront” already existed at the time of the prior refusal disposition, the conclusion is not different. In addition, with respect to the “request to reflect 25% public contribution” in the original refusal disposition, it is difficult to regard as identical the consideration factor of “the need to expand infrastructure due to local conditions or conditions of the relevant district, etc.,” which was examined and determined in the prior judgment, and the consideration factor of the need to establish a development plan consistent with the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan),” the “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront,” etc.\\n\\n4) The “Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan,” which was separately being formulated and advanced at the time of the decision at issue, aims at a broad-area urban management plan that systematically integrates and manages the existing apartment district development basic plans centered on individual redevelopment projects, which lack linkage with their surroundings, by comprehensively considering the residential environment and traffic conditions of the area, infrastructure such as roads, and linkage with surrounding areas. Accordingly, it has a different purpose from the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan),” which aims to present the highest-level standards for urban planning, and from the “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront,” which includes content presenting a basic framework to the extent of seeking type-specific alternative measures for the abolition of existing apartment districts. Therefore, it cannot necessarily be said that the public-interest factors considered in the “Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan” overlap with those in the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan)” or the “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront.” If so, the need for a comprehensive and integrated urban management plan concerning existing apartment districts may be regarded as a new circumstance not considered at the time of the prior refusal disposition, independently of whether the “2030 Seoul Urban Master Plan (2030 Seoul Plan)” or the “Basic Plan for Management of the Han River Waterfront” was considered.\\n\\nMeanwhile, since the fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City publicly announced, through a press release on April 19, 2017, the promotion of the formulation of the “Apartment District Improvement Implementation Plan” may be seen as externally expressing the future standards for formulating urban management plans, etc. concerning apartment districts, it is difficult to regard as unlawful the fact that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City considered, when making the decision at issue, that although the implementation plan had not yet been finalized, it would be finalized and implemented in the near future.\\n\\ne. In sum, after the prior judgment cancelling the prior refusal disposition became final, the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City, as a result of additionally considering new circumstances not considered at the time of the prior refusal disposition and conducting a new balancing of interests, made the decision at issue, which actively establishes an urban management plan. Moreover, the decision at issue does not as is include the “request to reflect 25% public contribution” or the “request to include the outdoor golf practice range among the prohibited uses,” which the prior judgment pointed out as defects in the balancing of interests of the prior refusal disposition. Therefore, it cannot be said that the decision at issue violates the binding force of the prior judgment. Nevertheless, the court below, based solely on the circumstances as determined in its opinion, held that the decision at issue violates the binding force of the prior judgment, and on that premise held that the Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan City cannot be deemed to have fulfilled the duty to re-dispose under the prior judgment in this case. The judgment below contains an error of misunderstanding the legal principles concerning planning discretion and the binding force of cancellation judgments, etc.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal of the Plaintiff, we reverse the judgment below and remand the case to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2021DU33593]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Circumstances of the case\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\na. The Plaintiff is a waste treatment company that has moved into the Ulsan-Mipo National Industrial Complex, which was designated and developed as a national industrial complex pursuant to the Act on Industrial Location and Development (hereinafter the “Industrial Location and Development Act”), and the Defendant is an administrative agency to which the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport delegated the authority to alter the industrial complex development plan for a national industrial complex pursuant to the statutes and regulations under the Industrial Location and Development Act.\\n\\nb. On March 14, 2019, the Defendant accepted the application of NC Ulsan Co., Ltd. (hereinafter “NC Ulsan”), another waste treatment company that had moved into the industrial complex at issue, and altered the industrial complex development plan so that NC Ulsan could add one business-site waste incineration facility (with a daily incineration capacity of 206 tons).\\n\\nc. On March 19, 2019, the Plaintiff applied to the Defendant for an alteration of the industrial complex development plan in order to add one business-site waste incineration facility (with a daily incineration capacity of 163 tons, hereinafter the “incineration facility at issue”) to the Plaintiff’s factory.\\n\\nd. On May 8, 2019, the Defendant prepared a “Review Report on Restrictions on the Installation of Air Emission Facilities (Incineration Facilities) in Special Air Conservation Countermeasure Areas for National Industrial Complexes” and decided to restrict, in the future, the expansion of business-site waste incineration facilities within its jurisdiction in order to reduce the emission of air pollutants in Ulsan Metropolitan City.\\n\\ne. On May 16, 2019, the Defendant rejected the Plaintiff’s application for alteration of the industrial complex development plan on the following grounds (hereinafter the “previous grounds for disposition”):\\n\\n1) According to the Clean Air Conservation Act, in a Special Countermeasure Area, the installation of emission facilities where the aggregate annual amount of dust, sulfur oxides, and nitrogen oxides among air pollutants is 10 tons or more may be restricted.\\n\\n2) The concentration of ultrafine particulate matter in Ulsan Metropolitan City exceeds the standards prescribed by the Framework Act on Environmental Policy, anxiety over the health of citizens is increasing, and, pursuant to the Special Act on the Improvement of Air Environment in Air Management Areas (hereinafter the “Air Management Area Act”), enacted and promulgated on April 2, 2019, the “total allowable emissions system for air pollutants by air management area” (hereinafter the “total allowable emissions system”) is expected to be implemented shortly. Business-site waste incineration facilities within the Defendant’s jurisdiction have a high proportion of treating business-site waste generated outside the jurisdiction. The Defendant is restricting the expansion of business-site waste incineration facilities in consideration of these circumstances.\\n\\nf. On August 9, 2019, the Plaintiff again applied to the Defendant for an alteration of the industrial complex development plan with the same content (hereinafter the “application at issue”), stated that it would install a nitrogen oxide reduction device and a chimney remote monitoring system in the incineration facility at issue, and submitted an environmental review report prepared by Blue Entec Co., Ltd. (hereinafter the “environmental review report at issue”).\\n\\ng. On September 6, 2019, the Defendant rejected the application at issue by adding to the previous grounds for disposition the following reason: “Although the Plaintiff asserts that thermal energy generated from the incineration facility at issue can be supplied to the nearby SKC factory to reduce the use of fossil fuels at the SKC factory, the use of fossil fuels only emits general air pollutants such as dust and nitrogen oxides, whereas in the waste incineration process various specific hazardous air pollutants that directly or indirectly harm citizens’ health and the environment, including dioxins, are emitted.” (hereinafter the “disposition at issue”).\\n\\n2. Judgment of the court below\\n\\nThe court below found that the disposition at issue was unlawful due to an abuse or excess of discretionary power, for the following reasons.\\n\\na. The incineration facility at issue appears to have the same daily incineration capacity as the K-2 model among the business-site waste incineration facilities currently operated by the Plaintiff, and its pollutant emissions also appear likely to be similar. However, since the Plaintiff began operating the K-2 model on January 1, 2016, the concentration of ultrafine particulate matter in Ulsan Metropolitan City has decreased from 2015 and has remained largely unchanged to date. In addition, according to the “2015 National Air Pollutant Emissions” and the “2016 National Air Pollutant Emissions,” the amount of ultrafine particulate matter generated by waste treatment companies accounts for only 0.2% to 0.3% of the total.\\n\\nb. The Plaintiff proposed air pollution prevention measures such as installing a nitrogen oxide reduction device and a chimney remote monitoring system in the incineration facility at issue, and according to the environmental review report at issue, the emission of air pollutants from the incineration facility at issue is unlikely to exceed the standards prescribed by the Clean Air Conservation Act. However, the Defendant did not present specific grounds as to, inter alia, the fact that specific hazardous air pollutants under the Clean Air Conservation Act are emitted from the incineration facility at issue in excess of the statutory standards.\\n\\nc. The location and scale of business-site waste treatment facilities should be determined at the national level. Therefore, the part of the grounds for the disposition at issue that states, “if the incineration facility at issue is installed, business-site waste generated outside Ulsan Metropolitan City may be brought in, thereby aggravating air pollution in Ulsan Metropolitan City,” cannot be regarded as a lawful ground for disposition.\\n\\nd. The Defendant may, at a later stage when deciding whether to grant permission to install an air pollutant emission facility under the Clean Air Conservation Act, require measures to reduce air pollutant emissions from the incineration facility at issue, and may also devise air pollution prevention measures even after the incineration facility at issue is installed.\\n\\ne. Considering that the Plaintiff’s factory is located only about 200 meters away from NC Ulsan’s factory, and that the incineration facility for which NC Ulsan applied for expansion has a greater daily incineration capacity than the incineration facility at issue, the disposition at issue should be viewed as contrary to the principle of equity when compared with the NC Ulsan case. The Defendant is also promoting the expansion of the incineration facility at the Seongam Incineration Plant.\\n\\n3. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\na. An administrative plan means a standard of activity established in order to realize a certain order at a certain point in the future by comprehensively coordinating relevant administrative means on the basis of professional and technical judgments concerning administration to achieve a specific administrative objective, or the act of establishing such a standard. When an administrative agency formulates and determines a specific administrative plan, it has a relatively broad discretion in formation. However, such discretionary power of the administrative agency in formation cannot be said to be unlimited, and administrative plans are subject to the limitation that the interests of the persons concerned must be properly compared and weighed, not only between the public interest and private interest, but also among public interests or among private interests. Accordingly, where an administrative agency, in formulating and determining an administrative plan, fails to perform any balancing of interests at all, omits matters that should properly have been included among the objects of consideration in balancing interests, or performs balancing of interests but lacks legitimacy and objectivity, the determination of such administrative plan may become unlawful due to a defect in the balancing of interests (see Supreme Court Decisions 2013DU21748 decided on October 15, 2015, 2015DU2338 decided on December 10, 2015, etc.). These legal principles apply equally where the person authorized to alter an industrial complex development plan under the Industrial Location and Development Act determines whether to alter the industrial complex development plan upon an application by an enterprise in the industrial complex, etc.\\n\\nIn reviewing whether there has been an excess or abuse of discretionary power in relation to a rejection disposition on an application for alteration of an industrial complex development plan on the ground that there is a risk of environmental damage or pollution, careful determination should be made by comprehensively considering the legislative intent and purpose of the Industrial Location and Development Act, the concrete local circumstances such as the land use conditions and living environment of nearby residents, the legislative intent of the various provisions concerning the protection of environmental rights, and the balancing of rights and interests among stakeholders with opposing interests. Furthermore, the administrative agency’s discretionary judgment on requirements requiring prediction of uncertain situations and ripple effects to arise in the future, such as the “risk of environmental pollution,” should be broadly respected unless its content manifestly lacks rationality or, when compared against opposing interests or values, is clearly contrary to the principle of equity or proportionality. In addition, the circumstance that a disposition exceeded or abused discretionary power must be alleged and proved by the person contesting the validity of that disposition (see Supreme Court Decisions 2016DU55490 decided on March 15, 2017, 2019DU45579 decided on December 24, 2019, etc.).\\n\\nb. In light of these legal principles and the record, it is difficult to view the Defendant’s discretionary judgment that granting the application at issue would raise concerns about air pollution as manifestly lacking in rationality or as clearly contrary to the principle of proportionality or the principle of equity. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) According to the former Clean Air Conservation Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 16305 on April 2, 2019; hereinafter the same), a person who intends to install an emission facility in a place designated as a Special Countermeasure Area under Article 38 of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy must obtain permission from the Mayor/Do Governor [Article 23, paragraph 1, Article 11, paragraph 1, item 2 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Clean Air Conservation Act (prior to amendment by Presidential Decree No. 29988 on July 16, 2019; hereinafter the same)], and the Mayor/Do Governor may restrict the installation of emission facilities in a Special Countermeasure Area where the aggregate annual amount of dust, sulfur oxides, and nitrogen oxides among air pollutants is 10 tons or more (Article 23, paragraph 6, Article 12, item 2 of the former Enforcement Decree of the Clean Air Conservation Act).\\n\\nHowever, the industrial complex at issue has been designated as a Special Air Conservation Countermeasure Area pursuant to Article 2, item 1 of the “Notice on Designation of Special Air Conservation Countermeasure Areas and Comprehensive Measures for Reducing Air Pollution within Such Areas,” which was publicly announced by the Minister of Environment under the delegation of Article 38, paragraph 1, of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy. In addition, the Plaintiff itself predicted through the application at issue that the incineration facility at issue would emit 1.67 tons of dust, 10.18 tons of sulfur oxides, and 29.49 tons of nitrogen oxides per year. Accordingly, if the Plaintiff later applies for permission to install an emission facility under the Clean Air Conservation Act, the Defendant may, absent any change in circumstances, issue a denial disposition on the ground that the incineration facility at issue constitutes a facility that emits, in aggregate, 10 tons or more per year of dust, sulfur oxides, and nitrogen oxides within a Special Air Conservation Countermeasure Area.\\n\\nIt appears that the Defendant took into advance consideration the fact that, even if the application at issue were granted immediately, the incineration facility at issue would qualify as an emission facility whose installation is restricted under the Clean Air Conservation Act and would thus be difficult to obtain final installation permission for. Such a decision by the Defendant does not appear manifestly unreasonable.\\n\\n2) Since environmental pollution is often nearly impossible to restore to its original state once it has occurred, there are limits to recovering damage caused by environmental pollution through ex post regulation alone. Accordingly, where there is a risk that the environment may be seriously polluted, preventing such pollution in advance is important. However, in light of the following, it is also difficult to view the air pollution prevention measures proposed by the Plaintiff as sufficient.\\n\\nAccording to the environmental review report at issue, the emission of air pollutants from the incineration facility at issue is predicted not to exceed the standards prescribed by the Clean Air Conservation Act. However, this is premised on the Plaintiff’s continuously investing substantial costs to maintain the performance of the nitrogen oxide reduction device at the highest level. Moreover, even according to that prediction, the amount of dust, sulfur oxides, and nitrogen oxides emitted from the incineration facility at issue still exceeds the standard prescribed by the former Enforcement Decree of the Clean Air Conservation Act for allowing the Mayor/Do Governor to restrict the installation of emission facilities in a Special Countermeasure Area. In addition, the chimney remote monitoring system can measure, among the air pollutants under the Clean Air Conservation Act, only dust, oxygen saturation, nitrogen oxides, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride, ammonia, and carbon monoxide, and cannot measure the remaining air pollutants under the Clean Air Conservation Act or specific hazardous air pollutants such as dioxins, chromium, lead, and cadmium.\\n\\n3) The Defendant’s decision on May 8, 2019, to restrict the expansion of business-site waste incineration facilities within its jurisdiction appears to be one of the appropriate measures that could be selected in order to reduce the emission of ultrafine particulate matter. This is because the emission of ultrafine particulate matter by waste treatment companies in Ulsan Metropolitan City in 2016 was approximately 75 tons, accounting for about 3% of the total emission of ultrafine particulate matter in Ulsan Metropolitan City during the same period (approximately 2,501 tons), which is greater than the emission of ultrafine particulate matter by waste treatment companies in other Special Metropolitan Cities and Metropolitan Cities during the same period (approximately 11 tons in Seoul, 10 tons in Busan, 4 tons in Daegu, 8 tons in Incheon, 2 tons in Gwangju, and 5 tons in Daejeon), and because the annual average concentration of ultrafine particulate matter in Ulsan Metropolitan City exceeds the standards prescribed by Article 12, paragraph 2 of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy and [Appendix 1] of Article 2 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act.\\n\\nIn addition, after the Plaintiff filed the application for alteration of the industrial complex development plan on March 19, 2019, the Air Management Area Act, which includes the introduction of the total allowable emissions system, was enacted and promulgated as Act No. 16305 on April 2, 2019. Although Article 1 of the supplementary provisions of that Act provides that the effective date of the Act shall be one year after the date of promulgation, it appears that the Defendant also needed to establish and implement air pollution prevention measures proactively and actively in anticipation of the implementation of the total allowable emissions system.\\n\\n4) It is difficult to view the disposition at issue as clearly contrary to the principle of equity when compared with the NC Ulsan case. This is because, if the person authorized to alter an industrial complex development plan has altered the industrial complex development plan so that a particular waste treatment company may expand its waste incineration facility, and if one were to hold that, under the principle of equity, the industrial complex development plan must necessarily be altered so that nearby companies in the same line of business can also enjoy the same benefit, the system of industrial complex development plans, which is intended to promote balanced national land development and sustained industrial development through the rational placement of various industries within the industrial complex, could be rendered a dead letter. In addition, the Defendant altered the industrial complex development plan so that NC Ulsan could add one business-site waste incineration facility before the Air Management Area Act was enacted and promulgated, whereas the Plaintiff’s application at issue and the Defendant’s disposition at issue were made afterward.\\n\\nThe Seongam Incineration Plant is a facility operated by the Defendant to treat household waste discharged from its jurisdiction pursuant to Article 14, paragraph 1, of the Waste Management Act, and differs from the incineration facility at issue, which is for the treatment of business-site waste, in both the object of incineration and the legal basis. Accordingly, the disposition at issue cannot be viewed as contradictory to the Defendant’s plan to expand the incineration facility of the Seongam Incineration Plant.\\n\\nc. If the circumstances are as such, the court below should have conducted further review as to whether the Defendant’s discretionary judgment restricting the expansion of the incineration facility at issue in order to prevent environmental pollution manifestly lacked rationality or was clearly contrary to the principle of equity or proportionality, or should have held the Plaintiff to its burden of proof and dismissed the Plaintiff’s claim. Nevertheless, the court below found, solely on the basis of the circumstances as determined in its decision, that the disposition at issue was unlawful due to an excess or abuse of discretionary power. In so doing, the court below erred by misunderstanding the legal principles on excess or abuse of discretionary power and the allocation of the burden of proof, and by failing to conduct the necessary review, thereby affecting the judgment. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the judgment."}
