question: Which of the following correctly combines the statements that are true (○) and those that are false (X) regarding the following case? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law) A intended to collect mukcho from the X River flowing through City A. Accordingly, A applied to B, the Mayor of City A, who is the administrative authority for the X River, for a river occupation permit under the River Act and its subordinate statutes. However, even after receiving A's application, B has not responded in any way for a considerable period of time. A now seeks to file an action for confirmation of the illegality of omission against B.
label: A
supporting_precedents: {"[2008DU10560]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. On grounds 1 and 5 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nTaking Articles 8 and 38(1) of the Local Public Officials Act, and Article 38-3 of the Local Public Officials Appointment Decree together, the promotion appointment of public officials of Grade 2 through Grade 4 shall be made by the appointing authority taking into account administrative performance, ability, experience, field of major study, character, and aptitude, etc., and shall be subject to prior deliberation by the Personnel Committee. Accordingly, if a Grade 4 public official is determined, after deliberation by the Personnel Committee of the relevant local government, to be a candidate for promotion to Grade 3, and the appointing authority has even publicly announced that fact both internally and externally, then that public official, as a person having a legal interest in promotion appointment, has, vis-à-vis the appointing authority, a right under general legal principles to apply for promotion appointment to Grade 3, and the administrative agency that has received an application for promotion appointment through a petition for appeal review from such public official has a legal duty to respond to grant the application by an affirmative disposition or to render a negative disposition such as dismissal as inadmissible or dismissal on the merits within a reasonable period. Nevertheless, if the administrative agency is taking no affirmative or negative disposition whatsoever with respect to the application of such right-holder, such inaction on the part of the administrative agency is unlawful in itself.\\n\\nAccording to the reasons of the judgment below, it can be seen that, after publicly announcing both internally and externally that the Plaintiff had been determined, following deliberation by the Personnel Committee, to be a candidate for promotion to Grade 3, the Defendant took no action whatsoever with respect to the Plaintiff’s application for promotion appointment through appeal review dated 2005. 9. 30. until the close of the fact-finding oral argument in this case; in light of the legal principle stated above, such inaction on the part of the Defendant is unlawful in itself.\\n\\nAlthough it is not appropriate that the court below further determined whether the Defendant’s failure to promote appoint the Plaintiff was justified, its conclusion that the Defendant’s inaction in taking no measures whatsoever with respect to the Plaintiff’s application for promotion appointment is unlawful is proper, and there is no error such as misapprehension of legal principles as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. On ground 2 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nThis part of the grounds of appeal, to the effect that the Defendant, by appointing the Plaintiff to the post of Director of the Municipal Folk Museum on 2004. 8. 9., rendered a disposition refusing promotion appointment with respect to the Plaintiff, is an argument raised only at the appellate stage and cannot constitute a proper ground of appeal.\\n\\n3. On ground 3 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nIn light of the fact that the Plaintiff filed this action for confirmation of illegality of inaction after going through the appeal review procedure seeking performance of the promotion appointment, the court below’s determination rejecting the Defendant’s argument that this action is improper because it did not go through the mandatory prior adjudicative procedure is proper, and there is no error that affected the outcome of the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning prior procedures, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n4. On ground 4 of the grounds of appeal\\n\\nAn action for confirmation of illegality of inaction should be deemed to have an interest in seeking confirmation of illegality so long as the state of inaction continues, and thus, in principle, it is not subject to any limitation period for filing. However, in light of the fact that Article 38(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act applies mutatis mutandis Article 20 of the same Act, which prescribes the filing period, to an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction, where a prior procedure such as administrative appeal review has been gone through, an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction should be filed within the filing period prescribed by Article 20 of the Administrative Litigation Act. Nevertheless, whether an administrative agency is in a state of inaction or has rendered a negative disposition in response to an application based on a party’s statutory or general-principle right may not be clear because the issue of legal evaluation based on the same factual relations is involved, and if a negative disposition is made while an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction is pending, the action for confirmation of illegality of inaction loses its benefit of action and becomes improper, in which case an action for revocation of the negative disposition must be brought; thus, an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction has a supplementary character to an action for revocation. In light of such supplementary character of an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction, it may be said that, in an action for revocation seeking cancellation of a refusal disposition concerning the same application, unless there are special circumstances, it also includes the purport of seeking confirmation of the illegality of inaction concerning that application. Taking these circumstances together, where a party brought an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction with respect to the same application, but thereafter, deeming that a negative disposition had been made, changed the action alternately to an action for revocation of disposition, and then additionally joined the action for confirmation of illegality of inaction thereto, if the original action for confirmation of illegality of inaction had been filed within the lawful filing period, it is reasonable to deem that the filing period has still been complied with despite the process of such alternation to and additional change into the action for revocation of disposition.\\n\\nAccording to the facts lawfully determined by the court below and the record, on 2004. 9. 30. the Plaintiff filed a petition for appeal review with the Appeal Review Committee of □□ Metropolitan City to the effect that “the Defendant shall promote and appoint the Plaintiff as a Local Deputy Director-General (Grade 3),” and the said Appeal Review Committee dismissed the Plaintiff’s petition for appeal review on 2006. 2. 20.; the Plaintiff received the written decision around that time; the Plaintiff filed this action for confirmation of illegality of inaction on 2006. 3. 8., within the lawful filing period from the date of service of the said written decision, with the second alternative claim in this case as the prayer for relief; thereafter, at the first hearing date in the court of first instance on 2006. 8. 17., the second alternative claim in this case was changed alternately into an action for revocation to the effect that “the disposition refusing promotion appointment as Local Deputy Director-General made by the Defendant against the Plaintiff on 2006. 3. 30. is revoked,” and then, at the first hearing date before remand in the court below on 2007. 7. 26., the second alternative claim in this case was additionally changed; thereafter, by the remand judgment in this case, it was found that the disposition refusing promotion appointment dated 2006. 3. 30., which the Plaintiff sought to revoke in the action for revocation, did not exist, etc. As can be seen, in light of the legal principle stated above, it is manifest from the chronology that this action for confirmation of illegality of inaction was filed on 2006. 3. 8., within the lawful filing period from 2006. 2. 20., when the appeal review decision was rendered. Therefore, the mere fact that thereafter the prayer for relief was changed alternately and additionally in the manner stated above does not render the lawfully filed action for confirmation of illegality of inaction improper.\\n\\nAlthough the court below’s determination to the effect that an action for confirmation of illegality of inaction is not subject to any limitation period for filing contains a misapprehension of the legal principle concerning the filing period for such action, its conclusion rejecting the Defendant’s argument that this action for confirmation of illegality of inaction is improper because it was not filed within the filing period is proper, and ultimately there is no error that affected the outcome of the judgment.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the appellate costs shall be borne by the losing party. The participating Justices of the Supreme Court concurred, and the judgment is rendered as stated in the Disposition."}

{"[2009MU153]": "We examine the grounds for reappeal.\\n\\nThe lower court, by citing the first-instance order, made the following determination. That is, in the action for declaratory judgment on unlawfulness of omission brought by the applicant against the respondent, the applicant obtained a final and binding judgment granting the applicant’s second alternative claim. The purport of that judgment is merely to confirm that the respondent’s failure to take any measure whatsoever with respect to the applicant’s application for promotion appointment to a Deputy Director-General position in Gwangju Metropolitan City is unlawful. Accordingly, not only in the case where the respondent issues a disposition appointing the applicant to promotion appointment, but also in the case where the respondent issues a disposition refusing promotion appointment, it would be deemed that a disposition has been made in accordance with the purport of the said final and binding judgment. However, after the said final and binding judgment was rendered, the respondent issued a disposition refusing the applicant’s promotion appointment. Therefore, in the end, the applicant’s application for indirect enforcement in this case did not satisfy the necessary requirements.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination by the lower court is justifiable and acceptable, and it cannot be said that there was any illegality, as alleged in the grounds for reappeal, in misunderstanding the content of the judgment confirming unlawfulness of omission or in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning an action for declaratory judgment on unlawfulness of omission.\\n\\nTherefore, the reappeal is dismissed, and the costs of the reappeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so decided, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the disposition."}

{"[89NU4758]": "Regarding the grounds for final appeal,\\n\\n1. According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below found as follows: In appointing new faculty members at Seoul National University of Education, the dean, through the prescribed screening procedures, finally determines the candidate for appointment and has the person serve as a full-time instructor for a period of one year, then evaluates qualifications as a professor, ability, student guidance performance, and work status, etc., and thereafter decides whether to appoint the person as a full-time faculty member, and then appoints or recommends appointment as a full-time lecturer or assistant professor; in appointing the above full-time instructors and full-time faculty members, the dean must obtain the consent of the University Personnel Committee in each case. Accordingly, on 1987.1.1., the Defendant made a recruitment notice for professors stating that a candidate for new appointment as a professor would, after serving as a full-time instructor for one year, be appointed as a full-time faculty member if the work performance evaluation result during that period was a passing determination, but would be automatically dismissed if it was a failing determination, and after going through the prescribed procedures selected the Plaintiff, who had applied for the above faculty recruitment, as the appointment candidate for the Department of Science Education, and on 1987.2.1. appointed the Plaintiff as a full-time instructor in the University’s General Education Division for a period of one year from that date until 1988.1.31., expressly stating that if, as a result of the work evaluation during the appointment period, the Plaintiff passed, the Plaintiff would be appointed as a full-time faculty member. Thereafter, when the Plaintiff had completed the duties as a full-time instructor by lecturing in earth science during the above period, the Defendant first evaluated the Plaintiff’s work performance in order to appoint the Plaintiff as a regular faculty member, and as a result the Plaintiff passed, so the Defendant requested the University Personnel Committee for consent to appointment; however, the Committee’s resolution resulted in rejection, and thus the consent for appointment was not obtained. On that basis, the court below held that the Defendant’s failure to appoint the Plaintiff as a regular faculty member was unavoidable procedurally, and even if there were some defect in the University Personnel Committee’s resolution not to consent to the Plaintiff’s appointment, the Defendant, as dean, could not disregard it; nor could it be said that the Defendant by words or conduct caused the Plaintiff to trust that consent of the Personnel Committee was unnecessary for appointment as a regular faculty member. For these reasons, the court below dismissed the principal claim in this case, which sought a declaration that the Defendant’s omission in failing to appoint the Plaintiff as a regular faculty member was unlawful, and further dismissed the alternative claim seeking cancellation of the refusal disposition on the ground that the existence of a refusal disposition was not recognized.\\n\\n2. However, Article 2(1)1 of the Education Public Officials Act defines as one of the education public officials the teachers prescribed in Article 75(1)1 through 4 of the Education Act who work at educational institutions. According to Article 75(1)2, 5, and 6 of the Education Act, universities, teachers’ colleges, colleges of education, and junior colleges shall have a dean (a president in the case of a university), professors, associate professors, assistant professors, full-time lecturers, and assistants; each school shall also have necessary administrative staff in addition to teachers, and matters concerning the quotas of teachers and administrative staff shall be prescribed by Presidential Decree; and under Article 35 of the Enforcement Decree thereof, each school may have lecturers, as needed, in addition to the quota, for the purpose of assisting teachers’ duties, among whom those who work on a full-time basis are to be called full-time lecturers, and those who do not work on a full-time basis are to be called part-time lecturers. According to Article 26 of the Education Public Officials Act, full-time lecturers and assistants shall be appointed by the president or dean with the consent of the relevant University Personnel Committee. Meanwhile, under Article 29(1) of the State Public Officials Act, in principle, when newly appointing a Grade 5 public official, the person is appointed on a probationary basis for one year, and when newly appointing a public official of Grade 6 or lower or a technical public official, the person is appointed on a probationary basis for six months, and if the work performance during that period is good, the person is to be appointed as a regular public official, thereby establishing the so-called probationary appointment system. Further, according to the draft amendment to the Regulations on New Appointments of Faculty Members at Seoul National University of Education (Exhibit A No. 8), Article 3 provides that the rank for new appointment of faculty members shall be full-time lecturer, but in the case of a person with a doctorate and special research experience, appointment as assistant professor is permitted; Article 4 provides that new appointments of faculty members shall, in principle, be made through open recruitment, and that the selection of candidates for appointment shall be made by the Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice President for Student Affairs, the relevant dean or department chair, based on the application documents submitted by the applicant, after document screening according to the prescribed appointment qualification standards, who then recommends the candidate to the dean with an opinion letter attached; the dean shall make a final determination of the candidate for appointment from among the recommended persons through screening, have the person serve as a full-time instructor for one year, then evaluate qualifications as a professor, ability, student guidance performance, and work status, etc., decide whether to appoint the person as a full-time faculty member, and thereafter appoint or recommend appointment as a full-time lecturer or assistant professor. Article 7 provides that when the dean appoints a full-time instructor or seeks to appoint or recommend appointment of a faculty member, the matter shall be submitted to the Personnel Committee and consent obtained. Also, according to the Regulations on Full-time Instructors at Seoul National University of Education (Exhibit A No. 9), Article 2 provides that a full-time instructor means a person appointed for one year pursuant to the above Regulations on New Appointments and who works full-time at this university; Article 6 provides that the evaluators of work performance are the Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice President for Student Affairs, the relevant dean of education or the relevant department chair, and the principal of the national elementary school used for practical training in the field of education, each of whom evaluates based on the evaluation form and submits it to the dean; the dean, by reference thereto, conducts the final work performance evaluation by dividing each item into five levels; Article 7(1) provides that appointment of a full-time instructor as a full-time faculty member shall be limited to a person whose final work performance evaluation, when comprehensively considered, is at least level 2, but consent of the University Personnel Committee must be obtained; and Article 9 provides that matters concerning service and work other than those in the present Regulations shall be governed mutatis mutandis by the Regulations on Public Officials’ Service and the Regulations on Public Officials’ Work Matters.\\n\\nExamining the above relevant provisions, a person hired as a full-time instructor at Seoul National University of Education under the full-time instructor system operated by the university refers to a full-time lecturer who works on a full-time basis to assist teachers’ duties beyond the quota prescribed in Article 35(2) of the Enforcement Decree of the Education Act; however, since this is distinct from the full-time lecturer, who is a regular teacher prescribed in Article 75(1)2 of the Education Act, the said full-time instructor system is not a method of appointing teachers having an express basis under the Education Act or the Education Public Officials Act. Rather, according to the purpose and content of the said full-time instructor system, in the case of appointing new faculty members of full-time lecturer rank or higher at the university, the appointment candidate must necessarily undergo a one-year period, and only a person who is determined to be qualified may be appointed as a regular faculty member; thus, it must be regarded as corresponding to a public official conditionally hired under the so-called probationary appointment system under the State Public Officials Act.\\n\\nThe State Public Officials Act, with the objective of establishing the fundamental standards of personnel administration applicable to all State public officials working in each level of agency (see Article 1), provides in Article 26 that the appointment of public officials shall be based on examination scores, work performance, and other demonstrations of ability, thereby declaring the so-called merit principle, and in Article 29 establishes the above probationary appointment system. By contrast, the Education Public Officials Act (see Article 1), which aims to prescribe special provisions applicable to education public officials concerning qualifications, appointment, remuneration, training, and status guarantees in light of the special nature of the duties and responsibilities of education public officials vis-à-vis the State Public Officials Act, also declares the merit principle in appointing education public officials (see Article 10), but does not contain an express provision regarding the above probationary appointment system. The purpose and objective of that system is understood to be, in view of the fact that open competitive examinations for new appointment of public officials or special recruitment examinations (see Article 28(1) and (2) of the same Act) cannot be said to fully demonstrate the public official’s ability to perform duties, to perfect the merit principle of appointing public officials based on demonstrated ability by facilitating the exclusion, through actual practice, of those among public officials initially hired through examination, etc., who are later determined not to possess the requisite qualifications. In particular, in light of the fact that the Education Public Officials Act, which provides special provisions to the State Public Officials Act, excludes the application of other provisions of the State Public Officials Act in Article 53 while, peculiarly, excluding only the provision of Article 29 of the State Public Officials Act concerning the probationary appointment system, the probationary appointment or conditional hiring system is likewise permissible under the Education Public Officials Act because there is a rational basis for it in the new appointment of education public officials. Accordingly, the full-time instructor system at Seoul National University of Education in this case, which appears to be operated within the scope of the purpose and objective of that system, is lawful; and the Plaintiff, who was hired as a full-time instructor accordingly, in the probationary appointment or conditional hiring at that time, acquires, on the condition that during the prescribed conditional employment period the work performance is satisfactory and a determination of qualification is obtained, the right to be appointed as a regular public official immediately upon the expiration of that period, absent special circumstances, and the appointing authority bears the corresponding legal duty. Further, while enjoying the status as an education public official through probationary appointment under the Education Public Officials Act, if during the conditional employment period the person receives a status-disadvantageous disposition such as dismissal or disciplinary action, or if after the expiration of the probationary appointment period appointment as a regular public official or faculty member is refused, the person must also be regarded as having the right to request adjudication of a petition under Article 52 of the Education Public Officials Act as a prerequisite procedure for filing an administrative lawsuit.\\n\\n3. Meanwhile, an action for confirmation of the illegality of omission is intended to, in cases where an administrative agency has a legal duty to respond, within a reasonable period, to an application based on a person’s statutory rights or rights under general principles of law by making a certain disposition, namely, a positive disposition granting the application or a negative disposition such as dismissal or rejection, but fails to do so, promptly induce the administrative agency’s response by confirming the unlawfulness of the omission as of the time of judgment (the close of oral argument in the fact-finding proceedings), thereby eliminating the negative unlawful state called omission or non-response; further, because it is a system intended ultimately to protect the rights and interests of the people by causing the administrative agency, through the binding force of the relevant judgment, to make a disposition, etc., and, if there is an objection to the disposition, etc. at that time, to contest the disposition, etc., when the omission state is remedied before or after the filing of the suit and by the time of judgment through the administrative agency’s making a positive or negative disposition with respect to the application, the interest in the suit is lost and the relevant action cannot avoid dismissal as inadmissible.\\n\\nAnd in order to say that there has been a certain disposition from the administrative agency, especially a refusal disposition, which extinguishes the administrative agency’s omission state, it is not enough merely that there was a factual decision within the administrative agency for the disposition or that a written document containing the content of that decision was drafted or prepared; only where the decision has been expressed externally in some form by a person with authority in the administrative agency and the purport that the application was refused or dismissed has been accurately communicated to the applicant without misunderstanding, placing the applicant in a state where the applicant can know it, can it be said that such a disposition existed. According to the original judgment and the record, in this case, when the Plaintiff had completed the duties as a full-time instructor, the Defendant, in order to appoint the Plaintiff as a regular faculty member, first evaluated the Plaintiff’s work performance through the prescribed procedures, and as a result the Plaintiff passed. Accordingly, the Defendant requested the University Personnel Committee for consent to appointment; however, the Committee’s resolution resulted in rejection, and thus consent for appointment was not obtained. Notwithstanding this, the Defendant did not accurately communicate that purport to the Plaintiff. Consequently, around 1988.3.10., the Plaintiff sent the Defendant a registered mail letter requesting that the Plaintiff be appointed as a regular faculty member, while also sending a petition with the same content to the Ministry of Education. When the Defendant received the petition transferred from the Ministry of Education, the Defendant, only then, in the form of a notice of the result of processing a civil petition document, sent the Plaintiff, around 1988.3.15., a letter containing the explanation that, although the Plaintiff’s work performance evaluation as a full-time instructor disclosed no special disqualifying reason, appointment as a regular faculty member was not possible because the consent to appointment was rejected in the Personnel Committee consent procedure. According to this, the Defendant had been in a state of omission in that the Defendant had not, immediately after the expiration of the Plaintiff’s full-time instructor service period, made a disposition appointing the Plaintiff as a regular faculty member, and indeed had not made any disposition refusing such appointment; thus, after the lapse of a reasonable period, the Defendant’s above omission became unlawful. However, thereafter, at the Plaintiff’s request, the Defendant made clear the intention to refuse the appointment in the form of a notice of the result of processing a civil petition document, so at least around that time, it must be regarded that the Defendant had made a refusal disposition against the Plaintiff.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the court below, ex officio, should have dismissed the Plaintiff’s principal claim in this case, premised on the continued existence of the Defendant’s omission state, as improper for lack of interest in the suit; on the other hand, since there had thereafter been a refusal disposition by the Defendant, the court below should have proceeded to the merits and determined the propriety of the Plaintiff’s alternative claim seeking cancellation thereof. Nevertheless, instead of doing so, the court below, conversely, regarded the Defendant’s omission state as still continuing, proceeded to a merits determination on the principal claim and dismissed it as groundless, and as to the alternative claim, found that there was no refusal disposition and dismissed it. This constitutes a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning an action for confirmation of the illegality of omission and a refusal disposition by an administrative agency that is the subject of an administrative lawsuit, and also an error affecting the judgment due to a mistake of fact. Accordingly, the argument is well-founded.\\n\\nAccordingly, without even considering the grounds for final appeal on the merits of the Plaintiff’s principal and alternative claims in this case, the original judgment is reversed in its entirety; as to the portion dismissing the principal claim, the facts established by the court below are sufficient for this Court to determine, so this portion of the action is dismissed as inadmissible, and as to the portion dismissing the alternative claim, since the Defendant’s refusal disposition, which is the subject of the action for cancellation, exists, the case is remanded to the court below, the Seoul High Court, so that it may proceed to the merits and review and determine the matter. The opinions of the participating Justices being unanimous, it is so adjudged as ordered."}

{"[90NU3553]": "With respect to the Plaintiff’s grounds of appeal (the supplemental grounds of appeal stated in the supplemental brief of grounds of appeal submitted after the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal had expired, to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal), the Court determines as follows.\\n\\n1. Whether to reopen closed oral proceedings is a matter within the discretion of the court; according to the record, the reason the Plaintiff applied for reopening of the oral proceedings concerns the merits, and the lower court, having declined to accept this and dismissed the action on the ground that all claims in this case were improper, was proper, and the lower court judgment cannot be said to contain the illegality alleged. Accordingly, the argument is without merit.\\n\\n2. The lower court held that what the Plaintiff seeks in this lawsuit can broadly be divided into, first, a part seeking confirmation of the facts and, second, a part seeking confirmation of the existence of a duty to act. The first part concerns, in the issuance, distribution, arrangement, and display of various books, such as the History of the Independence Movement published and distributed by Defendant the Administrator of the Office of Veterans Affairs as Chairman of the Fund Management Committee, textbooks of Korean history for middle and high schools authored and distributed by Defendant the Minister of Education, and various explanatory texts and exhibits at the Independence Hall of Korea managed by Defendant the Minister of Culture, the misdescription or mistaken arrangement and display of the activities of groups such as Daehan Gukminhoe, Daehan Dongnipgun, Gwangbokgun, Gunjeongseo, and Daehan Dongnip Giseong Chonghoe, and of Hong Beom-do, Kim Jwa-jin, Lee Beom-seok, Ahn Jung-geun, Yun Bong-gil, Lee Dong-hwi, and Ma Jin, Yang Hyeong-in, Ma Cheon-ryong, and Ma Cheon-mok, the Plaintiff’s adoptive father, who participated in various independence movements at home and abroad, such as the Battle of Cheongsanri, the Battle of Bongodong, and the March 1 Movement under Japanese colonial rule, thereby causing their historical significance to be wrongly assessed; and, for that reason, it seeks confirmation of those facts. It also seeks confirmation that Defendant the Administrator of the Office of Veterans Affairs, by misunderstanding the activities of these independence activists and exercising the authority to recommend honors and decorations in veterans affairs, improperly exercised such recommendation authority, and thus seeks confirmation that the exercise or non-exercise of such recommendation authority is null and void as a matter of course, or confirmation that the omission is unlawful. The second part seeks confirmation that the Defendants have a duty, because the exercise of the recommendation authority for honors and decorations for these independence activists was improper, to correct this and recommend them again, to correct the misdescribed activities of the independence activists and republish and redistribute the books such as the History of the Independence Movement, and to correct the erroneous parts among the explanatory texts and exhibits in the exhibition halls of the Independence Hall of Korea and display and arrange them again. The lower court determined that the first category of claims seeks confirmation of matters concerning the existence or nonexistence of past historical facts, or matters concerning factual relationships that are not specific legal relationships under public law, or targets a mere omission by an administrative agency, and therefore are not subject to administrative appeal litigation; and that the second category of claims, as actions for confirmation of a duty to act, are likewise not subject to administrative appeal litigation. Accordingly, it held that this lawsuit in its entirety failed to satisfy the requirements for an administrative suit and was therefore unlawful.\\n\\nIn light of the record, the content of the relevant statutes and regulations, and this Court’s judgments in the cases in which the Plaintiff was a party and had filed suit (83NU570 decided on September 25, 1984; 85NU607 decided on November 26, 1985; 88NU3116 decided on January 24, 1989; 88NU3147 decided on January 24, 1989; 88NU3314 decided on January 24, 1989, etc.), the above determination of the lower court is justified and persuasive, and the lower court judgment cannot be said to contain the illegality alleged. The judgments of this Court cited by the arguments as precedents all concern different factual circumstances from this case and are not suitable for invocation here. The argument is also without merit.\\n\\n3. All other arguments concern the merits or cannot serve as legitimate grounds of appeal, and therefore cannot be accepted.\\n\\n4. Therefore, the Plaintiff’s appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal are borne by the losing Plaintiff. It is so adjudged, with the concurrence of all participating Justices."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning administrative litigation are correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a) In a case where the Superintendent of Education issued to the chairperson and the principal of a private school corporation a corrective order stating that, because the conversion of equivalent career experience into salary steps for their subordinate employees had been reflected excessively, salary recovery would be ordered for the employees whose salary steps had been calculated excessively, and that if this was not complied with, subsidy support for those employees would be suspended, and further ordered that the salary steps be re-determined on the basis of the corrected salary steps and the results of the measures be submitted, this constitutes a case in which the employees of the private school were infringed with interests protected by law by the above orders issued to their respective private school corporations.

(b) Since a change of action from civil litigation to appeal litigation is permitted, there is no reason to construe that there is no identity of the factual basis of the claim merely because public-law party litigation and civil litigation are different litigation procedures, and thus to disallow a change of action between the two.

(c) Where a judgment canceling a refusal disposition has become final and conclusive, if the ground for cancellation was due to illegality in the procedure or method of the administrative disposition, the administrative agency that made the disposition may, in accordance with the purport of the final judgment, supplement the illegality and again issue a refusal disposition with respect to the previous application.

(d) When filing an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation in the sense of declaring an administrative disposition void ab initio, it is not necessary to satisfy the filing requirements for a revocation action, such as compliance with the filing period.

On the Propriety of the Action\\n\\nThe court below held, in substance, that Article 9(3) of the Broadcasting Act (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) provides that “where a relay cable broadcasting business operator falling under the standards prescribed by Presidential Decree seeks to engage in the cable broadcasting business, it shall obtain approval from the Broadcasting Commission.” Article 7 of the Enforcement Decree of the Act provides in paragraph (1) that, where a relay cable broadcasting business operator seeks to obtain approval for the cable broadcasting business, the facility conversion plan must conform to the technical standards for the cable broadcasting business and the number of subscribers of the relay cable broadcasting business operator must secure at least the ratio announced by the Defendant out of the total number of households within the relevant broadcasting service area, and that, upon satisfying such requirements, the operator shall attach a facility conversion plan to the application for approval and submit it to the Defendant; while paragraph (2) provides that, when the Defendant receives such application for approval, it shall examine the foregoing matters and the matters set forth in each item of Article 10(1) of the Act, and after going through prescribed procedures, notify the applicant of the result. On a comprehensive consideration of the contents of the relevant statutes, it held that Article 9(3) of the Act is a provision intended to grant a relay cable broadcasting business operator the right to apply for approval for the cable broadcasting business (hereinafter referred to as the “application for conversion approval”), and that whether a relay cable broadcasting business operator that has applied for conversion approval must secure a number of subscribers at least equal to the ratio announced by the Defendant out of the total number of households within the relevant broadcasting service area is a matter to be examined in order to determine whether to grant conversion approval to that operator, and therefore should be determined on the merits.\\n\\nIn light of the provisions of the relevant statutes, the reasoning of the court below is proper and persuasive, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality, such as an error of law concerning the existence of the right to apply, which is a prerequisite for recognizing the dispositive nature of the refusal disposition, as argued in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\nThe Supreme Court decision cited by the Defendant in the grounds of appeal concerns a different case and is therefore not appropriate for citation in this case.\\n\\n2. On the purport and binding force of the final judgment, and the grounds to be considered upon re-disposition\\n\\na. The court below, based on the evidence cited in its opinion, found the following facts: on December 30, 2000, the Defendant publicly announced matters concerning applications for conversion approval for 53 cable broadcasting service areas (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Public Notice”), including the matters to be approved (approval of the cable broadcasting business for a relay cable broadcasting business operator, hereinafter referred to as “conversion approval”), the number of operators to be approved (no more than one operator per broadcasting area), eligibility to apply for approval, application procedures, review of approval applications (review method: in the case of an area with applications from multiple operators, absolute evaluation, and if there are multiple passing operators, comparative evaluation), and implementation schedule (operator approval: scheduled for the end of April 2001); that it received an application for conversion approval (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Conversion Approval Application”) from the Plaintiff, a relay cable broadcasting business operator in the Chungcheongnam-do Cheonan-si, Asan-si, and Yeongi-gun area (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Broadcasting Area”), one of the above 53 service areas; that on April 30, 2001, it selected the Defendant-intervenor, Korea Cable T.V. Cheonan Broadcasting Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the “Intervenor”), another relay cable broadcasting business operator that had applied for conversion approval for the Instant Broadcasting Area, as the operator slated for approval, and issued a disposition not approving the Plaintiff’s Instant Conversion Approval Application (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Prior Refusal Disposition”); that, however, on April 2, 2001, prior to the Instant Prior Refusal Disposition, Taekwang Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Taekwang Industrial”), which owned 100% of the shares of the Intervenor, was designated as a large business group (hereinafter referred to as a “large enterprise group”), and thus the issue arose whether Article 8(4) of the former Broadcasting Act (the version before its amendment by Act No. 6905 on May 29, 2003, hereinafter referred to as the “former Act”), which provides that such a large enterprise group may not own more than 33/100 of the total number of shares of a cable broadcasting business operator, applied; nevertheless, the Defendant received from the Intervenor a document to the effect that Taekwang Industrial would thereafter disperse the shares it owned, and, as above, selected the Intervenor as the operator slated for approval, and then, when Taekwang Industrial’s shareholding ratio fell to 33%, on October 22 of the same year, issued a conversion approval disposition for the Instant Broadcasting Area to the Intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Prior Approval Disposition,” and, together with the Instant Prior Refusal Disposition, the “Instant Prior Dispositions”); that the Plaintiff filed on May 29, 2001, a lawsuit with Seoul Administrative Court Case No. 2001GU20659 seeking revocation of the Instant Prior Refusal Disposition, and the Seoul Administrative Court, on December 26 of the same year, rendered a judgment to the effect that “if, in violation of Article 8(4) of the former Broadcasting Act, a large enterprise group owns more than 33% of the total shares of a relay cable broadcasting business operator that has applied for conversion approval and conversion approval is nevertheless granted, such approval disposition is unlawful; furthermore, if, while postponing the examination of whether the above provision has been violated, the approval disposition is made solely on the basis of the remaining requirements, thereby definitively excluding the rival applicant and then later granting approval on the ground that the provision has come not to be violated, the reference point for reviewing the legal requirements for the rival applicant and the reference point for reviewing the legal requirements for the person who received approval will differ; moreover, since the evaluation points obtainable by the Intervenor may change if the composition of shareholders changes in the process in which Taekwang Industrial reduces its shareholding ratio in the Intervenor, the possibility that the result of the comparative evaluation with the Plaintiff may change cannot be ruled out. Therefore, the Defendant’s decision, on the condition that Taekwang Industrial reduce its shareholding ratio in the Intervenor to 33% or less, to designate the Intervenor as the operator slated for approval and definitively exclude the Plaintiff, and then, once that condition was fulfilled, to grant conversion approval to the Intervenor, is unlawful as a designation of an operator slated for approval and an approval disposition in respect of the Intervenor, who is substantively disqualified from receiving an approval disposition; procedurally, too, it is unlawful because it examined the Intervenor and the Plaintiff by applying different reference points in time. Accordingly, the Instant Prior Refusal Disposition constitutes an abuse and deviation of discretion.” In substance, the court rendered a judgment revoking the foregoing Prior Refusal Disposition, and that judgment became final and conclusive on January 13, 2002; that the Defendant, on July 3, 2002, ex officio revoked the Instant Prior Approval Disposition granted to the Intervenor, constituted a reexamination committee, and, as a result of reexamination considering changed circumstances after the date of conclusion of oral argument in the above final judgment (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Final Judgment”), selected the Intervenor as the operator to be granted conversion approval upon finding that the Intervenor obtained a higher score, and, on July 30 of the same year, issued a disposition not granting conversion approval to the Plaintiff’s conversion approval application (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Re-Refusal Disposition”), and, on August 16 of the same year, issued a conversion approval disposition to the Intervenor (hereinafter referred to as the “Instant Re-Approval Disposition,” and, together with the Instant Re-Refusal Disposition, the “Instant Re-Dispositions”).\\n\\nBased on the facts found above, the court below held that, according to the purport of the Instant Public Notice, the Plaintiff and the Intervenor were in a so-called rival relationship; in light of the need for protection of legitimate expectations regarding the Instant Public Notice (approval schedule for operators) and the fact that the reference point held by the Instant Final Judgment to be unlawful as to the Instant Prior Approval Disposition was April 30, 2001, the purport of the Instant Final Judgment is that, as of the end of April 2001, the Defendant should evaluate the Plaintiff’s and the Intervenor’s applications for approval according to the review method announced by the Defendant, exclude applicants who obtained a score below the cutoff score or who lacked qualification to apply for approval, and, if there are multiple applicants who passed, select the applicant with the higher evaluation score and issue an approval disposition; according to this, as of the end of April 2001, the Intervenor lacked qualification to apply for approval because Taekwang Industrial, a large enterprise group, owned 100% of its shares, and the Plaintiff obtained a score above the cutoff score, so the Defendant should have issued an approval disposition to the Plaintiff and a refusal disposition to the Intervenor unless a new ground for disapproval arose against the Plaintiff after the date of conclusion of oral argument in the Instant Final Judgment; nevertheless, the Instant Re-Dispositions, in which conversion approval was granted to the Intervenor instead of to the Plaintiff as a result of reexamination based on July 30, 2002, violate the binding force of the Instant Final Judgment.\\n\\nb. However, this determination by the court below is difficult to accept.\\n\\nAccording to Article 30(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, where a judgment revoking an administrative agency’s refusal disposition becomes final and conclusive, the administrative agency that issued the disposition shall be under a duty to make a re-disposition concerning the prior application in accordance with the purport of the judgment; however, if the ground for revocation lies in illegality in the procedure or method of the administrative disposition, the administrative agency that issued such disposition may supplement the illegality in accordance with the purport of the final judgment and again issue a refusal disposition concerning the prior application, and such disposition also falls under a re-disposition prescribed in the above provision (see Supreme Court Decision 91NU5242 dated May 26, 1992, and Decision 2002MU30 dated January 15, 2004, among others).\\n\\nAccording to the record, the Instant Final Judgment, after explaining that conversion approval for a relay cable broadcasting business operator in which a large enterprise group owns more than 33% of the total shares is unlawful as being in violation of Article 8(4) of the former Act, and thus approval cannot be granted to such a relay cable broadcasting business operator, proceeded on the premise that if, while postponing the examination of whether that provision was violated, only the remaining requirements are examined and the rival applicant is definitively excluded in advance, and conversion approval is then permitted on the ground that the disputed requirement has been satisfied, the reference point for review of the legal requirements for the rival applicant and the reference point for review of the legal requirements for the person who received approval will, as a result, differ, contrary to the principle of equity; then, in the instant case, taking into account that the designation of Taekwang Industrial as a large enterprise group was a circumstance that the Intervenor could not have foreseen, and that the condition of violation of the shareholding restriction could be resolved within a certain period of time, the review point could have been postponed by setting an appropriate grace period, but such a method was not adopted, and because if the shareholder composition changes in the process in which Taekwang Industrial reduces its shareholding ratio in the Intervenor, the evaluation score obtainable by the Intervenor may change and the possibility that the comparative evaluation with the Plaintiff may change cannot be ruled out, it is apparent that the Instant Prior Refusal Disposition, which evaluated the Plaintiff and the Intervenor by applying different reference points in time and, by determining the Intervenor as the operator slated for approval on the condition that Taekwang Industrial reduce its shareholding ratio in the Intervenor to 33% or less and definitively excluding the Plaintiff, was held to be unlawful as an abuse and deviation of discretion. Since the legality of an approval disposition is determined not at the time of designation of the prospective approved operator but at the time of the approval disposition itself, so long as Taekwang Industrial, a large enterprise group, did not own more than 33% of the Intervenor’s shares at the time of the Instant Prior Approval Disposition, it cannot be said that the Instant Prior Approval Disposition was unlawful on the ground of excessive share ownership by a large enterprise group. Furthermore, in the Instant Final Judgment, despite the possibility that the evaluation result may change if the review is conducted after lowering Taekwang Industrial’s shareholding ratio in the Intervenor, it was held that evaluating the Plaintiff and the Intervenor by applying different reference points in time constituted an abuse and deviation of discretion, and, additionally, it was stated that it would also be possible to postpone the review point by setting an appropriate grace period. In light of these points, the purport of the Instant Final Judgment is that, because the Defendant’s evaluation of the Plaintiff and the Intervenor by using different reference points in time was unlawful, the Defendant should determine whether to grant conversion approval based on the result of a fresh review of the Plaintiff and the Intervenor using the same point in time as the standard; it cannot be said to be intended to require conversion approval to be granted to the Plaintiff without reexamination.\\n\\nAccordingly, the Instant Re-Refusal Disposition, among the Instant Re-Dispositions made as a result of the Defendant’s reexamination of the Plaintiff and the Intervenor on the same basis as of around the time of the Instant Re-Dispositions after the Instant Final Judgment, is a refusal disposition again made concerning the prior application by supplementing the illegality in accordance with the purport of the Instant Final Judgment, and therefore falls under a re-disposition prescribed in Article 30(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act; the Instant Re-Approval Disposition is likewise a disposition in accordance with the purport of the Instant Final Judgment.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below understood the purport of the Instant Final Judgment as meaning that, unless a new ground for disapproval arose against the Plaintiff after the date of conclusion of oral argument in the Instant Final Judgment, approval should be granted to the Plaintiff and disapproval should be rendered against the Intervenor, and held that the Instant Re-Dispositions, based on reexamination considering circumstances that arose after that date of conclusion of oral argument, violated the binding force of the Instant Final Judgment. Accordingly, this court below judgment is erroneous in that it misapprehended the purport of the Instant Final Judgment, the binding force of a final judgment, and the grounds to be considered upon re-disposition.\\n\\n3. On Deviation from and Abuse of Discretion\\n\\na. The court below, premising that the fundamental purpose of the conversion approval system under Article 9(3) of the Act is to activate the cable television industry by granting qualified cable broadcasting business operators the status of cable broadcasting business operators, recognizing multiple cable broadcasting business operators within the same broadcasting area, and thereby inducing expanded opportunities to watch cable TV through fair competition among them, while also encouraging market integration of relay cable broadcasting and cable broadcasting, held, based on the evidence cited in its opinion, that Taekwang Industrial, at the time of the Instant Prior Dispositions, owned 47.06% of the shares of Jungbu Broadcasting and 100% of the shares of the Intervenor, but when the issue of shareholding ratio arose, dispersed the remaining shares, except for 33%, to LG Home Shopping Co., Ltd. and others; that a substantial part of the representative directors, directors, auditors, and other officers of Jungbu Broadcasting and the Intervenor overlapped at the time of the Instant Prior Dispositions and the Instant Re-Dispositions; that the Intervenor intended, at the time of the Instant Reexamination, to use Jungbu Broadcasting’s broadcasting building and share broadcasting facilities such as studios, and after the Instant Re-Dispositions, was sharing broadcasting facilities such as Jungbu Broadcasting’s studios, displaying both the Intervenor’s and Jungbu Broadcasting’s company logos on its outgoing screen, having officers and employees use both the Intervenor’s and Jungbu Broadcasting’s names on their business cards, and jointly operating customer centers and otherwise conducting joint business; and then held that, in light of these facts, the Intervenor, not only at the time of the Instant Conversion Approval Application but also at the time of the Instant Re-Dispositions, was substantially the same operator as Jungbu Broadcasting and, as a cable broadcasting business operator equal to Jungbu Broadcasting, had no reasonable expectation of being able to achieve the purposes of the conversion approval system described above through fair competition, and thus could not be regarded as an operator conforming to the purpose of that system or as an operator satisfying the standard of “regional, social, and cultural necessity and appropriateness” prescribed in Article 10(1) item 3 of the Act; therefore, if the Intervenor, who had a defect in qualification as an approval target as above, obtained a higher score than the Plaintiff as a result of review according to the detailed standards established by the Defendant, then this would mean that the detailed review standards established by the Defendant were set contrary to the purpose of the conversion approval system, or that the evaluation of each item was conducted with a manifest lack of rationality, and thus resulted from an abuse and deviation of discretion. Accordingly, the court held that the Instant Re-Dispositions were unlawful.\\n\\nb. However, this determination by the court below is also difficult to accept.\\n\\nConversion approval under Article 9(3) of the Act is an administrative act by which a relay cable broadcasting business operator is permitted to engage in the cable broadcasting business. In light of the fact that the Defendant is a collegial administrative agency composed of nine Broadcasting Commissioners with expertise and representativeness in various fields of society, and that it deliberates and resolves overall matters concerning broadcasting, as well as the relevant provisions of the Broadcasting Act, the Defendant may establish specific criteria and methods for review of conversion approval through procedures such as hearing the opinions of viewers and announcing whether those opinions were reflected, taking into account the purpose of the Act—to protect the rights and interests of viewers, foster democratic public opinion formation and the improvement of national culture, and contribute to the development of broadcasting and the promotion of the public welfare—and the purpose of the above conversion approval system. Even if review is conducted in accordance with such established criteria and methods, in order to conclude that a disposition based on the result of such review is unlawful, circumstances such as that the criteria themselves violate statutory provisions, or are objectively and manifestly lacking in rationality or appropriateness in light of the purpose of the Broadcasting Act and the conversion approval system, or that the evaluation of each item set out in the review criteria was conducted without appropriateness, would need to be present.\\n\\nHowever, according to the record, it appears that at the time of the Instant Re-Dispositions, both the Intervenor and Jungbu Broadcasting were affiliates of Taekwang Industrial, that a substantial portion of their officers overlapped, and that the Intervenor intended to conduct joint business with Jungbu Broadcasting if it received conversion approval; nevertheless, these circumstances alone make it difficult to conclude that the Intervenor and Jungbu Broadcasting were substantially the same operator at the time of the Instant Re-Dispositions, and therefore it cannot be said that the Intervenor was not an operator conforming to the purpose of the Act and the above conversion approval system, or an operator satisfying the standard of “regional, social, and cultural necessity and appropriateness” set forth in Article 10(1) item 3 of the Act.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below held that, because the Intervenor was substantially the same operator as Jungbu Broadcasting and thus difficult to regard as an operator satisfying the purpose of the conversion approval system or the standard in Article 10(1) item 3 of the Broadcasting Act, the fact that the Intervenor received a higher evaluation than the Plaintiff in the reexamination based on the standards established by the Defendant means that the detailed review standards established by the Defendant were set contrary to the purpose of the conversion approval system or that the evaluation of each item was conducted with a manifest lack of appropriateness, and on that basis held that all of the Instant Re-Dispositions were unlawful. Accordingly, this court below judgment is erroneous in that it misapprehended the law concerning abuse and deviation of discretion in conversion approval dispositions under Article 9(3) of the Act.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The participating Justices of the Supreme Court are of the same opinion, and it is so adjudged as ordered."}

{"[2022DU44262]": "The grounds for final appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the First Ground for Final Appeal\\n\\nA. According to the reasons stated in the judgment below and the record, it can be seen that the Plaintiff filed against the Defendant a claim for confirmation of nonexistence of debt to the effect that the settlement money obligation owed by the Plaintiff to the Defendant under Article 41 of the Urban Development Act does not exist in excess of 3,534,050,553 won, that while the case was pending in the first instance the Plaintiff paid the Defendant a total of 3,957,827,600 won under the name of settlement money, and that, accordingly, the Plaintiff submitted to the court below on 2022. 4. 6. an application to amend the petitum and cause of action, stating that it would amend the existing petitum so as to seek payment of 423,777,047 won paid in excess (= total 3,957,827,600 won paid by the Plaintiff to the Defendant while the case was pending in the first instance – 3,534,050,553 won, which the Plaintiff asserts to be the proper settlement money) and delay damages thereon.\\n\\nB. The court below determined that, whereas the existing lawsuit seeking confirmation of partial nonexistence of the settlement money obligation is a public-law party litigation, the claim seeking return as unjust enrichment of the 423,777,047 won in settlement money overpaid by the Plaintiff pursuant to the application to amend the petitum dated 2022. 4. 6. must be litigated through civil procedure. In light of the relevant legal principles and the record, such determination of the court below is proper, and there is no illegality, such as misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the subject matter of public-law party litigation, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal. The Plaintiff’s First Ground for Final Appeal disputing this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. As to the Second Ground for Final Appeal\\n\\nA. Whether amendment of the action from a public-law party litigation to a civil action is permitted\\n\\n1) The Administrative Litigation Act provides only for cases in which a public-law party litigation is changed into an appeal litigation (Administrative Litigation Act Articles 42 and 21) or where the action is changed due to a change in the disposition (Administrative Litigation Act Article 44(1) and Article 22), and does not contain an express provision on whether a public-law party litigation may be changed into a civil action.\\n\\n2) However, it cannot be said that amendment of the action from a public-law party litigation to a civil action is prohibited. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\na) Since Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act provides that the Civil Procedure Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to administrative litigation, in the case of a public-law party litigation as well, unless it is deemed inappropriate in light of the nature of administrative litigation, the petitum may be amended under Article 262 of the Civil Procedure Act until the conclusion of oral argument, to the extent that the factual basis of the claim is not changed.\\n\\nb) Meanwhile, the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that, where a matter that should have been brought as appeal litigation under the Administrative Litigation Act was mistakenly filed as a civil action, the court seised of the case must exercise its authority to clarify matters so as to have the Plaintiff amend the action into appeal litigation and adjudicate the case according to the procedures prescribed by the Administrative Litigation Act (see Supreme Court Decision 2020. 1. 16. rendered 2019DA264700, etc.). Since amendment from a civil action to appeal litigation is thus permitted, there is no reason to construe that there is no identity of the factual basis of the claim merely because a public-law party litigation and a civil action constitute different procedural forms of litigation, and thereby not permit amendment of the action between the two.\\n\\nc) For ordinary citizens, it is not easy to distinguish the subject matter of public-law party litigation from that of civil action, and there are also cases where, due to changes in circumstances during the progress of the litigation, it becomes necessary to amend a public-law party litigation into a civil action. Even where the necessity of amendment of the action is recognized, requiring withdrawal of the already filed action and the filing of a new civil action merely because the litigation procedure would differ depending on the amendment of the action is not desirable from the standpoint of relief of the party’s rights or judicial economy.\\n\\n3) Accordingly, it is reasonable to construe that amendment from a public-law party litigation to a civil action is also possible, to the extent that the factual basis of the claim is not changed.\\n\\nB. Whether the Plaintiff’s amendment of the action should be permitted\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff’s existing petitum seeking confirmation that the settlement money obligation prescribed by Article 41 of the Urban Development Act does not exist in excess of 3,534,050,553 won, and the petitum seeking return on the ground that the settlement money paid in excess of the said 3,534,050,553 won constitutes unjust enrichment, both presuppose the same assertion that the settlement money obligation under Article 41 of the Urban Development Act is 3,534,050,553 won, and thus there is identity of the factual basis of the claim. Accordingly, the Plaintiff’s aforementioned application dated 2022. 4. 6. to amend the petitum and cause of action must be allowed.\\n\\n2) Nevertheless, the court below’s determination that changing a public-law party litigation into a civil action involves a change in the basis of the claim and therefore cannot be permitted in light of Article 21(1) of the Administrative Litigation Act contains an error affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the identity of the factual basis of the claim, which is a requirement for amendment of the action. The Plaintiff’s Second Ground for Final Appeal pointing this out has merit.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment below is reversed and the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination, and it is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2022DU56630]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. Course of the case and the judgment below\\n\\na. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiffs are employees of a private school.\\n\\n2) On 2020. 8. 5., the Defendant issued a corrective order to the chairperson and the principal of the school foundation to which the Plaintiffs belong, on the ground that the conversion of similar-service careers into salary steps for the employees belonging to that foundation had been excessively reflected, requiring recovery, within the scope of 5 years, of salaries pursuant to the correction of salary steps for employees whose salary steps had been excessively calculated. The above corrective order states that, for a noncomplying school foundation, payment of financial-deficit subsidies (personnel expenses) for employees whose salary steps were excessively reflected will be suspended pursuant to Article 9, subparagraph 7 of the Gangwon-do Ordinance on Financial Subsidies for Private Schools.\\n\\n3) On 2020. 9. 2., the Defendant ordered the chairperson and the principal of the school foundation to which the Plaintiffs belong to carry out re-determination of salary steps based on the corrected salary steps and to submit the results of the measures by 2020. 9. 7. (hereinafter, the corrective order dated 2020. 8. 5. and the order dated 2020. 9. 2. are collectively referred to as ‘the orders at issue’).\\n\\nb. Judgment below\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its holding, the court below upheld the first-instance judgment dismissing this action on the ground that the Plaintiffs, who are not the direct addressees of the disposition, lack standing to sue to challenge the orders at issue.\\n\\n2. Judgment of the Supreme Court\\n\\na. Even a third party who is not the direct addressee of an administrative disposition has standing to bring an action for revocation and obtain a determination on the merits as to its propriety when he/she has suffered an infringement of legally protected interests due to the relevant administrative disposition. The legally protected interests referred to here mean individual, direct, and concrete interests protected by the statutes forming the basis of the relevant disposition and related statutes, and do not include cases where the person merely has factual and economic interests, such as general, indirect, and abstract interests commonly held by the public as a result of the protection of the public interest. In addition, legally protected interests under the statutes forming the basis of the relevant disposition and related statutes include legally protected interests expressly protected by the express provisions of the statutes forming the basis of the relevant disposition; legally protected interests expressly protected by the statutes forming the basis of a series of step-by-step related dispositions for achieving the administrative purpose of the relevant disposition, although not protected by the statutes forming the basis of the relevant disposition; and even where there is no express provision in the statutes forming the basis of the relevant disposition or related statutes that expressly protects the interest, cases in which, upon a reasonable interpretation of the basis statutes and related statutes, the reason those statutes constrain the administrative agency is construed to include the purport of protecting not only pure public interests but also individual, direct, and concrete interests (see Supreme Court Decision 2011DU33044, decided 2013. 9. 12., among others).\\n\\nb. 1) The orders at issue are administrative dispositions having legal binding force that do not merely recommend the chairpersons and principals of each private school foundation to recover salaries and correct salary steps, but also contemplate measures such as suspension of subsidy payments against school foundations that fail to comply.\\n\\n2) a) Among the statutes and regulations forming the basis of the orders at issue, Article 43(2)2 of the former Private School Act (as amended by Act No. 17659 before amendment on 2020. 12. 22.; hereinafter the same) provides to the effect that, when the budget of a school foundation that has received subsidies from or support by a local government is deemed inappropriate in light of the purpose of the support, necessary corrective measures may be recommended with respect to such budget. Since this provision was enacted for the purpose of securing the propriety of the budget of a school foundation that receives financial support, such as subsidies, it may be difficult to view this provision alone as protecting the direct and concrete interests of the Plaintiffs, who are employees of a private school.\\n\\nb) However, because the orders at issue were issued on the ground that the Plaintiffs’ salary steps had been excessively calculated, Article 70-2(1) of the former Private School Act, which prescribes the calculation of salary steps and remuneration for office employees of school foundations, the articles of incorporation of each private school foundation, and the Regulation on Remuneration of Local Public Officials must also be regarded as the statutes forming the basis of the orders at issue or related statutes. Article 70-2(1) of the former Private School Act provides that matters concerning the remuneration of office employees belonging to a school foundation shall be prescribed by the articles of incorporation of the school foundation, and, pursuant to that delegation, the articles of incorporation of each school foundation to which the Plaintiffs belong provide, with respect to the remuneration of office employees, that the remuneration regulations for local public officials shall apply mutatis mutandis (Article 86 of the Articles of Incorporation of Sangji Munhakwon, Article 81 of the Articles of Incorporation of Jingwanghakwon) or that the remuneration regulations and allowance regulations for public officials (public officials of the general service, etc.) shall apply mutatis mutandis (Article 85 of the Articles of Incorporation of Jeonin Hakwon). In addition, Article 8(2) of the Regulation on Remuneration of Local Public Officials provides that the initial salary step of a public official shall be determined in accordance with Attached Table 1, and Attached Table 1 specifically provides how, if an individual public official has public-service experience and similar experience prescribed in Attached Table 2 before appointment, such experience is to be reflected in the initial salary step.\\n\\nc) In this way, the former Private School Act requires the remuneration of private school employees to be prescribed by the articles of incorporation, and the articles of incorporation of each school foundation to which the Plaintiffs belong provide that the remuneration of those employees shall follow the example of public officials, in order to secure the stability and predictability of the remuneration of office employees belonging to private schools and thereby ensure that private school education can be smoothly conducted in a manner consistent with the public purpose, while at the same time guaranteeing the economic livelihood stability and welfare improvement of those office employees; therefore, these provisions may be viewed as provisions that individually, directly, and concretely protect the interests of office employees of private schools.\\n\\n3) Furthermore, the orders at issue direct the school foundations to re-determine the salary steps of their office employees and to recover, within the scope of 5 years, the salaries paid in excess accordingly, and as a result the Plaintiffs will suffer direct and concrete harm in that their salaries will in substance be reduced or they will be required to return salaries already paid; therefore, the Plaintiffs may be regarded as having an individual, direct, and concrete interest in challenging the orders at issue.\\n\\nc. Nevertheless, the court below dismissed this action on the ground that the Plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the orders at issue; therefore, the judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles on “standing of the plaintiff in an action for revocation.”\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the judgment of the court below is quashed, and the Supreme Court, deciding the case itself, annuls the first-instance judgment. Pursuant to Article 8(2) of the Administrative Litigation Act, Article 425 and the main text of Article 418 of the Civil Procedure Act, the case is remanded to the first-instance court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[92NU11039]": "1. First, ex officio with respect to the Plaintiff’s principal claim, even in a case where an administrative lawsuit is filed seeking revocation of an administrative disposition in the sense of declaring it null and void ab initio, the requirements for instituting a revocation action, such as compliance with the filing period, must be satisfied (see this Court’s decisions rendered on 1984.5.29. in 84NU175; on 1987.6.9. in 87NU219; on 1990.12.26. in 90NU6279, etc.). Accordingly, insofar as the Plaintiff is seeking revocation of the objection adjudication at issue by way of a principal claim, even if the purport is to seek revocation in the sense of declaring the said objection adjudication null and void ab initio, the filing period prescribed in Article 75-2 of the Land Expropriation Act must be observed. However, according to the record, it is clear that the Plaintiff initially filed an administrative lawsuit seeking revocation of the original adjudication, and even after receiving the written adjudication on the objection filed in this case, only changed the statement of claim to seek revocation of the objection adjudication on 1990.11.1., which was well over one month later. Therefore, this lawsuit was filed beyond the immutable period and is thus unlawful, and the defect cannot be cured. Nevertheless, the judgment of the court below, which treated the principal claim in this case as lawful and rendered a judgment on the merits, contains an error of law in misapprehending the legal principles concerning the filing period for a revocation action; accordingly, without even examining the grounds of appeal, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning this matter cannot escape reversal.\\n\\n2. All of the grounds of appeal regarding the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the alternative claim are matters relating to the merits and therefore cannot constitute lawful grounds of appeal against the judgment of the court below. The argument is without merit.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the judgment of the court below concerning the principal claim is reversed, and this Court has decided to render judgment directly thereon; accordingly, this portion of the action is dismissed, and the appeal concerning the alternative claim is without merit and is therefore dismissed. The total costs of litigation shall be borne by the losing Plaintiff. The opinions of the participating Justices having been unanimous, the judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition."}

question: Which of the following statements concerning reports under administrative law is incorrect? (Where there is any dispute, according to case law)
A: Where a report for temporary use of a mountainous area is filed for the purpose of opening a temporary road and satisfies the requirements prescribed by statutes, unless there is a defect in the report form or attached documents, or the report was filed by false or other improper means, the administrative agency must accept the report and cannot refuse to accept the report on grounds other than the reasons prescribed by statutes.
