B: Where a building owner who intends to commence construction of a building for which permission was obtained or a report was filed has filed a report of the construction plan (commencement report) pursuant to the statutes, and the administrative agency has returned it, the building owner may challenge this return by an administrative appeal litigation.
C: In a building report under the Building Act in which another license is deemed by law to have been granted, the administrative agency may refuse to accept the report on the ground that the report does not satisfy the licensing standards prescribed by other statutes.
D: If a person initially reported that an outdoor assembly would be held, but contrary to the contents of the report no outdoor assembly was actually held and only an indoor assembly, whose scope and identity are recognized as the same as that of the reported outdoor assembly, was held in a building adjacent to the reported place, the person shall not be punished for deviating from the scope of the report.
E: In a report requiring acceptance, even where the report act itself is invalid because of grounds such as falsification of the report form, if the administrative agency accepts the report, such acceptance act is merely unlawful and cannot be said to be void ab initio.
label: E
supporting_precedents: {"[2010DU14954]": "The appeal is dismissed. The costs of appeal shall be borne by the Plaintiff."}

{"[2010DU7321]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nThe issue of whether an act by an administrative agency can be the subject of an appeal litigation cannot be determined abstractly and generally; in a specific case, keeping in mind that an administrative disposition is an act that directly affects the rights and obligations of the people as the enforcement of law concerning concrete facts performed by an administrative agency as the bearer of public authority, it must be determined individually by considering the content and purpose of the relevant statutes, the subject, content, form, and procedure of the act, the substantive nexus between the act and the disadvantage suffered by the other party and other interested persons, as well as the principle of administrative rule of law and the attitudes of the administrative agency and the interested persons regarding the act in question (see Supreme Court Decision 91NU1714 rendered on January 17, 1992, and Supreme Court en banc Decision 2008DU167 rendered on November 18, 2010, etc.).\\n\\nAccording to the relevant provisions of the former Building Act (as in force before its entire revision by Act No. 8974 on March 21, 2008), even in the case of a commencement report, where construction is commenced without such report, the administrative agency may issue a corrective order, such as an order to suspend construction, demolish, or prohibit use, against the building owner, etc. (Article 69(1)); where a building that has received such corrective order is not complied with, the administrative agency may request that permission for business or other acts to be carried out using such building under other statutes not be granted (Article 69(2)); a person who has received such request shall comply therewith unless there is a special reason (Article 69(3)); furthermore, the administrative agency may impose a compulsory performance surcharge on the building owner, etc. who fails to comply with the corrective order (Article 69-2(1)1); and a person who fails to file a commencement report may be punished by a fine not exceeding 2,000,000 won (Article 80(1), Article 9).\\n\\nThus, if the commencement report is rejected, the building owner, etc. will be placed in an unstable position because, if construction of the relevant building is commenced, there is a risk of being subject to a corrective order, a compulsory performance surcharge, or a fine, or of being denied permission for acts to be carried out using the relevant building. Therefore, at the stage where the commencement report is rejected, allowing the party to contest the legality of the rejection and thereby resolve the legal uncertainty before proceeding with construction, so as to open the way for escaping in advance from possible future risks, and enabling the early and fundamental resolution of disputes surrounding the proliferation of unlawful buildings and their demolition, is consistent with the principle of administrative rule of law. Therefore, it is correct to regard the act of rejecting the commencement report in this case as subject to an appeal litigation.\\n\\nAccordingly, the court below should have examined whether the commencement report in this case was lawfully made with the requirements and procedures prescribed by the former Building Act, and determined whether the defendant’s act of giving notice that the commencement report could not be processed was unlawful. Nevertheless, the court below merely upheld the first-instance judgment, which dismissed all of the Plaintiffs’ actions on the ground that the act of rejecting the commencement report does not directly cause a concrete change in rights and obligations, such as establishing any rights or imposing any obligations on the reporter; thus, this appellate judgment contains an error that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning whether the act of rejecting a commencement report constitutes the subject of an appeal litigation. The appellant’s argument on this point is meritorious.\\n\\nTherefore, without needing to determine the remaining grounds for final appeal, the appellate judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating, as stated in the order."}

{"[2011DO13023]": "The grounds for appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to Ground 1 of the appeal\\na. The Act on Assemblies and Demonstrations (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) provides that a person who intends to organize an outdoor assembly or demonstration shall submit to the chief of the competent police station a report stating the purpose, date and time, place, organizer, contact person in charge, the address, name, occupation, and contact information of the order keeper, the organizations and number of persons expected to participate, and, in the case of a demonstration, the method thereof (Article 6(1)); it further provides that the organizer of an assembly or demonstration shall not engage in acts that clearly deviate from the scope of the purpose, date and time, place, method, etc. reported as above (Article 16(4)3), and punishes a person who violates this provision (Article 22(3)). As such, the Act requires prior reporting for outdoor assemblies or demonstrations and further punishes acts that deviate from the scope of the report, but it does not contain any provision requiring reporting for indoor assemblies. Therefore, where a person who initially reported that he or she would hold an outdoor assembly instead does not hold any outdoor assembly at all contrary to the reported contents and holds only an indoor assembly in a building adjacent to the reported place, etc., it may be said that, apart from whether this constitutes another crime such as the crime of unlawful entry into a building, such person cannot be punished for violating the Act on the ground that he or she committed an act deviating from the reported scope in the course of holding the reported outdoor assembly.\\n\\nb. The court below held that, although the Defendant had originally reported that he would hold an outdoor assembly on the sidewalk in front of the Busan Regional Employment and Labor Office (hereinafter referred to as the “Busan Labor Office”), in fact the acts described in this portion of the facts charged, in that the Defendant, Non-Indicted Person 1, Non-Indicted Person 2, Non-Indicted Person 7, and 121 union members of the Busan and Ulsan Branches of the National Federation of Public Transport Workers, Airport and Port Transport Headquarters, National Port Tugboat Branch (hereinafter referred to as the “Tugboat Union”) did not hold an outdoor assembly at the reported place and, pursuant to prior communication among the assembly participants, immediately entered the Busan Labor Office building and occupied the first-floor lobby to hold an indoor assembly, could not be deemed to fall under Article 16(4)3 of the Act, even though there was illegality in that they trespassed into the Busan Labor Office building managed by another person without authorization, and on that basis found the Defendant not guilty of this portion of the facts charged.\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principle, examining the reasons stated in the judgment below, the above determination by the court below is proper, and there is no illegality, such as violation of the rules of logic and experience, exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence, or misapprehension of the law on outdoor assemblies deviating from the reported scope, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. With respect to Ground 2 of the appeal\\na. The gist of this portion of the facts charged is that the Defendant, together with Non-Indicted Person 1, Non-Indicted Person 2, Non-Indicted Person 3, and 121 union members of the Busan Branch and Ulsan Branch of the Tugboat Union, sat in the lobby of the Busan Labor Office on October 13, 2009, demanding an interview with the head of the Busan Labor Office, and while holding an assembly by singing labor songs and chanting slogans, he was ordered to disperse three times on the ground that, upon being entrusted by the chief of Busan Yeonje Police Station, he had committed disorderly conduct by trespassing into the Busan Labor Office building, and that he had continued an assembly that clearly deviated from the scope of the reported assembly, including the place and method thereof, and yet he did not disperse without delay.\\nIn response, the court below held that, in order to issue an order to disperse under Article 20(1)5 of the Act, it must fall under an “assembly that cannot maintain order due to acts falling under any one of the subparagraphs of Article 16(4),” and that, taking the circumstances as found by the court into comprehensive consideration, even if the Defendant and others’ act of entering the Busan Labor Office ultimately constituted the crime of unlawful entry into a building against the will of the building manager, unless conduct equivalent to separate assault, intimidation, damage, or arson was added, the acts of the Defendant and others alleged in this portion of the facts charged alone could not be deemed to constitute “acts disturbing order by assault, intimidation, damage, arson, etc.” under Article 16(4)2 of the Act; furthermore, it could not be deemed that the assembly in this case fell under an “assembly that cannot maintain order” under Article 20(1)5 of the Act on account of such acts, and on that basis found this portion of the facts charged not guilty.\\n\\nb. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n(1) The freedom of assembly is a basic right guaranteed by the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, but where necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare, it may be restricted by law to the extent that it does not infringe upon its essential content (Article 37(2) of the Constitution). It is also in this context that the Act provides that, in certain cases, such as “an assembly that cannot maintain order due to acts disturbing order by assault, intimidation, damage, arson, etc.,” voluntary dispersal may be requested and, if such request is not complied with, an order to disperse may be issued (Article 20(1) of the Act).\\nMeanwhile, although an indoor assembly may be held without prior reporting under the Act, its freedom may likewise be restricted where necessary to protect other important legal interests. Accordingly, even where an indoor assembly is held in a building managed by another person, if the assembly, in light of its purpose, number of participants, method of assembly, and manner of conduct, constitutes “an assembly that cannot maintain order due to acts disturbing order by assault, intimidation, damage, arson, etc.” (Article 20(1)5 and Article 16(4)2 of the Act), or otherwise poses a direct and clear danger to the infringement of another person’s legal interests or to other public peace and order, it should be regarded as subject to an order to disperse. Even if the place of the assembly is indoors in a public building such as a government office, unless it is an open place where assemblies are generally permitted, if the participants occupy it without authorization, thereby disturbing the peace of the building or causing danger to the performance of its normal functions, and further reaching the level of being unable to maintain order, such conduct exceeds the scope of activities protected by freedom of assembly; accordingly, it would be the same that it is subject to an order to disperse.\\n\\n(2) The reasons stated in the judgment below and the evidence duly admitted by the court below reveal the following facts, among others. ① The Busan Labor Office is a government office that performs public duties such as job creation and employment stability, protection of working conditions, prevention and mediation of labor-management disputes, and promotion of workers’ welfare in the jurisdiction covering Busan Metropolitan City, Ulsan Metropolitan City, and Gyeongsangnam-do. ② After the Busan Branch and Ulsan Branch of the Tugboat Union went on a full strike on August 7, 2009, the workers belonging to the Busan Branch held a total of 15 assemblies on the sidewalk in front of the Busan Labor Office up to October 12, 2009, for the purpose of urging government intervention in mediation and bargaining. ③ The Defendant, who was the branch head of the Ulsan Branch of the Tugboat Union, Non-Indicted Person 1, who was the chairperson of the Busan Headquarters of the National Federation of Public Transport Workers (the head of the Tugboat Struggle Headquarters), Non-Indicted Person 2, who was the branch head of the Busan Branch of the Tugboat Union, and Non-Indicted Person 3, who was the organizational chief of the Airport and Port Transport Headquarters of the National Federation of Public Transport Workers, planned that, in connection with the National Assembly Environment and Labor Committee’s audit of state administration scheduled to be held at the Busan Labor Office on October 14, 2009, they would occupy the first-floor lobby of the Busan Labor Office and stage a sit-in on October 13, 2009, the day before, thereby using it as an opportunity to resume bargaining; however, they planned to use the existing assembly report for an outdoor assembly on the sidewalk in front of the Busan Labor Office, which the Busan Branch of the Tugboat Union had already submitted to the chief of the competent police station, for that purpose. ④ On October 13, 2009, around 11:00 a.m., the Defendant and Non-Indicted Persons 1 and 2 visited the Busan Labor Office and, while meeting with Non-Indicted Person 4, the chief of the Labor Improvement Guidance Division 3, and others, demanded an interview with the head of the Busan Labor Office, and in the meantime, 121 union members of the Busan Branch and Ulsan Branch of the Tugboat Union, who had gathered nearby pursuant to their instructions, unlawfully entered the first-floor lobby of the Busan Labor Office between around 11:20 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. on the same day. ⑤ Thereafter, from that time until around 2:50 p.m. on the same day, they sat on the floor there, demanded an interview with the head of the Busan Labor Office, and continued the assembly by chanting slogans such as “The head of the Labor Office should awaken,” and singing labor songs. ⑥ The Busan Labor Office is a four-story building, with a civil complaints office on the first floor and the Labor Improvement Guidance Divisions 1, 2, and 3 on the first and second floors; due to the sit-in, the work of the civil complaints department of the Busan Labor Office and the passage of complainants were obstructed, and some of the employees of the Busan Labor Office were unable to perform their original normal duties because they were preparing for building security duties on the stairs and corridors of the building, among other things. ⑦ Accordingly, the head of the Busan Labor Office requested the Defendant and the union members to leave around 11:57 a.m. on the same day; Non-Indicted Person 6, the chief of the Security and Traffic Division of that police station, who had been delegated authority by Non-Indicted Person 5, the chief of Busan Yeonje Police Station, issued a request for voluntary dispersal at around 12:10 p.m. on October 13, 2009, a first order to disperse at around 12:20 p.m. on the same day, and a second order to disperse at around 1:55 p.m. on the same day, and Non-Indicted Person 5 issued a third order to disperse at around 2:35 p.m. on the same day, but the Defendant and the union members did not comply.\\n\\n(3) In light of the various circumstances discernible from the foregoing facts, namely, that the Busan Labor Office is a government office that performs public duties such as employment stability and mediation of labor-management disputes, and is difficult to regard as an open place where the general public or complainants, etc. are allowed to hold assemblies at will inside the building; the background by which the Defendant and others led the union members to enter the building lobby, which was the place of the assembly in this case; the purpose and scale of the assembly; the manner and duration of the assembly carried out while disregarding the request for evacuation by the person with managerial authority over the building; the size and structure of the space inside the building where the assembly in this case was held; the extent to which the entry and exit of complainants visiting that place or the performance of duties by public officials were obstructed; and other circumstances surrounding the progress of the assembly in this case, there is sufficient room to view that, after the Defendant and others collectively trespassed into the Busan Labor Office building and occupied the lobby, they continued an indoor assembly for a prolonged period by chanting slogans and singing songs, while failing to comply with the request to leave, and thus caused a disturbance of order by infringing upon others’ legal interests, such as the peace of the building and the right of management of its facilities, thereby rendering public peace and order incapable of being maintained.\\nNevertheless, the court below concluded, solely on the basis of the reasons stated in its opinion, that no lawful ground for an order to disperse was established with respect to the assembly in this case. Accordingly, this judgment of the court below contains an error that affected the conclusion of the judgment by misapprehending the law concerning the requirements and subject matter of an order to disperse under the Act and by failing to conduct the necessary examination. The grounds of appeal pointing this out are well-founded.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the portion of the judgment below concerning the Defendant’s violation of the Act on Assemblies and Demonstrations due to his failure to comply with the order to disperse is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination on this point. It is so adjudged, in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2018DU33593]": "We consider the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. a. Article 36(1) of the former Act on Long-Term Care Insurance for the Aged (prior to amendment by Act No. 13647 of December 29, 2015) provides that the head of a long-term care institution shall report to the Special Self-Governing City Mayor, the Special Self-Governing Province Governor, the Mayor, the County Governor, or the Head of the District Office no later than 30 days before the scheduled date of closure or suspension of operations, where he or she intends to close or suspend operations. Meanwhile, Article 40(1) of the former Welfare of Senior Citizens Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 13646 of December 29, 2015) provides that where a person who has established a senior medical welfare facility pursuant to Article 35(2) changes any of the matters stated in the establishment report that are prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Health and Welfare, or intends to abolish or suspend such facility, he or she shall give prior notice to the Mayor, County Governor, or Head of the District Office in accordance with the Presidential Decree.\\n\\nb. Such a closure report for a long-term care institution and abolition report for a senior medical welfare facility correspond to the so-called “report requiring acceptance,” which is accepted by the administrative agency after examining whether it satisfies the requirements prescribed by the relevant statutes. However, even if the administrative agency has accepted the report, if the reporting act itself is invalid due to reasons such as forgery of the report, the acceptance act is void because there is no valid object of acceptance; and it is naturally void without even considering whether the acceptance act itself has grave and obvious defects (see Supreme Court Decision 2005DO3554, rendered on December 23, 2005).\\n\\n2. a. According to the reasoning of the judgment below and the lawfully admitted evidence, the following facts may be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff completed the establishment report for ○○ Silver Center, a long-term care institution and senior medical welfare facility, on January 8, 2009.\\n\\n2) The Non-party, on December 12, 2013, forged the Plaintiff’s name and submitted to the Defendant a “Report of Abolition of Senior Medical Welfare Facility and Closure of Long-Term Care Institution due to Change of Representative (hereinafter referred to as ‘the reports at issue’)”, and the Defendant accepted the reports at issue on December 19, 2013.\\n\\n3) On July 14, 2017, the Non-party was sentenced to a fine of KRW 2,000,000 for the criminal facts that he or she used a forged report of abolition of a senior medical welfare facility and a forged report of closure of a long-term care institution in the Plaintiff’s name before an official of Bucheon City Hall, and the said judgment became final and conclusive as it stood around that time.\\n\\nb. In light of the foregoing relevant provisions and legal principles, as applied to these facts, the reports at issue filed using forged documents are ineffective, and the Defendant’s act of accepting the reports is also void ab initio.\\n\\n3. Nevertheless, the court below, on the incorrect premise that the acceptance act itself must have grave and obvious defects in order to be void ab initio regardless of whether the reporting act is valid or invalid, held that the disposition accepting the reports at issue was not void ab initio. In such determination by the court below, there is an error of law affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning defects in the reporting act and the validity of the ensuing acceptance disposition.\\n\\n4. Therefore, omitting consideration of the remaining grounds for appeal, we reverse the judgment below and remand the case to the court below for a new trial and determination, and hereby render judgment with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[2022DU50588]": "We examine the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n1. Outline of the case and the judgment of the court below\\nA. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be ascertained.\\n\\n1) The Plaintiff is the owner of forest land measuring 15,762 square meters in Taean-gun, Chungcheongnam-do (address omitted) (hereinafter referred to as “the forest land at issue”).\\n\\n2) On 2018. 12. 21., the Plaintiff received a provisional permit for spring water development from the Governor of Chungcheongnam-do to the effect that, pursuant to Article 10 of the former Drinking Water Management Act (before amendment by Act No. 17840 on 2021. 1. 5.; hereinafter the same shall apply) and Article 4(3) of the Enforcement Rule of the same Act (before amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Environment No. 931 on 2021. 7. 23.; hereinafter the same shall apply), spring water could be developed for two years from 2018. 12. 21. to 2020. 12. 20. at the forest land at issue, with two intake wells (300㎥/day) (hereinafter referred to as “the provisional permit at issue”).\\n\\nThe provisional permit at issue is subject to conditions, including that “the provisional permit shall be revoked if the environmental impact investigation report is not submitted within two years without justifiable grounds,” and the permit certificate also states, inter alia, that “prior explanation to residents and resolution of complaints are necessary because there are residents’ objections due to concerns over changes in the water flow of nearby groundwater and the problem of depletion of groundwater used for agricultural water,” and that “conflict must be resolved in the future by sufficiently reflecting the opinions of local residents.”\\n\\n3) In order to conduct an environmental impact investigation on the forest land at issue, on 2020. 7. 23. the Plaintiff filed with the Defendant a report on temporary use of mountainous district land under Article 15-2 of the former Mountainous Districts Management Act (before amendment by Act No. 18263 on 2021. 6. 15.; hereinafter the same shall apply) for the purpose of constructing a temporary road with respect to 2,025 square meters of the forest land at issue (hereinafter referred to as “the report at issue”); however, on 2020. 8. 18., the Defendant issued a notice that acceptance of the report on temporary use of mountainous district land was impossible, on the ground that “the condition attached to the provisional permit, namely prior explanation to residents and resolution of complaints, had not been fulfilled, and therefore acceptance of the report on temporary use of mountainous district land is impossible” (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition at issue”).\\n\\nB. The court below held that the Plaintiff, who had only obtained a provisional permit for spring water development, could not be deemed to have a legal status equivalent to that of the permit-granting authority for spring water development prescribed in Article 9(1) of the former Drinking Water Management Act; that there was no provision allowing the construction of a temporary road on mountainous district land in order to conduct an environmental impact investigation while being in a state of having only such provisional permit; and that it also appeared unlikely that the Plaintiff would obtain a permit for spring water development in the future unless the Plaintiff fulfilled the conditions of the provisional permit. On those grounds, the court below held that the temporary road the Plaintiff intended to install could not be regarded as an access road that may be installed pursuant to Article 18-3(4) of the Enforcement Decree of the Mountainous Districts Management Act and [Attached Table 3-3] 3. (d), and therefore determined that the disposition at issue, which did not accept the report at issue, was not erroneous.\\n\\n2. The Supreme Court’s determination\\nA. However, the foregoing determination by the court below is difficult to endorse. The reasons are as follows.\\n\\n1) Article 13(1) of the former Drinking Water Management Act provides, “Among those who intend to obtain a permit for the development of spring water, a person who intends to engage in the manufacturing business of drinking spring water, etc. shall conduct an environmental impact investigation, prepare a report thereon, and submit it to the Mayor/Do Governor when applying for the development permit.” Article 10(1) of the same Act provides, “A Mayor/Do Governor may provisionally permit the development of spring water, etc. on the condition that a person who intends to develop spring water, etc. subject to an environmental impact investigation under Article 13(1) conducts an environmental impact investigation and submits the report thereon.”\\n\\nAs stated above, the Plaintiff received the provisional permit at issue on the condition that an environmental impact investigation be conducted and the report thereon be submitted within two years, before obtaining a spring water development permit. Not only must the Plaintiff fulfill the conditions attached to the provisional permit in order to maintain the provisional permit at issue, but the Plaintiff must also conduct an environmental impact investigation and submit the report thereon in order to apply for a permit to develop drinking spring water.\\n\\nIf so, in the Plaintiff’s case, it must be deemed that the Plaintiff may seek temporary use of mountainous district land for the construction of a temporary road to the extent necessary to conduct an environmental impact investigation on the forest land at issue, and that the competent administrative agency cannot refuse this without justifiable grounds.\\n\\n2) In light of the legal nature of a report of temporary use of mountainous district land and the form and content of the provisions on such report in Article 15-2(4) through (6) of the former Mountainous Districts Management Act, Article 18-3(4) of the Enforcement Decree of the Mountainous Districts Management Act, and [Attached Table 3-3], a county governor, etc. who has received such a report must accept the report if, unless there is a defect in the report or attached documents or the report was filed by false or other wrongful means, the contents of the report satisfy the standards, conditions, subject facilities, scope of acts, installation area, and installation conditions prescribed by law; and the county governor, etc. cannot refuse to accept the report on grounds other than those prescribed by law (see Supreme Court Decisions 2011Du31970 dated 2012. 9. 27. and 2011Du31987 dated 2012. 9. 27., etc.).\\n\\nThe report at issue concerns the Plaintiff’s use of part of the forest land at issue for a certain period for the purpose of constructing a temporary road, and thereafter restoring it, in order to conduct an environmental impact investigation in preparation for an application for a spring water development permit or for the performance of the conditions attached to the provisional permit at issue.\\n\\nThe mere circumstance that the Plaintiff is only a provisional permit holder, or that the Plaintiff has not fulfilled the conditions attached to the provisional permit, cannot be deemed to mean that the contents of the report at issue do not satisfy the requirements of Article 18-3(4) of the Enforcement Decree of the Mountainous Districts Management Act and [Attached Table 3-3] 3. (d), concerning the standards and conditions for the report, the subject facilities, the scope of acts, the installation area, and the installation conditions. Nor is there any material to find that the contents of the report at issue otherwise fail to satisfy the statutory requirements concerning the standards and conditions for the report, and the Defendant does not rely on such grounds as the basis for the disposition at issue. In addition, there is no circumstance suggesting that there are defects in the documents for the report at issue or that the report at issue was made by false or other wrongful means.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing circumstances and the legal principles stated above, even if the Plaintiff failed to properly fulfill the matters stated in the permit certificate for the provisional permit at issue, such as “prior explanation to residents and resolution of complaints,” it is reasonable to conclude that such circumstances cannot be invoked to refuse acceptance of the report at issue.\\n\\nB. Nevertheless, the court below held that the disposition at issue, which did not accept the report at issue, was lawful for the reasons stated in its judgment. In the judgment below, there is an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal status of a person who has obtained a provisional permit for spring water development pursuant to Article 10 of the former Drinking Water Management Act and the legal principles concerning a report of temporary use of mountainous district land. The ground of appeal asserting this point is well taken.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, without examining the remaining grounds of appeal, the judgment below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for a further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question:
The Minister B, who is the appointing authority, imposed a suspension-from-office disposition on public official A, who belonged to the ministry, pursuant to the “State Public Officials Act,” which provides that “a position may be denied to a person against whom a disciplinary resolution corresponding to dismissal, removal, demotion, or suspension is being requested.” After the period of A’s suspension from office had expired, B again imposed a dismissal ex officio disposition on A. Which of the following explanations concerning this matter are correct? (If there is any dispute, according to precedents)

(a) Because a suspension from office under the State Public Officials Act is an infringing disposition that directly and indirectly produces adverse effects on the public official in various respects, such as remuneration, promotion, and salary step increases, the same procedural safeguards as those required for disciplinary action as a punitive sanction are required.

(b) A suspension-from-office disposition cannot be justified merely on the formal ground that a request for a disciplinary resolution corresponding to dismissal, removal, demotion, or suspension has been made; a high probability of receiving such disciplinary action must be recognized.

(c) If A did not file a request for review of a grievance appeal against the suspension-from-office disposition, A cannot, in a lawsuit seeking revocation of the later dismissal ex officio disposition, assert the illegality of the dismissal ex officio disposition on the basis of a ground for revocation, rather than a ground of voidness, of the suspension-from-office disposition.

(d) If B imposed a suspension-from-office disposition on A on the basis of new grounds for suspension from office, it is reasonable to regard the prior suspension-from-office disposition as having been implicitly withdrawn.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2012DU26180]": "We determine the grounds for appeal.\\n\\n1. On the First Ground of Appeal\\n\\nEven if, while a lawsuit seeking a declaration of invalidity or revocation of a disposition of suspension from office under the State Public Officials Act is pending, a public official cannot restore his status as a public official through a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the disposition of suspension from office after exceeding the mandatory retirement age, where such declaration of invalidity or revocation makes it possible to seek payment of reduced salary, etc. for the period from the date of suspension from office until the date of dismissal ex officio, there is a legal interest in seeking a declaration of invalidity or revocation of the disposition of suspension from office (see Supreme Court Decision 2007DO18406 dated July 29, 2010, Supreme Court Decision 2011DO5001 dated February 23, 2012, etc.).\\n\\nOn the same purport, the lower court properly determined the merits on the premise that the Plaintiff, whose mandatory retirement age had passed while the trial on the merits was pending, had a legal interest in seeking revocation of the disposition of suspension from office at issue, and there is no illegality in misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning legal interest as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n2. On the Second through Fourth Grounds of Appeal\\n\\nA. The lower court, based on the evidence it admitted, found the following facts: the Plaintiff was a public official promoted to Grade 5 Administrative Officer at the Ministry of Employment and Labor on March 9, 2006; after the Ministry of Employment and Labor established, around June 2010, a plan to strengthen the capabilities of mid-level managers, it conducted a multilateral evaluation by an evaluation panel composed of 130 subordinates at Grade 6 or below for 37 public officials who had been promoted to Grade 5 and had served for four years or more, and then sequentially held meetings of the Seoul Regional Employment and Labor Office and the Ministry of Employment and Labor’s selection committee for capability-strengthening targets, selecting 20 persons, including the Plaintiff, as subjects for capability strengthening; the Seoul Regional Employment and Labor Office implemented programs such as capability-strengthening training and on-site support activities against the Plaintiff and other subjects for approximately three months from around July 2010, and the Ministry of Employment and Labor held a results evaluation committee and assigned the Plaintiff an evaluation grade of “unsatisfactory”; the Defendant, on January 6, 2011, issued a disposition of suspension from office against the Plaintiff pursuant to Article 73-3(1)2 of the State Public Officials Act on the ground that the Plaintiff’s ability to perform duties was markedly insufficient (hereinafter referred to as “the disposition at issue”); and, meanwhile, the Plaintiff received the lowest grade of “Fair” in all four performance evaluations from the second half of 2008 through the first half of 2010. The lower court then held that a public official subject to a disposition of suspension from office is unable to perform duties and will receive unfavorable treatment with respect to promotions, advancement, and payment of remuneration, etc.; therefore, a disposition of suspension from office constitutes an adverse personnel disposition that imposes obligations on a public official or restricts his rights and interests; the item constituting the ground for suspension from office in relation to the Plaintiff, namely, “a person lacking ability to perform duties or with extremely poor work performance,” is prescribed in a general, inclusive, and relative form in terms of its standard as compared to grounds for disciplinary action; accordingly, there is a great necessity to afford the public official subject to the disposition advance notice and an opportunity to submit opinions; in light of the circumstances and content of the disposition at issue, it is difficult to regard the disposition at issue as a disposition that, by its nature, is recognized as making it difficult or unnecessary to undergo administrative procedures such as advance notice of the disposition or hearing of opinions; and there is no provision in the State Public Officials Act requiring procedures equivalent to administrative procedures with respect to a disposition of suspension from office. On that basis, the lower court determined that, in order to make the disposition at issue, advance notice and opinion-hearing procedures had to be conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Procedures Act, and therefore held that the disposition at issue, which was made without advance notice to the Plaintiff and without affording him an opportunity to submit opinions, had procedural defects in violation of Article 21(1) and Article 22(3) of the Administrative Procedures Act and was thus unlawful.\\n\\nB. However, the lower court’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\nArticle 3(2) of the former Administrative Procedures Act (before its amendment by Act No. 11498 on October 22, 2012; hereinafter the same) provides that “this Act shall not apply to the following matters,” and Item 9 thereof provides that, as cases to which the Administrative Procedures Act is excluded from application, “matters that, due to the nature of the relevant administrative action, are recognized as making it difficult or unnecessary to go through administrative procedures, and matters prescribed by Presidential Decree as having undergone procedures equivalent to administrative procedures, such as conscription and call-up under the Military Service Act, entry and exit of foreigners, recognition of refugees, naturalization, disciplinary action or other dispositions under laws and regulations relating to the personnel affairs of public officials, or mediation, coordination, arbitration, adjudication, or other dispositions under laws and regulations for the purpose of adjustment of interests.” The former Enforcement Decree of the Administrative Procedures Act (before its amendment by Presidential Decree No. 23383 on December 21, 2011), enacted pursuant to such delegation, provides in Article 2 that “the term ‘matters prescribed by Presidential Decree’ in Article 3(2)9 of the Act means the following matters,” and Item 3 thereof provides for “matters concerning disciplinary action or other dispositions under laws and regulations relating to the personnel affairs of public officials.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, suspension from office prescribed in Article 73-3(1) of the State Public Officials Act (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) is, in general, a measure that, in cases where a public official lacks ability to perform duties, has extremely poor work performance, is under disciplinary proceedings, or is indicted in a criminal case, temporarily does not assign a position to the relevant public official and thereby prevents him from engaging in duties, as a provisional and injunctive measure in order to prevent anticipated obstacles in work, interference with the execution of public duties, and impairment of the fairness of administration and public trust therein, should the public official continue to be assigned duties in the future. Accordingly, by its nature, it cannot be required to satisfy the same procedural guarantees as those demanded for discipline and other punitive sanctions imposed for the purpose of maintaining public service order in response to misconduct by public officials in the past (see Supreme Court Decision 2003DO5945 dated October 10, 2003, Supreme Court Decision 2012DA64833 dated May 9, 2013, Constitutional Court Full Bench Decision 2004HEONBA12 dated May 25, 2006, etc.). Article 73-3(1)2 and paragraph 3 of the Act concerning suspension from office provide that the appointing authority may issue a disposition of suspension from office to a person lacking ability to perform duties or having extremely poor work performance, and that a person suspended from office shall be ordered to remain on standby within a range of three months; moreover, under Articles 75 and 76(1) of the Act, when a public official is suspended from office, the person with authority to make the disposition or the person authorized to propose the disposition must deliver a written explanation stating the grounds for the disposition, and if the public official who received the written explanation of the grounds for disposition contests the disposition, he may file a request for grievance review within 30 days from the date he received that written explanation. In this way, the appointing authority is required, when effecting a disposition of suspension from office, to invariably deliver a written explanation of the grounds for disposition, which requires a concrete and specific statement of facts, thereby guaranteeing the relevant public official an opportunity to prepare a defense and contest the disposition and ensuring the care and rationality of the appointing authority’s judgment. A public official who has received a disposition of suspension from office is also guaranteed a sufficient opportunity to state opinions and submit materials through a grievance procedure or administrative litigation after the fact. In addition, if a person placed on standby as above is recognized as unlikely to be able to improve his ability or work performance during that period, he may be subject to dismissal ex officio under Article 70(1)5 of the Act; however, in that case, consent from the disciplinary committee is required pursuant to the proviso of paragraph 2 of the same Article, thereby strengthening procedural safeguards.\\n\\nAccordingly, because a disposition of suspension from office under the State Public Officials Act falls under matters that, due to the nature of the relevant administrative action, are recognized as making it difficult or unnecessary to go through administrative procedures, or matters that have undergone procedures equivalent to administrative procedures, pursuant to Article 3(2)9 of the former Administrative Procedures Act and Article 2(3) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, it is reasonable to regard the provisions of the Administrative Procedures Act concerning advance notice of disposition and hearing of opinions, etc. as not separately applicable.\\n\\nNevertheless, the lower court, based solely on the reasons stated in its opinion, determined that, in order to make the disposition at issue, advance notice and opinion-hearing procedures had to be conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Administrative Procedures Act, and thereby upheld the Plaintiff’s claim in this case; thus, the lower court judgment contains illegality that affected the judgment by misunderstanding the legal doctrine concerning the scope of exclusion from application of the Administrative Procedures Act and the reasons for exception thereto.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nWithout addressing the remaining grounds of appeal, we reverse the lower court judgment and remand the case to the lower court for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

{"[2022DU45623]": "The grounds of appeal are examined.\\n\\n1. As to the claim for payment of the amount equivalent to ungranted welfare points\\n\\nFor the reasons stated in its judgment, the court below held that the Plaintiff could not seek payment from the Defendant of the amount equivalent to the ungranted welfare points.\\n\\nExamining the reasons of the court below’s judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the record, there is no error in this part of the court below’s determination that affected the judgment by violating the rules of logic and experience or by exceeding the bounds of the principle of free evaluation of evidence in finding facts, or by misconstruing the legal principles concerning the amount equivalent to ungranted welfare points during the period of no post assignment.\\n\\n2. As to the claim for payment of remuneration\\n\\nA. Relevant legal principles\\n\\n1) The suspension from position prescribed in Article 73-3(1) of the State Public Officials Act is a provisional measure that prevents the relevant public official from performing duties by temporarily not assigning a position to that public official in order to prevent obstacles in official duties expected to arise if the official continues to perform duties in the future, and it means that the appointing authority unilaterally deprives the official of the post. Such suspension from position differs in legal nature from disciplinary action, which is a punitive sanction for a public official’s misconduct (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2003DU5945 dated October 10, 2003), but because it is an invasive disposition that directly or indirectly produces adverse effects on the public official in various respects, such as remuneration, promotion, and salary increment, if it is unjustifiably prolonged, it inherently has the possibility of causing a level of disadvantage comparable, in effect, to dismissal. Accordingly, the requirements for suspension from position and the time of expiration or extinguishment of its effect must be strictly construed in accordance with the wording, and, in particular, in light of not only the perspective of protection of status for public officials under Article 7(2) of the Constitution and Article 68 of the State Public Officials Act, but also the constitutional principle of proportionality, no analogical or expansive interpretation unfavorable to the person subject to the suspension from position disposition may be made.\\n\\n2) Article 73-3(1)3 of the State Public Officials Act provides that a suspension from position disposition may be made against a person for whom a disciplinary resolution corresponding to removal from office, dismissal, demotion, or suspension from office is pending (hereinafter referred to as a “resolution for major disciplinary action”), and this is intended to prevent in advance the concern that if a public official who has been requested to undergo a resolution for major disciplinary action continues to hold the position and perform duties, there may arise a concrete risk of impairing the fairness of the execution of public duties and the public’s trust therein. In light of the purpose and intent of this system of suspension from position, as well as the degree of disadvantage resulting therefrom and the nature of an invasive disposition, a suspension from position disposition cannot be justified merely on the formal ground that there has been a “request for a resolution for major disciplinary action”; rather, on the premise that the person subject to the suspension from position disposition is highly likely to receive major disciplinary action, all circumstances concerning whether, given the nature of the person’s position, post, and duties, his or her continued performance of duties would create a concrete risk to the fair execution of public duties must be closely considered in determining whether the requirements are satisfied.\\n\\n3) Meanwhile, Article 73-3(2) of the State Public Officials Act expressly provides that even where a suspension from position disposition has been made, the position shall be restored without delay once the ground therefor ceases to exist. This relates to the meaning of “a person for whom a resolution for major disciplinary action is pending,” one of the requirements in Article 73-3(1)3, and to the interpretation of the terminus of “request for a resolution for major disciplinary action.” The State Public Officials Act clearly distinguishes and provides for each stage of the disciplinary procedure, such as “request for disciplinary resolution (Article 78), disciplinary resolution (Article 82(1)), notice of disciplinary resolution (Article 18 of the Public Officials Disciplinary Decree), disciplinary action (Article 78 and Article 19 of the Public Officials Disciplinary Decree), or request for review or re-review (Article 82(2) and Article 24 of the Public Officials Disciplinary Decree),” and by expressly providing that “request for a re-disciplinary resolution (Article 78-3)” is limited to cases where the disciplinary action has become void or has been revoked, it is also clear from the wording that “request for review or re-review” is not included therein. In light of the wording and structure of these relevant provisions, it is appropriate to view “a person for whom a resolution for major disciplinary action is pending” as limited to the period until a disciplinary resolution is made pursuant to Article 82(1) of the State Public Officials Act and Article 12 of the Public Officials Disciplinary Decree.\\n\\n4) If, unlike the case where disciplinary action is immediately taken in accordance with a disciplinary resolution, the effect of suspension from position is deemed to continue until the decision on a request for review or re-review where the person empowered to request the disciplinary resolution has filed a request for review or re-review against the disciplinary resolution, this would not only run counter to the interpretation of the wording and structure of the State Public Officials Act and the Public Officials Disciplinary Decree, but would also connect the terminus of a suspension from position, which is a disposition corresponding to a considerable degree of disadvantage, to the unilateral will and judgment of whether the person empowered to request the disciplinary resolution files a request for review or re-review, thereby causing public officials to be placed in an unstable status for a prolonged period and thus creating a strong risk of violating the guarantee of status for public officials prescribed by the Constitution and the State Public Officials Act; moreover, it would amount to analogical or expansive interpretation unfavorable to the person subject to the suspension from position disposition, which is impermissible. Furthermore, where “minor disciplinary resolution” is made in accordance with lawful procedures against a person who was subject to a suspension from position disposition on the ground that the person was “a person for whom a resolution for major disciplinary action is pending,” it is appropriate to view that, even taking into account the possibility of modification through a request for re-review, the state has become one in which it is not easy to recognize that there is a “high likelihood of receiving major disciplinary action.” Given the nature of a suspension from position disposition as a provisional measure, it must be operated to the minimum extent necessary within an appropriate scope consistent with its grounds and purpose; in this respect, even if the initial suspension from position constituted a lawful disposition at the time it was made, it must be understood that the suspension from position disposition loses effect from the day after the disciplinary resolution corresponding to the date on which the ground ceases to exist or is extinguished.\\n\\nB. Supreme Court’s determination\\n\\nComprehensively considering the relevant legal principles together with the circumstances ascertainable from the reasons of the court below’s judgment and the record, the court below’s determination is difficult to accept for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) On February 28, 2017, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport requested the Central Disciplinary Committee to make a resolution for major disciplinary action against the Plaintiff, and at the same time made a suspension from position disposition against the Plaintiff pursuant to Article 73-3(1)3 of the State Public Officials Act. On February 23, 2018, the Central Disciplinary Committee made a minor disciplinary resolution against the Plaintiff (a reduction in pay for 2 months). On March 13, 2018, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport filed a request for review with the Central Disciplinary Committee against the foregoing minor disciplinary resolution, but the Central Disciplinary Committee dismissed it on June 22, 2018, and on July 11, 2018, the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport imposed a disciplinary punishment of a reduction in pay for 2 months on the Plaintiff.\\n\\n2) The meaning of “a person for whom a resolution for major disciplinary action is pending,” which constitutes the requirements and grounds for the suspension from position disposition against the Plaintiff, is limited to the period up to February 23, 2018, when the disciplinary resolution against the Plaintiff was made; and, in particular, because a disciplinary resolution corresponding to a reduction in pay for 2 months, which is a minor disciplinary action, was made against the Plaintiff, it may be viewed that from at least the following day, February 24, 2018, the requirements and grounds for the suspension from position disposition, namely the “high likelihood of receiving major disciplinary action,” had ceased to exist or been extinguished. Therefore, it is appropriate to view that the suspension from position disposition against the Plaintiff lawfully maintained its effect only from July 28, 2017, to February 23, 2018.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the court below, relying only on the reasons stated in its judgment, held that the effect of the suspension from position disposition against the Plaintiff still continued from July 28, 2017, until June 22, 2018, when the decision dismissing the Minister of Land, Infrastructure and Transport’s request for review was rendered, and calculated the unpaid remuneration amount on that premise. In this regard, the court below erred in a manner that affected the judgment by misconstruing the legal principles concerning the terminus of the effect of suspension from position.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the part of the court below’s judgment adverse to the Plaintiff concerning the claim for payment of remuneration is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The remaining appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged in unanimous agreement of the participating Justices as stated in the disposition."}

{"[84NU191]": "We examine the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nThe judgment of the court below, in its reasons, stated that, with respect to the murder case of printer Choi Hyun-seok, which occurred at around 23:30 on 1981.6.24 in a chili pepper field located at 670, Hyoja-dong 1-ga, Jeonju-si, the Plaintiff, who had performed the duties of the head of the investigation headquarters, was, as of 1982.9.30, subjected to a disposition of suspension from office under Article 50(1) of the former Police Officials Act (before amendment by Act No. 3606 of 1982.12.31) on the ground of a marked lack of ability to perform duties and to direct and supervise subordinates, and thereafter, because he had not been assigned a position even after three months had elapsed, was subjected to a disposition of dismissal on 1983.1.14; that, for the investigation of the murder case of Choi Hyun-seok, an investigation headquarters consisting of the Plaintiff as head of the investigation headquarters and Hyeong Byeong-gwon and 20 others as investigators was established on 1981.6.28 at Jarimwon, located in Hyoja-dong, Jeonju-si, near the scene of the incident; that the said investigation headquarters, on the basis of a clue found at the scene of the incident, namely one T-shirt, conducted canvassing investigations and, as a result, came to arrest Nonparty 1, a laborer, as a strong suspect on 1981.7.12; but when Nonparty 1 persistently denied the offense, the headquarters secured Nonparty 1’s person by causing him to be detained for 5 days for acts of drunken disturbance committed in the past at Hanbat Restaurant near the Jeonju University construction site, and, while at the same time organizing a dedicated team to interrogate Nonparty 1, Sergeant Nonparty 2, Nonparty 3, Corporal Nonparty 4, and others belonging to that team took Nonparty 1 around to places such as the Jeonju Police Station Jinbuk 2-dong Police Box and the Jarimwon warehouse, which was the investigation headquarters, instead of the police station detention room, beat him on the head with their fists, tied two chairs together facing each other and fixed them in place, laid Nonparty 1 across them with his hands and feet handcuffed, beat him with clubs, bound his upper body with a bicycle tube so as to make breathing difficult, shone a flashlight on the victim’s belongings while making him say, “Hyun-seok, I am sorry that I killed you,” and, if he refused, beat him with clubs and deprived him of sleep, thereby continuing cruel treatment and forcing a confession, as a result of which Nonparty 1 came to make a false confession on 1981.7.16, merely 4 days after his arrest, that he had murdered the said Choi Hyun-seok; that the Plaintiff, although having received from Inspector Hyeong Byeong-gwon, who was in the position of deputy chief of the said investigation headquarters, a report that Nonparty 1 denied the offense and that a dedicated team should therefore be organized, neglected without inquiry to examine the place where Nonparty 1 was detained or the investigative process of the dedicated team; that, even after receiving a report that Nonparty 1 had vehemently denied the offense and only confessed after 4 days, he did not personally interrogate the suspect or attempt to determine whether the confession was true; and that he participated only near the end of the on-site investigation conducted on 1981.7.17; and then, on the basis of the evidence cited in the judgment, recognized those facts and held that, according to the facts so found, the Plaintiff had a marked lack of ability to perform the duties of head of the investigation headquarters or to direct and supervise his subordinates, and therefore fell under the grounds for suspension from office prescribed in Article 50(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2 of the former Police Officials Act, and that there was no dispute between the parties that the Plaintiff had not been assigned a position for 3 months after the said suspension from office, so that the disposition of dismissal on that ground was lawful.\\n\\nHowever, the disposition of dismissal that is the subject of the present litigation was a disposition received under Article 50(3) of the same Act on the ground that the Plaintiff had received a disposition of suspension from office because he fell under a person having the disqualifying grounds prescribed in Article 50(1) subparagraphs 1 and 2 of the former Police Officials Act (before amendment by Act No. 3606 of 1982.12.31), and thereafter had not been assigned a position for 3 months; thus, if the Plaintiff had not filed an application for review with the Appeal Review Committee pursuant to Article 52 of the former Police Officials Act with respect to the prior disposition of suspension from office, then even if there were grounds of illegality in that disposition of suspension from office, it cannot be challenged unless they are grounds for nullity ab initio; and, on the other hand, although the disposition of suspension from office under Article 50(1) of the former Police Officials Act and the disposition of dismissal under Article 50(3) of the same Act are premised on the former, they are administrative dispositions that, respectively and step by step, produce separate legal effects, so that grounds of illegality in the prior disposition of suspension from office are not succeeded to by the disposition of dismissal, and therefore the effect of the disposition of dismissal cannot be contested on the basis of grounds of illegality in the prior disposition of suspension from office (see Supreme Court Decision 71NU96, rendered 1971.9.28); according to the record, it is clear that the Plaintiff never underwent a lawful request for review prescribed in Article 52 of the former Police Officials Act with respect to the prior disposition of suspension from office, yet he is contesting the effect of the dismissal disposition in this case merely by asserting that the prior disposition of suspension from office was unlawful, so the Plaintiff’s claim for revocation of the dismissal disposition in this case cannot be accepted on that point alone, without any need to determine whether the prior disposition of suspension from office was lawful.\\n\\nAccordingly, regardless of the reason by which the court below rejected the Plaintiff’s claim, its conclusion is, as a result, correct; therefore, even if the action it took of recognizing the facts as stated in the judgment and determining that those facts constituted grounds for suspension from office as to the Plaintiff, and thus, even if there were error in fact-finding in violation of the rules of evidence or error of law as asserted in the grounds of final appeal, such illegality cannot be a ground that affected the result of the judgment below.\\n\\nUltimately, the grounds of final appeal are without merit; therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of final appeal are borne by the losing party, and the judgment is rendered as set forth in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}
