The Plaintiff’s remaining appeal is dismissed. The costs of litigation for the reversed portion and the appellate costs for the portion for which the appeal is dismissed shall all be borne by the Plaintiff."}

question:
Administrative Agency A issued to A a corrective order under the Building Act on the ground that a building owned by A was in violation of laws and regulations, and intends to impose a compulsory performance penalty if A fails to perform the obligations specified in the corrective order. Which of the following is the correct combination of the statements that are correct (○) and incorrect (X)? (Where there is a dispute, according to case law)

(a). Even if Administrative Agency A neglects the imposition and collection of the compulsory performance penalty against A, this is an act not directly related to finance and accounting, and therefore does not fall within matters subject to a resident suit.
(b). If a compulsory performance penalty is imposed on A after A's death, the obligation to pay is succeeded to by A's heirs.
(c). Even if A performed the obligations specified in the corrective order before Administrative Agency A imposed the compulsory performance penalty, if A performed those obligations after the period specified in the corrective order had elapsed, Administrative Agency A may impose the compulsory performance penalty on A.
(d). If A, as a proper means of performing the obligations in accordance with the purpose of the corrective order, made a report to Administrative Agency A, but Administrative Agency A unlawfully rejected it so that the rejection disposition cannot escape revocation, then, absent special circumstances, Administrative Agency A cannot impose the compulsory performance penalty on A on the ground of non-performance of the corrective order.
label: D
supporting_precedents: {"[2006MA470]": "The Court rules ex officio.\\n\\n1. The compulsory performance fine under the former Building Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 7696 of 2005. 11. 8.) is a kind of indirect compulsory enforcement imposed on a building owner, etc. who fails to comply, within the rectification period after receiving a rectification order for a violation prescribed by the former Building Act (see Supreme Court Decision dated 2002. 8. 16., 2002MA1022), and the obligation to pay such compulsory performance fine is of a personal nature that cannot be succeeded to by an heir or any other person; therefore, an administrative disposition or decision imposing a compulsory performance fine on a person already deceased is void ab initio, and if, after judicial proceedings under the Non-Contentious Case Procedure Act have been commenced upon the objection of the person on whom the compulsory performance fine was imposed, that objecting person dies, the case itself should be regarded as having lost its object and the proceedings terminated.\\n\\n2. According to the record, however, the court of first instance decided on 2003. 12. 16. to impose a compulsory performance fine of 10,000,000 won on the Re-Appellant, and when the Re-Appellant appealed therefrom, the court below, by Decision dated 2006. 4. 14., modified the decision of the court of first instance and decided to impose a compulsory performance fine of 7,000,000 won on the Re-Appellant (it is clear that “penalty” in the disposition and reasons of the decision below is a clerical error for “compulsory performance fine”); however, it can be found that the Re-Appellant had already died around 2004. 8. 21., which was after the decision of the court of first instance and before the decision of the court below. In light of the legal principle seen above, the decision of the court below is void ab initio, and the instant re-appeal filed in the name of the already deceased Re-Appellant is defective in a manner that cannot be cured and is therefore unlawful.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the instant re-appeal is dismissed, and the decision is made as ordered, by the unanimous opinion of the Justices involved."}

{"[2013DU16746]": "1. Before examining the grounds for appeal, the Court examines ex officio.\\n\\n(1) Article 17(1) of the Local Autonomy Act provides that a resident who has requested an audit concerning matters of expenditure of public funds, matters concerning the acquisition, management, and disposal of property, matters concerning the conclusion and performance of sale, lease, or work contracts or other contracts with the relevant local government as a party, or matters concerning the neglect to impose and collect local taxes, usage fees, charges, fines for negligence, etc. may file a lawsuit against the head of the relevant local government with respect to illegal acts or facts of neglect related to the matters for which the audit was requested, and Article 17(2) provides that “the lawsuits that may be filed by residents pursuant to paragraph (1) shall be as follows,” and in each subparagraph lists, inter alia, “a lawsuit seeking cancellation or modification of the relevant act, which is an administrative disposition, or seeking confirmation of whether the effect of such act does or does not exist or whether such act exists or does not exist” (Subparagraph 2), and “a lawsuit seeking confirmation of the illegality of the facts of neglect” (Subparagraph 3). This resident lawsuit system is intended to secure the lawfulness of administration concerning local finance and accounting by enabling residents to seek prevention or correction of unlawful fiscal and accounting acts of local governments. Therefore, under the above provisions, the “matters concerning the management and disposal of property” or the “matters concerning the neglect to impose and collect public funds” that become the subject of a resident lawsuit mean acts directly intended to maintain, preserve, or realize the value of property belonging to a local government, or acts neglecting to impose and collect public funds related thereto, and other acts unrelated to finance and accounting do not fall under the “matters concerning the management and disposal of property” or the “matters concerning the neglect to impose and collect public funds” that are subject to a resident lawsuit, even if they affect the finances of a local government in some way.\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, the Plaintiff, by this action, which is a resident lawsuit prescribed in Article 17(1) and (2) of the Local Autonomy Act, alleged that Shinsegae Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “Shinsegae”) unlawfully changed the use of part of the attached parking lot of the Shinsegae Department Store Yeongdeungpo Branch B Building (hereinafter referred to as “the department store building at issue”), and that, although all of the parking spaces required for the department store building at issue under the traffic impact analysis and improvement measures pursuant to the Urban Traffic Improvement Promotion Act had to be secured as an attached parking lot, 109 of them were installed in a separate parking-only building, and sought cancellation or confirmation of nullity (Article 17(2), Subparagraph 2 of the Local Autonomy Act) of the approval for use of the department store building at issue made by the Defendant against Shinsegae, and, alternatively, sought confirmation of illegality with respect to the Defendant’s failure to take, in relation to the illegality concerning the failure to secure the number of parking spaces in the above attached parking lot, measures such as cancellation of approval for use, corrective orders, imposition of a performance fine, or disposition to enter the contents of the violation in the building registry under the Building Act, or its failure to take necessary measures, restoration to the original condition, administrative execution, or corrective measures under the Parking Lot Act or the Urban Traffic Improvement Promotion Act (Article 17(2), Subparagraph 3 of the Local Autonomy Act).\\n\\n(3) Examining this case in light of the legal principles stated above, a performance fine is one of the sources constituting the fiscal revenue of a local government, and the Act on the Collection, etc. of Local Non-Tax Revenues specifically provides matters necessary for the efficient collection of performance fines, thereby regulating their imposition and collection also from the perspective of finance and accounting; accordingly, an act of neglecting to impose and collect a performance fine falls under the matter of neglecting to impose and collect public funds, which is the subject of a resident lawsuit.\\n\\nHowever, as to the remainder of the claims in this case other than the portion concerning the imposition of the performance fine, namely, the portions relating to the approval for use, cancellation of approval for use or corrective orders, disposition to enter the contents of the violation in the building registry, restoration to the original condition, administrative execution, and corrective measures, it is evident that they do not constitute finance-and-accounting acts that are the subject of a resident lawsuit; therefore, the lawsuit concerning those portions is unlawful.\\n\\n(4) Therefore, the court below erred in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning, inter alia, the standing to bring a resident lawsuit in holding that the lawsuit concerning the remainder of the claims excluding the above portion concerning the imposition of the performance fine was lawful and proceeding to determine the merits. However, the court below, by applying the principle against unfavorable alteration and dismissing the Plaintiff’s appeal, maintained the conclusion of the court of first instance that had dismissed this portion of the lawsuit, and since such action by the court below is substantively proper, the above error cannot be said to have affected the judgment, and thus does not constitute a ground for reversal of the court below’s judgment.\\n\\n2. The Court examines the grounds for appeal (including the supplementary statement of grounds for appeal and the additional supplementary written statement filed after the period for submitting the statement of grounds for appeal, to the extent that they supplement the grounds for appeal).\\n\\n(1) In order for the fact that public funds were unlawfully neglected to be imposed and collected, which is a requirement for a resident lawsuit under Article 17(1) and Article 17(2), Subparagraph 3 of the Local Autonomy Act, to be recognized, as a prerequisite, the requirements under the relevant statutes must be satisfied so that the executive agency of the local government, etc. can impose and collect such public funds. Meanwhile, a performance fine under the Building Act and the corrective order that is its prerequisite may be issued only where the building, etc. violates the Building Act or orders or dispositions under the Building Act (Article 79(1) and Article 80 of the Building Act).\\n\\n(2) According to the reasons of the judgment of the court below and the record, with respect to the change of use of part of the attached parking lot of the department store building at issue into sales facilities, Shinsegae obtained lawful approval from the competent administrative agency pursuant to the then-current provisions of the Building Act and subordinate statutes and obtained approval for use for the change of use; therefore, it is difficult to find that Shinsegae violated the Building Act or orders, etc. under the Building Act.\\n\\n(3) Although there are some insufficiencies in the statement of reasons by the court below, the conclusion of the court below that the Defendant’s failure to impose a performance fine under the Building Act on Shinsegae does not constitute a fact of unlawfully neglecting to impose public funds is proper, and there is no error, such as misunderstanding the legal principles concerning the requirements for recognition of a resident lawsuit or the requirements for imposition of a performance fine under the Building Act.\\n\\n3. Therefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of the appeal are to be borne by the losing party. The judgment is rendered as stated in the disposition by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

{"[2015DU35116]": "The grounds of appeal are examined (the contents of a supplemental brief on the grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for submitting the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement the grounds of appeal).\\n\\n1. As to the grounds of appeal regarding the rejection disposition in this case\\na. Whether the failure to submit a “land use consent letter” constitutes a lawful ground for rejection (Ground of appeal No. 1)\\n(1) Article 20(2) of the former Building Act (prior to amendment by Act No. 12246 of Jan. 14, 2014; hereinafter referred to as the “Building Act”) provides that, in order to erect a temporary building for a use prescribed by Presidential Decree, a report thereof shall be filed with the mayor, etc., and Article 15(5) subparagraphs of the former Enforcement Decree of the Building Act (prior to amendment by Presidential Decree No. 24621 of June 17, 2013; hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Decree”) enacted pursuant to such delegation enumerates the temporary buildings subject to such report.\\n\\nMeanwhile, according to paragraphs 8 and 9 of the Enforcement Decree and Article 13(1) of the former Enforcement Rule of the Building Act (prior to amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport No. 40 of Nov. 28, 2013; hereinafter referred to as the “Enforcement Rule”), a person intending to erect a temporary building subject to report shall submit to the mayor, etc., a “construction report” together with a “site plan/floor plan” and a “land use consent letter,” and the mayor, etc. shall, after verifying the contents thereof, issue a construction report certificate to the reporter. By contrast, Article 15(7) of the Enforcement Decree and Article 13(5) and (6) of the Enforcement Rule provide that a person intending to extend the period of existence of a temporary building whose period of existence has expired shall submit to the mayor, etc. a “report of extension of the period of existence,” and the mayor, etc. shall, after verifying the stated contents, issue a report receipt certificate, thereby not providing, with respect to a report for extension of the period of existence, any provision concerning documents to be attached to the report form, unlike in the case of a construction report.\\n\\n(2) Since a temporary building is not a “building” under the Building Act, the rule is that it may be installed without a building permit or building report; however, as to certain temporary buildings, there is a need to control risks by treating them analogously to buildings, and thus they are regulated as subjects of report. In light of the purpose of such reporting system, when the owner of a building, etc. intending to extend the period of existence of a temporary building files a report for extension with the administrative agency with all documents and requirements prescribed by law, the administrative agency shall, in principle, accept it and issue a report receipt certificate, and may not refuse acceptance on grounds other than those prescribed by law. Therefore, the administrative agency shall not refuse acceptance of a report for extension of the period of existence of a temporary building on grounds that documents such as a “land use consent letter,” which are not even required by law, were not submitted, or that there is no consent to use by the landowner.\\n\\n(3) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, when the Plaintiffs filed a report for extension of the period of existence (hereinafter referred to as the “extension report in this case”) with respect to the temporary building in this case, for which the construction report had been accepted as a “temporary building for construction purposes of a size necessary for the construction work” prescribed in Article 15(5) subparagraph 3 of the Enforcement Decree, the Defendant rejected the extension report in this case (hereinafter referred to as the “rejection disposition in this case”) solely on the ground that the Plaintiffs had not submitted the “land use consent letter” of some co-owners of the relevant site at the time of the above extension report.\\n\\nIn light of the foregoing legal principles, these circumstances show that the rejection disposition in this case, which refused acceptance of the extension report for the temporary building solely on the ground that the “land use consent letter,” which did not even constitute a statutory requirement for a report for extension of the period of existence of a temporary building, had not been submitted, is unlawful.\\n\\n(4) Among the reasons stated in the judgment below, the part viewing the act of accepting the extension report in this case as a discretionary act is not appropriate; however, the conclusion reached by the court below, namely, that the rejection disposition in this case is unlawful because acceptance of the extension report in this case could not be refused solely because the “land use consent letter” had not been submitted, is proper, and there is no error, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misapprehending the legal principles regarding the requirements for acceptance of a report for extension of the period of existence of a temporary building.\\n\\nb. Whether the rejection disposition in this case is lawful because the temporary building was no longer being used for construction purposes at the time of the extension report in this case (Ground of appeal No. 2)\\n(1) In an administrative litigation seeking revocation of an administrative disposition, the agency may not assert, as a ground for the disposition, separate facts that are not identical in basic factual relation to the grounds presented by the agency as the basis for the original disposition (see Supreme Court Decision 2016DO44186, rendered Aug. 29, 2017, etc.).\\n\\n(2) The Defendant, however, while arguing in the course of the lawsuit and also as a ground of appeal that the rejection disposition in this case is lawful because the temporary building in this case was erected in order to implement an order for remediation of contaminated soil in connection with the Yongsan Station area international business district development project, but the said development project was in effect scrapped and the said order for remediation of contaminated soil was also withdrawn, and thus the temporary building was no longer being used for construction purposes, is also making the same argument as a ground of appeal.\\n\\n(3) However, in light of the foregoing legal principles, it is difficult to find identity in basic factual relation between the newly added ground, “the temporary building for construction purposes is no longer being used for construction purposes,” and the original ground for the disposition, “the land use consent letter of some co-owners of the site was not submitted.” Accordingly, it is not permissible for the Defendant to add this as a new ground for the disposition.\\n\\n(4) The court below erred in judging the Defendant’s above argument in relation to whether there was an abuse or deviation from discretion, while overlooking the foregoing legal principles; however, since the court below ultimately held that the rejection disposition in this case is unlawful, such error did not affect the result of the judgment. Therefore, the ground of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.\\n\\n2. As to the grounds of appeal regarding each of the dispositions imposing the indirect coercive fines in this case (Ground of appeal No. 3)\\na. The indirect coercive fine under the Building Act is not a sanction for a past violation, namely, non-performance of a corrective order, but rather a means of administrative indirect coercion that indirectly compels performance of the obligation by imposing psychological pressure on the obligor through ordering performance of the obligation subject to the corrective order and notifying the obligor that if the obligation is not performed within the performance period, an indirect coercive fine will be imposed. In light of the nature of such indirect coercive fine, if the obligor subject to the corrective order performs the obligation before the indirect coercive fine is imposed, the indirect coercive fine cannot be imposed even if performance was after the period prescribed in the corrective order (see Supreme Court Decision 2013DO15750, rendered Dec. 11, 2014, etc.).\\n\\nFurthermore, if the obligor subject to the corrective order files an application or report with the administrative agency by a lawful means to perform the obligation consistent with the purpose of the corrective order, but the administrative agency unlawfully refuses or rejects it, resulting in the eventual revocation of that disposition, then, absent special circumstances, it is consistent with the purpose of the above indirect coercive fine system to view that an indirect coercive fine may not be imposed on the ground of non-performance of the corrective order.\\n\\nb. According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following circumstances can be found.\\n\\n(1) Around early June 2013, the Defendant notified the Plaintiffs to file a report for extension of the period of existence concerning the temporary building in this case.\\n\\n(2) On July 3, 2013, the Defendant issued to the Plaintiffs a corrective order requiring removal of the temporary building in this case on the ground that the period of existence had expired.\\n\\n(3) On July 5, 2013, the Plaintiffs filed a report for extension of the period of existence concerning the temporary building in this case, but withdrew that extension report after the Defendant requested supplementation by submitting land use consent letters from all landowners.\\n\\n(4) Meanwhile, on August 5, 2013 and August 26, 2013, the Defendant twice issued corrective orders requiring removal of the temporary building in this case.\\n\\n(5) On August 30, 2013, the Plaintiffs filed the extension report in this case again, but the Defendant rendered the rejection disposition in this case on September 30, 2013 on the ground that the land use consent letter of some co-owners with respect to the site had not been submitted.\\n\\n(6) On October 1, 2013, the Defendant imposed each of the indirect coercive fines in this case on the ground that the Plaintiffs had failed to comply with each of the above corrective orders.\\n\\nc. Examining these facts in light of the foregoing legal principles, the extension report in this case may be viewed as a lawful means of performing the obligation in order to eliminate the illegality of the temporary building itself, which is the premise of the corrective order; and, as noted above, the Defendant unlawfully rejected the extension report in this case, so that the rejection disposition in this case must be revoked. Therefore, it is reasonable to view that the Defendant may not impose an indirect coercive fine on the Plaintiff on the ground of non-performance of each corrective order issued before the rejection disposition in this case.\\n\\nd. Although there are some deficiencies in the reasoning of the court below, the conclusion of the court below that each of the dispositions imposing the indirect coercive fines in this case is unlawful is proper, and thus some errors in the court below’s factual findings cannot be said to have affected the result of the judgment. Accordingly, there is no error in the judgment below, such as misapprehension of the legal principles regarding the requirements for imposing an indirect coercive fine under the Building Act or the preclusive force, etc. of a demolition order, as alleged in the grounds of appeal.\\n\\n3. Conclusion\\nTherefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party. It is so adjudged as stated in the dispositive part by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating."}

question:
Which of the following statements concerning property rights and compensation for losses are correct? (In the event of a dispute, according to case law)

(a) Even if the project implementer includes nonresident owners within the scope of persons eligible for relocation measures beyond the scope of persons eligible for relocation measures prescribed by law, the relocation measures provided to nonresident owners who are not persons eligible for relocation measures prescribed by law are not obligations under law, but are of a gratuitous nature.

(b) The “just compensation” prescribed in Article 23(3) of the Constitution means that the objective property value of the expropriated property must be fully compensated; therefore, calculating the amount of compensation for losses by excluding development gains resulting from the implementation of the relevant public works project runs counter to the principle of just compensation.

(c) Article 23(3) of the Constitution does not limit the subject of expropriation of property rights; thus, if it is not an issue that the State expropriates land in a project recognized as being for public necessity, it cannot be said that the judgment on public necessity in that project is essentially different merely because a private person has the right of expropriation in the same project.

(d) In calculating the amount of compensation for expropriation of land subject to restrictions under public law, if such restrictions were imposed not for the direct purpose of implementing the relevant public project, the land must be appraised as it stands under such restrictions; however, if such restrictions were imposed after the implementation of the relevant public project, it must be appraised as if it were not subject to such restrictions.
