{"[2007HEONBA114]": "1. Outline of the Case and Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\na. Outline of the Case\\n\\n(1) The non-party OO Electronics Co., Ltd. submitted to the Mayor of Asan, on 2004. 2. 23., a “Request for Approval of Designation of an Industrial Complex” pursuant to Article 11 of the Act on Industrial Sites and Development (hereinafter referred to as the “Industrial Sites Act”) and Article 13 of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, with respect to 3,261,281㎡ of land in OO-ri, DD-ri, and TT-ri, Tangjeong-myeon, Asan-si, Chungcheongnam-do, and the Mayor of Asan delivered the above request to the Governor of Chungcheongnam-do on 2004. 4. 19. together with a written opinion on the request, etc. Accordingly, the Governor of Chungcheongnam-do designated and approved OO Electronics as the project implementer, on 2004. 7. 31., for 2,113,759㎡ of land in OO-ri, DD-ri, and TT-ri, Tangjeong-myeon, Asan-si, as the “Tangjeong No. 2 General Local Industrial Complex,” and thereafter, on 2004. 8. 5., pursuant to Article 7-3 of the Industrial Sites Act, publicly notified this by Chungcheongnam-do Public Notice No. 2004-159.\\n\\n(2) Petitioners are landowners who own land within the above industrial complex, and the land owned by Petitioners located within the above industrial complex was designated as land subject to expropriation pursuant to the above public notice. OO Electronics consulted with the Petitioners concerning the acquisition, etc. of the above land, but as no agreement was reached, it applied to the Chungcheongnam-do Local Land Expropriation Committee for an adjudication, and the Chungcheongnam-do Local Land Expropriation Committee, on 2006. 5. 22., rendered an expropriation award with respect to the above land and structures thereon.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, on 2006. 7. 24., Petitioners filed a suit with the Daejeon District Court against the Chungcheongnam-do Local Land Expropriation Committee seeking revocation of the expropriation disposition at issue (Daejeon District Court 2006GUHAP2239), and during the pendency of the said litigation, on the ground that Article 11(1) of the Industrial Sites Act, etc. violate Article 23(3) and Article 37(2) of the Constitution, and that item (j) of Article 2(6) of the Industrial Sites Act is contrary to the principle of clarity, they filed an application for referral for constitutional review (Daejeon District Court 2005A163); however, when this was dismissed on 2007. 9. 19., they filed the present constitutional complaint on October 29 of the same year.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Adjudication\\n\\nThe Petitioners seek review of the constitutionality of item (j) of Article 2(6), Article 11(1) and (3), Article 16(1)3, and Article 22(1) and (2) of the Industrial Sites Act. However, the essence of the Petitioners’ argument lies in the constitutionality of the relevant statutory provisions that grant expropriation power to private corporations in the name of industrial complex development; since Article 11(1) and (3), Article 16(1)3, and Article 22(2) of the Industrial Sites Act cannot be said to be directly related to the expropriation case at issue, or since the Petitioners do not appear to be actively making their own constitutional arguments against them, it is reasonable to limit the subject matter of adjudication in this case to item (j) of Article 2(6) of the Industrial Sites Act (hereinafter referred to as the “definition provision at issue”) and the portion of Article 22(1) concerning “Article 16(1)3” among the “project implementer” portion (hereinafter referred to as the “expropriation provision at issue”). The contents of the provision subject to adjudication and the relevant provisions are as follows.\\n\\n[Provision Subject to Adjudication]\\n\\nIndustrial Sites and Development Act (as amended by Act No. 5111 on 1995. 12. 29.) Article 2 (Definitions) The definitions of terms used in this Act are as follows.\\n\\n6. “Industrial complex development project” means any of the following projects implemented for the creation of an industrial complex.\\n\\nj. Other projects incidental to the projects under subparagraphs (a) through (i)\\n\\nIndustrial Sites and Development Act (as amended by Act No. 6406 on 2001. 1. 29.) Article 22 (Expropriation of Land) (1) A project implementer (excluding a project implementer under Article 16(1)6; the same shall apply in this Article) may expropriate or use land, buildings, or things affixed to land necessary for an industrial complex development project, and rights other than ownership in relation thereto, mining rights, fishing rights, and rights concerning the use of water.\\n\\nArticle 16 (Project Implementer of Industrial Complex Development Project) (1) An industrial complex development project shall be implemented by a person designated by the person authorized to designate the industrial complex, among the following persons, as prescribed in the industrial complex development plan.\\n\\n3. A person who installs facilities suitable for the relevant industrial complex development plan and seeks to occupy the complex, or a person recognized as capable of developing an industrial complex suitably under the relevant industrial complex development plan and who satisfies the requirements prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n\\n[Relevant Provisions]\\n\\nAs set forth in the attached sheet.\\n\\n2. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments, the Grounds for the Court’s Dismissal of the Application for Constitutional Review, and the Summary of the Interested Parties’ Opinions\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) Although Article 23(3) of the Constitution provides that property rights may be expropriated only in cases of “public necessity,” the expropriation provision at issue allows private corporations to expropriate the land of other private persons merely because they are creating an industrial complex. In the case of a private corporation that is not a subsistence-support corporation but a profit-seeking private corporation, the purpose is profit-seeking, and even if increases in tax revenue are generated from such economic activity, it is difficult to say that this satisfies public necessity on that basis; moreover, in that the provision does not even contain any recapture rule for profits generated from development, the expropriation provision at issue may be said to lack public necessity, and therefore it violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution, and even if there is public necessity, it violates the principle of excessive restriction under Article 37(2) of the Constitution.\\n\\nIn addition, even if the project implementer is one carrying out a public works project, in the case of a private corporation, since profit-seeking is its ultimate objective, stricter standards must be applied in granting land expropriation power, as compared with cases where the State, a local government, or a public corporation becomes the project implementer; however, while the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act and the Special Act on the Development of Enterprise Cities, when granting land expropriation power to private corporations, grant such unilateral land expropriation power only when, at a minimum, more than 50 percent of the project land and, at most, more than 67 percent of the land are purchased by consultation, and when consent is obtained from more than 50 percent to 80 percent of the total number of landowners, the Industrial Sites Act recognizes full land expropriation power for private corporations that become project implementers without imposing any certain land acquisition conditions. Accordingly, as compared with other laws, merely because an industrial complex has been designated under the Industrial Sites Act, landowners within the industrial complex face a greater risk of losing ownership of their land through expropriation; thus, this also violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution, and further, as discrimination lacking a rational basis, it violates the constitutional right to equality.\\n\\nMeanwhile, Petitioners have the constitutional right to pursue happiness and the freedom of residence and movement to spend their old age while enjoying the leisure of a peaceful life, farming on the land they own, and the expropriation provision at issue infringes such fundamental rights.\\n\\n(2) The definition provision at issue is contrary to the principle of clarity because the concept of “incidental project” is extremely vague.\\n\\nb. Summary of the Court’s Grounds for Dismissing the Application for Constitutional Review\\n\\n(1) The expropriation provision at issue is intended to contribute to the sound development of the national economy by promoting balanced land development and continued industrial development through the smooth supply of industrial sites and the rational placement of industry, and thus public necessity is recognized; and once public necessity is recognized, it cannot be said to be contrary to Article 23(3) of the Constitution merely because the project implementer is a private corporation.\\n\\nIn addition, the above expropriation provision is intended to realize the legislative purpose of the Industrial Sites Act; its purpose is legitimate, and if the project implementer is limited to the State or a local government in developing an industrial complex, problems such as budgetary difficulties or uncertainty regarding companies’ entry may arise, so it may be efficient to have the final end users of industrial sites directly develop them. Furthermore, in light of the fact that the Industrial Sites Act limits the qualifications of private corporations that may develop industrial complexes and also provides methods that can appropriately restrict the profit-seeking of private corporations serving as project implementers, the appropriateness of the means is also recognized. Therefore, it cannot be said to violate Article 37(2) of the Constitution, and thus, even if the Petitioners’ land is expropriated by the expropriation disposition at issue, causing inconvenience such as being required to relocate their residence, this does not infringe the right to pursue happiness or the freedom of residence and movement.\\n\\nUnder the Industrial Sites Act, industrial complex development projects have a strong public necessity, and not only are institutional devices provided to restrict the profit-seeking of private corporations, but the legislative purpose is different from that of the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act, etc., which impose certain restrictions on the land expropriation power of private corporations; therefore, the fact that the expropriation provision at issue does not impose the same restrictions as other laws in exercising land expropriation power cannot be said to be discrimination lacking a rational basis.\\n\\n(2) The definition provision at issue does not specify in detail every individual facility necessary in developing an industrial complex; however, the “incidental project” in this provision can be sufficiently predicted as a project accompanying projects such as the creation of factory sites, etc., and thus it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nc. Summary of the Opinions of the Interested Party OO Electronics Co., Ltd. and the Chungcheongnam-do Local Land Expropriation Committee\\n\\n(1) Since the legislative purpose of the Industrial Sites Act is to achieve public interest, the public character of the industrial complex development project cannot be said to change merely because a private corporation becomes the project implementer; the basic spirit of the Industrial Sites Act lies in seeking to achieve both the development of industrial complexes by private corporations and the public interest of national economic development through harmonization of the profit-seeking of private corporations and public necessity; and in light of the fact that the Industrial Sites Act provides various legal devices capable of solving the problems that may arise from a private corporation becoming a project implementer, the expropriation provision at issue cannot be said to violate Article 23(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\nAlso, Article 23(3) of the Constitution does not require “acquisition by consultation of land exceeding a certain ratio,” and since the Industrial Sites Act and other laws that impose certain restrictions on the exercise of land expropriation power by private corporations differ in their legislative purposes, regulated projects, and degree of public interest, there is a rational basis for the expropriation provision at issue, which stipulates different requirements for land expropriation power from those of other laws; therefore, it cannot be said that the Petitioners, to whom this provision applies, have had their right to equality infringed.\\n\\nThat the Petitioners’ freedom of residence and movement was restricted due to the expropriation disposition at issue is merely a problem that always arises in cases of land expropriation, and insofar as the expropriation provision at issue does not infringe property rights or the right to equality, it does not infringe the right to pursue happiness or the freedom of residence and movement either.\\n\\n(2) The definition provision at issue is a case in which its meaning can be determined through interpretation, including by considering the interrelationship with other provisions, and in light of the fact that many of the laws in force in our country that contain definition provisions regarding various projects adopt the same form as the definition provision at issue, it cannot be said to violate the principle of clarity.\\n\\nd. Summary of the Opinion of the Interested Party, the Minister of Construction and Transportation\\n\\nIt is generally the same as the grounds stated by the court for dismissing the application for constitutional review and the opinions of OO Electronics Co., Ltd. and the Chungcheongnam-do Local Land Expropriation Committee.\\n\\n3. Decision\\n\\na. Determination on the Expropriation Provision at Issue\\n\\n(1) Whether it violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution, etc.\\n\\nThe Petitioners argued, inter alia, that since the expropriation provision at issue allows a private corporation engaged in profit-oriented activities to expropriate land in order to create an industrial complex, it violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution, which assumes the State as the subject of expropriation; that it does not satisfy public necessity; and that even if there is public necessity, it is contrary to Article 37(2) of the Constitution. We examine this in order below.\\n\\n(a) Whether expropriation by a private corporation itself is unconstitutional\\n\\n1) Article 23(3) of the Constitution provides for the possibility of expropriation, etc. of property rights on the premise of just compensation, but it does not limit the subject of property expropriation. This means that at the normative level of the Constitution there is no specific determination as to whether, in relation to expropriation of property, the subject of expropriation must be limited to the State, etc., or whether it may also be permitted to private corporations. Therefore, there is no reason to interpret the subject of expropriation, etc. as limited to public institutions such as the State.\\n\\nThe core of the above constitutional provision lies in whether the expropriation at issue conforms to public necessity and whether just compensation is being paid, rather than in whether the subject of expropriation is the State or a private corporation. For example, if the State expropriates land for a project recognized as having public necessity, there is no issue; likewise, it cannot be said that the judgment concerning public necessity in that project essentially changes merely because a private corporation has expropriation power for the same project.\\n\\nAlso, even in a case like the present one where a private corporation becomes the subject of expropriation, the granting of expropriation power to that private corporation is done by the State or a local government, which performs the designation of the industrial complex, etc.; this ultimately means that the final authority to judge the public necessity required for expropriation is reserved to a public institution such as the State. Whether the State or another public institution directly becomes the subject of expropriation, or whether a private corporation becomes the subject of expropriation under the final approval and determination of such public institution, there does not appear to be any essential difference between the two in terms of the judgment on public necessity and the scope of expropriation. As long as the public institution such as the State retains a leading role and final decision-making authority in the overall process of determining the public necessity of the project and reviewing whether expropriation is permissible, even if a private corporation becomes the subject of expropriation, this is merely the concrete implementation of the above decision by the State, etc. However, if the benefit of expropriation accrues first to a private corporation whose purpose is profit-seeking rather than to a public institution, then even if such expropriation has public necessity, it is appropriate that it be institutionally regulated so that the original public-interest objective is not undermined by excessive pursuit of private gain by the private corporation; we will return to this point below.\\n\\n2) Today, the scale of our industry has grown to a degree incomparable with the past, and national industrial policy is a serious matter that determines the economic course of the community, so the capital invested in the development of industrial complexes may also be required on a large scale. In such cases, if the project implementer in developing an industrial complex were limited to the State or a local government, there could be difficulties in promoting the development project due to budgetary constraints. Also, if the State were to develop industrial complexes and then supply them to companies, adhering solely to the so-called public development method, the industrial complex might not correspond to the intentions of the actual end-user companies even if enormous public capital were invested in its development, and accordingly there is a probability that resources will be inefficiently consumed by developing industrial complexes that do not match demand, such as where companies cannot smoothly move in. If companies are allowed to develop industrial complexes directly, there would also be an aspect in which participation by companies may be encouraged.\\n\\nSince the legislative purpose of the Industrial Sites Act is achieved by granting private corporations the authority to develop industrial complexes, if land expropriation power is necessary for the project implementer in order for such development to proceed effectively, recognizing such power would be consistent with the legislative intent of the Industrial Sites Act. On the other hand, where a Mayor/Do Governor designates a general industrial complex upon application by a private corporation, notice through the method of public notice, the granting of an opportunity for residents and relevant experts, etc. to submit opinions, and deliberation by the Industrial Sites Policy Deliberation Council for the approval of the Minister of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs are guaranteed, so that the process of designation of an industrial complex proceeds in accordance with the principle of due process; this Court has already confirmed this through a separate case (Constitutional Court 2007. 4. 26. 2006HEONBA10, Court Reports 19-1, 482, 500). Our legal system also provides effective remedies through administrative litigation, etc. in the event of defects in concrete administrative acts such as the designation disposition or the expropriation disposition in this case.\\n\\n3) Taking the above into comprehensive consideration, one cannot declare unconstitutional the mere fact that a private corporation is prescribed as the subject of expropriation; furthermore, the legislative judgment that it is necessary, in developing an industrial complex for public interest purposes, to allow a private corporation designated as the project implementer to expropriate land when necessary for the implementation of the project appears to have a rational basis.\\n\\n(b) Whether public necessity is recognized\\n\\n1) The expropriation provision at issue seeks to contribute to the sound development of the national economy by promoting balanced national land development and continued industrial development through the smooth supply of industrial sites and the rational placement of industry (Article 1 of the Industrial Sites Act), and further, it aims to promote the proper regional dispersion of industry and the revitalization of the regional economy (Article 2(5)(b)(1) of the Industrial Sites Act).\\n\\nAn industrial complex means a parcel of land designated and developed in accordance with a comprehensive plan in order to collectively install factories, facilities related to knowledge industries, etc., and the educational, research, business, support, information-processing, and distribution facilities related thereto, as well as residential, cultural, and environmental facilities, etc., for enhancing the functions of these facilities; thus, if industrial sites are supplied smoothly, construction of industrial complexes can be facilitated, and therefore effective economic development or growth can be expected through the construction of industrial complexes.\\n\\nThe development of industrial complexes, which began along with the promotion of the economic development plan in the early 1960s, has played a central role in our country’s industrial policy over the past decades. Through the development of industrial complexes, the State was able to supply individual companies with sites equipped with infrastructure, etc., thereby promoting corporate activities. As industrial complexes were developed, individual companies could relatively easily use facilities that would be difficult to secure on their own, and from the State’s perspective, it could promote national and regional industry through the activities and enhancement of competitiveness of companies, thereby creating employment and dispersing industry nationwide to induce balanced development of the national territory. In addition, industrial complexes also played a major role in preventing disorderly development of industrial land use and contributing to the clustering of new and relocated factories, thereby realizing environmentally friendly use of national territory and the economies of scale.\\n\\nFurthermore, the economic development resulting from industrial complex development has also been a major cornerstone in the social and cultural development of our society. Looking back historically, the social significance of industrial complex development can be confirmed in that such economic development has been a major driving force that has elevated the civilizational level of the life led in the relevant national community.\\n\\n2) Meanwhile, as mentioned above, unlike the State, private corporations fundamentally pursue profit in their economic activities; therefore, if there is a case where, being absorbed in the private interest of profit-seeking, the public interest obtainable from the activities of a private corporation is significantly undermined or lost, such legislation may be in violation of Article 23(3) of the Constitution. However, in light of the contents of the following provisions under the Industrial Sites Act, it is difficult to say that there is a lack of institutional regulation to ensure that the public-interest objective originally intended to be achieved and maintained by creating an industrial complex is not undermined by the private corporation, the project implementer, becoming excessively focused on its own profit-seeking.\\n\\nAccording to the Industrial Sites Act, when a project implementer completes an industrial complex development project, it must, without delay and as prescribed by Presidential Decree, obtain completion approval from the authority approving the implementation plan (Article 37(1) of the same Act); and if the completion inspection results show that it was not completed as per the implementation plan, the authority approving the implementation plan must, without delay, order necessary measures such as supplementary construction (Article 37(4) of the same Article); and companies entering the industrial complex must, absent special reasons, preferentially employ relocated persons or residents of nearby areas (Article 36(2) of the same Act). Meanwhile, if the project implementer intends to sell, lease, or transfer land, facilities, etc. within the project area, it must prepare a disposition plan and consult with the management agency under Article 30 of the Act on the Promotion of Industrial Cluster and Factory Establishment (Article 38(1) of the same Act), and comply with the basic industrial complex management plan (Article 38-2 of the same Act). In this process, the sale price cannot be determined arbitrarily by the project implementer; if the land is sold as industrial facility land, the price is determined as the development cost or the development cost plus a reasonable profit, and the reasonable profit is normatively limited so as not to exceed a certain range (Article 40(1) and (2) of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act), while the sale price of land supplied for purposes other than industrial facility land is prescribed as the appraised value determined by an appraiser under Article 2(9) of the Act on Public Announcement of Real Estate Values and Appraisal of Real Estate (Article 40(6) of the same Act). On the other hand, when, after an industrial complex has been developed, readjustment of the industrial complex is necessary due to changes in industrial structure, expansion of urban areas, and aging of industrial facilities, etc., the person authorized to designate the industrial complex may carry out an industrial complex readjustment project directly or upon request of the Minister of Commerce, Industry and Energy and the heads of the relevant central administrative agencies or the head of the Si/Gun/Gu, after hearing the opinions of the tenant companies and the heads of the relevant local governments and consulting with the heads of the relevant administrative agencies (Article 38-3 of the same Act), and by applying mutatis mutandis the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (hereinafter referred to as the “Public Works Act”), the Industrial Sites Act provides in advance that a right of repurchase shall arise when land designated as an industrial complex is later excluded from the industrial complex or loses its utility as an industrial complex (Article 22(4) of the same Act).\\n\\n3) Considering the legislative purpose above, and at the same time thoroughly examining the institutional devices intended to ensure that public interest is not undermined, the expropriation provision at issue appears to satisfy the “public necessity” requirement under Article 23(3) of the Constitution.\\n\\n(c) Whether it violates the principle of excessive restriction\\n\\n1) Legitimacy of the objective and appropriateness of the means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the expropriation provision at issue is as confirmed above when examining the public necessity of the expropriation provision at issue, and it is clear that this is a legitimate legislative purpose for pursuing the public welfare. And through the expropriation provision at issue, the project implementer can appropriately purchase, at market value, the land of those who do not respond to consultation and thus be able to proceed with the project smoothly; therefore, it is recognized that the above expropriation provision is a highly effective means for achieving the above legislative purpose.\\n\\n2) Least infringement\\n\\n(a) Taking the following into account, the expropriation provision at issue does not appear to impose an unnecessarily excessive restriction on the property rights of the expropriated party.\\n\\nSince the Public Works Act applies mutatis mutandis except where the Industrial Sites Act contains special provisions regarding expropriation (Article 22(4) of the Industrial Sites Act), the project implementer under the Industrial Sites Act is still obligated to sincerely consult with landowners and interested persons concerning compensation for land, etc. (Article 16 of the Public Works Act), and, as seen above, when land designated as an industrial complex is later excluded from the industrial complex or loses its utility as an industrial complex, a right of repurchase arises and the rights of the original owner are restored (Article 22(4) of the same Act). Even if expropriation occurs upon the project implementer’s application for adjudication, the project implementer must pay just compensation to the person subject to expropriation (Article 23(3) of the Constitution), and, as noted above, the process leading up to expropriation under the Industrial Sites Act is guaranteed to proceed in accordance with the principle of due process; thus, institutional procedures are provided so that various interests and opinions concerning industrial complex development may be expressed and evenly reflected. Furthermore, as mentioned above, our legal system has also prepared effective means of remedies through administrative litigation, etc. where there are defects in a concrete expropriation disposition.\\n\\n(b) Meanwhile, the scope of the object of expropriation under the expropriation provision at issue does not appear to exceed the necessary range. The expropriation provision at issue prescribes as objects of expropriation “land, buildings, or things affixed to land necessary for an industrial complex development project, and rights other than ownership in relation thereto, mining rights, fishing rights, and rights concerning the use of water,” and, in addition, the industrial complex in this case means “a parcel of land designated and developed according to a comprehensive plan in order to collectively install factories, facilities related to knowledge industries, facilities related to cultural industries, facilities related to information and communications industries, resource stockpiling facilities, etc., and the educational, research, business, information-processing, distribution facilities related thereto, and residential, cultural, medical, tourism, sports, and welfare facilities for workers and users of these facilities in order to enhance the functions of these facilities” (Article 2(5) of the Industrial Sites Act). Factories and facilities related to knowledge industries, etc. may be said to constitute the core of the industrial complex, and educational and research facilities related thereto, etc., and residential, cultural, and medical facilities for workers and users of these facilities in order to enhance the functions of these facilities, are facilities deemed necessary in the context of reducing the risk that an industrial complex may not function effectively by relying on other external facilities or institutions, and of ensuring that it can efficiently perform its core tasks as an organic unit; therefore, they appear to fall within a reasonable range in light of the purpose of an industrial complex. Accordingly, the scope of land expropriation power granted to the project implementer, a private corporation, under the Industrial Sites Act is within the bounds of public necessity in light of the legislative purpose and enactment intent of the Industrial Sites Act, as seen above, and it is difficult to say that expropriation power beyond the necessary scope was granted.\\n\\n(c) Even if the expropriation provision at issue recognizes full land expropriation power without imposing certain land acquisition requirements, etc. as conditions for expropriation, it is difficult to say, on that ground alone, that it violates Article 23(3) of the Constitution or runs counter to the principle of least infringement.\\n\\nArticle 23(3) of the Constitution provides “public necessity” and “just compensation” as the legal requirements for public expropriation; therefore, whether expropriation is permissible should naturally be determined by whether the above two requirements are satisfied. Accordingly, if a project does not have public necessity, expropriation power should not be granted to the project implementer even if it satisfies certain land acquisition requirements; conversely, if a project is strongly recognized as having public necessity, expropriation power may be granted even if certain land acquisition requirements are not imposed on the project implementer. Certain land acquisition requirements in land expropriation should be understood in a policy context aimed at promoting the smooth progress of expropriation procedures based on the broader will of the people or preventing abuse of expropriation authority; the mere absence of such requirements does not make the statute unconstitutional.\\n\\n3) Balance of legal interests\\n\\nIn addition, considering the role that industrial complexes have played in our national community, the public-interest significance of the sound development of the national economy, the promotion of the regional dispersion of industry, and the revitalization of the regional economy pursued by the expropriation provision at issue is not small; and even if the property rights of the person subject to expropriation are somewhat restricted by the expropriation provision at issue, when the institutional procedures leading up to expropriation and the compensation system are comprehensively considered, the degree of restriction cannot be said to be heavier than the public interest guaranteed by the expropriation provision at issue. Therefore, the expropriation provision at issue cannot be said to disregard the balance between public and private interests, and thus does not violate the principle of balance of legal interests.\\n\\n4) Sub-conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, the expropriation provision at issue cannot be said to violate Article 23(3) and Article 37(2) of the Constitution (in light of the foregoing grounds, the Petitioners’ arguments, whose main thrust is that the freedom of residence and movement and the right to pursue happiness were infringed by the above provision, are likewise without merit.).\\n\\n(d) Determination on other arguments\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that, because there is no system for recapturing development gains when a private corporation project implementer develops a general local industrial complex, this is unconstitutional; however, according to Article 5(1)2 of the Act on Restitution of Development Gains and [Attached Table 1] of the Enforcement Decree of the same Act, the general local industrial complex development project falls within the projects subject to the imposition of development charges, so if the project implementer has development gains, there are also means such as imposing development charges on the project implementer; therefore, the Petitioners’ argument on this point is also without merit without need for further examination.\\n\\nOn the other hand, the Petitioners argue that, due to the expropriation provision at issue, the project implementer exercised expropriation power beyond the necessary scope, and therefore the above expropriation is contrary to the principle of excessive restriction; however, the grounds of the Petitioners’ argument may be grounds for illegality, such as that the designation and expropriation disposition in this case deviated from the scope of discretion, but cannot be regarded as grounds for unconstitutionality of the expropriation provision at issue, and thus the Petitioners’ argument on this point is also without merit without need for further examination.\\n\\n(2) Whether the right to equality has been infringed\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that, while the Urban and Residential Environment Improvement Act and the Special Act on the Development of Enterprise Cities, etc. require the acquisition of land exceeding a certain ratio, etc. when granting land expropriation power to private corporations, the expropriation provision at issue recognizes full land expropriation power without imposing certain land acquisition requirements, etc., and thus, as compared with other laws, landowners within industrial complexes under the Industrial Sites Act face a greater risk of losing ownership of their land through expropriation; therefore, this constitutes discrimination lacking a rational basis and infringes the constitutional right to equality.\\n\\nHowever, as noted above, certain land acquisition requirements in land expropriation should be understood in a policy context aimed at promoting the smooth progress of expropriation procedures based on the broader will of the people or preventing abuse of expropriation authority; accordingly, whether or not to impose certain land acquisition requirements when expropriating land is left to the legislative policy judgment based on the public necessity of the project in question.\\n\\nTurning back to the expropriation provision at issue, it grants land expropriation power within the scope of the specific necessity of industrial complex development for the purpose of sound development of the national economy, and, as seen above, industrial complex development has played a central role in our country’s industrial policy over the years and through it the State and regional industries could be developed, employment created, and balanced development of the national territory induced through nationwide dispersion of industry; in this respect, the Industrial Sites Act has a public-interest purpose and content different from that of the other laws referred to in the Petitioners’ arguments. In addition, taking into account that under the Industrial Sites Act the project implementer is obligated to sincerely consult with landowners and interested persons (Article 16 of the Public Works Act), even if the expropriation provision at issue does not require the acquisition of land exceeding a certain ratio when granting land expropriation power to private corporations, this is attributable to the rational judgment of the legislature as above, and it is difficult to say that such treatment constitutes arbitrary discrimination infringing the right to equality.\\n\\nb. Determination on the Definition Provision at Issue\\n\\nThe Petitioners argue that the concept of “incidental project” prescribed in the definition provision at issue is extremely vague and thus violates the principle of clarity of statutes.\\n\\n(1) Intensity of review under the principle of clarity\\n\\nUnder the principle of clarity, the degree of clarity required is not the same for all statutes; it may vary depending on the nature of each statute or statutory provision, and may differ according to the special characteristics of each element of the offense and the background or circumstances under which such statute was enacted. In other words, in criminal statutes governed by the principle of nulla poena sine lege, the degree of clarity is heightened and a stricter standard is applied (the principle of clarity under nulla poena sine lege). However, in general statutes, the degree of clarity is not required so strongly, and therefore a relatively relaxed standard is applied (general principle of clarity) (Constitutional Court 2008. 11. 27. 2007HEONBA51, Court Reports 20-2, lower volume, 273, 280).\\n\\nThe definition provision at issue does not itself constitute an element of a crime or prescribe conditions for punishment. Accordingly, this is not a case where the very strict principle of clarity related to due process or criminal punishment applies; rather, it is a case where the general principle of clarity derived from the general theory of the rule of law applies.\\n\\n(2) Specific determination\\n\\nThe “incidental project” in the definition provision at issue can be predicted, in light of the structure and wording of the provision, as a project carried out in addition to the main projects such as those in Article 2(6)(a) through (i) of the Industrial Sites Act; and since the method of first listing the main items and then regulating, in the final item, work or projects “incidental” to the preceding items is a normative form commonly adopted by other statutes, it is difficult to say that it lacks clarity. Even if the above provision contains some degree of ambiguity, it can sufficiently be resolved through systematic and harmonized interpretation with other provisions or interpretation according to the legislative purpose and enactment intent of the statute in question. Therefore, the meaning of the above provision cannot be said to deviate from the standard of clarity, and at the very least a person of sound common sense and ordinary legal sentiment can be said to be able roughly to predict the semantic core of the above provision. Accordingly, the Petitioners’ above argument is not accepted.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, since the expropriation provision at issue and the definition provision at issue do not violate the Constitution, the decision is rendered as stated in the Order by the unanimous opinion of the remaining participating Justices, except for the dissenting opinion of Justice Kim Jong-dae as set forth in 5. below.\\n\\n5. Dissenting Opinion of Justice Kim Jong-dae\\n\\nUnlike the majority opinion, I conclude that the provisions at issue infringe property rights under our Constitution, and state as follows.\\n\\na. The constitutional ideal of the guarantee of property rights\\n\\nThe guarantee of property rights, based on the private ownership system and the principle of private autonomy in economic activity, is to enable each citizen, within the capitalist market economic order, to satisfy the basic needs of life through free economic activity, and to guarantee the free use, profit, disposition, and inheritance of private property. This is based on the ideal that such a guarantee is the shortcut to guaranteeing freedom and creativity and, ultimately, the best means of enhancing human dignity and value (see, e.g., Constitutional Court 1993. 7. 29. 92HEONBA20, Court Reports 5-2, 36, 44).\\n\\nSince its emergence in the Petition of Right and the Bill of Rights of England, which may be regarded as the gestation period of modern constitutionalism, the spirit of such guarantee of property rights has been treated as an important matter and has established itself as a core value in the history of modern constitutionalism. The State cannot be an end in itself; the liberal and democratic understanding of the Constitution today would be that it has the character of a kind of means devised to guarantee the people’s basic freedoms and rights, and no one can deny that property rights belong among such basic freedoms of the people.\\n\\nb. Restrictions on property rights and their limits\\n\\nHowever, even property rights cannot be absolutely protected. Since the contents of property rights are determined by statute, the legislature may be granted a certain degree of legislative discretion in that process, and because the exercise of property rights itself entails the constitutional demand that it be suitable for the public welfare, broader restrictions may be imposed on the exercise of property rights that have a high degree of social relevance (see Constitutional Court 2004. 10. 28. 99HEONBA91, Court Reports 16-2, lower volume, 104, 126-127). And where there is public necessity, property rights may be expropriated by statute in return for just compensation. But apart from such reasons, arbitrary restriction or deprivation of an individual’s property rights is constitutionally prohibited. In particular, in the case of expropriation, it directly deprives the people of their property rights, and furthermore may infringe freedom of contract derived from Article 10 of the Constitution, and if the object of expropriation is the expropriatee’s residence, it may even involve infringement of the expropriatee’s freedom of residence and movement because forced relocation follows after the expropriation; therefore, since it can in fact cause restrictions on many constitutional values, the examination of unconstitutionality must be conducted carefully.\\n\\nc. The unconstitutionality of the provisions at issue\\n\\nArticle 23(3) of the Constitution provides only for “expropriation of property rights by public necessity.” In response, the expropriation provision at issue seeks to comply with the constitutional demand for public necessity by invoking such nominal purposes as “sound development of the national economy.” However, the substance of the expropriation provision at issue lies in seeking to give priority to guaranteeing the profit-seeking of private corporations in the name of economic development of our society, and this must be deemed to violate Article 23(3) and Article 37(2) of the Constitution for the following reasons.\\n\\n(1) Activities of private economic entities and public necessity\\n\\nThe profit-oriented economic activities of private economic entities, insofar as they are carried out within the community of society, indirectly or incidentally satisfy public necessity.\\n\\nHowever, the activities of private economic entities have, after all, the primary purpose of their own profit-oriented activities, and the public-interest outcomes arising from such activities are merely secondary in nature. If, by approaching such cases inversely, one broadly recognizes that private economic activity may, as a result, conform to public necessity, there is a risk of moving in a direction that is inconsistent with the spirit of property rights guaranteed under our Constitution, such as allowing the ownership of land originally held by one individual to be taken away and transferred to another at any time merely because there is a possibility that another person could use that land more efficiently and usefully and thereby contribute more greatly to the public interest. Indeed, even in this case, the structure is such that the expropriation is justified on the basis that OO Electronics Co., Ltd.’s use of the land subject to expropriation would economically benefit the State and society more than the expropriatees’ use of that land would; this idea not only runs counter to the spirit of the guarantee of individual property rights under our Constitution, but also may cause the State and the powerful to become allied under the pretext of public necessity, thereby causing serious obstacles to fair social development. And this may also have negative consequences for the constitutional order as a whole, which seeks to guarantee fundamental rights to the maximum extent and achieve equal enhancement of people’s life.\\n\\n(2) Constitutional requirements for expropriation by private corporations and whether those requirements have been violated\\n\\nTraditionally, the subject of expropriation was a public institution such as the State. Therefore, it may be said that the situation in which a private corporation becomes the subject of expropriation is an exceptional phenomenon. This originated from the reason that, in order to satisfy the requirement of public necessity demanded for expropriation, it is appropriate that a public institution such as the State implement it so that the benefit arising from expropriation is not appropriated by a particular individual or group but is publicly attributed or enjoyed.\\n\\nThat is, if the State, etc. becomes the subject of expropriation, the normative ought and expectation that the benefit of such expropriation will accrue to the interests of the entire community, including the expropriatee, lead the expropriatee to endure such expropriation.\\n\\nBy contrast, if a private corporation becomes the subject of expropriation, such trust or normative ought is difficult to operate. If both the expropriator and the expropriatee are equal private persons, such expropriation is nothing other than forcing the transfer of one private person’s property to another private person. Therefore, compared with the case in which the State becomes the subject of expropriation and assumes the role of spreading the benefit of expropriation to the entire community, in such a case there is a weaker guarantee that the benefit of expropriation will accrue publicly; accordingly, in order for such expropriation to be justified, more intensified legislative measures that can ensure the public necessity of the expropriation in question and publicly attribute the benefit through expropriation must be accompanied. For example, one should institutionally regulate so that the rich fruits borne through expropriation are enjoyed together by the community, including the expropriator and the expropriatee, by adding measures such as guaranteeing continuous recapture measures for development gains arising from expropriation of the relevant project, devising methods for public use of the profits from business operations generated by the corporation’s expropriation, or implementing mandatory employment quotas for local residents.\\n\\nAlthough, as the majority opinion states, the Industrial Sites Act and related statutes provide for the recapture of development gains (where development gains here refer merely to the increase in land value accruing to the person implementing the development project or the landowner, in excess of the normal increase in land prices, according to the implementation of the development project or changes in land-use plans, or other social or economic factors; see Article 2(1) of the Act on Restitution of Development Gains), and take measures such as ensuring certain supervisory procedures by administrative authorities, this is still markedly insufficient to control the expropriation fruits from accruing unilaterally to a particular private corporation.\\n\\nAlso, although the Industrial Sites Act and related statutes guarantee the right of repurchase under the Public Works Act even in the expropriation procedures under the expropriation provision at issue, in the case of expropriation by a private corporation the scope in which the right of repurchase is recognized should be broader than in the case of expropriation by the State, etc., and for the same reason, in expropriation by a private corporation, the public necessity of the expropriation should also be more strictly limited. Because the Industrial Sites Act very broadly defines the scope of industrial complex development projects (Article 2(6) of the Industrial Sites Act), and in particular regulates them in the vague form of “incidental project” as in Article 2(6)(j) of the same Act, it should also be supplemented that there is always concern that the scope of industrial complex development projects may be expanded beyond what is necessary, thereby unjustly infringing the property rights of the person subject to expropriation.\\n\\nUnless these legal and institutional supplements are made, expropriation by a private corporation under the provisions at issue is difficult to reconcile with the constitutional value of the guarantee of property rights.\\n\\n(3) Violation of the principle of least infringement\\n\\nThe various fundamental rights guaranteed by our Constitution function as a safety net preventing the strong majority from unjustly infringing the interests of the weak minority when seeking to realize their own interests. And even if there is a constitutional demand that the rights of the minority be restricted for the sake of the majority, such restriction must be limited to the minimum necessary.\\n\\nTherefore, even if it is unavoidable to grant expropriation authority to a private corporation pursuant to the provisions at issue, it would still be fully possible to seek various measures to mitigate the loss of the landowner’s property rights caused by the project implementer’s unilateral will, such as by prescribing as a legal requirement that the project implementer acquire a certain ratio of land in advance before the expropriation award is rendered. As in other statutes, by requiring that a private corporation satisfy certain land acquisition requirements in advance in order to exercise expropriation authority, it would be possible to substantially compel transfer of property rights by consultation and, even when expropriation is unavoidable for the promotion of the project in the public interest, to strive to minimize the damage by reducing the extent to which the expropriatee’s property rights are unilaterally restricted; the absence of such legislative consideration does not conform to the spirit of the constitutional principle of excessive restriction.\\n\\nd. Conclusion\\n\\nUltimately, the provisions at issue cannot but be deemed to infringe property rights under our Constitution and thus to violate the Constitution.\\n\\nJustices Lee Kang-guk (Presiding Justice), Lee Gong-hyeon, Cho Dae-hyeon, Kim Hee-ok, Kim Jong-dae, Min Hyeong-gi, Lee Dong-heub (unable to sign and seal due to an overseas business trip), Mok Young-joon, and Song Doo-hwan\\n\\n[Attached Sheet] Relevant Provisions\\n\\nIndustrial Sites and Development Act (as amended by Act No. 6842 on 2002. 12. 30.) Article 2 (Definitions) The definitions of terms used in this Act are as follows.\\n\\n5. “Industrial complex” means a parcel of land designated and developed in accordance with a comprehensive plan in order to collectively install factories, facilities related to knowledge industries, facilities related to cultural industries, facilities related to information and communications industries, resource stockpiling facilities, etc., and the educational, research, business, information-processing, distribution facilities related thereto, and residential, cultural, medical, tourism, sports, and welfare facilities, etc. for workers and users of these facilities in order to enhance the functions of these facilities, and refers to the following:\\n\\na. National industrial complex: an industrial complex designated pursuant to Article 6 in order to develop as an industrial complex regions that foster national core industries, advanced science and technology industries, etc., or underdeveloped regions requiring development promotion, or regions spanning two or more Special Cities, Metropolitan Cities, or Provinces (hereinafter referred to as “cities and provinces”)\\n\\nb. Local industrial complex: an industrial complex classified as follows:\\n\\n(1) General local industrial complex: an industrial complex designated pursuant to Article 7 in order to promote the proper regional dispersion of industry and revitalize the regional economy\\n\\n(2) Urban high-tech industrial complex: an industrial complex designated pursuant to Article 7-2 within an urban planning zone under the Urban Planning Act in order to foster advanced industries such as knowledge industries, cultural industries, and information and communications industries\\n\\nc. Agro-industrial complex: an industrial complex designated pursuant to Article 8 in order to attract and foster industries for increasing the income of farmers and fishermen in rural and fishing areas prescribed by Presidential Decree\\n\\n6. “Industrial complex development project” means any of the following projects implemented in order to create an industrial complex.\\n\\na. Site creation project for factories, facilities related to knowledge industries, facilities related to cultural industries, facilities related to information and communications industries, resource stockpiling facilities, etc.\\n\\nb. Site creation project for educational and research facilities for the development of advanced science and technology industries\\n\\nc. Site creation project for business facilities, information-processing facilities, exhibition facilities, distribution facilities, etc. for enhancing the efficiency of the industrial complex\\n\\nd. Site creation project and park creation project for residential facilities, cultural facilities, medical and welfare facilities, sports facilities, tourism and recreation facilities, etc. for enhancing the functions of the industrial complex\\n\\ne. Project for facilities supplying industrial and domestic water\\n\\nf. Road, railroad, harbor, track, canal, balancing reservoir, and reservoir construction project\\n\\ng.
