{"[2009HEONBA142]": "1. Summary of the Case and Subject Matter of Review\\n\\na. Summary of the Case\\n\\n(1) The Mayor of Seoul Metropolitan Government, on February 10, 2004, lifted the designation of a Development Restriction Zone for a tract of land in the area that had formerly been incorporated into a Natural Green Area and a Development Restriction Zone and included land owned by petitioner Shin ○ Ja, namely, land 368-1, ○○-dong, Eunpyeong-gu, Seoul, and land 371-3, the same dong, owned by petitioner Park ○ Seo (hereinafter referred to as “the land at issue”), and on February 25, 2004, designated and publicly notified the area as the Eunpyeong New Town Urban Development Zone while changing the land use designation of the land at issue from a Natural Green Area to a Second-Class General Residential Area.\\n\\n(2) SH Corporation, the implementer of the above urban development project, applied for expropriation adjudication with respect to the land at issue and other land for which acquisition by agreement had not been achieved, and the Seoul Metropolitan Government Local Land Expropriation Committee, on November 10, 2006, rendered an expropriation adjudication setting the compensation for the land at issue at KRW 955,790,530 with respect to petitioner Shin ○ Ja and KRW 1,979,065,020 with respect to petitioner Park ○ Seo.\\n\\n(3) Accordingly, petitioner Shin ○ Ja filed a lawsuit seeking payment of KRW 1 billion and petitioner Park ○ Seo filed a lawsuit seeking payment of KRW 2 billion in compensation and delay damages, and when only part of their claims was granted, they appealed. During the pendency of the appellate proceedings, they applied for a motion to request a constitutional review on the ground that Article 67(2), etc. of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects was unconstitutional, but when that motion was denied, they filed the present constitutional complaint.\\n\\nb. Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of review in this case is whether Article 67(2) and Article 70(4) of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (enacted by Act No. 6656 on February 4, 2002; hereinafter referred to as the “Public Works Act”), and Article 70(1) of the former Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (before amendment by Act No. 8665 on October 17, 2007; hereinafter referred to as the “former Public Works Act”) are unconstitutional, and the content of the provisions at issue in this case and the related provisions is as follows.\\n\\n[Provisions at Issue]\\n\\nAct on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (enacted by Act No. 6656 on February 4, 2002)\\n\\nArticle 67 (Price Time Point, etc. for Compensation Amount) ② In calculating the amount of compensation, where there is a change in the price of land, etc. due to the public works project concerned, such change shall not be taken into account.\\n\\nArticle 70 (Compensation for Land to Be Acquired) ④ In the case of acquisition after project authorization, the officially announced land price under paragraph (1) shall be the officially announced land price whose public reference date is a point in time before the date of public notice of project authorization, and among the officially announced land prices publicly announced at the time of the formation of agreement or adjudication concerning the land concerned, it shall be the officially announced land price publicly announced at the point closest to the date of public notice of project authorization.\\n\\nFormer Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (before amendment by Act No. 8665 on October 17, 2007)\\n\\nArticle 70 (Compensation for Land to Be Acquired) ① With respect to land acquired by agreement or adjudication, compensation shall be made on the basis of the officially announced land price under the Act on Public Notice of Values and Appraisal of Real Estate, but it shall be compensated at an appropriate price evaluated by considering the land-use plan under the relevant statutes from the public reference date to the price time point, the land price fluctuation rate in the region not affected by the land value due to the relevant public works project, as prescribed by Presidential Decree, the producer price increase rate (meaning the rate calculated by the Producer Price Index investigated and announced by the Bank of Korea pursuant to Article 86 of the Bank of Korea Act), and, inter alia, the location, shape, environment, and use status of the relevant land.\\n\\n[Related Provisions]\\n\\nAct on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (enacted by Act No. 6656 on February 4, 2002)\\n\\nArticle 19 (Expropriation or Use of Land, etc.) ① When necessary for the performance of a public works project, the project implementer may expropriate or use land, etc. pursuant to this Act.\\n\\nArticle 67 (Price Time Point, etc. for Compensation Amount) ① The calculation of the amount of compensation shall be based, in the case of agreement, on the price at the time the agreement is formed, and in the case of adjudication, on the price at the time of adjudication of expropriation or use.\\n\\nArticle 70 (Compensation for Land to Be Acquired) ② The amount of compensation for land shall be calculated by considering the actual state of use and the objective conditions according to the general method of use as of the price time point, but temporary states of use, the subjective value held by the landowner or interested person, and cases premised on use for a special purpose shall not be taken into account.\\n\\nFormer Act on Public Notice of Values and Appraisal of Real Estate (wholly amended by Act No. 7335 on January 14, 2005, and before amendment by Act No. 8409 on April 27, 2007)\\n\\nArticle 9 (Application of Officially Announced Standard Land Prices) ① When the State, local governments, government-invested institutions under the Framework Act on the Management of Government-Invested Institutions, or other public organizations prescribed by Presidential Decree calculate the price of land for the purposes set forth in each subparagraph below, they shall ensure that the price of the relevant land and the officially announced standard land price maintain balance, based on one or more officially announced standard land prices of standard lots deemed to have similar utility value to the relevant land. Provided, that where deemed necessary, the calculated land price may be adjusted upward or downward and applied according to the purposes set forth in each subparagraph below.\\n\\n2. Petitioners’ Arguments, Reasons for the Court’s Denial of the Motion for Constitutional Review, and the Opinions of the Relevant Authorities\\n\\na. Summary of the Petitioners’ Arguments\\n\\n(1) Argument concerning exclusion of development gains\\n\\n“Just compensation” as prescribed in Article 23(3) of the Constitution means full compensation, and the implementer of a public works project is merely a private economic actor seeking to acquire land necessary for a development project; however, the provisions at issue in this case prescribe that, in calculating the amount of compensation for loss, development gains arising from the implementation of the relevant public works project shall be excluded. As a result, the development gains excluded from the just compensation that should be paid to the landowners accrue to the project implementer, who is a private economic actor, and therefore this violates the principle of freedom of contract, the principle of equality, the principle of legality in taxation, and the social state principle.\\n\\n(2) Argument concerning the basis of officially announced land price\\n\\nIn the case of eminent domain, in order to achieve full compensation, the amount of compensation to the landowner should be calculated on the basis of market value, which is the normal transaction price. Nevertheless, Article 70(1) of the former Public Works Act and Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act limit the method of price calculation by prescribing that, in compensating for land expropriation, the price of the expropriated land shall be calculated on the basis of the officially announced land price of the standard lot, thereby violating the principle of just compensation, the principle of equality, the principle of proportionality, and the principle of market economic order.\\n\\nb. Reasons for the Court’s Denial of the Motion for Constitutional Review\\n\\n(1) Regarding the argument concerning exclusion of development gains\\n\\nPrices formed through speculative transactions cannot be regarded as normal objective property values; therefore, excluding them does not run contrary to the principle of full compensation. Development gains arising from the rise in land prices due to the implementation of a public works project arise from the investment of the project operator and are not generated by the efforts or capital of the expropriated landowner; accordingly, such development gains, in light of the notion of equity, are of a nature that should accrue not to the landowner but rather to the investor, namely the project operator, or ultimately to all the people. Moreover, because development gains arise only through the implementation of a public works project, they cannot be deemed included in the objective value of the expropriated land at the time of expropriation. Therefore, it cannot be said that the relevant provisions of the Public Works Act, by prescribing exclusion of development gains arising from the implementation of the public works project when calculating the amount of loss compensation for the expropriated person, violate the principle of just compensation prescribed by the Constitution or the principle of freedom of contract, the principle of equality, the principle of legality in taxation, or the social state principle.\\n\\n(2) Regarding the argument concerning the basis of officially announced land price\\n\\nFirst, the officially announced land price under Article 70(1) of the former Public Works Act properly reflects the objective value of the standard lot as of the public reference date, the selection of the standard lot is appropriate so as to recognize price similarity between the standard lot and the land subject to land price appraisal, and the method of point-in-time adjustment that calculates market value fluctuations from the public reference date until expropriation appears to be appropriate; therefore, it does not violate the principle of just compensation prescribed by Article 23(3) of the Constitution. Nor can it be regarded as exceeding the reservation to law under the above constitutional provision or violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\nNext, the provision in Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act, which prescribes that the officially announced land price that serves as the basis for calculating the amount of loss compensation shall be the officially announced land price whose public reference date is a point in time before the date of public notice of project authorization, and among the officially announced land prices publicly announced at the time of the formation of agreement or adjudication concerning the relevant land, shall be the officially announced land price publicly announced at the point closest to the date of public notice of the relevant project authorization, is intended to prevent development gains from being included in the officially announced land price that serves as the basis for point-in-time adjustment; thus, the provision constitutes an appropriate means for calculating the amount of loss compensation with development gains excluded.\\n\\nTherefore, it cannot be said that Article 70(1) of the former Public Works Act and Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act, which require that the price of the expropriated land be calculated on the basis of the officially announced land price of the standard lot, are contrary to the principle of just compensation, the principle of equality, the principle of proportionality, or the principle of market economic order and thus unconstitutional.\\n\\nc. Summary of the Opinion of the Minister of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs\\n\\nExcept for the arguments below, it is substantially the same as the summary of the court’s reasons for denying the motion for constitutional review.\\n\\nThe principle of equality prescribed in Article 11(1) of the Constitution by no means means absolute equality that denies all differential treatment; rather, it means that discrimination based on irrational conditions must not be made in the application of law or legislation. Therefore, even though no institutional mechanism has been established to recover all development gains, including the development gains retained by the owner of land that was not expropriated, requiring landowners who hold expropriated land within an area where an officially announced land price has been publicly notified to return such gains cannot be said to discriminate against landowners according to whether they are subject to expropriation, without rational reason.\\n\\nd. Summary of the Opinion of Defendant SH Corporation in the Relevant Case\\n\\nIt is substantially the same as the summary of the court’s reasons for denying the motion for constitutional review.\\n\\n3. Determination on the Merits\\n\\na. Whether Article 67(2) of the Public Works Act Is Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Existence of precedents\\n\\nOn September 24, 2009, in Decision 2008HEONBA112, the Constitutional Court held that Article 67(2) of the Public Works Act does not violate the Constitution, and the gist of its reasons is as follows.\\n\\n⌈Article 67(2) of the Public Works Act is a provision that excludes development gains arising from the relevant public works project in calculating the amount of compensation. Development gains arising from an increase in land prices due to the implementation of a public works project result from the investment of the project operator and are not generated by the efforts or capital of the expropriated landowner. Accordingly, in light of the notion of equity, such development gains are not of a nature that should naturally accrue to the landowner, but rather are of a nature that should accrue to the investor, namely the project operator, or ultimately to all the people. Moreover, because development gains arise only through the implementation of a public project, they cannot be regarded as included in the objective value of the expropriated land at the time of expropriation, and, temporally, they can only be actualized once the relevant public works project is carried out smoothly; therefore, considering the portion of the rise in land prices that has increased in expectation of development gains before the public works project has even been implemented is nothing more than a subjective value attribution that holds the public works project hostage. Since the loss suffered by the owner through land expropriation and the gains arising from the implementation of the public works project are separate issues, including in the compensation amount the rise in land prices reflecting in advance the increase in utility value expected from the implementation of the public works project would amount to calculating compensation in excess of the objective value of the expropriated land at the time of project implementation. Therefore, development gains, by their nature, cannot be regarded as losses of the expropriated person included within the scope of full compensation, and thus excluding such development gains in calculating the amount of loss compensation does not contravene the principle of just compensation prescribed by the Constitution.⌉\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\nThe above reasoning of the decision is fully applicable in this case as well, and there is no circumstance requiring it to be changed.\\n\\nb. Whether Article 70(1) of the former Public Works Act and Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act Are Unconstitutional\\n\\n(1) Existence of precedents\\n\\n(a) On November 29, 2007, in Decision 2006HEONBA79 (Court Cases Collection 19-2, 576), the Constitutional Court held that Article 70(2) and (4) of the Public Works Act, Article 70(1) and (5) of the former Public Works Act, and Article 9(1)1 of the former Act on Public Notice of Values and Appraisal of Real Estate do not violate the Constitution, and the gist of its reasons is as follows.\\n\\n⌈In Decisions 93HEONBA20 et al. dated April 20, 1995 (Court Cases Collection 7-1, 519), 98HEONBA13 et al. dated December 23, 1999 (Court Cases Collection 11-2, 721), and 2000HEONBA31 dated April 26, 2001 (Court Cases Collection 13-1, 932), the Constitutional Court held that calculating the amount of compensation for expropriated land on the basis of officially announced land prices does not violate the Constitution, and the gist of the reasons for such holdings is as follows.\\n\\n“Just compensation” prescribed in Article 23(3) of the Constitution means, in principle, full compensation, which completely compensates for the objective property value of the expropriated property. The fact that Article 46(2) of the former Land Expropriation Act and Article 10(1)1 of the Act on the Public Notice of Land Prices etc. prescribe that the amount of loss compensation arising from land expropriation be calculated on the basis of officially announced land prices while excluding development gains, and that point-in-time adjustment from the public reference date to the time of adjudication be carried out by means of the price fluctuation rate of nearby land and the wholesale price increase rate, etc., is not contrary to the principle of just compensation prescribed by Article 23(3) of the Constitution, because the officially announced land price under the above statutory provisions properly reflects the objective value of the standard lot as of the public reference date, the selection of the standard lot is appropriate so as to recognize price similarity between the standard lot and the land subject to land price appraisal, and the method of point-in-time adjustment that calculates market value fluctuations from the public reference date until expropriation appears to be appropriate. Nor can it be said to exceed the reservation to law under the above constitutional provision or to violate the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.”\\n\\nMeanwhile, in Decision 98HEONBA13 et al., in addition to the above gist of the holding, the Court also determined, as follows, that the provision prescribing the public reference date of the officially announced land price that serves as the basis for calculating the amount of loss compensation does not violate the Constitution.\\n\\n“Article 46(3) of the Land Expropriation Act is a provision concerning the base date of the officially announced land price. The provision that the officially announced land price that serves as the basis for calculating the amount of loss compensation shall be the officially announced land price whose public reference date is a point in time before the date of public notice of project authorization, and among the officially announced land prices publicly announced at the time of the formation of agreement or adjudication concerning the relevant land, shall be the officially announced land price publicly announced at the point closest to the date of public notice of the relevant project authorization, is intended to prevent development gains from being included in the officially announced land price that serves as the basis for point-in-time adjustment, and thus constitutes an appropriate means for calculating the amount of loss compensation with development gains excluded.”\\n\\nThe provisions of the former Public Works Act at issue in this case are identical in content to Article 46 of the former Land Expropriation Act, which was the subject of review in the above precedents of the Constitutional Court, except that the name of the Act and the term “officially announced land price under the Act on the Public Notice of Land Prices and Appraisal of Land, etc.” were changed, in accordance with the change in the name of the Act, to “officially announced land price under the Act on Public Notice of Values and Appraisal of Real Estate,” and that, among the listed consideration factors, “wholesale price increase rate” was changed to “producer price increase rate” in accordance with the change in terminology. Article 9(1)1 of the former Real Estate Appraisal Act is also identical in content to Article 10(1)1 of the Act on the Public Notice of Land Prices and Appraisal of Land, etc., except that only the name of the Act changed. Since no special change in circumstances appears that would require a different determination from those precedents in this case, those precedents shall be maintained as they are.⌉\\n\\n(b) In addition, on July 30, 2009, in Decision 2007HEONBA76, the Constitutional Court, citing the above precedent, held that Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act does not violate the Constitution, and on September 24, 2009, in Decision 2008HEONBA112, citing the above precedent, held that Article 70(1) of the former Public Works Act and Article 70(4) of the Public Works Act do not violate the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Determination\\n\\nThe above reasoning of the decision is fully applicable in this case as well, and there is no circumstance requiring it to be changed.\\n\\nc. Determination on the Petitioners’ Other Arguments\\n\\nThe petitioners additionally argue that the provisions at issue in this case violate the principle of freedom of contract and the principle of the market economy, etc., but as noted above, insofar as the provisions at issue in this case do not infringe property rights, they cannot be said to violate the constitutional principle of freedom of contract, the principle of the market economy, etc.\\n\\n4. Conclusion\\n\\nAccordingly, since the provisions at issue in this case do not violate the Constitution, the decision shall be made as stated in the operative part. This decision is based on the unanimous opinion of the other participating Justices, except for the dismissal opinion of Justice Cho Dae-hyeon as set forth in 5. below.\\n\\n5. Opinion of Justice Cho Dae-hyeon on Dismissal\\n\\nIn a constitutional complaint under Article 68(2) of the Constitutional Court Act, the purpose of which is normative review, it is appropriate to regard a case as the same case under Article 39 of the Constitutional Court Act if the provisions of law at issue and the issues are identical (see the dissenting opinion in the decision rendered on January 17, 2007, in 2006HEONBA39). The subject matter of review and the issues in this case are identical to those in 2006HEONBA79, 2008HEONBA112, and other cases already adjudicated by the Constitutional Court as not violating the Constitution, as stated by the majority opinion. Therefore, even if the parties and the relevant case in this case are different from those in the cases already adjudicated, they should be regarded as the same case under Article 39 of the Constitutional Court Act.\\n\\nAccordingly, insofar as there is no particular need to adjudicate anew on whether the provisions at issue in this case are unconstitutional, the petition in this case seeking a determination of unconstitutionality of the provisions at issue in this case should be dismissed by applying Article 39 of the Constitutional Court Act."}

{"[2012DU7950]": "The grounds for final appeal (the statements in each supplemental brief submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds for final appeal shall be considered only to the extent that they supplement it) are examined.\\n\\n1. With respect to the Plaintiff's grounds for final appeal Nos. 1 and 3 and the Defendant's ground for final appeal No. 1\\n\\na. 1) Article 70(2) of the former Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (prior to amendment by Act No. 11017 on August 4, 2011; hereinafter the \"Act\") provides that \"the amount of compensation for land shall, in principle, be calculated by taking into consideration the actual use condition at the price-point date and the objective circumstances based on ordinary methods of use, and temporary use conditions, etc. shall not be taken into consideration.\" Article 70(6) of the Act, which delegates the specific method of calculating and appraising the amount of compensation to be prescribed by Ordinance of the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, is implemented by Article 24 of the former Enforcement Rules of the Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (prior to amendment by Ordinance of the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs No. 427 on January 2, 2012; hereinafter the \"Enforcement Rules\"), which provides that \"with respect to land that has been altered in shape without obtaining permission or filing a report, although permission or a report is required under related statutes (hereinafter referred to as 'illegally shape-altered land'), the land shall be appraised on the assumption of the use condition at the time the land was altered in shape.\" According to this, since the amount of compensation for land is, in principle, calculated according to the actual use condition, where a party asserting the application of such an exceptional method of calculating the amount of compensation seeks to calculate the amount of compensation based on the original use condition or the use condition at the time of the shape alteration on the ground that the use condition of the land subject to expropriation is temporary or that it is illegally shape-altered land, that party must prove that the land subject to expropriation is illegally shape-altered land (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2011DU2521 decided on April 26, 2012).\\n\\nHowever, the provision to the effect that, in cases of illegal shape alteration, appraisal shall be made based on the condition at the time of the shape alteration was first newly enacted in Article 6(6) of the former Enforcement Rules of the Act on Special Cases Concerning the Acquisition of Public Land and the Compensation for Losses (repealed by Article 2 of the Supplementary Provisions to the Enforcement Rules of the Act on the Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects [Ordinance of the Ministry of Construction and Transportation No. 344, December 31, 2002]) when the former Enforcement Rules were amended by Ordinance of the Ministry of Construction and Transportation No. 3 on January 7, 1995. Article 4 of the Supplementary Provisions thereto contained a transitional provision stating that, where land was incorporated into a public works project district before the enforcement of the above Enforcement Rules, the previous provisions would apply, and Article 6 of the Supplementary Provisions to the Enforcement Rules (December 31, 2002) also provides that, with respect to illegally shape-altered land incorporated into a public works project district as of January 7, 1995, compensation shall, notwithstanding Article 24, be made according to the actual use condition. Therefore, as to land that had already been incorporated into a public works project district before January 7, 1995, such as by being decided and publicly notified as the site of an urban planning facility, and had been unlawfully shape-altered, Article 6(6) of the above Enforcement Rules or Article 24 of the Enforcement Rules, which provides for appraisal on the assumption of the land use condition at the time of the shape alteration, cannot be applied; instead, the land must be appraised according to the actual use condition unless the use condition is temporary (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DU16007, 16014 decided on May 15, 2008).\\n\\n2) Article 23(1) of the Enforcement Rules, which is delegated by Article 70(6) of the Act, provides that \"land subject to public-law restrictions shall be appraised as restricted; provided, however, that where the public-law restriction has been imposed directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project, the land shall be appraised on the assumption that there is no restriction.\" Paragraph (2) provides that \"with respect to land for which the use district or use zone, etc. has been changed directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project, the land shall be appraised on the basis of the use district or use zone, etc. before the change.\" Accordingly, when calculating the amount of compensation for land subject to public-law restrictions, if the relevant public-law restriction is a general planning restriction, such as the designation or alteration of a use district, use zone, or area (hereinafter \"use district, etc.\"), which achieves its restriction purpose by itself and is not directly related to a specific urban planning project, the land must be appraised as restricted; however, even if the restriction arises from the designation or alteration of a use district, etc. that constitutes a general planning restriction, if such designation or alteration of the use district, etc. is for the implementation of a particular public works project, it shall be regarded as a restriction imposed directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project, and the land must be appraised on the assumption that such restriction does not exist (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2012DU1020 decided on May 24, 2012). Meanwhile, both the proviso to Article 23(1) and Article 23(2) of the Enforcement Rules are legislatively intended to exclude the effect of the relevant public works project and thereby realize just compensation (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DU11507 decided on July 12, 2007).\\n\\nIn addition, the designation or alteration of a use district, etc. is a kind of administrative planning carried out on the basis of professional and technical judgment and is thus a discretionary act; however, such planning discretion held by the administrative authority must involve a proper comparative balancing of the interests of those concerned with the administrative plan, not only between the public interest and private interest, but also between public interests themselves and between private interests themselves, and such comparative balancing must conform to the principle of proportionality. Therefore, if, in formulating and deciding an administrative plan, the administrative authority fails to conduct any balancing of interests at all, omits an important matter that should properly have been included among the subjects of consideration in the balancing of interests, or conducts balancing of interests but in a manner contrary to the principle of proportionality, the decision on the administrative plan is unlawful as an abuse or excess of discretionary authority (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2002DU5474 decided on March 10, 2005; Supreme Court Decision 2011DU31093 decided on May 10, 2012).\\n\\nTaking into comprehensive consideration the content, interrelationship, and legislative purpose of Article 23(1) and (2) of the Enforcement Rules, the legal nature of the designation or alteration of a use district, etc. and the scope of judicial review thereof, the significance of the effect that a use district, etc. has on land price formation, and the point that, in appraising land prices for calculating the amount of compensation for land acquired for a public works project, even a designation or alteration of a use district, etc. that constitutes a general planning restriction must be regarded as a restriction directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project if it is for such implementation, then, where the failure to designate or alter a use district, etc. at a specific point in time with respect to a certain land subject to expropriation is for the implementation of a specific public works project, this should be regarded as a restriction directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project, and the land price must be appraised on the assumption that such designation or alteration of the use district, etc. has been made. In order to conclude that the designation or alteration of a use district, etc. was not made for the implementation of a specific public works project, it must be objectively clear that, if the circumstance that the land is to be provided for a specific public works project is excluded, the act of not designating or altering the use district, etc. would constitute an abuse or excess of planning discretion.\\n\\nb. 1) According to the reasons of the appellate judgment, the following facts can be ascertained.\\n\\na) The 2,959 square meters of forest land at (Address 1 omitted), Gangnam-gu, Seoul (hereinafter the \"Land in this Case\"), is located at the foot of Maebongsan, and its land category is forest land. On July 9, 1977, it was decided and publicly notified as the site of a neighborhood park, which is an urban planning facility. At that time, to the north and west of the Land in this Case there was a forest area in a natural forest state, to the east there was a residential area consisting of houses and an agricultural area consisting of paddy fields and dry fields, and to the south it abutted a large road that appeared to be an unpaved road.\\n\\nb) In the 1980s, the farmland south of the above large road began to be converted into building sites, and from around 1988, construction work for the opening of Nonhyeon-ro was carried out to the west of the Land in this Case, and the forest area west of Nonhyeon-ro was converted into building sites.\\n\\nc) The Land in this Case had been classified as a residential area or a general residential area and was designated as Type 1 General Residential Area in or around October 20, 2003, pursuant to the Intervenor's subdivision measure for general residential areas. Meanwhile, according to the Seoul Metropolitan Government Manual for Subdivision of General Residential Areas, Type 1 General Residential Area refers to an area necessary to create a convenient residential environment centered on low-rise houses, Type 2 General Residential Area refers to an area necessary to create a convenient residential environment centered on mid-rise houses, and Type 3 General Residential Area refers to an area necessary to create a convenient residential environment centered on mid- and high-rise houses.\\n\\nd) The Land in this Case is currently located west of Maebong Station on Subway Line 3 in Dogok-dong, Gangnam-gu, Seoul, with Nambu Sunhwan-ro to the south and Nonhyeon-ro to the west. Across Nonhyeon-ro from the Land in this Case there is a large apartment complex, and across Nambu Sunhwan-ro there are neighborhood living facilities and houses, while to the east and north there is a forest area around an urban area in a pure natural forest state.\\n\\ne) At the time of the public notice of project authorization on September 16, 2002, the Land in this Case consisted of four parcels of land, namely 856 square meters of forest land at (Address 1 omitted), Gangnam-gu, Seoul; 117 square meters of forest land at (Address 2 omitted); 102 square meters of forest land at (Address 3 omitted); and 1,884 square meters of forest land at (Address 4 omitted) (hereinafter, the land at (Address 1 omitted) shall be referred to as the \"Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation,\" and the remaining lands shall be identified by their lot numbers), and they were consolidated into the Land in this Case in or around May 11, 2007. The portion of the Land in this Case corresponding to the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation had been unlawfully shape-altered since around 1977, with landscape trees, etc. planted thereon; the portion of the land at (Address 2 omitted) had also been unlawfully shape-altered and was being used as a parking space; whereas the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) are lands in a natural forest state densely covered with miscellaneous trees such as oak trees.\\n\\nf) Of the lands in the vicinity of the Land in this Case directly abutting Nambu Sunhwan-ro or Nonhyeon-ro, most have been designated as Type 3 General Residential Area and are being used as commercial sites or large apartment sites, except for cases where, like the Land in this Case, they were decided and publicly notified as sites for neighborhood parks (Dogok Park).\\n\\n2) The court below held that: a) the meaning of the provision that no public-law restriction is assumed is that, in general cases, the amount of compensation for loss is evaluated on the basis of the land use condition before the public-law restriction directly for the purpose of implementing the relevant public works project was imposed; however, where special circumstances exist, such as where, as a result of a comprehensive review of various circumstances including the current status of the land subject to expropriation and surrounding lands, the course of changes in their use conditions, and the content of related public-law restrictions, there is a high degree of probability that the use condition of the relevant land would have changed to another use condition at the price-point date had no public-law restriction been imposed, the amount of compensation for loss may exceptionally be determined based on the use condition at the price-point date so presumed; and then b) it determined that, if the Land in this Case had not been designated as park land under the relevant public works project, there is a high degree of probability that the portion of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the portion of the land at (Address 2 omitted) would have been classified as Type 3 General Residential Area at the price-point date and used as commercial sites, and thus the amount of compensation for loss for those portions must be calculated on the premise that the use district is Type 3 General Residential Area and the land is used as commercial sites, while it held that, with respect to the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted), it is difficult to conclude from the materials submitted alone that, taking into account their use condition as forest land and other public-law restrictions on use, they would have been changed to the different use condition asserted by the Plaintiff at the price-point date.\\n\\nc. As to the circumstances stated by the court below regarding the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) among the Land in this Case, namely, ① that, in view of their current condition, they are located on the rear upper portion not fronting a road and are mainly planted with natural forest, it is appropriate to regard them as lands on the extension line of the surrounding forest area, and they clearly show a different use condition from the lands located on the lower portion; ② that they correspond to a steep hilly area with a slope of 10 degrees or more, and the standing tree density also appears to comfortably exceed 51%, which is the level restricting permission for development activities; ③ that they are not at all equipped with urban infrastructure, conversion of their use condition is expected to require considerable cost, and they may be regarded as having preservation value from the standpoint of the urban ecological environment; and considering these circumstances comprehensively, when judged after excluding the circumstance that these portions of the land were designated as park land, it cannot be said that the Intervenor's classification and designation of these portions of the land as Type 1 General Residential Area, rather than Type 2 General Residential Area or Type 3 General Residential Area, at the time of the subdivision measure for general residential areas in or around October 20, 2003, objectively and clearly constituted an abuse or excess of planning discretion.\\n\\nAccordingly, although the court below contained improper portions in its statement of reasons, its decision to adopt the appraisal result based on the assumption that the use district of the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) was Type 1 General Residential Area and the use condition was forest land, as in fact, is justifiable, and there is no illegality affecting the judgment, such as a violation of the rules of logic and experience in breach of the principle of free evaluation of evidence or a misapprehension of the law concerning the method of appraising compensation for expropriation of land subject to public-law restrictions, as alleged in the Plaintiff's grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nd. However, among the determinations of the court below, the part that held that the amount of compensation for loss must be calculated on the assumption that the use district of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted) was changed to Type 3 General Residential Area cannot be readily upheld for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) In light of the legal principles and factual relations discussed above, the Land in this Case had already been decided and publicly notified as the site of an urban planning facility before January 7, 1995, and the portion of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation among the Land in this Case had been unlawfully shape-altered since around 1977, with landscape trees, etc. planted thereon, while the portion of the land at (Address 2 omitted) had also been unlawfully shape-altered and used as a parking space. Therefore, absent the Defendant's assertion and proof of special circumstances such as that the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted) were unlawfully shape-altered only after January 7, 1995, or that the use condition resulting from such shape alteration was merely temporary, the compensation value must be appraised according to the actual use condition, regardless of whether the shape alteration was lawful.\\n\\n2) Yet the circumstances stated in the court below's judgment concerning the portions of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted), namely, ① that they had long shown a use condition clearly distinguished from neighboring lands, including forest areas, by being used as parking lots or having landscape trees planted thereon; ② that the slope was not very steep and, except for landscape trees planted for sale, the standing tree density fell far short of the level restricting permission for development activities; ③ that they are adjacent to a major arterial road, have a favorable transportation environment, fall within a station-area zone, and have locational conditions as Type 3 General Residential Area in that there is a need to promote harmony with nearby residential and neighborhood commercial facilities through improvement; ④ that, among the nearby lands, most of those with similar locational characteristics or current status to these portions of the land were designated as Type 3 General Residential Area at the time of the Intervenor's subdivision measure for general residential areas and are being used as commercial sites; and ⑤ that, in light of the location and shape of the land, etc., development costs do not appear to become excessively large depending on changes in the use condition, do not clearly establish that, when judged after excluding the circumstance that these portions of the land were designated as park land, the Intervenor's failure to classify and designate these portions of the land as Type 3 General Residential Area at the time of the subdivision measure for general residential areas in or around October 20, 2003, objectively and clearly constituted an abuse or excess of planning discretion.\\n\\nThe court below should have, in accordance with the legal principles discussed above, further examined in detail, on the basis of the altered state of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted), such as their use as parking lots or the planting of landscape trees, whether the designation status of use districts, etc. of lands that were not designated as park land and that had the same or similar characteristics and current status in terms of location, area, shape, etc. as these portions of the land at the time of the Intervenor's subdivision measure for general residential areas, as well as the content of the Seoul Metropolitan Government Manual for Subdivision of General Residential Areas, which served as the operational standard for the exercise of planning discretion, were consistent with each other; and then, assuming that these portions of the land had not been designated as park land, it should have sequentially determined whether the failure to classify and designate them as Type 3 General Residential Area at the time of the subdivision measure for general residential areas objectively and clearly constituted an abuse or excess of planning discretion, and if not, whether the failure to classify and designate them as Type 2 General Residential Area objectively and clearly constituted an abuse or excess of planning discretion. Only where, as a result of examining these matters, the abuse or excess of planning discretion is objectively and clearly recognized, may the amount of compensation for loss for these portions of the land be determined on the premise that the use district is Type 3 or Type 2 General Residential Area.\\n\\n3) Nevertheless, the court below, without examining the above matters, held merely for the reasons stated in its judgment that the use district of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted) was Type 3 General Residential Area and that the amount of compensation for loss must be calculated on the premise that the above portions of the land were used as commercial sites. In this determination of the court below, there is illegality in that it misapprehended the legal principles concerning Article 70(2) of the Act and Article 23 of the Enforcement Rules and failed to conduct the necessary examination. The Defendant's ground for final appeal pointing this out is well taken.\\n\\n2. With respect to the Plaintiff's ground for final appeal No. 2\\n\\nThe court below held that, although the Land in this Case corresponds to one parcel at the price-point date, this is merely the result of consolidation in or around May 11, 2007 at the Plaintiff's request; that the Land in this Case had been owned and managed as four separate parcels since the time of purchase in 1971 until such consolidation; and that, considering that appraisal is made on the assumption that there was no public-law restriction, it is reasonable to examine separately, by parcel, the use district and use condition of the Land in this Case, taking into account whether development activity permits were restricted according to the relevant laws and regulations then in force during that period, and it rejected the Plaintiff's argument that the Land in this Case is one parcel and thus should be appraised as a whole in a single manner.\\n\\nIn light of the relevant legal principles and the record, the above determination of the court below is justifiable, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of the law concerning the appraisal of a tract of land, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n3. With respect to the Defendant's ground for final appeal No. 2\\n\\na. As to the argument that the selection of the standard parcel was unlawful\\n\\nThe comparable standard parcel should, absent special circumstances, be selected by giving priority to the use district in urban areas and to the actual land category based on the actual use condition outside urban areas. In addition, where the land subject to expropriation is located in an urban area and there are multiple comparable standard parcels with the same use district, one should select, as the comparable standard parcel to be applied to the relevant land, a land whose natural and social conditions are the same as or similar to those of the land subject to expropriation, taking into account all characteristics such as actual use condition, land category in the public register, surrounding environment, and location; but if such a land does not exist, then one should select a land whose natural and social conditions are the same as or most similar to those of the land to be appraised, taking into account all characteristics such as land category, use, surrounding environment, and location. Even if there are some differences between the standard parcel and the land to be appraised in terms of use district or surrounding environment, such matters are merely to be taken into account in the comparative equivalence assessment through analysis of regional factors or individual factors, etc., and cannot be deemed to render the selection of the standard parcel itself erroneous (see, e.g., Supreme Court Decision 2006DA64627 decided on September 10, 2009; Supreme Court Decision 2009DU4340 decided on September 8, 2011).\\n\\nThe court below, with respect to the selection of the comparable standard parcel for the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) among the Land in this Case, stated that: ① in the appraisal conducted at the time of the expropriation award and the objection award, the 7,322 square meters of forest land at (Address 5 omitted), Gangnam-gu, Seoul, selected as the comparable standard parcel, was a land whose officially assessed land price at the base date was only KRW 150,000 per square meter and which had been incorporated into the same park land as the Land in this Case, so there is a certain limitation in correcting it to a state not subject to public-law restrictions through upward adjustment of administrative conditions, etc.; ② the 307 square meters of land at (Address 6 omitted), Gangnam-gu, Seoul, although its land category and use condition do not exactly coincide with those of the Land in this Case, such matters can be appropriately taken into account in the comparative equivalence assessment through analysis of regional factors or individual factors, and the use district at the base date was the same as that of the subject land, namely, a general residential area, and it was not incorporated into park land; and ③ in this case, it is realistically difficult to find a standard parcel in the Gangnam-gu, Seoul area that is in a forest land state and not designated as park land. Based on these considerations, the court below adopted the appraisal result of the first court appraisal (supplemented) in which the above 307 square meters of land at (Address 6 omitted) was selected as the comparable standard parcel and the appraisal was conducted, on the ground that it properly evaluated the objective value of the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) among the Land in this Case.\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, the above determination of the court below is justifiable, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of the law concerning the selection of a comparable standard parcel or contradictory reasoning, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\nb. As to the argument that taking account of compensation precedents was unlawful\\n\\nTaking a comprehensive view of the relevant statutory provisions concerning the calculation of the amount of compensation for loss, while it is not necessarily required, when calculating the amount of compensation for land subject to expropriation, to investigate and take into account transaction cases or compensation precedents, if there are cases in which nearby similar lands were traded or compensated and it is proven that the price is normal and can affect the proper assessment of the amount of compensation, the normal transaction price of such land may be taken into account, and if a compensation precedent concerns nearby similar land and serves as an important basis for evaluating the proper price of the land subject to expropriation, it is reasonable to take it into account (see Supreme Court Decision 2006DU11507 decided on July 12, 2007).\\n\\nIn light of the above legal principles and the record, it is justifiable to regard as proper the court below's acceptance of the result of the first court appraisal (supplemented), which appraised the portions of the land at (Address 3 omitted) and (Address 4 omitted) among the Land in this Case by taking into account as a compensation precedent the 333 square meters of paddy field at (Address 7 omitted), Gangnam-gu, Seoul, and there is no illegality such as a misapprehension of the legal principles concerning the principle for calculating the amount of compensation for loss as to land, as alleged in the grounds for final appeal.\\n\\n4. Scope of reversal\\n\\nThe portion of the appellate judgment that held that the amount of compensation for loss must be calculated on the assumption that the use district of the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted) was changed to Type 3 General Residential Area and that they were used as commercial sites cannot be maintained as is, as stated above. Since the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation, the land at (Address 2 omitted), the land at (Address 3 omitted), and the land at (Address 4 omitted) are all parts of a single parcel, and where the compensation amount for some items among the objects of an administrative lawsuit is too low and the compensation amount for other items is too high, the excess and deficiency among such items must be offset and the total amount of compensation determined by adding the excessive and deficient portions together, the entire portion of the appellate judgment against the Defendant, including not only the portions concerning the Land at (Address 1 omitted) before consolidation and the land at (Address 2 omitted) but also the portions concerning the land at (Address 3 omitted) and the land at (Address 4 omitted), as well as the portion of compensation for trees standing on the Land in this Case, must be reversed.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nTherefore, the portion of the appellate judgment adverse to the Defendant is reversed, and this case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. The Plaintiff's final appeal is dismissed. It is so adjudged by the unanimous opinion of the Justices of the Supreme Court as stated in the order."}

{"[2013DU7520]": "The grounds of appeal are determined (the statements in the supplemental brief on the grounds of appeal submitted after the expiration of the period for filing the statement of grounds of appeal are considered only to the extent that they supplement such grounds).\\n\\nUnder Article 24 of the Urban Development Act and Article 78(1) of the Act on Acquisition of and Compensation for Land, etc. for Public Works Projects (hereinafter referred to as the \"Public Works Projects Act\"), the project implementer shall, as prescribed by Presidential Decree, establish and implement relocation measures or pay relocation settlement funds for persons who, by providing a residential building due to the implementation of an urban development project, lose the basis of their livelihood (hereinafter referred to as \"persons subject to relocation measures\"). Meanwhile, Article 40(3) of the Enforcement Decree of the Public Works Projects Act provides that, in principle, owners of buildings (hereinafter referred to as \"non-resident owners\") who have not continuously resided in the relevant building from the date on which a public notice, etc. pursuant to the relevant statutes for a public works project was made until the date of conclusion of the contract or the expropriation adjudication are excluded from persons subject to relocation measures; accordingly, it is permissible for the project implementer to establish and implement standards expanding the scope of persons subject to relocation measures prescribed by the above statutes (see Supreme Court Decision 2009DU9819 rendered on September 24, 2009).\\n\\nWhere the project implementer expands the scope of persons subject to relocation measures prescribed by law and implements relocation measures even for non-resident owners, etc. outside that scope, the relocation measures implemented for non-resident owners, etc. are not pursuant to a statutory duty but are of a benevolent nature; therefore, the standards established by the project implementer for such relocation measures should be respected unless there are special circumstances showing that they are objectively unreasonable, such as being contrary to equity, and the mere fact that such standards differ from the law does not make them unlawful. Even if the project implementer, for a date earlier than the \"date on which a public notice, etc. pursuant to the relevant statutes was made\" under Article 40(3)2 of the Enforcement Decree of the Public Works Projects Act, additionally required the condition that \"all household members have no house other than the house in question within the project area\" and selected only non-resident owners satisfying that condition as persons subject to relocation measures, this too is a standard established for benevolent relocation measures, and the same reasoning applies.\\n\\nAfter partially citing the reasons of the first-instance judgment and recognizing the facts as stated therein, the court below held that the Plaintiff acquired ownership of Unit 303 of B Housing in Gangseo-gu, Seoul, located within the development project area at issue, on 2005. 12. 9., but had never resided therein and therefore did not fall under the persons subject to relocation measures prescribed by Article 74(1) of the Public Works Projects Act and Article 40(3) of the Enforcement Decree of the Public Works Projects Act; that, according to the selection criteria for persons subject to relocation measures of the development project at issue established and announced by the Defendant, the project implementer, even a non-resident owner falls under persons subject to relocation measures if \"all household members, other than the dwelling in question, have had no house from before the relocation measures reference date (2005. 12. 30.) until the compensation plan announcement date (2008. 8. 29.)\"; however, because the Plaintiff's spouse C had acquired ownership of an apartment outside the project area on 2003. 5. 1. and had transferred it to a third party on 2006. 9. 22., the Plaintiff did not satisfy this requirement either; and that, meanwhile, the Mayor of Seoul announced the development project formation plan of the present case to the press on 2005. 12. 20. and thereafter even gave public notice on 2005. 12. 30. setting the relocation measures reference date for the development project at issue as that same day, so that the contents of the development project at issue and the relocation measures reference date appear to have become widely known around that time, and therefore the establishment of the above relocation measures reference date cannot be deemed unlawful for lack of reasonableness or propriety. On these grounds, the court below rejected the Plaintiff's assertion that the Plaintiff fell under the persons subject to relocation measures for the development project at issue.\\n\\nThe court below's determination is in accordance with the foregoing legal principles and is proper, and there is no illegality, as alleged in the grounds of appeal, in misunderstanding the legal principles concerning persons subject to relocation measures, such as the standard date for satisfying the no-house condition or the distinction between persons subject to relocation measures and the person who is to establish and implement relocation measures, or in omitting to make a determination.\\n\\nTherefore, the appeal is dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the losing party, and it is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the Justices who participated."}
